The crafty old blade, by my crafty tricks, have I compelled and constrained to believe me in everything.
4.4.645: Then, for the son of the old gentleman, my master here in love, together with whom I drink, with whom I eat and go a-courting, I have procured regal and golden trea sures, that he may take from thence at home, and not go seeking abroad. Those Parmenos and those Syruses,
4.4.650: please me not, who filch some two or three minae from their masters. There’s nothing more worthless than a servant without skill—worthless, if he has not a breast mightily well-stocked, so that, whenever there is necessity, he may draw his supply from his own breast. No one can be a person well to do
4.4.655: unless he understands both how to do good and how to do evil. With rogues he must be a rogue; with thieves let him filch whatever he can. It befits him who is truly wise, to be a person that can shift his very skin.
4.4.659: Good with the good let him be, bad with the bad: just as things are, so let him ever frame his humour. But I should like to know how much gold my master has taken for himself, and what he has given up to his father.
4.4.665: If he is a prudent person, he has made a Hercules of his parent: he has given him the tenth part, and has kept back nine for himself. But, see! the person whom I was looking for; he meets me most opportunely. (To MNESILOCHUS.) Has any of your money fallen down, my master, that thus, in silence, you are looking down upon the ground?
4.4.669: Why do I see you two sad and sorrowful?
4.4.670:
I like it not; and ’tis not without some reason. Are you going now to give me any answer?
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.671:
I’m undone, Chrysalus.
CHRYSALUS
Perhaps you took too little of the gold.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.672:
How, a plague, too little? Why, yes, indeed, a very great deal less than too little.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.673: Why the mischief then, simpleton, since by my skill an opportunity was procured for that very purpose, that you might take as much as you pleased,
4.4.675:
did you thus take it up with the tips of two fingers? Or, didn’t you know how rarely an opportunity of that kind presents itself to a person?
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.677:
You are mistaken.
CHRYSALUS
Why, surely, ’tis you yourself that were mistaken, when you dip’t your fingers in not deep enough.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.678:
I’ faith, you’d upbraid me more than now you do, if you knew the matter better. I’m undone.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.679:
My mind is now foreboding further mischief from those words.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.680:
I’m ruined.
CHRYSALUS
How so?
MNESILOCHUS
Because I’ve given all up to my father, with every particle of it.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.681:
Given it up?
MNESILOCHUS
Given it up.
CHRYSALUS
What, all?
MNESILOCHUS
Every jot.
CHRYSALUS
We are done for. How came it into your mind to do this deed so foul?
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.683: I had a suspicion, Chrysalus, by reason of a charge, that Bacchis and he (pointing to PISTOCLERUS) had been playing me false; for that reason, in my anger, I gave up all the gold
4.4.685:
to my father.
CHRYSALUS
What did you say to your father when you gave up the gold?
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.686:
That I had at once received this gold from his host, Archidemides.
CHRYSALUS
Eh! by that speech you have this day consigned Chrysalus to the torture; for, when he shall set eyes on me, the old gentleman will carry me off that instant to the executioner.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.689:
I’ve besought my father.
CERYS.
I suppose, to do, in fact, the thing that I was speaking of?
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.690:
Nay, not to punish you, or to blame you at all on account of this business. And with some difficulty I’ve prevailed. Now, Chrysalus, this must be your care.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.692:
What do you wish should be my care?
MNESILOCHUS
That once again you should make a second inroad upon the old gentleman. Contrive, devise, invent whatever you please; frame your plans, so that this day you may cleverly deceive the old man unawares, and carry off the gold.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.695:
It scarcely seems possible to be done.
MNESILOCHUS
Set about it, and you’ll easily effect it.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.696:
How the plague easily, for me, whom he has this moment caught out in a lie? Should I entreat him not to believe me at all, he would not venture even to believe me in that.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.698:
Aye, and if you were to hear what things he said about you in my presence.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.699:
What did he say?
MNESILOCHUS
That if you were to say that this sun was the sun,
4.4.700:
he would believe it was the moon, and that that is the night which is now the day.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.701:
By my troth, I’ll bamboozle the old chap right well this very day, so that he shan’t have said that for nothing.
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.702:
Now, what would you have us do?
CHRYSALUS
Why, nothing, except that I beg you’ll still love on. As for the rest, ask of me as much gold as you please; I’ll find it you. Of what use is it for me to have the name of Chrysalus, unless I give proofs by fact?
4.4.705:
But now, tell me, Mnesilochus, how much gold is requisite for you.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.706:
There’s occasion for two hundred pieces at once, to pay the Captain for Bacchis.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.707:
I’ll find it you.
MNESILOCHUS
Then we have need of some for current expenses.
CHRYSALUS
Aye, aye, I wish us to do each thing deliberately; when I’ve accomplished the one, then I’ll set about the other. First, for the two hundred pieces, I shall direct my engine of war against the old gentleman.
4.4.710:
If with that engine I batter down the tower and the outworks, straight at the gate that instant I’ll attack the old town and the new one; if I take it, then carry to your friends the gold in baskets, just as your heart wishes.
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.713:
Our hearts are with you, Chrysalus.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.714:
Now, do you go in-doors to Bacchis, Pistoclerus, and quickly bring out—
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.715:
What?
CHRYSALUS
A pen, some wax, tablets, and some cord.
PISTOCLERUS
I’ll have them here this instant.
(Goes into the house.)
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.716:
What now are you about to do? Do tell me that.
CHRYSALUS
Let a breakfast be prepared; there will be you two, and your mistress will make a third with you.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.718:
Just as you say.
CHRYSALUS
Pistoclerus has no mistress?
MNESILOCHUS
O yes, she’s here; he’s in love with the one sister, I with the other, both of the name of Bacchis.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.720:
What were you going to say?
MNESILOCHUS
This; how we are to manage.
CHRYSALUS
Where are your couches laid out?
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.721:
Why o you ask that?
CHRYSALUS
So the matter stands; I wish to be informed. You know not what I am about to do, nor what a great exploit I shall attempt.
MINES.
4.4.723:
Give me your hand, and follow me close, to the door. Peep in.
(CHRYSALUS looks in at the door of the house of BACCHIS.)
CHRYSALUS
4.4.724:
Hurra! ’Tis a very pretty place, this, and exactly as I could wish it to be.
(Re-enter PISTOCLERUS, with pen and tablets.)
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.726:
The things that you ordered—what’s ordered for a good purpose is forthwith done by the obedient.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.727:
What have you brought?
PISTOCLERUS
Everything that you bade me bring.
CHRYSALUS
(to MNESILOCHUS.)
4.4.728:
Do you take the pen at once, and these tablets.
MNESILOCHUS
(taking them.)
What then?
CHRYSALUS
4.4.729: Write there what I shall bid you; for I wish you to write for this reason,
4.4.730: that your father may know the hand when he reads it.
4.4.731:
Write now.
MNESILOCHUS
What shall I write?
CHRYSALUS
Health to your father, in your own language.
(MNESILOCHUS writes.)
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.732:
Suppose he were to write disease and death, in preference, that would be much better.
CHRYSALUS
4.4.733:
Don’t you interrupt us.
MNESILOCHUS
What you have ordered is now written on the wax.
CHRYSALUS
Tell me in what terms.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.734:
Mnesilochus sends health to his father.
CHRYSALUS
Write this, too, quickly:
4.4.735:
My father, Chrysalus is always and everywhere talking at me, and in no measured terms, because I gave you up the gold, and because I did not cheat you of it.
(MNESILOCHUS writes.)
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.737:
Stop till he has written it.
CHRYSALUS
It befits the hand of a lover to be active.
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.738:
I’ faith, that hand is more active by far at lavishing than at writing.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.739:
Say on; that’s written down.
CHRYSALUS
Now, my dear father, do you henceforth be on your guard against him,
4.4.740:
for he is forming knavish plans to deprive you of the gold, and has declared that he will have it beyond a doubt. Write legibly.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.742:
You only dictate.
(Writes.)
CHRYSALUS
And he promises that he will give this gold to me, for me to give away to naughty women, and to consume it and live like a Greek in dens of infamy. But, father, do you take care that he does not impose on you this day; I entreat you, do beware.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.745:
Only say on.
CHRYSALUS
Just write on, then.
MNESILOCHUS
Only say what I am to write
CHRYSALUS
(MNESILOCHUS writing.)
4.4.746:
But, father, what you promised me I beg that you will remember, that you will not beat him, but keep him in chains at your house at home. Do you give me the wax and cord forthwith. Come, fasten it, and seal it in an instant.
MNESILOCHUS
(sealing the tablets.)
4.4.749: Prithee, what use is there in this writing after such a fashion,
4.4.750:
that he is to give no credence to you, and to keep you in chains at home?
CHRYSALUS
4.4.751:
Because it pleases me so. Can’t you possibly take care of your own self, and have no thought about me? In confidence in myself I undertook the task, and at my own peril do I carry on the matter.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.753:
You say what’s true.
CHRYSALUS
Give me the tablets.
MNESILOCHUS
(giving them.)
Take them.
CHRYSALUS
Give attention now; Mnesilochus, and you, Pistoclerus, do you take care that each of you goes at once and reclines on his couch
4.4.755:
with his mistress; so ’tis requisite; and on that same spot where the couches are now laid, do you forthwith commence to carouse.
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.757:
Anything else?
CHRYSALUS
This, and this especially: when you shall have once taken your places together, don’t you arise anyhow, until the signal shall be given by me.
PISTOCLERUS
4.4.759:
O skilful commander!
CHRYSALUS
You ought by this time to have taken your second draught.
MNESILOCHUS
4.4.760:
Capital; let’s go.
CHRYSALUS
Do you take care of your duty, and I’ll do mine.
(MNESILOCHUS and PISTOCLERUS go into the house.)

4.5.761:
(CHRYSALUS, alone.) CHRYSALUS
A tremendously great business am I undertaking, and I have my fears how in this one day I may accomplish it. But now I have occasion for the old blade to be fierce and savage at me. For it suits not this plan of mine
4.5.765:
that the old fellow should be calm when he has beheld me in his presence. I’ll turn him about this day, finely, if I live. I’ll have him parched as well as ever pea was parched. I’ll walk before the door, that when he comes out, at once as he comes up, I may put the letters in his hand.
(Stands near the door of BACCHIS.)

4.6.770:
(Enter NICOBULUS, at a distance.) NICOBULUS
This is a matter of great vexation to me, that Chrysalus has thus escaped me this day.
CHRYSALUS
(aside.)
4.6.772:
I’m all right: the old fellow is in a passion. Now’s my time for me to accost my man.
NICOBULUS
4.6.773:
Who speaks hard by? (Looking round.) Why surely this is Chrysalus, I think.
CHRYSALUS
(aside.)
4.6.775: My honest servant, hail to you. What’s doing now? How soon do I set sail for Ephesus, to bring back the gold home from Theotimus? What—silent? I swear by all the Gods, if I didn’t love my son so much as to wish everything done for him that he desires
4.6.779:
that your sides should be wealed now right well with rods, and that in irons at the mill you should be lingering out your life. I’ve learnt of Mnesilochus all your wicked pranks.
CHRYSALUS
4.6.783:
Has he accused me? ’Tis very good; I am a bad one, I am a cursed one—a wicked one. Only reflect upon the matter. I’ll utter not one word.
NICOBULUS
4.6.785:
What? Hangdog, do you even threaten me?
CHRYSALUS
4.6.786:
You’ll find out before long what sort of man he is. He ordered me just now to carry this letter to you. He requested that that which is there written may be done.
NICOBULUS
4.6.789:
Give it me.
CHRYSALUS
Take notice of the seal.
(Gives him the tablets.)
NICOBULUS
I know it. Where is he himself?
CHRYSALUS
I don’t know.
4.6.790:
I ought to know nothing now; I’ve forgotten everything. I know that I’m a slave; I know not even that which I do know. (Aside.) Now from the springe this thrush is catching at the worm; he’ll be finely noosed this day, so well I’ve set the snare.
NICOBULUS
4.6.794:
Stay here but a moment; I’ll return to you directly, Chrysalus.
(Goes into his house.)
CHRYSALUS
4.6.795: How he does dissemble with me; how ignorant I am of the business he’s about. He has gone to fetch slaves from in-doors to bind me. The ship speeds prosperously on; finely, too, is this craft boarding it. But I’ll hold my tongue, for I hear the door opening.

4.7.799:
(Re-enter NICOBULUS, with SLAVES carrying fetters.) NICOBULUS
Artamo, do you fasten the hands of that fellow this very instant.
(The SLAVES bind him.)
CHRYSALUS
4.7.800:
What have I done?
NICOBULUS
Pitch your fist into him if he mutters a word. (To CHRYSALUS, pointing at the tablets.) What does this letter say?
CHRYSALUS
4.7.801:
Why do you ask me? As I received it from him, so I’ve brought it sealed to you.
NICOBULUS
4.7.803: Come now, you rascal, have you not shamefully abused my son in your talk, because he gave me up that gold,
4.7.805:
and said that you would still take that gold away from me by some knavish trick?
CHRYSALUS
4.7.806:
Have I said so?
NICOBULUS
You have.
CHRYSALUS
4.7.807:
What person is there, who says that I’ve said so?
NICOBULUS
Hold your tongue. No person says so; this letter which you have brought me accuses you. See, ’tis this that requests you to be chained.
(Points to the open tablets.)
CHRYSALUS
4.7.810:
Ah! your son has been making a Bellerophon of me; I myself brought this letter, for the purpose that I might be bound. Be it so.
NICOBULUS
4.7.812:
This I am doing for this reason, because you persuade my son to live like a Greek with you, you thrice-dotted villain.
CHRYSALUS
(aside.)
4.7.814: O fool, fool, you know not that you are at this moment on sale;
4.7.815:
and that you are standing on the very stone as the auctioneer puts you up.
NICOBULUS
(overhearing him.)
4.7.816:
Answer me; who is selling me?
CHRYSALUS
He whom the Gods favour dies in youth, while he is in his health, has his senses and judgment sound. This person (pointing to NICOBULUS), if any God had favoured him, ought to have been dead more than ten years—aye, more than twenty years ago.
4.7.820:
’Tis for long, he has walked, a nuisance, on the earth; so devoid is he of either judgment or sense. He is of as much value as a rotten mushroom is.
NICOBULUS
4.7.822:
Do you think that I am a nuisance to the earth? Away with him in-doors, and tie him tightly to the post. You shall never take away any gold from here.
CHRYSALUS
4.7.824:
No, but you’ll soon be giving it me.
NICOBULUS
4.7.825:
I, give it you?
CHRYSALUS
You’ll be entreating me, too, of your own accord to receive it, when you shall come to know this accuser of mine, in how great danger and in what a dreadful situation he is. Then will you be offering his liberty to Chrysalus; but I certainly shan’t accept it.
NICOBULUS
4.7.830:
tell me, in what danger is my son Mnesilochus.
CHRYSALUS
4.7.831:
Follow me this way; I’ll soon let you know.
NICOBULUS
Where on earth shall I follow you?
CHRYSALUS
4.7.832:
Only three steps.
NICOBULUS
Aye, ten even.
CHRYSALUS
Come, then, Artamo, do you open you this door out a very little way; softly, don’t make it creak. (The door of the house of BACCHIS is opened.) That’s enough. Now, step you hither. (To NICOBULUS, who looks in.) Do you see the entertainment?
NICOBULUS
(still looking in.)
4.7.835:
I see Pistoclerus and Bacchis right opposite.
CHRYSALUS
4.7.836:
Who are upon that other couch?
NICOBULUS
(looking on the other side.)
Wretch that I am, I’m undone.
CHRYSALUS
4.7.837:
Do you recognize that person?
NICOBULUS
I do recognize him.
CHRYSALUS
Now tell me, if you please, does that woman seem of handsome appearance?
NICOBULUS
4.7.839:
Well, do you take her to be a courtesan?
NICOBULUS
Why not?
CHRYSALUS
4.7.840:
You are mistaken.
NICOBULUS
Who is she then, prithee?
CHRYSALUS
You’ll find out from me. indeed, you’ll get no more information to-day.

4.8.842:
(Enter CLEOMACHUS, at a distance.) CLEOMACHUS
(aloud.)
Is this Mnesilochus, the son of Nicobulus, by force to detain my own mistress? What proceeding is this?
NICOBULUS
4.8.844:
Who’s this?
CHRYSALUS
(aside.)
This Captain’s opportunely come for me.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.845:
He doesn’t consider that I am a soldier, but a woman, who cannot defend myself and mine. But may neither Bellona nor Mars ever put confidence in me, if I don’t put him out of life, if I meet him, or if I don’t make him lose possession of his existence.
NICOBULUS
4.8.850:
Chrysalus, who’s this that’s threatening my son?
CHRYSALUS
4.8.851:
This is the husband of that woman with whom he is now reclining.
NICOBULUS
4.8.852:
What! The husband?
CHRYSALUS
The husband, I say.
NICOBULUS
Prithee, is she married then?
CHRYSALUS
4.8.853:
You’ll know before very long.
NICOBULUS
Wretch that I am; I’m utterly undone.
CHRYSALUS
4.8.854: How now? Does Chrysalus seem such a villain to you?
4.8.855:
Come, chain me now, and do listen to your son. Didn’t I tell you that you would discover what sort of person he is?
NICOBULUS
4.8.857:
What shall I do now?
CHRYSALUS
Order me at once to be released, if you please; for, if I’m not released, he’ll just now be overpowering the young man in our presence.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.859: There’s no gain that I should this day take so much delight in making,
4.8.860:
as I should in falling upon him as he reclines with her, so that I might kill them both.
CHRYSALUS
(to NICOBULUS.)
4.8.861:
Don’t you hear what he says Why don’t you order me to be released?
NICOBULUS
(to the SLAVES.)
4.8.862:
Unbind him. I’m ruined; wretch that I am! I’m in a dreadful fright.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.863:
Then I’d make her, who publicly puts up her person for sale, not to say that she has got a person for her to laugh at.
CHRYSALUS
(to NICOBULUS.)
4.8.865:
You may make terms with him for a little money.
NICOBULUS
4.8.866:
Make terms, then, I beg, for what you like; so that he mayn’t, in our presence, fall upon the young man, or kill him outright.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.868:
Unless the two hundred Philippeans are repaid to me at once, I’ll this instant swallow the lives of them both outright.
NICOBULUS
(to CHRYSALUS.)
4.8.870:
Make terms with him, if you can; prithee, do make haste; agree for any sum you like.
CHRYSALUS
4.8.871:
I’ll go, and do it carefully. (Goes up to CLEOMACHUS.) Why are you exclaiming so?
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.872:
Where’s your master?
CHRYSALUS
Nowhere; I don’t know. Do you wish the two hundred pieces to be promised you at once, so as to make no riot or disturbance here?
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.875:
There’s nothing that I would desire more.
CHRYSALUS
And that I may heap many a curse upon you?
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.876:
Just as you please.
CHRYSALUS
(aside.)
How the villain does cringe.
4.8.877:
(To CLEOMACHUS.) This is the father of Mnesilochus: follow me; he shall promise it you. Do you ask for the gold. As to the rest, a word’s enough.
(They go up to NICOBULUS.)
NICOBULUS
4.8.879:
What has been done?
CHRYSALUS
I’ve struck the bargain for two hundred Philippeans.
NICOBULUS
Well done! Goddess Salvation,
4.8.880:
thou hast saved me. Well, how soon am I to say I’ll pay it?
CHRYSALUS
(to CLEOMACHUS.)
4.8.881:
Do you ask it of him; and (to NICOBULUS) do you promise it him.
NICOBULUS
I promise it. (To CLEOMACHUS.) Come, ask me.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.882:
Will you give me two hundred golden Philippean pieces, lawful money?
CHRYSALUS
4.8.883:
They shall be given, say: do answer him.
NICOBULUS
I’ll give them.
CHRYSALUS
4.8.884: Well, now, filthy fellow is there anything owing to you?
4.8.885: Why are you plaguing him? Why are you frightening him about death? Both I and he wish you every ill luck. If you have a sword, still we have a spit at home; with which, in fact, if you provoke me,
4.8.890:
I’ll make you more full of holes than a rat’s skin when caught in a trap. I’ faith, for my part, some time since I found out what suspicion it was that tormented you; namely, that he was with that wife of yours.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.892:
Yes; and so he is.
CHRYSALUS
So may Jupiter, Juno, Ceres, Minerva, Hope, Latona, Ops, Virtue, Venus, Castor, Pollux, Mars, Mercury, Hercules,
4.8.895:
Summanus, the Sun, Saturn, and all the Deities, prosper me, he neither reclines with her, nor walks, nor kisses, nor does that which is wont to be reported.
NICOBULUS
(aside.)
4.8.898:
How he does swear! He’s saving me, however, by his perjury.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.899:
Where then, at this moment, is Mnesilochus?
CHRYSALUS
His father has sent him into the country.
4.8.900:
And she has gone hence to the citadel, to see the temple of Minerva. The door’s open now; go in, and see if he’s there.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.902:
I’ll be off to the Forum next.
CHRYSALUS
Or rather, by my troth, to very perdition.
CLEOMACHUS
4.8.903:
Am I to demand this gold to-day?
CHRYSALUS
Demand it, and go hang yourself; don’t you suppose, you worthless fellow, that we shall be entreating of you. (Exit CLEOMACHUS.)
4.8.905:
He’s taken himself off. Permit me, master, I entreat you by the immortal Gods, to go in-doors here to your son.
(Pointing to the house of BACCHIS.)
NICOBULUS
4.8.907:
But why go in there?
CHRYSALUS
That with many words I may rebuke him, since after this fashion he has been going on this way.
NICOBULUS
4.8.909:
Well, I beg you will do so, Chrysalus; and I entreat you not to spare him in your talking to him.
CHRYSALUS
4.8.910:
And do you instruct even myself? Isn’t it sufficient, if this day he shall hear from me more harsh things than ever Clinias heard from Demetrius?
(Goes into the house of BACCHIS.)
NICOBULUS
4.8.913: This servant of mine is very like a running eye; if you have it not, you don’t wish for it or desire it;
4.8.915: if you have it, you can’t keep off from rubbing it. But if he hadn’t, by lucky chance, been here to-day, the Captain would have surprised Mnesilochus with his wife, and have killed him as an adulterer detected in the fact. Now, in a manner have I ransomed my son with the two hundred Philippeans
4.8.920:
which I have promised to give to the Captain; which, however, I shall not rashly pay him down, before I have met with my son. By my troth, I’ll never rashly give credence in anything to Chrysalus. But I have a mind even once again to read over this letter; ’tis right that when a letter is sealed we should give credence to it.
(Goes into his house.)

4.9.925:
(Enter CHRYSALUS from the house of BACCHIS.) CHRYSALUS
The two brothers, the sons of Atreus, are said to have done a most famous deed, when, with arms, and horses, and an army, and with chosen warriors, and with ships a thousand in number, after the tenth year, they subdued Pergamus, the native land of Priam, founded by hands divine. Not more decidedly did it fall by the engine of war, than I shall storm my master here,
4.9.930: without a fleet, and without an army and so great array of soldiers. I have won, I have taken by storm this gold from his father for my master’s son, in his amour. Now, before the old man comes here, I wish to lament until he does come out. O Troy! O my country! O Pergamus! O Priam! old man, you are undone, you, who’ll be wretchedly and shockingly choused out of four hundred golden Philippeans.
4.9.935: For those tablets, sealed on the one side and on the other, they are not tablets, but the horse which the Greeks sent, of wood. Pistoclerus is the Epeus; from him were these received. Mnesilochus is the Simon left behind. Behold him! not in Achilles’ tomb, but on a couch he reclines: he has Bacchis with him; just as the other formerly had the fire with which to give the signal;
4.9.940: so now does she inflame himself. I am Ulysses, by whose advice they do these things. Then, the characters which there are written, are the soldiers in this horse, armed and of high courage. So even thus far has the matter prospered with me. This horse, too, will be making his attack, not on a citadel, but on a coffer A ruin, a destruction, a cleaner-out of the old man’s gold, will this horse prove this day.
4.9.945: To this silly old man of ours, in fact, I give the name of Ilium; the Captain is Menelaüs; I, Agamemnon; I, too, am Ulysses, the son of Laërtes; Mnesilochus is Alexander, who will be the destruction of his father’s fortunes; he has borne off the Helen, on whose account I am now carrying on the siege of Ilium. For there I have heard say that Ulysses was both bold and full of mischief, just as I am.
4.9.950: I have been detected in my tricks—he, discovered in a beggar’s guise, had almost perished, while he was spying out there the doings of the Trojans. Similarly has it happened to myself to-day. I have been bound, but by my devices I have redeemed myself; he, too, preserved himself by artifice. I have heard that there were three destinies attending Troy, which were fatal to it; if the statue should be lost from the citadel; whereas the second was the death of Troilus;
4.9.955: the third was when the upper lintel of the Phrygian gate should be demolished. Just so are there three fatalities for this Troy of ours, corresponding with those three; for, first of all, when, a short time since, as I told our old gentleman the lying story about his host, and the gold, and the bark, then, that instant, did I steal the statue from the citadel. And even then two fatalities were remaining, and no further had I taken this city.
4.9.960: Afterwards, when I carried the letter to the old man, then I killed my Troilus. When he supposed, just now, that Mnesilochus was with the Captain’s wife, from that, with difficulty, did I disengage myself. And that danger do I compare to what they say, how that Ulysses, recognized by Helen, was betrayed to Hecuba. But as, in olden time, by his coaxing arts, he liberated himself from her, and persuaded her to let him go,
4.9.965: so I, by my devices, have rescued myself from the danger, and have deceived the old man. Afterwards, I engaged with the blustering Captain, who, unarmed, takes cities with his words, and there I repulsed my man. Then I engaged in fight with the old gentleman; straightway by one lying device did I vanquish him; by one blow, in a moment, did I take the spoils away from him. He now will give the two hundred Philippean pieces to the Captain,
4.9.970: which he has promised that he will give. Now, I have occasion for another two hundred, to be distributed when Ilium is taken, that there may be the usual draught of honeyed wine with which the soldiers may celebrate their triumph. But this Priam is far superior to him of old. Not fifty sons only has he, but four hundred, and all choice ones, without a blemish;
4.9.975: all these this day will I cut off at two single blows. Now, if there were any purchaser for this Priam of ours, I would sell the old fellow in the lump, whom I have on sale the moment that J shall have taken the city. But, lo! I see our Priam standing before the door; I’ll go and speak to him.

4.10.979:
(Enter NICOBULUS from his house.) NICOBULUS
Pray, whose voice is it that sounds near me?
CHRYSALUS
O Nicobulus!
NICOBULUS
What’s the matter?
CHRYSALUS
4.10.980:
O, capital!
NICOBULUS
Well, have you done aught of what I sent you upon?
CHRYSALUS
What—ask you that? Step closer this way.
NICOBULUS
(coming nearer.)
Well, I do come closer.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.981:
I am an excellent pleader. By rebuking him, and by whatever hard language I really was able to think of, I forced the fellow to tears.
NICOBULUS
4.10.985:
he bade me deliver them to you. (Gives him the tablets.) But I am afraid that they sing to the same tune that the former ones did. Observe the seal, is it his?
NICOBULUS
4.10.986:
I recognize it. I’d like to read them over.
(Goes to a distance.)
CHRYSALUS
Read them through. (Aside.) Now is the upper lintel being cut down, now is the destruction of Troy near at hand. The wooden horse is shaking it right cleverly.
NICOBULUS
4.10.988:
Chrysalus, just step here while I am reading these through.
CHRYSALUS
Prithee, what need is there for me to be near you?
NICOBULUS
4.10.989:
That you may know what’s written here.
CHRYSALUS
I don’t care, and I don’t wish to know.
NICOBULUS
4.10.990:
Still, do come here.
CHRYSALUS
What need is there?
NICOBULUS
Hold your tongue.
CHRYSALUS
I’ll stay.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.993:
I won’t, I say.
NICOBULUS
But I will, I say.
CHRYSALUS
What need is there?
NICOBULUS
Still do you only do that which I bid you.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.994:
I’ll come. ’Tis right to do so; your own servant ought to be obedient at your command.
(Goes up to him.)
NICOBULUS
(looking at the tablets.)
4.10.996:
Heyday! he hasn’t been sparing of his wax or pen. But whatever it is, I’m resolved to read it through. Attend to me, please, this very instant.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.995:
When you choose, read on; I devote to you the attention of my ears.
NICOBULUS
(looking close.)
Give your attention then.
4.10.991:
Bless me! the letters are small.
CHRYSALUS
To one, indeed, who cannot see well with his eyes but they are quite large enough for one who can see well.
NICOBULUS
4.10.997:
(He reads.) Father, I beseech you, do give two hundred Philippeans to Chrysalus, if you wish me to be safe or alive for you—
CHRYSALUS
4.10.999:
By my troth, really a very great mistake,
I tell you.
NICOBULUS
What’s the matter?
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1000:
He hasn’t first written the salutation to you.
NICOBULUS
(looking.)
I don’t see it anywhere.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1006: Even from its very commencement the letter is an impertinent one.
4.10.1001:
If you are wise, you’ll not give it; but at the best, if you give it him, why, let him find out some other porter for himself, if he is wise; for I won’t carry it if you order me ever so much. I’ve been quite enough suspected as it is, when I was guiltless of a fault.
NICOBULUS
4.10.1005: Listen on now, while I read through what’s written.
4.10.1007: (Reading.) I am ashamed, father, to appear before you in your presence; such disgraceful conduct of mine have I heard that you are aware of, that I have formed an intercourse with the wife of a strange Captain.
4.10.1010:
By my troth, you are not joking there; for I have saved your life from the consequences of this foul deed with two hundred golden Philippeans.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1012:
There’s not a particle of these things but what I’ve told him.
NICOBULUS
(reading.)
4.10.1013: I confess that I have acted foolishly. But I beseech you, father, do not forsake me, if, in my folly, I have transgressed.
4.10.1015:
Of fierce desires, and eyes uncontrolled, have I been; I have been urged on to do a deed of which I am now ashamed. It were proper, then, that you should have taken heed before you were ashamed.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1018:
All these very same words did I say to him only just now.
NICOBULUS
(reading.)
4.10.1019: I beseech you, father, to consider that it is enough that Chrysalus
4.10.1020:
has reproached me with many cutting words, and by his advice has made me a better man, so that ’tis right that you should return him sincere thanks.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1023:
Is that written there?
NICOBULUS
Look and see, then you’ll know.
(Shows him the letter.)
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1024:
He that has so offended, how humble to all he is, and of his own accord.
NICOBULUS
(reading.)
4.10.1025:
Now, father, if even yet I may be allowed to ask anything of you, do give me two hundred Philippean pieces, I do entreat you.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1027:
By my troth, now, not one even, if you are wise.
NICOBULUS
Let me read on. (Reading.) In set form I have taken an oath that I would give this to the woman this day before nightfall,
4.10.1030: ere she leaves me. Now, father, have a care that I be not forsworn, and take me hence away from her as soon as you can, on whose account I have incurred so much loss and guilt. Take care and let not the two hundred pieces be a cause of annoyance to you; I will repay you innumerable times as much, if I live.
4.10.1035:
Farewell, and do attend to these matters. Now, Chrysalus, what do you think?
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1036: I won’t give you one bit of advice this day, and I won’t run the risk, that if any mistake is made, you should say that you had done it by my counsel. But, as I conceive, if I were in your place,
4.10.1040:
I would rather give the gold than suffer him to be corrupted. There is a twofold choice consider which you would adopt; either to lose the gold, or for a lover to be forsworn. I neither order you, nor forbid you, nor do I persuade you.
NICOBULUS
4.10.1044:
I’m sorry for him.
CHRYSALUS
You don’t do anything surprising—he is your son.
4.10.1045:
If still more must be lost, ’tis better for it to go, than for this disgrace to be everywhere proclaimed.
NICOBULUS
4.10.1047: By my troth, I certainly had much rather he had been at Ephesus, so long as he was well, than that he had returned home. But why don’t I hasten to get rid of that which is doomed to be squandered away?
4.10.1050:
I’ll bring you just now from in-doors twice two hundred Philippeans, both those which, a little time since, to my sorrow, I promised to the Captain, and these others. Wait there; I’ll be out to you, Chrysalus, this instant.
(Goes into his house.)
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1053: Troy is laid waste, the chiefs have razed Pergamus. I knew some time ago that I should be the ruin of Pergamus.
4.10.1055:
I’ faith I wouldn’t dare make a bet with him who should say that I was deserving of severe torture; so great confusion am I making. But the door makes a noise; the plunder’s being brought forth from Troy. For the present I’ll hold my tongue.
(with the money in two bays.)
NICOBULUS
4.10.1059: Take you this gold, Chrysalus; go, carry it to my son.
4.10.1060:
But I’ll go hence to the market-place to pay this to the Captain.
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1061:
For my part, I’ll not receive it; do you seek somebody at once to take it. I won’t have it entrusted to me.
NICOBULUS
4.10.1062:
But do take it; you’re worrying me now.
(Holds it to him.)
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1063:
For my part, I’ll not take it.
NICOBULUS
But, prithee do.
CHRYSALUS
I am telling you what is the fact.
NICOBULUS
4.10.1064:
You are delaying me.
CHRYSALUS
I don’t want, I say, the gold to be entrusted to me. At all events, find some person to keep a watch upon me.
NICOBULUS
4.10.1066:
Well, give it me, if it must be so.
(Holds out his hand.)
NICOBULUS
(gives him the money.)
Take care of it. I’ll be back here just now.
(Exit.)
CHRYSALUS
4.10.1067: I’ve taken care—that you shall be a most wretched old fellow; this is bringing an undertaking to a fair ending; even as it has proved my lot to go rejoicing, laden with the spoil.
4.10.1070: With safety to myself, and the city taken by stratagem, I now bring home my whole army unhurt. But, Spectators, don’t you now be surprised that I don’t go in triumph; ’tis such a common thing, I don’t care for it. Still however, the soldiers shall be received with the usual honeyed wine.
4.10.1075:
Now I’ll carry off all this booty at once to the Quaestor.
(Goes into the house of BACCHIS.)
PHILOXENUS
(Enter PHILOXENUS.)
4.10.1076: The more I revolve it in my breast, what disturbances my son has raised, into what a course of life, and into what habits he unwittingly has headlong plunged himself, the greater is my concern, and the more do I dread lest he may be ruined or corrupted. I know it; I once was of the same age, and I did all these things; but in a quiet way.
4.10.1080: I was gay, I had my mistress, I drank, I feasted, I made presents, but still it was seldom I did so. The methods, too, please me not which I see parents in general employ towards their sons. I have determined to give some latitude to my son, that he may have some scope for his inclinations. I think that’s right; but still, I don’t wish him to give way too much to sloth and wantonness. Now I’m going to Mnesilochus,
4.10.1084:
to see whether, as I requested, by his endeavours he has turned him for me to virtue and to sobriety; as, indeed, I am sure he has done if he has met him, of such a disposition is he by nature.
(Exit.)

5.1.1087:
(Enter NICOBULUS, wringing his hands.) NICOBULUS
Whoever there are in any place whatsoever, whoever have been, and whoever shall be, in time to come, fools, blockheads, idiots, dolts, sots, oafs, lubbers, I singly by far exceed them all in folly and absurd ways.
5.1.1090: I’m undone. I’m ashamed of myself; that I at this time of life should disgracefully have been twice made a fool of! The more I think of this confusion which my son has made, the more am I incensed. I’m ruined, and I’m utterly destroyed; I’m distracted in every possible way. All plagues harass me, by all modes of death do I perish. This day has Chrysalus rent me in pieces; Chrysalus has plundered wretched me;
5.1.1095: he, the villain, by his clever tricks, has shaved, to the very quick, simple me, just as he has pleased. For the Captain says that she is a Courtezan, whom that fellow said was his wife; and he has informed me of everything, as each particular happened; how that she had been hired by him for this year; how that that much gold was left to be repaid, which I, most simple man, had promised him. ’Tis this, this, I say, through which my breast boils with indignation; ’tis this, in fine, by which I am distracted;
5.1.1100:
that I, at my time of life, should be made a fool of, aye, by Heaven, so made a very sport of, and with my hoary head and white beard, that wretched I should be bamboozled out of my gold. Undone am I, inasmuch as this slave of mine has dared in this way to set not the value of a nutshell upon me. And I—if any other way I had lost a greater sum—I should have taken it less amiss, and have deemed it less of a loss to me.
(Enter PHILOXENUS.)
PHILOXENUS
(as he enters.)
5.1.1104: For sure, some person, I know not who, seems to be talking near to me. But who’s this I see?
5.1.1105:
Really, ’tis the father of Mnesilochus.
NICOBULUS
Hah! I see a partner in affliction. Save you, Philoxenus!
PHILOXENUS
5.1.1106:
And you; whence are you betaking yourself?
NICOBULUS
From a place whence comes a wretched and a luckless mortal.
PHILOXENUS
5.1.1107:
Why, troth, I’m surely on the earth, the spot where it befits a wretched and a luckless mortal to be.
NICOBULUS
5.1.1108:
We now, as we are of like age, are meeting with similar fortunes.
PHILOXENUS
So it is. But as to yourself, what’s the matter with you?
NICOBULUS
5.1.1109:
I’ faith, mine’s the same mishap as your own.
PHILOXENUS
5.1.1110:
Does this misfortune in any way relate to your son?
NICOBULUS
5.1.1111:
Such is the fact.
PHILOXENUS
The same disease exists in my own breast.
NICOBULUS
5.1.1112:
Aye, and that very worthy fellow, Chrysalus, has been ruining my son, myself, and all my fortunes.
PHILOXENUS
5.1.1114:
Pray now, what is this mishap of yours about your son?
NICOBULUS
You shall know:
5.1.1115:
together with your own son he’s undone; both of them are keeping mistresses alike.
PHILOXENUS
5.1.1116:
How do you know?
NICOBULUS
I have seen them.
PHILOXENUS
Ah! wretch that I am! I’m ruined outright.
NICOBULUS
5.1.1117:
Why do we hesitate a moment to knock and to call them both hither out of doors.
PHILOXENUS
5.1.1118:
I don’t object.
NICOBULUS
(knocks at the door of the house of BACCHIS.)
Hallo there! Bacchis! Bid the door to be opened this instant, if you please, unless you had rather the door and the posts be knocked to bits with hatchets.

5.2.1120:
(Enter FIRST BACCHIS and SECOND BACCHIS from the house.) 1st BACCHIS
Who is it that calls out my name with such a noise and tumult, and is knocking so hard at the door?
NICOBULUS
5.2.1121:
I and this person here.
(Pointing to PHILOXENUS.)
1st BACCHIS
Pray, what’s the matter now? Who has been driving these sheep to us?
NICOBULUS
5.2.1122:
These most shocking hussies call us sheep.
2nd BACCHIS
Their shepherd’s asleep, as they come straying thus from the flock.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1124:
But, i’ faith, they are not white; they both look dirty.
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1125:
Because they have both been shorn just now.
PHILOXENUS
How they seem to be laughing at us.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1126:
Let them, just as long as they please.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1127:
Don’t you think that these sheep are shorn three times a year?
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1128:
I’ faith, to-day one of them has been already shorn twice, that’s sure.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1129:
They are old and fleeceless, both of them.
2nd BACCHIS
But I think they have been in good plight once.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1130:
Prithee, do you see how they are looking with a sheep’s eye at us?
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1131:
By my troth, I really do believe they are without any ill design.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1132:
This happens to us deservedly, for having come here.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1133:
Well, let them be driven in-doors to fold.
2nd BACCHIS
I don’t know what occasion there is for that, as they have neither milk nor wool. Let them stand as they are.
5.2.1135: Of whatever value they have been, they are now out of date; all their fruit has fallen off them by this. Don’t you see, how, straying unattended, they are ranging about at liberty? Why, I fancy that they must be dumb with age; they don’t bleat even, though they are absent from the rest of the flock.
5.2.1139:
They seem both silly and worthless.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1140:
Let’s return in-doors, sister.
NICOBULUS
Stay where you are, both of you; these sheep want you.
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1141:
Why, surely this is a prodigy; sheep are addressing us with a human voice.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1142:
These sheep will return you the heavy and great injury which they owe to you.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1143:
If you owe me aught, I forgive it you; keep it to yourself; I’ll never demand it of you. But what is the reason that you are threatening mischief to us?
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1145:
Because they say that our two lambs are shut up here.
(Pointing to the house.)
NICOBULUS
5.2.1146:
And besides those lambs, my dog is there concealed that bites. If they are not now produced to us and sent out of the house, we shall be furious rams; we shall attack you forthwith.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1149:
Sister, I have something to say to you in private.
2nd BACCHIS
How now, prithee?
(They go apart.)
NICOBULUS
Whither are they going?
FIRST BACCHIS
5.2.1150:
Sister, I give to you that old fellow that’s farthest off, that you may have him cleverly smoothed down; I’ll now attack this other one that’s angry; if we can only entice them here indoors.
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1152:
I’ll manage my task with cleverness, although ’tis to caress an old skeleton.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1153:
Take care and do your best.
2nd BACCHIS
Be quiet; do you do yours; I’ll manage what I have said.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1154:
Why are these two women holding a council here in private?
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1155:
What say you, my good fellow—?
NICOBULUS
What would you with me?
PHILOXENUS
I really am ashamed to tell you a certain thing.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1156:
What is it that you’re ashamed about?
PHILOXENUS
Still, as you are a person, a friend of mine, I’m determined to entrust you with what I could wish. (Whispers.) I’m good for nought.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1157:
I’ve known that this long time; but tell me why you’re good for nought?
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1158:
I’ve been terribly touched with birdlime: troth, my heart is pierced by the goad.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1159: I’ faith, ’twere much better if your flanks were goaded, you worthless fellow.
5.2.1160:
But what is it? Although I suspect that I myself pretty well know already what it is; still, I should even like to hear it from yourself.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1161:
Do you see that woman?
(Pointing to the SECOND BACCHIS.)
NICOBULUS
I see her.
PHILOXENUS
She’s not an uncomely person.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1162:
Troth, but she is decidedly uncomely; and you are a good-for-nothing fellow.
PHILOXENUS
Why more? I’m in love.
NICOBULUS
You, in love?
PHILOXENUS
’Pon honor.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1163:
And do you, you rotten creature, presume to become a lover at your time of life?
PHILOXENUS
Why not?
NICOBULUS
5.2.1164:
Because it’s a disgrace.
PHILOXENUS
What need of words? I am not vexed with my son, nor yet is it right you should be vexed with yours: if they are in love, they do wisely.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1166:
Follow me this way.
(They approach the old men.)
NICOBULUS
See, they are moving at last, these allurers and enticers to disgrace. (To the women.) How now? Do you this instant restore us our sons and my servant, or am I to try rougher means with you?
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1168:
Won’t you away with you? You surely are not a man, to address a pretty woman so rudely in that fashion.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1170:
Most worthy old gentleman, by whatsoever is upon the earth, let me entreat this of you, that you will cease to attack this error with such great vehemence.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1172:
If you don’t away with you, although you are so handsome, I’ll be doing you some great mischief just now.
1st BACCHIS
I shall endure it; I don’t apprehend that any blow that you can give, will cause me any pain.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1173:
How smooth of speech she is. O me! I am in alarm.
1st BACCHIS
(aside.)
5.2.1175:
(Aloud.) Step this way with me in-doors; and there, if you choose, correct your son.
(Takes his arm.)
NICOBULUS
5.2.1176:
Avaunt from me, abomination!
(Shakes her off.)
1st BACCHIS
Do, my love, let me prevail upon you.
NICOBULUS
You, prevail upon me?
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1177:
For sure, I shall prevail, at all events, upon this gentleman.
(Pointing to PHILOXENUS.)
PHILOXENUS
Yes, I beg of you to show me in-doors.
2nd BACCHIS
5.2.1178:
What a dear man you are.
PHILOXENUS
But do you know on what condition you are to show me in-doors?
2nd BACCHIS
That you are to be with me.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1179:
You mention all that I desire.
2nd BACCHIS
NICOBULUS
I have seen wicked men; but not one worse than yourself.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1180:
I am as I am.
1st BACCHIS
(to NICOBULUS.)
5.2.1181:
Step this way in-doors with me, where you may be elegantly received with viands, wine, and unguents.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1182:
Enough, enough now of your banquets; it matters not to me how I’m received. My son and Chrysalus have choused me out of four hundred Philippeans. If I don’t surely this day put him to the torture, may I never receive as large a sum again.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1185:
What, pray, if half the gold is paid you back? Will you go in-doors here with me, and so control your feelings as to forgive them their faults?
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1186:
He’ll do it.
(Takes his arm.)
NICOBULUS
Certainly not—I won’t—I don’t care—let me alone, now. (Shakes him off.) I had rather punish them both.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1188:
Take you care, you good-for-nothing man, that through your own fault you don’t lose even that which the favouring Gods offer you. One half of the gold is offered; take it, and carouse, and enjoy yourself with your partner.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1190:
What, am I to carouse in that very place where my son is being corrupted?
PHILOXENUS
You must carouse there.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1192:
Am I to be the witness of it when she is reclining with him at table?
1st BACCHIS
Nay, so far as I’m concerned, i’ faith, I’ll recline at table with your own self.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1193:
My head does itch so. (Aside.) I’m a ruined man—I can scarce deny her.
PHILOXENUS
5.2.1194: And has it not before this come into your mind, that if, while you live, you enjoy yourself,
5.2.1195:
that, i’ faith, is for no very long time; and that, if you lose the present day, it can never return to you after you are dead?
NICOBULUS
5.2.1196:
What am I to do?
PHILOXENUS
What are you to do? Do you even ask it?
NICOBULUS
I should like, and yet I’m afraid.
1st BACCHIS
What are you afraid of?
NICOBULUS
5.2.1197:
Lest I should be exposed before my son and my servant.
1st BACCHIS
Pray now, my honey; such things do happen. He’s your own son; whence do you suppose that he is to have money, except that only which you give him yourself? Let me obtain pardon of you for them both.
NICOBULUS
(aside.)
5.2.1199: How she does work her way.
5.2.1200:
She’s now prevailing on me against that which I was quite resolved upon.
1st BACCHIS
I will love you, and embrace you.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1201:
Through your doing, and for your sake am I corrupted.
1st BACCHIS
I certainly had rather ’twere for your own than for mine.
NICOBULUS
5.2.1191:
Come then, however that may be, although it is to my disgrace, I’ll submit; I’ll induce my feelings to do so.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1202:
Have I that solemnly promised?
NICOBULUS
What I have once said, I will not alter.
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1203:
The day wears apace. Come into the house, to take your places at table: your sons are expecting within—
NICOBULUS
5.2.1204:
How soon, in fact, we may be dead, d’ye mean?
1st BACCHIS
5.2.1205:
’Tis evening, already; come, follow us.
PHILOXENUS
Lead us in like bondsmen.
(They go into the house.)
1st BACCHIS
(to the SPECTATORS.)
5.2.1206:
Right cleverly are these persons entrapped themselves, who for their sons had laid a snare.
(Goes in.)
The COMPANY of COMEDIANS
5.2.1207: Had not these old men been worthless from their youth upwards, they would not, with their hoary heads, have this day done an action so disgraceful; nor, indeed, should we have represented this, if we had not, before this, seen it happen
5.2.1210: that fathers became the rivals of their sons in the houses of procurers. Spectators, we wish you Farewell! and that you will grant us loud applause.

0.0.1:
PROLOGUS
THESE two captives (pointing to PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS), whom you see standing here, are standing here because—they are both standing, and are not sitting. That I am saying this truly, you are my witnesses. The old man, who lives here (pointing to HEGIO’S house), is Hegio— his father (pointing to TYNDARUS.)
0.0.5: But under what circumstances he is the slave of his own father, that I will here explain to you, if you give attention. This old man had two sons; a slave stole one child when four years old, and flying hence, he sold him in Elis,
0.0.10: to the father of this captive (pointing to PHIILOCRATES.) Now, do you understand this? Very good. I’ faith, that man at a distance there (pointing) says, no. Come nearer then. If there isn’t room for you to sit down, there is for you to walk; since you’d be compelling an actor to bawl like a beggar. I’m not going to burst myself for your sake, so don’t you be mistaken.
0.0.15: You who are enabled by your means to pay your taxes, listen to the rest; I care not to be in debt to another. This runaway slave, as I said before, sold his young master, whom, whom he fled, he had carried off, to this one’s father. He, after he bought him, gave him as his own
0.0.20: private slave to his son of his, because they were of about the same age. He is now the slave at home of his own father, nor does his father know it. Verily, the Gods do treat us men just like footballs. You hear the manner now how he lost one son. Afterwards, the Aetolians are waging war with the people of Elis,
0.0.25: and, as happens in warfare, the other son is taken prisoner. The physician Menarchus buys him there in Elis. On this, this Hegio begins to traffic in Elean captives, if, perchance, he may be able to find one to change for that captive son of his. He knows not that this one who is in his house is his own son.
0.0.30: And as he heard yesterday that an Elean knight of very high rank and very high family was taken prisoner, he has spared no expense to rescue his son. In order that he may more easily bring him back home, he buys both of these of the Quaestors out of the spoil.
0.0.35: Now they, between themselves, have contrived this plan, that, by means of it, the servant may send away hence his master home. And therefore among themselves they change their garments and their names. He, there (pointing), is called Philocrates; this one (pointing), Tyndarus; he this day assumes the character of this one, this one of him.
0.0.40: And this one to-day will cleverly carry out this plot, and cause his master to gain his liberty; and by the same means he will save his own brother, and without knowing it, will cause him to return back a free man to his own country to his father. Just as often now, on many occasions,
0.0.45: a person has done more good unknowingly than knowingly. But unconsciously, by their devices, they have so planned and devised their plot, and have so contrived it by their design, that this one is living in servitude with his own father.
0.0.50: And thus now, in ignorance, he is the slave of his own father. What poor creatures are men, when I reflect upon it! This plot will be performed by us—a play for your entertainment. But there is, besides, a thing which, in a few words, I would wish to inform you of. Really, it will be worth your while to give your attention to this play.
0.0.55: ’Tis not composed in the hackneyed style, nor yet like other plays, nor are there in it any ribald lines unfit for utterance: here is neither the perjured procurer, nor the artful courtesan, nor yet the braggart captain. Don’t you be afraid because I’ve said that there’s war between the Aetolians and the Eleans.
0.0.60: There (pointing), at a distance, beyond the scenes, the battles will be fought. For this were almost impossible for a Comic establishmen, that we should at a moment attempt to be acting Tragedy. If, therefore, any one is looking for a battle, let him commence the quarrel;
0.0.65: if he shall find an adversary more powerful, I’ll cause him to be the spectator of a battle that isn’t pleasant to him, so that hereafter he shall hate to be a spectator them all. I now retire. Fare ye well, at home, most upright judges, and in warfare most valiant combatants.

1.1.69:
(Enter ERGASILUS.) ERGASILUS
The young men have given me the name of the mistress,
1.1.70: for this reason, because invocated I am wont to attend at the banquet. I know that buffoons say that this is absurdly said, but I affirm that it is rightly said. For at the banquet the lover, when he throws the dice, invokes his mistress. Is she then invocated, or is she not? She is, most clearly.
1.1.75: But, i’ faith, we Parasites with better reason are so called, whom no person ever either invites or invokes, and who, like mice, are always eating the victuals of another person. When business is laid aside, when people repair to the country, at that same moment is business laid aside for our teeth.
1.1.80: Just as, when it is hot weather, snails lie hidden in secret, and live upon their own juices, if the dew doesn’t fall; so, when business is laid aside, do Parasites lie hidden in retirement, and miserably live upon their own juices, while in the country the persons are rusticating whom they sponge upon.
1.1.85: When business is laid aside, we Parasites are greyhounds; when business recommences, like mastiffs, we are annoying-like and very troublesome-like. And here, indeed, unless, i’ faith, any Parasite is able to endure cuffs with the fist, and pots to be broken about his head,
1.1.90: why he may e’en go with his wallet outside the Trigeminian Gate. That this may prove my lot, there is some danger. For since my patron has fallen into the hands of the enemy—(such warfare are the Aetolians now waging with the Eleans; for this is Aetolia; this Philopolemus has been made captive in Elis, the son of this old man Hegio
1.1.95: who lives here (pointing to the house)—a house which to me is a house of woe, and which so oft as I look upon, I weep). Now, for the sake of his son, has he commenced this dishonorable traffic, very much against his own inclination.
1.1.100: He buys up men that have been made captives, if perchance he may be able to find some one for whom to gain his son in exchange. An object which I really do much desire that he may gain. For unless he finds him, there’s nowhere for me to find myself. I have no hopes in the young men; they are all too fond of themselves.
1.1.105:
He, in fine, is a youth with the old-fashioned nanners, whose countenance I never rendered cheerful without a return. His father is worthily matched, as endowed with like manners. Now I’ll go to him;—but his door is opening, the door from which full oft I’ve sallied forth drunk with excess of cheer.
(He stands aside.)

1.2.110:
(Enter, from his house, HEGIO and a SLAVE.) HEGIO
Now, give attention you, if you please. Those two captives whom I purchased yesterday of the Quaestors out of the spoil, put upon them chains of light weight; take off those greater ones with which they are bound. Permit them to walk, if they wish, out of doors, or if in-doors,
1.2.115:
but so that they are watched with the greatest care. A captive at liberty is like a bird that’s wild; if opportunity is once given for escaping, ‘tis enough; after that, you can never catch him.
A SLAVE
1.2.119:
Doubtless we all are free men more willingly than we live the life of slaves.
HEGIO
1.2.120:
You, indeed, don’t seem to think so.
A SLAVE
1.2.121:
If I have nothing to give, should you like me to give myself to flight?
HEGIO
1.2.122:
If you do so give yourself, I shall at once have something to be giving to you.
A SLAVE
1.2.123:
I’ll make myself just like the wild bird you were telling of.
HEGIO
1.2.124: ’Tis just as you say; for if you do so, I’ll be giving you to the cage.
1.2.125:
But enough of prating; take you care of what I’ve ordered, and be off. (The SLAVE goes into the house.) I’ll away to my brother’s, to my other captives; I’ll go see whether they’ve been making any disturbance last night. From there I shall forthwith betake myself home again.
ERGASILUS
(apart.)
1.2.129: It grieves me that this unhappy old man is following the trade of a slave-dealer,
1.2.130:
by reason of the misfortune of his son. But, if by any means he can be brought back here, I could even endure for him to become an executioner.
HEGIO
(overhearing him.)
1.2.133:
Who is it that’s speaking?
ERGASILUS
’Tis I, who am, pining at your affliction, growing thin, waxing old, and shockingly wasting away. Wretched man that I am,
1.2.135:
I’m but skin and bone through leanness; nor does anything ever do me good that I eat at home; even that ever so little which I taste out of doors, the same refreshes me.
HEGIO
1.2.138:
Ergasilus, save you!
ERGASILUS
(crying.)
May the Gods kindly bless you, Hegio!
HEGIO
1.2.139:
Don’t weep.
ERGASILUS
Must I not weep for him? Must I not weep for such a young man?
HEGIO
1.2.140:
I’ve always known you to be a friend to my son, and I have understood him to be so to you.
ERGASILUS
1.2.142: Then at last do we men know our blessings, when we have lost those things which we once had in our power. I, since your son fell into the power of the enemy,
1.2.145:
knowing by experience of what value he was, now feel his loss.
HEGIO
1.2.146:
Since you, who are no relation, bear his misfortune so much amiss, what is it likely that I, a father, should do, whose only son he is?
ERGASILUS
1.2.148: I, no relation to him? He, no relation to me? Oh, Hegio! never do say that, nor come to such a belief.
1.2.150:
To you he is an only child, but to me he is even more only than an only one.
HEGIO
1.2.151:
I commend you, in that you consider the affliction of your friend your own affliction. Now be of good heart.
ERGASILUS
(crying.)
1.2.153: ’Tis this afflicts him, that the army for guttling is now disbanded.
1.2.154:
Meanwhile, have you found no one to command for you the army that you mentioned as disbanded?
ERGASILUS
1.2.156:
What do you think? All to whom it used to fall are in the habit of declining that province since your son Philopolemus was taken prisoner.
HEGIO
1.2.158: I’ faith, ‘tisn’t to be wondered at, that they are in the habit of declining that province. You have necessity for numerous troops, and those of numerous kinds.
1.2.160:
Well, first you have need of the Bakerians. Of these Bakerians there are several kinds, You have need of Roll-makerians, you have need too of Confectionerians, you have need of Poultererians, you have need of Beccaficorians; besides, all the maritime forces are necessary for you.
ERGASILUS
1.2.165:
How the greatest geniuses do frequently lie concealed! How great a general now is this private individual!
HEGIO
1.2.167: Only have good courage; for I trust that in a few days I shall bring him back home. For see now; there’s a captive here, a young man of Elis,
1.2.170:
born of a very high family, and of very great wealth; I trust that it will come to pass that I shall get my son in exchange for him.
ERGASILUS
1.2.172:
May the Gods and Goddesses grant it so!
HEGIO
1.2.173:
But are you invited out anywhere to dinner?
ERGASILUS
Nowhere that I know of. But, pray, why do you ask me?
HEGIO
1.2.175:
for that reason I’d like you to be invited to dinner at my house.
ERGASILUS
1.2.177:
But if you can be content to eat a very little—
ERGASILUS
Aye, even ever so little; for on such fare as that do I enjoy myself every day at home.
HEGIO
1.2.179:
Come, then, please, set yourself up for sale.
ERGASILUS
I’ll put myself up for purchase, just like a landed estate, unless any one shall privately make a better offer that pleases myself and my friends more, and to my own conditions will I bind myself.
HEGIO
1.2.182:
You are surely selling me a bottomless pit, and not a landed estate. But if you are coming, do so in time.
ERGASILUS
1.2.183:
Why, for that matter, I’m at leisure even now.
HEGIO
1.2.184: Go then, and hunt for a hare; at present, in me you have but a ferret,
1.2.185:
for my fare is in the way of frequenting a rugged road.
ERGASILUS
1.2.186:
You’ll never repulse me by that, Hegio, so don’t attempt it. I’ll come, in spite of it, with teeth well shod.
HEGIO
1.2.188:
Really, my viands are but of a rough sort.
ERGASILUS
Are you in the habit of eating brambles?
HEGIO
1.2.189:
Mine is an earthy dinner.
ERGASILUS
A pig is an earthy animal.
HEGIO
1.2.190:
Earthy from its plenty of vegetables.
ERGASILUS
Treat your sick peoples at home with that fare? Do you wish anything else?
HEGIO
1.2.191:
Come in good time.
ERGASILUS
You are putting in mind one who remembers quite well.
(Exit.)
HEGIO
1.2.192:
I’ll go in-doors, and in the house I’ll make the calculation how little money I have at my banker’s; afterwards I’ll go to my brother’s, whither I was saying I would go.
(Goes into his house.)

2.1.195:
(Enter, from the house, PHILOCRATES, TYNDARUS, and SLAVES and CAPTIVES of HEGIO.) A SLAVE
If the immortal Gods have so willed it that you should undergo this affliction, it becomes you to endure it with equanimity; if you do so, your trouble will be lighter. At home you were free men, I suppose; now if slavery has befallen you, ‘tis a becoming way for you to put up with it, and by your dispositions to render it light, under a master’s rule.
2.1.200:
Unworthy actions which a master does must be deemed worthy ones.
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
Alas! alas! alas!
A SLAVE
2.1.201:
There’s no need for wailing; you cause much injury to your eyes. In adversity, if you use fortitude of mind, it is of service.
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
2.1.203:
But we are ashamed, because we are in bonds.
A SLAVE
But in the result it might cause vexation to our master, if he were to release you from chains,
2.1.205:
or allow you to be loose, whom he has purchased with his money.
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
2.1.206:
What does he fear from us? We know our duty, what it is, if he allows us to be loose.
A SLAVE
2.1.208:
Why, you are meditating escape. I know what it is you are devising.
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
2.1.209:
We, make our escape? Whither should we escape?
A SLAVE
To your own country.
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
Out upon you; it would ill befit us to be following the example of runaways.
A SLAVE
2.1.210:
Why, faith, should there be an opportunity, I don’t advise you not.
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
2.1.211:
Do you allow us to make one request.
A SLAVE
What is it, pray?
PHILOCRATES and TYNDARUS
2.1.212:
That you will give us an opportunity of conversing, without these and yourselves for overlookers.
A SLAVE
2.1.214:
Be it so; go you away from here, you people. Let’s step here, on one side.
(To the other CAPTIVES and SLAVES.)
2.1.215:
But commence upon a short conversation only.
PHILOCRATES
O yes, it was my intention so to do. Step aside this way.
(to TYNDARUS.)
A SLAVE
(to the other CAPTIVES.)
2.1.216:
Stand apart from them.
TYNDARUS
(to the SLAVE.)
We are both greatly obliged to you, by reason of your doing so, since you allow us to obtain what we are desirous of.
PHILOCRATES
2.1.219: Step here then, at a distance now, if you think fit,
2.1.220: that no listeners may be enabled to overhear our discourse, and that this plan of ours mayn’t be divulged before them for a stratagem is no stratagem, if you don’t plan it with art but it is a very great misfortune if it becomes disclosed. For if you are my master, and I represent myself as your servant,
2.1.225:
still there’s need of foresight, and need of caution, that this may be carried out discreetly and without overlookers, with carefulness and with cautious prudence and diligence. So great is the mutter that has been commenced upon; this must not be carried out in any drowsy fashion.
TYNDARUS
2.1.228:
Just as you shall desire me to be, I will be.
PHILOCRATES
I trust so.
TYNDARUS
2.1.229:
For now you see that for your precious life I’m setting at stake my own, as dear to me.
PHILOCRATES
2.1.231:
I know it.
TYNDARUS
But remember to know it when you shall be enjoying that which you wish for; for mostly, the greatest part of mankind follow this fashion; what they wish for, until they obtain it, they are rightminded; but when they have now got it in their power,
2.1.235:
from being rightminded they become most deceitful, and most dishonest; now I do consider that you are towards me as I wish. What I advise you, I would advise my own father.
PHILOCRATES
2.1.237:
I’ faith, if I could venture, I would call you father; for next to my own father, you are my nearest father.
TYNDARUS
2.1.240:
I understand.
PHILOCRATES
And therefore I remind you the more frequently, that you may remember it. I am not your master, but your servant; now this one thing I do beseech you. Inasmuch as the immortal Gods have disclosed to us their wishes, that they desire me to have once been your master, and now to be your fellow-captive; what formerly of my right I used to command you, now with entreaties do I beg of you,
2.1.245:
by our uncertain fortunes, and by the kindness of my father towards you, and by our common captivity, which has befallen us by the hand of the enemy, don’t you pay me any greater respect than I did you when you were my slave; and don’t you forget to remember who you were, and who you now are.
TYNDARUS
2.1.249:
I know, indeed, that I now am you, and that you are I.
PHILOCRATES
Well, if you are able carefully to remember that, 1 have some hope in this scheme of ours.

2.2.251:
(Enter HEGIO, from his house, speaking to those within.) HEGIO
I shall return in-doors just now, when I shall have discovered from these people what I want to know. (To the SLAVES.) Where are those persons whom I ordered to be brought out of doors here, before the house?
PHILOCRATES
2.2.253:
By my faith, I find that you have taken due precaution that we shouldn’t be missed by you, so walled in are we with chains and keepers.
HEGIO
2.2.255:
He that takes precaution that he mayn’t be deceived, is hardly on his guard, even while he’s taking precaution; even when he has supposed that he has taken every precaution, full often is this wary man outwitted. Was there not good reason, indeed, for me to watch you carefully, whom I purchased with so large a sum of ready money?
PHILOCRATES
2.2.259: Troth, it isn’t fair for us to hold you to blame, because you watch us closely;
2.2.260:
nor yet for you us, if we go away hence, should there be an opportunity.
HEGIO
2.2.261:
As you are here, so is my son a captive there among your people.
PHILOCRATES
2.2.262:
He, a captive?
HEGIO
Even so.
PHILOCRATES
We, then, have not proved the only cowards.
HEGIO
(to PHILOCRATES, supposing him to be the SERVANT of the other.)
2.2.263:
Step you aside this way, for there are some things that I wish to enquire of you in private, on which subjects I would have you not to be untruthful to me.
(They step aside.)
PHILOCRATES
2.2.265:
as to that which I shall know; if I shall not know anything, that which I don’t know I’ll tell you of.
TYNDARUS
(aside.)
2.2.266:
Now is the old fellow in the barber’s shop; now, at this very instant, is Philocrates wielding the razor. He hasn’t cared, indeed, to put on the barber’s cloth, so as not to soil his dress. But whether to say that he’s going to shave him close, or trim him through the comb, I don’t know; but if he’s wise, he’ll scrape him right well to the very quick.
HEGIO
(to PHILOCRATES.)
2.2.270:
Which would you? Would you prefer to be a slave, or a free man?—Tell me.
PHILOCRATES
2.2.271:
That which is the nearest to good, and the furthest off from evil, do I prefer; although my servitude hasn’t proved very grievous to me, nor has it been otherwise to me than if I had been a son in the family.
TYNDARUS
(aside.)
2.2.274: Capital! I wouldn’t purchase, at a talent’s price even, Thales the Milesian;
2.2.275:
for compared with this man’s wisdom, he was a very twaddler. How cleverly has he suited his language to the slave’s condition.
HEGIO
2.2.277:
Of what family is this Philocrates born?
PHILOCRATES
The Polyplusian; which one family is flourishing there, and held in highest esteem.
HEGIO
2.2.279:
What is he himself? In what esteem is he held there?
PHILOCRATES
In the highest, and that by the very highest men.
HEGIO
2.2.280:
Since, then, he is held in such great respect among the Eleans, as you tell of, what substance has he?—Of large amount?
PHILOCRATES
2.2.281:
Enough for him, even, when an old man, to be melting out the tallow.
HEGIO
2.2.282:
What is his father? Is he living?
PHILOCRATES
When we departed thence, we left him alive; whether he’s living now or not, Orcus, forsooth, must know that.
TYNDARUS
(aside.)
2.2.284:
The matter’s all right; he’s not only lying, but he’s even philosophizing now.
HEGIO
2.2.285:
What’s his name?
PHILOCRATES
Thesaurochrysonicocrœsides.
HEGIO
2.2.286:
That name has been given, I suppose, by reason of his wealth, as it were.
PHILOCRATES
2.2.287:
Troth, not so, but rather by reason of his avarice and grasping disposition; for, indeed, he was Theodoromedes originally by name.
HEGIO
2.2.289:
How say you? Is his father covetous?
PHILOCRATES
Aye, by my faith, he is covetous.
2.2.290:
Why, that you may even understand it the better,—when he’s sacrificing at any time to his own Genius, the vessels that are needed for the sacrifice he uses of Samian ware, lest the Genius himself should steal them; from this, consider how much he would trust other people.
HEGIO
(addressing TYNDARUS as though PHILOCRATES.)
2.2.293: Do you then follow me this way. (Aside.) The things that I desire to know, I’ll enquire of him. (Addressing TYNDARUS.) Philocrates, this person has done as it becomes an honest man to do.
2.2.295:
For from him I’ve learnt of what family you are sprung; he has confessed it to me. If you are willing to own these same things (which, however, understand that I already know from him), you will be doing it for your own advantage.
TYNDARUS
2.2.297: He did his duty when he confessed the truth to you, although, Hegio, I wished carefully to conceal both my rank and my wealth;
2.2.300: now, inasmuch as I’ve lost my country and my liberty, I don’t think it right for him to be dreading me rather than you. The might of warfare has made my fortunes on a level with himself. I remember the time when he didn’t dare to do it in word; now, in deed, he is at liberty to offend me. But don’t you see? Human fortune moulds and fashions just as she wills.
2.2.305:
Myself, who was a free man she has made a slave, from the very highest the very lowest. I, who was accustomed to command, now obey the mandates of another. And indeed, if I meet with a master just such as I proved the ruler in my own household, I shall not fear that he will rule me harshly or severely. With this, Hegio, I wished you to be acquainted, unless perchance you your self wish it not.
HEGIO
2.2.310:
Speak boldly out.
TYNDARUS
As free a man was I till lately as your son. As much did a hostile hand deprive me of my liberty as him of his. As much is he a slave among my people, as I am now a slave here with yourself. There is undoubtedly a God, who both hears and sees the things which we do. Just as you shall treat me here, in the same degree will he have a care for him.
2.2.315:
To the well-deserving will he show favour, to the ill-deserving will he give a like return. As much as you lament your son, so much does my father lament me.
HEGIO
2.2.317:
That I am aware of. But do you admit the same that lie has disclosed to me?
TYNDARUS
2.2.318: I confess that my father has very great wealth at home, and that I am born of a very noble family; but I entreat you, Hegio,
2.2.320:
let not my riches make your mind too prone to avarice, lest it should seem to my father, although I am his only son, more suitable that I should be a slave in your house, bountifully supplied at your expense and with your clothing, rather than be living the life of a beggar where ‘twould be far from honorable.
HEGIO
2.2.324: By the favour of the Gods and of my forefathers, I am rich enough.
2.2.325: I don’t quite believe that every kind of gain is serviceable to mankind. I know that gain has already made many a man famous; and yet there are occasions when it is undoubtedly better to incur loss than to make gain. Gold I detest: many a one has it persuaded to many an evil course. Now give your attention to this, that you may know as well what my wishes are.
2.2.330:
My son, taken prisoner. is in servitude at Elis there among your people; if you restore him to me, don’t you give me a single coin besides; both you and him, your servant, I’ll send back from here; on no other terms can you depart hence.
TYNDARUS
2.2.333:
You ask what’s very right and very just, and you are the very kindest person of all mankind. But whether is he in servitude to a private person or to the public?
HEGIO
2.2.335:
In private servitude to Menarchus, a physician.
PHILOCRATES
By my faith, that person’s surely his father’s dependant. Why really, that’s down as pat for you, as the shower is when it rains.
HEGIO
2.2.337:
Do you then cause this person, my son, to be redeemed.
TYNDARUS
I’ll do so: but this I beg of you, Hegio—
HEGIO
2.2.338:
Whatever you wish, so that you request nothing against my interest, I’ll do.
TYNDARUS
Listen then, and you’ll know. I don’t ask for myself to be released, until he has returned.
2.2.340:
But I beg of you to give me him (pointing to PHILOCRATES) with a price set upon him, that I may send him to my father, that this person, your son, may be redeemed there.
HEGIO
2.2.341:
Why no; I’d rather send another person hence, when there shall be a truce, to confer with your father there, and to carry your injunctions which you shall entrust him with, just as you wish.
TYNDARUS
2.2.344: But it’s of no use to send to him one that he doesn’t know; you’d be losing your labour.
2.2.345: Send this person; he’ll have it all completed, if he gets there. And you cannot send any person to him more faithful, nor one in whom he places more confidence, nor who is more a servant after his own mind; nor, in fact, one to whom he would more readily entrust your son. Have no fears; at my own peril I’ll make proof of his fidelity,
2.2.350:
relying upon his disposition; because he is sensible that I’m kindly disposed towards him.
HEGIO
2.2.351:
Well then, I’ll send him with a price set upon him, on the surety of your promise, if you wish it.
TYNDARUS
I do wish it; so soon as ever it can, I want this matter to be brought to completion.
HEGIO
2.2.353:
What reason is there, then, that if he doesn’t return, you should not pay me twenty minae for him?
TYNDARUS
2.2.354:
Yes—very good.
HEGIO
(to the SLAVES, who obey.)
Release him now forthwith;
2.2.355:
and, indeed, both of them.
(On being released, PHILOCRATES goes into the house.)
TYNDARUS
May all the Gods grant you all your desires, since you have deigned me honor so great, and since you release me from my chains. Really, this is not so irksome now, since my neck is free from the collar-chain.
HEGIO
2.2.358: The kindnesses that are done to the good, thanks for the same are pregnant with blessings. Now, if you are about to send him thither, direct, instruct him, give him the orders
2.2.360:
which you wish to be carried to your father. Should you like me to call him to you?
TYNDARUS
Do call him.
(HEGIO goes to the door, and calls PHILOCRATES.)

2.3.361:
(Enter PHILOCRATES, from the house) HEGIO
May this affair turn out happily for myself and for my son, and for yourselves. (To PHILOCRATES.) Your new master wishes you to pay faithful obedience to your former owner in what he wishes. For I have presented you to him, with the price of twenty minae set upon you:
2.3.365:
and he says that he is desirous to send you away hence to his father, that he may there redeem my son, and that an exchange may be made between me and him for our respective sons.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.368: My disposition takes its course straight in either direction, both to yourself and to him; as a wheel you may make use of me;
2.3.370:
either this way or that can I be turned, whichever way you shall command me.
HEGIO
2.3.371:
You yourself profit the most from your own disposition, when you endure slavery just as it ought to be endured. Follow me. (To TYNDARUS.) See here’s your man.
TYNDARUS
2.3.373: I return you thanks, since you give me this opportunity and permission
2.3.375: to send this messenger to my parents, who may relate all the matter in its order to my father, what I’m doing here, and what I wish to be done. (To PHILOCRATES.) Now, Tyndarus, thus is it arranged between myself and him, that I’m to send you, valued at a fixed price, to my father in Elis;
2.3.380:
so that, if you don’t return hither, I’m to give twenty minae for you.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.381:
I think that you’ve come to a right understanding. For your father expects either myself or some messenger to come from here to him.
TYNDARUS
2.3.383:
I wish you, then, to mind what message it is I want you to carry hence to my country to my father.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.385:
Philocrates, as up to this moment I have done, I will take all due care to endeavour that which may especially conduce to your interest, and to pursue the same with heart and soul, and with my ears.
TYNDARUS
2.3.388: You act just as you ought to act; now I wish you to give attention. In the first place of all, carry my respects to my mother and my father,
2.3.390:
and to my relations, and if any one else you see well-disposed towards me: say that I am in health here, and that I am a slave, in servitude to this most worthy man, who has ever honored me more and more with his respect, and does so still.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.393:
Don’t you be instructing me as to that; I can, still, easily bear that in mind.
TYNDARUS
2.3.394: For, indeed, except that I have a keeper, I deem myself to be a free man.
2.3.395:
Tell my father on what terms I have agreed with this party about his son.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.396:
What I remember, it is sheer delay to be putting me in mind of.
TYNDARUS
2.3.397:
To redeem him, and to send him back here in exchange for both of us.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.398:
I’ll remember it.
HEGIO
But as soon as he can that is especially to the interest of us both.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.399:
You are not more anxious to see your son, than he is to see his.
