HEGIO
2.3.400:
My son is dear to myself, and his own to every man.
PHILOCRATES
(to TYNDARUS.)
Do you wish any other message to be carried to your father?
TYNDARUS
2.3.401: Say that I am well here; and do you boldly tell him, Tyndarus, that we have been of dispositions for uninterrupted harmony between ourselves, and that you have neither been deserving of censure, nor that I have proved your enemy; and that still, amid miseries so great, you have shown implicit obedience to your master,
2.3.405: and that you have never abandoned me, either in deed or in fidelity, amid my wavering, unprosperous fortunes. When my father shall know this, Tyndarus, how well-disposed you have proved towards his son and himself, he will never be so avaricious but that he’ll give you your liberty for nothing. And by my own endeavours, if I return hence, I’ll make him do so the more readily.
2.3.410:
For by your aid and kindness, and good disposition and prudence, you have caused me to be allowed to return to my parents once again, inasmuch as to Hegio you have confessed both my rank and my wealth; by means of which, through your wisdom, you have liberated your master from his chains.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.414: The things which you mention I have done, and I am pleased that you remember this.
2.3.415:
Deservedly have they been done for you by me; for now, Philocrates, if I, too, were to mention the things that you have kindly done for me, the night would cut short the day. For, had you been my slave even, no otherwise were you always obliging to me.
HEGIO
2.3.418: Ye Gods, by our trust in you! behold the kindly disposition of these persons! How they draw the very tears from me!
2.3.420:
See how cordially they love each other, and with what praises the servant has commended his master.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.421:
I’ troth, he hasn’t commended me the one hundredth part of what he himself deserves to be commended in my praises.
HEGIO
(to PHILOCRATES.)
2.3.423:
Since, then, you have acted most becomingly, now there’s an opportunity to add to your good deeds in managing this matter with fidelity towards him.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.425:
I am not able more to wish it done, than by my endeavours to try to bring it about. That you may know this, Hegio, with praises do I call supreme Jove to witness that I will not prove unfaithful to Philocrates—
HEGIO
2.3.427:
You are a worthy fellow.
PHILOCRATES
2.3.428:
And that I will never in anything act otherwise towards him than towards my own self.
TYNDARUS
2.3.429: I wish you to put these speeches to the test, both by your deeds and your actions;
2.3.430: and inasmuch as I have said the less about you than I had wished, I wish you the more to give me your attention, and take you care not to be angry with me by reason of these words. But, I beseech you, reflect that you are sent hence home with a price set upon you at my risk, and that my life is here left as a pledge for you. Do not you forget me the very moment that you have left my presence,
2.3.435: since you will have left me here behind a captive in captivity for yourself, and don’t consider yourself as free, and forsake your pledge, and not use your endeavours for you to bring his son home again, in return for me. Understand that you are sent hence valued at twenty minae. Take care to prove scrupulously faithful; take care that you show not a wavering fidelity.
2.3.440: For my father, I am sure, will do everything that he ought to do. Preserve me as a constant friend to you, and find out this person so lately discovered. These things, by your right hand, holding you with my own right hand, do I beg of you; do not prove less true to me than I have proved to you. This matter do you attend to; you are now my master, you my patron, you my father;
2.3.445:
to you do I commend my hopes and my fortunes.
PHILOCRATES
You have given injunctions enough. Are you satisfied if I bring back accomplished what you have enjoined?
TYNDARUS
2.3.447:
According to your wishes, and
(to TYNDARUS) according to yours, will I return hither provided. Is there anything else?
TYNDARUS
2.3.448:
For you to return back as soon as ever you can.
PHILOCRATES
The business itself reminds me of that.
HEGIO
(to PHILOCRATES.)
2.3.449: Follow me, that I may give you your expenses for the journey at my banker’s;
2.3.450:
on the same occasion I’ll get a passport from the Praetor.
TYNDARUS
What passport?
HEGIO
2.3.451:
For him to take with him hence to the army, that he may be allowed to go home from here. (To TYNDARUS.) You go in-doors.
TYNDARUS
2.3.452:
Speed you well.
PHILOCRATES
Right heartily, farewell.
(TYNDARUS goes into the house.)
HEGIO
(aside.)
I’ faith, I compassed my design, when I purchased these men of the Quaestors out of the spoil. I have released my son from slavery, if so it pleases the Gods;
2.3.455: and yet I hesitated a long time whether I should purchase or should not purchase these persons. Watch that man indoors, if you please, you servants, that he may nowhere move a foot without a guard. I shall soon make my appearance at home; now I’m going to my brother’s, to see my other captives; at the same time I’ll enquire whether any one knows this young man.
2.3.460:
(To PHILOCRATES.) Do you follow, that I may despatch you. I wish attention first to be paid to that matter.
(Exeunt.)

3.1.461:
(Enter ERGASILUS.) ERGASILUS
Wretched is that man who is in search of something to eat, and finds that with difficulty; but more wretched is he who both seeks with difficulty, and finds nothing at all; most wretched is he, who, when he desires to eat, has not that which he may eat. But, by my faith, if I only could, I’d willingly tear out the eyes of this day;
3.1.465: —with such enmity has it filled all people towards me. One more starved out I never did see, nor one more filled with hunger, nor one who prospers less in whatever he begins to do. So much do my stomach and my throat take rest on these fasting holidays. Away with the profession of a Parasite to very utter and extreme perdition!
3.1.470: so much in these days do the young men drive away from them the needy drolls. They care nothing now-a-days for these Laconian men of the lowest benches—these whipping-posts, who have their clever sayings without provision and without money. They now-a-days seek those who, when they’ve eaten at their pleasure, may give them a return at their own houses. They go themselves to market, which formerly was the province of the Parasites.
3.1.475: They go themselves from the Forum to the procurers with face as exposed as the magistrates in court, with face exposed, condemn those who are found guilty; nor do they now value buffoons at one farthing; all are so much in love with themselves. For, when, just now, I went away from here, I came to some young men in the Forum: Good morrow, said I; whither are we going together to breakfast? On this, they were silent.
3.1.480: Who says, ‘here, at my house,’ or who makes an offer? said I. Just like dumb men, they were silent, and didn’t smile at me. Where do we dine? said I. On this they declined. I said one funny saying out of my best bon mots, by which I formerly used to get feasting for a month; not an individual smiled; at once I knew that the matter was arranged by concert.
3.1.485: Not even one was willing to imitate a dog when provoked; if they didn’t laugh, they might, at least, have grinned with their teeth. From them I went away, after I saw that I was thus made sport of. I went to some others; then to some others I came; then to some others—the same the result. All treat the matter in confederacy, just like the oil-merchants in the Velabrum.
3.1.490: Now, I’ve returned thence, since I see myself made sport of there. In like manner do other Parasites walk to and fro, to no purpose, in the Forum. Now, after the foreign fashion, I’m determined to enforce all my rights. Those who have entered into a confederacy, by which to deprive us of food and life,—for them I’ll name a day. I’ll demand, as the damages, that they shall give me ten dinners
3.1.495: at my own option, when provisions are dear: thus will I do. Now I’ll go hence to the harbour. There, is my only hope of a dinner; if that shall fail me, I’ll return here to the old gentleman, to his unsavoury dinner.

3.2.498:
(Enter HEGIO and ARISTOPHONTES.) HEGIO
(to himself.)
What is there more delightful than to manage one’s own interests well for the public good, just as I did yesterday,
3.2.500: when I purchased these men. Every person, as they see me, comes to meet me, and congratulates me on this matter. By thus stopping and detaining unlucky me, they’ve made me quite tired. With much ado have I survived from being congratulated, to my misfortune.
3.2.505: At last, to the Praetor did I get. There, scarcely did I rest myself. I asked for a passport; it was given me: at once I delivered it to Tyndarus. He started for home. Thence, straightway, after that was done, I passed by my house; and I went at once to my brother’s, where my other captives are. I asked about Philocrates from Elis, whether any one of them all knew the person.
3.2.510: This man (pointing to ARISTOPHONTES) called out that he had been his intimate friend; I told him that he was at my house. At once he besought and entreated me that I would permit him to see him. Forthwith I ordered him to be released from chains. Thence have I come. (To ARISTOPHONTES.) Now, do you follow me,
3.2.514:
that you may obtain what you have besought of me, the opportunity of meeting with this person.
(They go into the house.)

3.3.516:
(Enter TYNDARUS, from the house.) TYNDARUS
Now stands the matter so, that I would much rather that I had once existed, than that I still exist; now do my hopes, my resources, and my succour, desert me and spurn themselves. This is that day, when, for my life, no safety can be hoped; nor yet is death my end; nor hope is there, in fact, to dispel this fear for me;
3.3.520: nor cloak have I anywhere for my deceitful stratagems; nor for my devices or my subterfuges is there anywhere a screen presented to me. No deprecating is there for my perfidy; no means of flight for my offences. No refuge is there anywhere for my trusting; and no escape for my cunning schemes. What was concealed is now exposed; my plans are now divulged.
3.3.525: The whole matter is now laid open; nor is there any ado about this matter, but that I must perish outright, and meet with destruction, both on behalf of my master and myself. This Aristophontes has proved my ruin, who has just now come into the house. He knows me. He is the intimate friend and kinsman of Philocrates. Not Salvation herself can save me now, even if she wishes; nor have I any means of escape,
3.3.530:
unless, perchance, I devise some artifice in my mind. (He meditates.) Plague on it!-how? What can I contrive?—what can I think of? Some very great folly and trifling I shall have to begin with. I’m quite at a loss.
(He retires aside.)

3.4.533:
(Enter HEGIO, ARISTOPHONTES, and SLAVES, from the house) HEGIO
Whither am I to say, now, that this man has betaken himself from the house out of doors?
TYNDARUS
(apart.)
3.4.534: Now, for a very certainty, I’m done for; the enemies are coming to you, Tyndarus!
3.4.535:
What shall I say?—what shall I talk of? What shall I deny, or what confess? All matters are reduced to uncertainty. How shall I place confidence in my resources? I wish the Gods had destroyed you, before you were lost to your own country, Aristophontes, who, from a plot well concerted, are making it disconcerted. This plan is ruined outright, unless I find out for myself some extremely bold device.
HEGIO
(to ARISTOPHONTES.)
3.4.540:
Follow me. See, there is the man; go to him and address him.
TYNDARUS
(aside, and turning away.)
What mortal among mortals is there more wretched than myself?
ARISTOPHONTES
(coming up to him.)
3.4.541:
Why’s this, that I’m to say that you are avoiding my gaze, Tyndarus? And why that you are slighting me as a stranger, as though you had never known me? Why, I’m as much a slave as yourself; although at home I was a free man, you, even from your childhood, have always served in slavery in Elis.
HEGIO
3.4.545:
I’ faith, I’m very little surprised, if either he does avoid your gaze, or if he does shun you, who are calling him Tyndarus, instead of Philocrates.
TYNDARUS
3.4.547: Hegio, this person was accounted a madman in Elis. Don’t you give ear to what he prates about; for at home he has pursued his father and mother with spears,
3.4.550:
and that malady sometimes comes upon him which is spit out Do you this instant stand away at a distance from him.
HEGIO
(to the SLAVES.)
3.4.551:
Away with him further off from me.
ARISTOPHONTES
Do you say, you whipp’d knave, that I am mad, and do you declare that I have followed my own father with spears? And that I have that malady, that it’s necessary for me to be spit upon?
HEGIO
3.4.554: Don’t be dismayed; that malady afflicts many a person
3.4.555:
to whom it has proved wholesome to be spit upon, and has been of service to them.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.556:
Why, what do you say? Do you, too, credit him?
HEGIO
Credit him in what?
ARISTOPHONTES
That I am mad?
TYNDARUS
3.4.557:
Do you see him, with what a furious aspect he’s looking at you? ’Twere best to retire, Hegio; it is as I said, his frenzy grows apace; have a care for yourself.
HEGIO
3.4.559:
I thought that he was mad, the moment that he called you Tyndarus.
TYNDARUS
3.4.560:
Why, he’s sometimes ignorant of his own name, and doesn’t know what it is.
HEGIO
3.4.561:
But he even said that you were his intimate friend.
TYNDARUS
So far from that, I never saw him. Why, really, Alcmaeon, and Orestes, and Lycurgus besides, are my friends on the same principle that he is.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.563:
Villain, and do you dare speak ill of me, as well? Do I not know you?
HEGIO
3.4.564: I’ faith, it really is very clear
3.4.565:
that you don’t know him, who are calling him Tyndarus, instead of Philocrates. Him whom you see, you don’t know; you are addressing him as the person whom you don’t see.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.567:
On the contrary this fellow’s saying that he is the person who he is not; and he says that he is not the person who he really is.
TYNDARUS
3.4.568:
You’ve been found, of course, to excel Philocrates in truthfulness.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.569:
By my troth, as I understand the matter, you’ve been found to brazen out the truth by lying. But i’ faith, prithee, come then, look at me.
TYNDARUS
(looking at him.)
3.4.570:
Well!
ARISTOPHONTES
Say, now; do you deny that you are Tyndarus?
TYNDARUS
3.4.571:
I do deny it, I say.
ARISTOPHONTES
Do you say that you are Philocrates?
TYNDARUS
3.4.572:
I do say so, I say.
ARISTOPHONTES
(to HEGIO.)
And do you believe him?
HEGIO
More, indeed, than either you or myself. For he, in fact, who you say that he is
(pointing to TYNDARUS), has set out hence to-day for Elis, to this person’s father.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.574:
What father, when he’s a slave.
TYNDARUS
And so are
3.4.575:
you a slave, and yet you were a free man; and I trust that so I shall be, if I restore his son here to liberty.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.577:
How say you, villain? Do you say that you were born a free man [liber]?
TYNDARUS
3.4.578:
I really do not say that I am Liber, but that I am Philocrates.
ARISTOPHONTES
How’s this? How this scoundrel, Hegio, is making sport of you now.
3.4.580:
For he’s a slave himself, and never, except his own self, had he a slave.
TYNDARUS
3.4.581:
Because you yourself are destitute in your own country, and haven’t whereon to live at home, you wish all to be found like to yourself; you don’t do anything surprising. ’Tis the nature of the distressed to be ill-disposed, and to envy the fortunate.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.584: Hegio, take you care, please, that you don’t persist in rashly placing confidence in this man;
3.4.585:
for so far as I see, he is certainly now putting some device in execution, in saying that he is redeeming your son from captivity; that is by no means satisfactory to me.
TYNDARUS
3.4.587:
I know that you don’t wish that to be done; still I shall effect it, if the Gods assist me. I shall bring him back here, and he will restore me to my father, in Elis. For that purpose have I sent Tyndarus hence to my father.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.590:
nor is there any slave in Elis of that name, except yourself.
TYNDARUS
3.4.591:
Do you persist in reproaching me with being a slave—a thing that has befallen me through the fortune of war?
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.592:
Really, now, I cannot contain myself.
TYNDARUS
(to HEGIO.)
Ha! don’t you hear him? Why don’t you take to flight? He’ll be pelting us just now with stones there, unless you order him to be seized.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.594:
I’m distracted.
TYNDARUS
His eyes strike fire; there’s need of a rope, Hegio.
3.4.595:
Don’t you see how his body is spotted all over with livid spots? Black bile is disordering the man.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.596:
And, by my faith, if this old gentleman is wise, black pitch will be disordering you with the executioner, and giving a light to your head.
TYNDARUS
3.4.598:
He’s now talking in his fit of delirium; sprites are in possession of the man.
HEGIO
3.4.599:
By my troth, suppose I order him to be seized?
TYNDARUS
You would be acting more wisely.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.600:
I’m vexed that I haven’t a stone, to knock out the brains of that whip-scoundrel, who’s driving me to madness by his taunts.
TYNDARUS
3.4.602:
Don’t you hear that he’s looking for a stone?
ARISTOPHONTES
I wish to speak with you alone, separately, Hegio.
HEGIO
3.4.603:
Speak from where you are, if you want anything; though at a distance, I shall hear you.
TYNDARUS
3.4.604:
Yes, for, by my faith, if you approach nearer, he’ll be taking your nose off with his teeth.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.605:
By heavens, Hegio, don’t you believe that I am mad, or that I ever was so, or that I have the malady which that fellow avers. But if you fear anything from me, order me to be bound; I wish it, so long as that fellow is bound as well.
TYNDARUS
3.4.608:
Why really, Hegio, rather let him be bound that wishes it.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.609: Now hold your tongue! I’ll make you, you false Philocrates, to be found out this day to be a real Tyndarus.
3.4.611:
Why are you making signs at me?
TYNDARUS
I, making signs at you? (To HEGIO.) What would he do, if you were at a greater distance off?
HEGIO
3.4.612:
What do you say? What if I approach this madman?
TYNDARUS
Nonsense; you’ll be made a fool of; he’ll be prating stuff, to you, neither the feet nor the head of which will ever be visible.
3.4.615:
The dress only is wanting; in seeing this man, you behold Ajax himself.
HEGIO
3.4.616:
I don’t care; still I’ll approach him.
(Advances to ARISTOPHONTES.)
TYNDARUS
(aside.)
Now am I utterly undone; now between the sacrifice and the stone do I stand, nor know I what to do.
HEGIO
3.4.618:
I lend you my attention, Aristophontes, if there is anything that you would wish with me.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.619: From me you shall hear that truth, which now you think to be false, Hegio.
3.4.620:
But I wish, in the first place, to clear myself from this with you—that madness does not possess me, and that I have no malady, except that I am in captivity; and, so may the King of Gods and of men make me to regain my native land, that fellow there is no more Philocrates than either I or you.
HEGIO
3.4.623:
Come, then, tell me who he is?
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.624: He whom I’ve told you all along from the beginning.
3.4.625:
If you shall find him any other than that person, I show no cause why I shouldn’t suffer the loss with you both of my parents and of my liberty for ever.
HEGIO
(to TYNDARUS.)
3.4.627:
What say you to this?
TYNDARUS
That I am your slave, and you my master.
HEGIO
I didn’t ask that—were you a free man?
TYNDARUS
3.4.628:
I was.
ARISTOPHONTES
But he really wasn’t; he is deceiving you.
TYNDARUS
3.4.629: How do you know? Were you, perchance, the midwife of my mother,
3.4.630:
since you dare to affirm this so boldly?
ARISTOPHONTES
When a boy, I saw yourself, a boy.
TYNDARUS
3.4.631:
But, grown up, I now see you grown up; so, there’s for you, in return. If you did right, you wouldn’t be troubling yourself about my concerns; do I trouble myself about yours?
HEGIO
3.4.633:
Was his father called Thesaurochrysonicocrœsides?
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.634: He was not; and I never heard that name before this day.
3.4.635:
Theodoromedes was the father of Philocrates.
TYNDARUS
(aside.)
I’m downright undone. Why don’t you be quiet, heart of mine? Go and be stretched, and hang yourself; you are throbbing so, that unfortunate I can hardly stand up for my fear.
HEGIO
3.4.638:
Is a full assurance given me that this was a slave in Elis, and that he is not Philocrates?
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.639:
So fully, that you will never find this to be otherwise; but where is he now?
HEGIO
3.4.640:
Where I the least, and he the most could wish himself. In consequence, then, I’m cut asunder, disjointed, to my sorrow, by the devices of this scoundrel, who has bamboozled me by his tricks just as he has thought fit. But do, please, have a care that you are right.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.4.643:
Why, I assure you of this, as an ascertained and established fact.
HEGIO
3.4.644:
For certain?
ARISTOPHONTES
Why, nothing, I say, will you find more certain than this certainty.
3.4.645:
Philocrates, from when a boy, has ever since that time been my friend.
HEGIO
3.4.646:
But of what appearance is your friend Philocrates?
ARISTOPHONTES
I’ll tell you:
3.4.647:
with a thin face, sharp nose, light hair, dark eyes, somewhat ruddy, with hair rather crisp and curling,
HEGIO
3.4.649:
Aye, so much so, indeed, that I’ve this day, much to my sorrow, got into the midst of this, i’ faith. Woe to those unfortunate rods which this day will be meeting their end upon my back.
HEGIO
3.4.651:
I see that I’ve been imposed upon.
TYNDARUS
(aside.)
Why, fetters, do you delay to run towards me and to embrace my legs, that I may have you in custody?
HEGIO
3.4.653: And have these two rascally captives really deceived me this day with their tricks? The other one pretended that he was the servant, and this one that he himself was the master.
3.4.655:
I’ve lost the kernel; for a security, I’ve left the shell. To such a degree have they imposed upon me, both on this side and that, with their trickeries. Still, this fellow shall never have the laugh against me. Colaphus, Cordalio, Corax (to the SLAVES), go you away and bring out the thongs.
A SLAVE
3.4.658: Are we to be sent to gather faggots? (The SLAVES go and bring the thongs from the house.)

3.5.659:
(HEGIO, TYNDARUS, ARISTOPHONTES, and SLAVES) HEGIO
(to the SLAVES.)
Put the manacles on this whipp’d villain.
TYNDARUS
(whilst the SLAVES are fastening him.)
3.5.660:
What’s the matter? What have I done wrong?
HEGIO
Do you ask the question? You weeder and sower of villanies, and in especial their reaper.
TYNDARUS
3.5.662:
Ought you not to have ventured to say the harrower first? For countrymen always harrow before they weed.
HEGIO
3.5.664:
Why, with what assurance he stands before me.
TYNDARUS
3.5.665:
It’s proper for a servant, innocent and guiltless, to be full of confidence, most especially before his master.
HEGIO
(to the SLATES.)
3.5.667:
Bind this fellow’s hands tightly, will you.
TYNDARUS
3.5.668:
I am your own—do you command them to be cut off even. But what is the matter on account of which you blame me?
HEGIO
3.5.670: Because me and my fortunes, so far as in you singly lay, by your rascally and knavish stratagems you have rent in pieces, and have distracted my affairs and spoiled all my resources and my plans, in that you’ve thus robbed me of Philocrates by your devices,
3.5.675:
I thought that he was the slave, you the free man. So did you say yourselves, and in this way did you change names between you.
TYNDARUS
3.5.677: I confess that all was done so, as you say, and that by a stratagem he has got away from you, through my aid and cleverness;
3.5.680:
and prithee, now, do you blame me for that, i’ faith?
HEGIO
3.5.681:
Why, it has been done with your extreme torture for the consequence.
TYNDARUS
3.5.682: So I don’t die by reason of my misdeeds, I care but little. If I do die here, then he returns not, as he said he would; but when I’m dead, this act will be remembered to my honor,
3.5.685:
that I caused my captive master to return from slavery and the foe, a free man, to his father in his native land; and that I preferred rather to expose my own life to peril, than that he should be undone.
HEGIO
3.5.689:
Take care, then, to enjoy that fame at Acheron.
TYNDARUS
3.5.690:
He who dies for virtue’s sake, still does not perish.
HEGIO
3.5.691:
When I’ve tortured you in the most severe manner, and for your schemes put you to death, let them say either that you have perished or that you have died; so long as you do die, I don’t think it matters if they say you live.
TYNDARUS
3.5.695:
I’ faith, if you do do so, you’ll do it not without retribution, if he shall return here, as I trust that he will return.
ARISTOPHONTES
(aside.)
3.5.697: O ye immortal Gods! I understand it now; now I know what the case really is. My friend Philocrates is at liberty with his father, in his native land. ’Tis well;
3.5.700:
nor have I any person to whom I could so readily wish well. But this thing grieves me, that I’ve done this person a bad turn, who now on account of me and my talking is in chains.
HEGIO
(to TYNDARUS.)
3.5.703:
Did I not forbid you this day to utter anything false to me?
TYNDARUS
3.5.704:
You did forbid me.
HEGIO
Why did you dare to tell me lies?
TYNDARUS
3.5.705:
Because the truth would have prejudiced him whom I was serving; now falsehood has advantaged him.
HEGIO
3.5.706:
But it will prejudice yourself.
TYNDARUS
’Tis very good. Still, I have saved my master, whom I rejoice at being saved, to whom my elder master had assigned me as a protector. But do you think that this was wrongly done?
HEGIO
3.5.710: But I, who disagree with you, say, rightly. For consider, if any slave of yours had done this for your son, what thanks you would have given him. Would you have given that slave his freedom or not? Would not that slave have been in highest esteem with you?
3.5.715:
Answer me that.
HEGIO
I think so.
TYNDARUS
Why, then, are you angry with me?
HEGIO
3.5.716:
Because you have proved more faithful to him than to myself.
TYNDARUS
3.5.717: How now? Did you expect, in a single night and day, for yourself to teach me—a person just made captive, a recent slave, and in his noviciate—that I should rather consult your interest than his,
3.5.720:
with whom from childhood I have passed my life?
HEGIO
3.5.721: Seek, then, thanks from him for that. (To the SLAVES.) Take him where he may receive weighty and thick fetters, thence, after that, you shall go to the quarries for cutting stone. There, while the others are digging out eight stones, unless
3.5.725:
you daily do half as much work again, you shall have the name of the six-hundred-stripe man.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.5.727:
By Gods and men, I do entreat you, Hegio, not to destroy this man.
HEGIO
3.5.728: He shall be taken all care of For at night, fastened with chains, he shall be watched;
3.5.730:
in the daytime, beneath the ground, he shall be getting out stone. For many a day will I torture him; I’ll not respite him for a single day.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.5.732:
Is that settled by you?
HEGIO
Not more settled that I shall die. (To the SLAVES.) Take him away this instant to Hippolytus, the blacksmith; bid thick fetters to be rivetted on him.
3.5.735:
From there let him be led outside the gate to my freedman, Cordalus, at the stone-quarries. And tell him that I desire this man so to be treated, that he mayn’t be in any respect worse off than he who is the most severely treated.
TYNDARUS
3.5.739: Why, since you are unwilling, do I desire myself to survive?
3.5.740: At your own hazard is the risk of my life. After death, no evil have I to apprehend in death. Though I should live even to extreme age, still, short is the space for enduring what you threaten me with. Farewell and prosper although you are deserving for me to say otherwise.
3.5.745:
You, Aristophontes, as you have deserved of me, so fare you; for on your account has this befallen me.
HEGIO
(to the SLAVES.)
3.5.747:
But this one thing I beg, that, if Philocrates should come back here, you will give me an opportunity of meeting him.
HEGIO
(to the SLAVES.)
3.5.749:
At your peril, if you don’t this instant remove him from my sight.
(The SLAVES lay hold of TYNDARUS, and push him along.)
TYNDARUS
3.5.750:
I’ troth, this really is violence, to be both dragged and pushed at the same time. (He is borne off by the SLAVES.)
HEGIO
3.5.751: He has been led off straight to prison as he deserves. Let no one presume to attempt such an enterprise. Had it not been for you who discovered this to me,
3.5.755: still would they have been leading me by the bridle with their tricks. Now am I resolved henceforth never to trust any person in anything. This once I have been deceived enough; I did hope, to my sorrow, that I had rescued my son from slavery. That hope has forsaken me. I lost one son,
3.5.760: whom, a child in his fourth year, a slave stole from me; and, indeed, never since have I found either slave or son; the elder one has fallen in the hands of the enemy. What guilt is this of mine? As though I had become the father of children for the purpose of being childless. (To AISTOPHONTES.) Follow this way. I’ll conduct you back where you were.
3.5.765:
I’m determined to have pity upon no one, since no one has pity upon me.
ARISTOPHONTES
3.5.766:
Forth from my chains with evil omen did I come; now I perceive that with like ill omen to my bonds I must return.
(Exeunt.)

4.1.768:
(Enter ERGASILUS ERGASILUS
Supreme Jove! thou dost preserve me, and dost augment my means. Plenty, extreme and sumptuous, dost thou present to me;
4.1.770: celebrity, profit, enjoyment, mirth, festivity, holidays, sights, provisions, carousings, abundance, joyousness. And to no man have I now determined with myself to go a-begging; for I’m able either to profit my friend or to destroy my enemy, to such extent has this delightful day heaped delights upon me in its delightfulness.
4.1.775: I have lighted upon a most rich inheritance without incumbrances. Now will I wend my way to this old gentleman Hegio, to whom I am carrying blessings as great as he himself prays for from the Gods, and even greater. Now, this is my determination, in the same fashion that the slaves of Comedy are wont, so will I throw my cloak around my neck, that from me, the first of all, he may learn this matter.
4.1.780: And I trust that I, by reason of this news, shall find provision up to the end.

4.2.781:
(Enter HEGIO, at a distance.) HEGIO
(to himself.)
The more that I revolve this matter in my breast, the more is my uneasiness of mind increased. That I should have been duped in this fashion to-day! and that I wasn’t able to see through it!
4.2.785:
When this shall be known, then I shall be laughed at all over the city. The very moment that I shall have reached the Forum, all will be saying, This is that clever old gentleman, who had the trick played him. But is this Ergasilus, that I see coming at a distance? Surely he has got his cloak gathered up; what, I wonder, is he going to do?
ERGASILUS
(advancing, and talking to himself.)
4.2.790:
Throw aside from you all tardiness, Ergasilus, and speed on this business. I threaten, and I strictly charge no person to stand in my way, unless any one shall be of opinion that he has lived long enough. For whoever does come in my way, shall stop me upon his face.
(He runs along, flourishing his arms about.)
HEGIO
(to himself.)
4.2.793:
This fellow’s beginning to box.
ERGASILUS
(to himself.)
4.2.794: I’m determined to do it; so that every one may pursue his own path,
4.2.795:
let no one be bringing any of his business in this street; for my fist is a balista, my arm is my catapulta, my shoulder a battering-ram; then against whomsoever I dart my knee, I shall bring him to the ground. I’ll make all persons to be picking up their teeth, whomsoever I shall meet with.
HEGIO
(to himself.)
4.2.799:
What threatening is this? For I cannot wonder enough.
ERGASILUS
4.2.800:
I’ll make him always to remember this day and place, and myself as well. Whoever stops me upon my road, I’ll make him put a stop to his own existence.
HEGIO
(to himself.)
4.2.802:
What great thing is this fellow preparing to do, with such mighty threats?
ERGASILUS
4.2.803:
I first give notice, that no one, by reason of his own fault, may be caught—keep yourselves in-doors at home, and guard yourselves from my attack.
HEGIO
(to himself.)
4.2.805:
By my faith, ‘tis strange if he hasn’t got this boldness by means of his stomach. Woe to that wretched man, through whose cheer this fellow has become quite swaggering.
ERGASILUS
4.2.807: Then the bakers, that feed swine, that fatten their pigs upon refuse bran, through the stench of which no one can pass by a baker’s shop; if I see the pig of any one of them in the public way,
4.2.810:
I’ll beat the bran out of the masters’ themselves with my fists.
HEGIO
(to himself.)
4.2.811:
Royal and imperial edicts does he give out. The fellow is full; he certainly has his boldness from his stomach.
ERGASILUS
4.2.813: Then the fishmongers, who supply stinking fish to the public—who are carried about on a gelding, with his galloping galling pace—
4.2.815: the stench of whom drives all the loungers in the Basilica into the Forum, I’ll bang their heads with their bulrush fish-baskets, that they may understand what annoyance they cause to the noses of other people. And then the butchers, as well, who render the sheep destitute of their young—who agree with you about killing lamb, and then offer you lamb at double the price—
4.2.820:
who give the name of wether mutton to a ram—if I should only see that ram in the public way, I’ll make both ram and owner most miserable beings.
HEGIO
(to hieiself.)
4.2.823:
Well done! He really does give out edicts fit for an Aedile, and ‘tis indeed a surprising thing if the Aetolians haven’t made him inspector of markets.
ERGASILUS
4.2.825:
No Parasite now am I, but a right royal king of kings; so large a stock of provision for my stomach is there at hand in the harbour. But why delay to overwhelm this old gentleman Hegio with gladness? With him, not a person among mankind exists equally fortunate.
HEGIO
(apart.)
4.2.829:
What joy is this, that he, thus joyous, is going to impart to me?
ERGASILUS
(knocking at HEGIO’S door.)
4.2.830:
Hallo, hallo!—where are you? Is any one coming to open this door?
HEGIO
(apart.)
4.2.831:
This fellow’s betaking himself to my house to dine.
ERGASILUS
Open you both these doors, before I shall with knocking cause the destruction, piecemeal, of the doors.
HEGIO
(apart.)
4.2.833:
I’d like much to address the fellow. (Aloud.) Ergasilus!
ERGASILUS
Who’s calling Ergasilus?
HEGIO
4.2.834:
Turn round, and look at me.
ERGASILUS
(not seeing who it is.)
A thing that Fortune does not do for you, nor ever will do, you bid me to do.
4.2.835:
But who is it.
HEGIO
Look round at me. ’Tis Hegio.
ERGASILUS
(turning round.)
O me! Best of the very best of men, as many as exist, you have arrived opportunely.
HEGIO
4.2.837:
You’ve met with some one at the harbour to dine with; through that you are elevated.
ERGASILUS
4.2.838:
Give me your hand.
HEGIO
My hand?
ERGASILUS
Give me your hand, I say, this instant.
HEGIO
Take it.
(Giving him his hand.)
ERGASILUS
4.2.839:
Rejoice.
HEGIO
Why should I rejoice?
ERGASILUS
Because I bid you; come now, rejoice.
HEGIO
4.2.840:
I’ faith, my sorrows exceed my rejoicings.
ERGASILUS
’Tis not so, as you shall find; I’ll at once drive away every spot of sorrow from your body. Rejoice without restraint.
HEGIO
4.2.842:
I do rejoice, although I don’t at all know why I should rejoice.
ERGASILUS
4.2.843:
You do rightly; now order—
HEGIO
Order what?
ERGASILUS
A large fire to be made.
HEGIO
4.2.844:
A large fire?
ERGASILUS
So I say, that a huge one it must be.
HEGIO
What, you vulture, do you suppose that for your sake I’m going to set my house on fire?
ERGASILUS
4.2.845:
Don’t be angry. Will you order, or will you not order, the pots to be put on, and the saucepans to be washed out, the bacon and the dainties to be made warm in the heated cooking-stoves, another one, too, to go purchase the fish?
HEGIO
4.2.848:
This fellow’s dreaming while awake.
ERGASILUS
4.2.849:
Another to buy pork, and lamb, and pullets.
HEGIO
4.2.850:
You understand how to feed well, if you had the means.
ERGASILUS
Gammons of bacon, too, and lampreys, spring pickled tunny-fish, mackerel, and sting-ray; large fish, too, and soft cheese.
HEGIO
4.2.852:
You will have more opportunity, Ergasilus, here at my house, of talking about these things than of eating them.
ERGASILUS
4.2.853:
Do you suppose that I’m saying this on my own account?
HEGIO
4.2.854: You will neither be eating nothing here to-day, nor yet much more than usual, so don’t you be mistaken.
4.2.855:
Do you then bring an appetite to my house for your every-day fare.
ERGASILUS
4.2.856:
Why, I’ll so manage it, that you yourself shall wish to be profuse, though I myself should desire you not.
HEGIO
4.2.857:
What, I?
ERGASILUS
Yes, you.
HEGIO
Then you are my master.
ERGASILUS
Yes, and a kindly disposed one. Do you wish me to make you happy?
HEGIO
4.2.858:
Certainly I would, rather than miserable.
ERGASILUS
4.2.859:
Give me your hand.
HEGIO
(extending his hand.)
Here is my hand.
ERGASILUS
All the Gods are blessing you.
HEGIO
I don’t feel it so.
ERGASILUS
4.2.860:
Why, you are not in a quickset hedge, therefore you don’t feel it; but order the vessels, in a clean state, to be got for you forthwith in readiness for the sacrifice, and one lamb to be brought here with all haste, a fat one.
HEGIO
4.2.862:
Why?
ERGASILUS
That you may offer sacrifice
HEGIO
4.2.863:
To which one of the Gods?
ERGASILUS
To myself, i’ faith, for now am I your supreme Jupiter. I likewise am your salvation, your fortune, your life, your delight, your joy.
4.2.865:
Do you at once, then, make this Divinity propitious to you by cramming him.
HEGIO
4.2.866:
You seem to me to be hungry.
ERGASILUS
For myself am I hungry, and not for you.
HEGIO
4.2.867:
I readily allow of it at your own good will.
ERGASILUS
I believe you; from a boy you were in the habit—
HEGIO
4.2.868:
May Jupiter and the Gods confound you.
ERGASILUS
I’ troth, ‘tis fair that for my news you should return me thanks; such great happiness do I now bring you from the harbour.
HEGIO
4.2.870:
Now you are flattering me.
Begone, you simpleton; you have arrived behind time, too late.
ERGASILUS
4.2.871: If I had come sooner, then for that reason you might rather have said that. Now, receive this joyous news of me which I bring you; for at the harbour I just now saw your son Philopolemus in the common fly-boat, alive, safe and sound, and likewise there that other young man together with him,
4.2.875:
and Stalagmus your slave, who fled from your house, who stole from you your little son, the child of four years old.
HEGIO
4.2.877:
Away with you to utter perdition! You are trifling with me.
ERGASILUS
So may holy Gluttony love me, Hegio, and so may she ever dignify me with her name, I did see—
HEGIO
4.2.879:
My son?
ERGASILUS
Your son, and my good Genius.
HEGIO
4.2.880:
That Elean captive, too?
ERGASILUS
Yes, by Apollo
HEGIO
The slave, too? My slave Stalagmus, he that stole my son—?
ERGASILUS
4.2.882:
So long a time ago?
ERGASILUS
Yes, by Praeneste!
HEGIO
Is he arrived?
ERGASILUS
Yes, by Signia!
HEGIO
4.2.883:
For sure?
ERGASILUS
Yes, by Phrysinone!
HEGIO
Have a care, if you please.
ERGASILUS
Yes, by Alatrium!
HEGIO
4.2.884:
Why are you swearing by foreign cities?
ERGASILUS
Why, because they are just as disagreable as you were declaring your fare to be.
HEGIO
4.2.886:
Because that you don’t believe me at all in what I say in sober earnestness. But of what country was Stalagmus, at the time when ne departed hence?
HEGIO
4.2.888:
A Sicilian.
ERGASILUS
But now he is not a Sicilian—he is a Boian; he has got a Boian woman. A wife, I suppose, has been given to him for the sake of obtaining children.
HEGIO
4.2.890:
Tell me, have you said these words to me in good earnest?
ERGASILUS
In good earnest.
HEGIO
4.2.891:
Immortal Gods, I seem to be born again, if you are telling the truth.
ERGASILUS
4.2.892:
Do you say so? Will you still entertain doubts, when I have solemnly sworn to you? In fine, Hegio, if you have little confidence in my oath, go yourself to the harbour and see.
HEGIO
4.2.894:
I’m determined to do so. Do you arrange in-doors what’s requisite. Use, ask for, take from my larder what you like; I appoint you cellarman.
ERGASILUS
4.2.896:
Now, by my troth, if I have not prophesied truly to you, do you comb me out with a cudgel.
HEGIO
4.2.897:
I’ll find you in victuals to the end, if you are telling me the truth.
ERGASILUS
4.2.898:
Whence shall it be?
HEGIO
From myself and from my son.
ERGASILUS
Do you promise that?
HEGIO
I do promise it.
ERGASILUS
4.2.899:
But I, in return, promise you that your son has arrived.
HEGIO
4.2.900:
Manage as well as ever you can.
ERGASILUS
A happy walk there to you, and a happy walk back.
(Exit HEGIO.)

4.3.901:
(ERGASILUS, alone) ERGASILUS
He has gone away from here, and has entrusted to me the most important concern of catering. Immortal Gods how I shall now be slicing necks off of sides; how vast a downfall will befall the gammon; how vast a belabouring the bacon! How great a using-up of udders, how vast a bewailing for the brawn!
4.3.905:
How great a bestirring for the butchers, how great a preparation for the porksellers! But if I were to enumerate the rest of the things which minister to the supply of the stomach, ‘twould be sheer delay. Now will I go off to my government, to give laws to the bacon, and, those gammons that are hanging uncondemned, to give aid to them.
(Goes into the house.)

4.4.909:
(Enter a LAD, a servant of HEGIO.) A LAD
May Jupiter and the Deities confound you, Ergasilus, and your stomach,
4.4.910: and all Parasites, and every one who henceforth shall give a dinner to Parasites. Destruction and devastation and ruin have just now entered our house. I was afraid that he would be making an attack on me, as though he had been an hungry wolf. And very dreadfully, upon my faith, was I frightened at him; he made such a gnashing with his teeth. On his arrival, the whole larder, with the meat, he turned upside down.
4.4.915: He seized a knife, and first cut off the kernels of the neck from three sides. All the pots and cups he broke, except those that held a couple of gallons; of the cook he made enquiry whether the salting pans could be set on the fire to be made hot. All the cellars in the house he has broken into, and has laid the store-closet open. (At the door.) Watch him, servants, if you please; I’ll go to meet the old gentleman.
4.4.920:
I’ll tell him to get ready some provisions for his own self, if, indeed, he wishes himself to make use of any. For in this place, as this man, indeed, is managing, either there’s nothing already, or very soon there will be nothing.
(Exit.)

5.1.922:
(Enter HEGIO, PHILOPOLEMUS, PHILOCRATES, and behind them, STALAGMUS.) HEGIO
To Jove and to the Deities I return with reason hearty thanks, inasmuch as they have restored you to your father, and inasmuch as they have delivered me from very many afflictions,
5.1.925:
which, while I was obliged to be here without you, I was enduring, and inasmuch as I see that that fellow (pointing to STALAGMUS) is in my power, and inasmuch as his word (pointing to PHILOCIATES) has been found true to me.
PHILOPOLEMUS
5.1.928: Enough now have I grieved from my very soul, and enough with care and tears have I disquieted myself. Enough now have I heard of your woes, which at the harbour you told me of.
5.1.930:
Let us now to this business.
PHILOCRATES
What now, since I’ve kept my word with you, and have caused him to be restored back again to freedom?
HEGIO
5.1.931:
Philocrates, you have acted so that I can never return you thanks enough, in the degree that you merit from myself and my son.
PHILOPOLEMUS
5.1.933: Nay, but you can, father, and you will be able, and I shall be able; and the Divinities will give the means for you
5.1.935:
to return the kindness he merits to one who deserves so highly of us; as, my father, you are able to do to this person who so especially deserves it.
HEGIO
5.1.937:
What need is there of words? I have no tongue with which to deny whatever you may ask of me.
PHILOCRATES
5.1.938: I ask of you to restore to me that servant whom I left here as a surety for myself; who has always proved more faithful to me than to himself;
5.1.940:
in order that for his services I may be enabled to give him a reward.
HEGIO
5.1.941:
Because you have acted thus kindly, the favour shall be returned, the thing that you ask; both that and anything else that you shall ask of me, you shall obtain. And I would not have you blame me, because in my anger I have treated him harshly.
PHILOCRATES
5.1.944:
What have you done?
HEGIO
I confined him in fetters at the stone-quarries,
5.1.945:
when I found out that I had been imposed upon.
PHILOCRATES
Ah wretched me! That for my safety misfortunes should have happened to that best of men.
HEGIO
5.1.947:
Now, on this account, you need not give me even one groat of silver for him. Receive him of me without cost that he may be free.
PHILOCRATES
5.1.948:
On my word, Hegio, you act with kindness; but I entreat that you will order this man to be sent for.
HEGIO
5.1.950:
(To the attendants, who immediately obey.) Where are you? Go this instant, and bring Tyndarus here. (To PHILOPOLEMUS and PHILOCRATES.) Do you go in-doors; in the meantime, I wish to enquire of this statue for whipping, what was done with my younger son. Do you go bathe in the meantime.
PHILOPOLEMUS
5.1.953:
Philocrates, follow me this way in-doors.
PHILOCRATES
I follow you. (They go into the house.)

5.2.954:
(HEGIO and STALAGMUS.) HEGIO
Come you, step this way, you worthy fellow, my fine slave.
STALAGMUS
5.2.955:
What is fitting for me to do, when you, such a man as you are, are speaking false? I was never a handsome, or a fine, or a good person, or an honest one, nor shall I ever be; assuredly, don’t you be forming any hopes that I shall be honest.
HEGIO
5.2.958: You easily understand pretty well in what situation your fortunes are. If you shall prove truth-telling, you’ll make your lot from bad somewhat better.
5.2.960:
Speak out, then, correctly and truthfully; but never yet truthfully or correctly have you acted.
STALAGMUS
5.2.961:
Do you think that I’m ashamed to own it, when you affirm it?
HEGIO
5.2.962:
But I’ll make you to be ashamed; for I’ll cause you to be blushes all over.
STALAGMUS
5.2.963:
Heyday—you’re threatening stripes, I suppose, to me, quite unaccustomed to them! Away with them, I beg. Tell me what you bring, that you may carry off hence what you are in want of.
HEGIO
5.2.965:
Very fluent indeed. But now I wish this prating to be cut short.
HEGIO
5.2.966:
As you desire, so be it done.
HEGIO
(to the AUDIENCE.)
As a boy he was very obedient; now that suits him not. Let’s to this business; now give your attention, and inform me upon what I ask. If you tell the truth, you’ll make your fortunes somewhat better.
STALAGMUS
5.2.969:
That’s mere trifling. Don’t you think that I know what I’m deserving of?
HEGIO
5.2.970:
Still, it is in your power to escape a small portion of it, if not the whole.
STALAGMUS
5.2.971:
A small portion I shall escape, I know; but much will befall me, and with my deserving it, because I both ran away, and stole your son and sold him.
HEGIO
5.2.973:
To what person?
STALAGMUS
To Theodoromedes the Polyplusian, in Elis, for six minae.
HEGIO
5.2.974:
O ye immortal Gods! He surely is the father of this person, Philocrates.
STALAGMUS
5.2.975:
Why, I know him better than yourself, and have seen him more times.
HEGIO
5.2.976: Supreme Jove, preserve both myself and my son for me. (He goes to the door, and calls aloud.) Philocrates, by your good Genius, I do entreat you, come out, I want you.

5.3.978:
(Enter PHILOCRATES, from the house) PHILOCRATES
Hegio, here am I; if you want anything of me, command me.
HEGIO
He (pointing to STALAGMUS) declares that he sold my son to your father, in Elis, for six minae.
PHILOCRATES
(to STALAGMUS.)
5.3.980:
How long since did that happen?
STALAGMUS
This is the twentieth year, commencing from it.
PHILOCRATES
5.3.981:
He is speaking falsely.
STALAGMUS
Either I or you do. Why, your father gave you the little child, of four years old, to be your own slave.
PHILOCRATES
5.3.983:
What was his name? If you are speaking the truth, tell me that, then.
STALAGMUS
5.3.984:
Paegnium, he used to be called; afterwards, you gave him the name of Tyndarus.
PHILOCRATES
5.3.985:
Why don’t I recollect you?
STALAGMUS
Because it’s the fashion for persons to forget, and not to know him whose favour is esteemed as worth nothing.
PHILOCRATES
5.3.987:
Tell me, was he the person whom you sold to my father, who was given me for my private service?
STALAGMUS
5.3.988:
It was his son.
(pointing to HEGIO.)
HEGIO
5.3.989:
Is this person now living?
STALAGMUS
I received the money I cared nothing about the rest.
HEGIO
(to PHILOCRATES.)
5.3.990:
What do you say?
PHILOCRATES
Why, this very Tyndarus is your son, according, indeed, to the proofs that he mentions. For, a boy himself together with me from boyhood was he brought up, virtuously and modestly, even to manhood.
HEGIO
5.3.993: I am both unhappy and happy, if you are telling the truth. Unhappy for this reason, because, if he is my son, I have badly treated him.
5.3.995: Alas! why have I done both more and less than was his due. That I have ill treated him I am grieved; would that it only could be undone. But see, he’s coming here, in a guise not according to his deserts.

5.4.998:
(Enter TYNDARUS, in chains, led in by the SERVANTS.) TYNDARUS
(to himself.)
I have seen many of the torments which take place at Acheron often represented in paintings; but most certainly there is no Acheron equal
5.4.1000: to where I have been in the stone-quarries. There, in fine, is the place where real lassitude must be undergone by the body in laboriousness. For when I came there, just as either jackdaws, or ducks, or quails, are given to Patrician children, for them to play with, so in like fashion, when I arrived, a crow was given me with which to amuse myself.
5.4.1005:
But see, my master’s before the door; and lo! my other master has returned from Elis.
HEGIO
5.4.1006:
Hail to you, my much wished-for son.
TYNDARUS
Ha! how—my son? Aye, aye, I know why you pretend yourself to be the father, and me to be the son; it is because, just as parents do, you give me the means of seeing the light.
PHILOCRATES
5.4.1009:
Hail to you, Tyndarus.
TYNDARUS
And to you, for whose sake I am enduring these miseries.
PHILOCRATES
5.4.1010:
But now I’ll make you in freedom come to wealth. For (pointing to HEGIO) this is your father; (pointing to STALAGMUS) that is the slave who stole you away from here when four years old, and sold you to my father for six minae. He gave you, when a little child, to me a little child for my own service. He (pointing to STALAGMUS) has made a confession, for we have brought him back from Elis.
TYNDARUS
5.4.1015:
How, where’s Hegio’s son?
PHILOCRATES
Look now; indoors is your own brother.
TYNDARUS
5.4.1016:
How do you say? Have you brought that captive son of his?
PHILOCRATES
5.4.1017:
Why, he’s in-doors, I say.
TYNDARUS
5.4.1071:
By my faith, you’ve done both well and happily.
PHILOCRATES
(pointing to HEGIO.)
5.4.1018:
Now this is your own father; (pointing to STALAGMUS) this is the thief who stole you when a little child.
TYNDARUS
5.4.1019:
But now, grown up, I shall give him grown up to the executioner for his thieving.
PHILOCRATES
5.4.1020:
He deserves it.
TYNDARUS
I’ faith, I’ll deservedly give him the reward that he deserves. (To HEGIO.) But tell me I pray you, are you my father?
HEGIO
5.4.1021:
I am he, my son.
TYNDARUS
5.4.1022:
Now, at length, I bring it to my recollection, when I reconsider with myself: troth, I do now at last recall to memory that I had heard, as though through a mist, that my father was called Hegio.
HEGIO
5.4.1025:
I am he.
PHILOCRATES
I pray that your son may be lightened of these fetters, and this slave be loaded with them.
HEGIO
5.4.1026:
I’m resolved that that shall be the first thing attended to. Let’s go in-doors, that the blacksmith may be sent for, in order that I may remove those fetters from you, and give them to him. (They go into the house.)
STALAGMUS
5.4.1028:
To one who has no savings of his own, you’ll be rightly doing so.
COMPANY of PLAYERS
(coming forward.)
5.4.1029: Spectators, this play is founded on chaste manners.
5.4.1030: No wenching is there in this, and no intriguing, no exposure of a child, no cheating out of money; and no young man in love here make his mistress free without his father’s knowledge. The Poets find but few Comedies of this kind, where good men might become better. Now, if it pleases you,
5.4.1035: and if we have pleased you, and have not been tedious, do you give this sign of it: you who wish that chaste manners should have their reward, give us your applause.

0.0.1:
THE PROLOGUE
I bid you, most worthy Spectators, welcome; who most highly esteem the Goddess Faith, and Faith esteems you. If I have said the truth, then give me loud applause, that even now, from the very beginning forward, I may know that you are favourably disposed towards me.
0.0.5: Those who make use of aged wine, I deem to be wise; and those as well, who, through choice, are the spectators of ancient Plays. Since antique works and words are pleasing to you, ’tis just that ancient Plays should in preference please you; for the new Comedies which come out now-a-days
0.0.10: are much more worthless than the new-coined money. We, since we have heard the report in public, that you ardently wish for the Plays of Plautus, have brought forward this ancient Comedy of his, which you, who are among the older ones, have formerly approved.
0.0.15: But I am aware that those who are among the younger ones are not acquainted with it; still, that they may make acquaintance with it, we will carefully use our best endeavours. When this was first represented, it surpassed all other Plays. In those days there was the very elite of the poets, who have now departed hence to the place common to all.
0.0.20: But though departed, yet do they prove of advantage to those who are still existing. All of you, with the greatest earnestness, I would have entreated that you’ll kindly lend attention to this our company. Dismiss from your thoughts cares and monies due; let no man stand in dread of his duns.
0.0.25: ’Tis a holiday this—to the bankers a holiday has been given. ’Tis now a calm; about the Forum these are Halcyon days. Reasonably do they act: during the games they ask no man for money; but during the games to no one do they pay. If your ears are disengaged, give me your attention;
0.0.30:
I wish to mention to you the name of the Play. Clerumenae this Comedy is called in Greek; in Latin, Sortientes. Diphilus wrote it in Greek, and after that, over again, Plautus with the barking name in Latin afresh.
(Pointing to the house of STALINO.)
0.0.35: An old married man is living here; he has a son; he, with his father, is dwelling in this house. He has a certain slave, who with disease is confined—aye, faith, to his bed, he really is, that I may tell no lie. But sixteen years ago, it happened that on a time this servant,
0.0.40: at early dawn, beheld a female child being exposed. He went at once to the woman who was exposing it, and begged her to give it to himself. He gained his request: he took it away, and carried it straight home. He gave it to his mistress, and entreated her to take care of it, and bring it up.
0.0.45: His mistress did so; with great care she brought it up, as though it had been her own daughter, not much different. Since then she has grown up to that age to be able to prove an attraction to the men; but this old gentleman loves this girl distractedly, and, on the other hand, so does his son as well.
0.0.50: Each of them now, on either side, is preparing his legions, both father and son, each unknown to the other. The father has deputed his bailiff to ask her as his wife; he hopes that, if she’s given to him, an attraction out of doors will be, unknown to his wife, provided for him.
0.0.55: But the son has deputed his armour-bearer to ask her for himself as a wife. He knows that if he gains that request, there will be an object for him to love, within his abode. The wife of the old gentleman has found out that he is gratifying his amorousness; for that reason, she is making common cause together with her son.
0.0.60: But this father, when he found out that his son was in love with this same woman, and was a hindrance to him, sent the young man hence upon business abroad. His mother, understanding this, still lends him, though absent, her assistance. Don’t you expect it; he will not, in this Play, to-day,
0.0.65: return to the city. Plautus did not choose it: he broke down the bridge that lay before him in the way. There are some here, who, I fancy, are now saying among themselves, Prithee, what means this, i’ faith?—the marriage of a slave Are slaves to be marrying wives, or asking them for themselves?
0.0.70: They’ve introduced something new—a thing that’s done nowhere in the world. But I affirm that this is done in Greece, and at Carthage, and here in our own country, and in the Apulian country; and that the marriages of slaves are wont to be solemnized there with more fuss than even those of free persons.
0.0.75: If this is not the fact, if any one pleases, let him bet with me a stake towards a jug of honied wine, so long as a Carthaginian is the umpire in my cause, or a Greek in fact, or an Apulian. (A pause.) What now? You don’t take it? No one’s thirsty, I find. I’ll return to that foundling girl,
0.0.80: whom the two slaves are, with all their might, contending for as a wife. She’ll be found to be both chaste and free, of freeborn parents, an Athenian girl, and assuredly of no immodesty at all will she be guilty in this Comedy at least. But i’ faith, for sure, directly afterwards, when the Play is over,
0.0.85: if any one offers the money, as I guess, she’ll readily enter into matrimony with him, and not wait for good omens. Thus much I have to say. Farewell; be prosperous in your affairs, and conquer by true valour, as hitherto you’ve done.

1.1.89:
(Enter OLYMPIO, CHALINUS following him. OLYMPIO
Isn’t it to be allowed me for myself to speak and think about my own affairs by myself, just as I choose, without you as an overlooker? Why the plague are you following me about?
CHALINUS
1.1.91: Because I’m resolved, just like your shadow, wherever you go, to follow you about. Why troth, even if you are ready to go to the cross, I’m determined to follow you. Hence judge of the sequel,
1.1.95:
whether you can or not, by your artifices, slily deprive me of Casina for a wife, just as you are attempting.
OLYMPIO
1.1.97:
What business have you with me?
CHALINUS
What say you, impudence? Why are you creeping about in the city, you bailiff, so very valuable in this place?
OLYMPIO
1.1.99:
Because I choose.
CHALINUS
But why ain’t you in the country, at your post of command?
1.1.100:
Why don’t you rather pay attention to the business that has been entrusted to you, and keep yourself from meddling in city matters? Have you come hither to deprive me of my betrothed? Be off to the country—be off to your place of command, and be hanged to you.
OLYMPIO
1.1.104: Chalinus, I have not forgotten my duty.
1.1.105: I’ve given charge to one who will still take care that all’s right in the country. When I’ve got that for which I came hither to the city, to take her as my wife whom you are dying for—the fair and charming Casina, your fellow-servant—when I’ve carried her off with myself into the country as my wife,
1.1.110:
I’ll then stick fast in the country, at my post of command.
CHALINUS
1.1.111:
What, you marry her? By my faith, ’twere better I should die by a halter, than that you should be the winner of her.
OLYMPIO
1.1.113:
She’s my prize; do you put yourself in a halter at once.
CHALINUS
1.1.114:
Fellow, dug up from your own dunghill, is she to be your prize?
OLYMPIO
1.1.115:
You’ll find that such is the fact.
Woe be unto you!
in what a many ways, if I only live, I’ll have you tormented at my wedding!
CHALINUS
1.1.117:
What will you do to me?
OLYMPIO
What will I do to you? In the first place of all, you shall hold the lighted torch for this new-made bride of nine; that always, in future, you may be worthless, and not esteemed.
1.1.120: Then next after that, when you get to the country-house, a single pitcher shall be found you, and a single path, a single spring, a single brass cauldron, and eight casks; and unless these shall be always kept filled, I’ll load you with lashes. I’ll make you so thoroughly bent with carrying water,
1.1.125: that a horse’s crupper might be manufactured out of you. And then, in future, unless in the country you either feed on pulse, or, like a worm, upon the soil, should you require to taste of any better food, never, upon my faith, is hunger as full of hungriness as I’ll make you to be in the country.
1.1.130:
After that, when you’re tired out, and starved with famine, care shall be taken that, at night, you go to bed as you deserve.
CHALINUS
1.1.132:
What will you do?
OLYMPIO
You shall be shut up fast in a nook with bars, where you can listen while I’m caressing her, while she is saying to me, My soul, my own Olympio,
1.1.135: my life, my sweet, my delight, do let me kiss your dear eyes, my love! do, there’s a dear, let yourself be loved! my own day of happiness, my sparrow-chick, my own dove, my leveret! When these expressions shall be being uttered to me, then will you, you villain,
1.1.140:
be wriggling about like a mouse in the middle of the wall. Now, that you mayn’t be trying to give me an answer, I’ll off in-doors; I’m tired of your talk.
(Goes into the house of STALINO.)
CHALINUS
1.1.142:
I’ll follow you. Here, indeed, on my word, assuredly you shall do nothing without me for an overlooker.
(Follows him into the house.)

2.1.144:
(Enter CLEOSTRATA and PARDALISCA, from the house of STALINO.) CLEOSTRATA
(at the door, to the SERVANTS, within.)
Seal fast the store-rooms, bring back the signet to me.
2.1.145:
I’m going here to my next door neighbour; if my husband wants me for anything, take care and send for me thence.
PARDALISCA
2.1.147:
The old gentleman ordered a breakfast to be got ready for him to-day.
CLEOSTRATA
2.1.148: Tut! Hold your tongue, and be off. (PARDALISCA goes into the house.) I don’t prepare it, and it shan’t be cooked; since he sets himself against myself and his son,
2.1.150: for the sake of his passion and his appetite. A disgraceful fellow that! I’ll punish this lover with hunger, I’ll punish him with thirst, with abuse, with hardships.
2.1.153: By my faith, I’ll thoroughly worry him with disagreable speeches; I’ll make him to pass a life in future just as he deserves—fit food for Acheron, a hunter after iniquity, a stable of infamy!
2.1.160: Now I’ll away hence to my neighbours, to lament my lot. But the door makes a noise; and see, she’s coming out of doors herself. On my word, I’ve not started for my call at a convenient time.

2.2.163:
(Enter MYRRHINA, from the house of ALCESIMUS.) MYRRHINA
(to her SERVANTS, at the door.)
Follow me, my attendants, here next door. You there! Does any one hear this that I say? I shall be here, if my husband or any person shall seek me. Did I order my distaff to be taken there? For when I’m at home alone, drowsiness takes effect upon my hand.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.171:
Good morrow, my dear Cleostrata. But, prithee, why are you sad?
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.172:
So all are wont to be who are unfortunately married; at home and abroad, there’s always enough to make them sad. But I was going to your house.
MYRRHINA
2.2.177:
And, troth, I was coming here to yours. But what is it that now distresses your mind? For the thing that distresses you, that same is a trouble to me.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.181:
On my word, I do believe you. For with good reason no female neighbour of mine do I love better than yourself, nor any one with whom I have more ties of intimacy, to afford me pleasure.
MYRRHINA
2.2.183:
I thank you kindly, and I long to know what this is.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.186:
My husband has put slights upon me in a most unworthy manner.
MYRRHINA
2.2.187:
Hah! What is it? Prithee, repeat that same again; for, on my word, I don’t in my mind sufficiently comprehend your complaints.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.189: My husband has put slights upon me in a most unworthy manner,
2.2.190:
and I have not the advantage of enjoying my own rights.
MYRRHINA
2.2.191:
’Tis surprising, if you say the truth; for husbands can scarce obtain from their wives what’s their own right.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.193: Why, against my will, he demands a female servant of me, who belongs to myself, and was brought up at my own expense,
2.2.195:
for him to give to his bailiff. But he is in love with her himself.
MYRRHINA
2.2.196:
Pray, do hold your tongue.
CLEOSTRATA
(looking round.)
2.2.197:
But here we may speak at present; we are alone—
MYRRHINA
2.2.198: It is so. But whence did you get her? For a good wife ought to have no property
2.2.200:
unknown to her husband; and she who has got any, it is not to her credit, for she must either have purloined it from her husband, or obtained it by unfaithfulness. Whatever is your own, all that I take to be your husband’s.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.203:
Surely, you’re saying all this out of opposition to your friend.
MYRRHINA
2.2.204:
Do hold your tongue, will you, simpleton, and attend to me. Do you forbear to oppose him, will you. Let him love on; that which he chooses let him do, so long as nothing’s denied you at home.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.207:
Are you quite in your senses? For really, you are saying these things against your own interest.
MYRRHINA
Silly creature, do you always take care and be on guard against this expression from your husband—
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.211:
What expression?
MYRRHINA
Woman! out of doors with you!
CLEOSTRATA
(in a low voice.)
2.2.212:
’St! be quiet.
MYRRHINA
What’s the matter?
CLEOSTRATA
Hush!
(Looks in a particular direction.)
MYRRHINA
Who is it that you see?
CLEOSTRATA
Why look, my husband’s coming; go you in-doors. Make all haste; be off, there’s a dear.
MYRRHINA
2.2.213:
You easily prevail; I’m off.
CLEOSTRATA
2.2.214:
At a future time, when you and I shall have more leisure, then I’ll talk to you. For the present, adieu!
MYRRHINA
2.2.216: Adieu! (Goes into her house. CLEOSTRATA stands aside.)

2.3.217:
(Enter STALINO.) STALINO
(to himself.)
I do believe that love excels all things and delights that are exquisite. It is not possible for anything to be mentioned, that has more relish and more that’s delicious in it. Really, I do much wonder at the cooks, who employ sauces so many,
2.3.220: that they don’t employ this one seasoning, which excels them all. For where love shall be the seasoning, that I do believe will please every one; nor can there be anything relishing or sweet, where love is not mixed with it. The gall which is bitter, that same it will make into honey; a man from morose into one cheerful and pleasant. This conjecture do I form rather from myself at home than from anything I’ve heard;
2.3.225:
who, since I’ve been in love with Casina, more than in my young days have excelled Neatness herself in neatness; I give employment to all the perfumers; wherever an unguent is excellent, I perfume myself, that I may please her. And I do please her, as I think. But inasmuch as she keeps living on, my wife’s a torment. (Catches sight of his WIFE, and speaks in a low voice.) I espy her standing there in gloominess. This plaguy baggage must be addressed by me with civility. (Going towards her.) My own wife and my delight, what are you about?
(Takes hold of her.)
CLEOSTRATA
(shaking him off.)
2.3.229:
Get you gone, and keep your hand off!
STALINO
2.3.230:
O fie! my Juno. You shouldn’t be so cross to your own Jupiter. Where art come now?
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.231:
Let me alone. (Moves as if going.)
STALINO
Do stay.
CLEOSTRATA
(still going.)
I shan’t stay.
STALINO
I’ troth, then I’ll follow you. (Follows her.)
CLEOSTRATA
(turning round.)
2.3.232:
Prithee, are you in your senses?
STALINO
In my senses, inasmuch as I love you.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.233:
I don’t want you to love me.
STALINO
You can’t have your way there.
CLEOSTRATA
You plague me to death.
STALINO
2.3.234:
I only wish you spoke the truth.
CLEOSTRATA
There I believe you. (Moves on.)
STALINO
2.3.235:
Do look back, O my sweet one.
CLEOSTRATA
About as much, I suppose, as you are to me. Whence is this strong smell of perfumes, prithee?
STALINO
(aside.)
2.3.236:
O dear, I’m undone; to my misfortune, I’m caught in the fact. Why delay to rub it off my head with my cloak? (Rubs his head with his cloak.) May good Mercury confound you, you perfumer, who provided me with this.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.239: How now, you worthless grey gnat! I can hardly restrain myself from saying what you deserve.
2.3.240:
In your old age, good-for-nothing, are you walking along the streets reeking with perfumes?
STALINO
2.3.241:
I’ faith, I lent my company to a certain friend of mine, while he was purchasing some perfumes.
CLEOSTRATA
How readily he did trump that up. Are you ashamed of anything?
STALINO
2.3.242:
Of everything that you like.
CLEOSTRATA
In what dens of iniquity have you been lying?
STALINO
(with an air of surprise.)
2.3.243:
I, in dens of iniquity?
CLEOSTRATA
I know more than you think I do.
STALINO
What is it that you know?
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.244: That not one among all the old men is more worthless than yourself, an old man.
2.3.245:
Whence come you, good-for-nothing? Where have you been? In what den amusing yourself? Where have you been drinking? You are come, on my word; look at his cloak, how it’s creased. (Points at it.)
STALINO
2.3.246:
May the Gods confound both me and yourself, if I this day have put a drop of wine into my mouth.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.247: Very well then; just as you like:
2.3.248:
drink, eat, and squander away your property!
STALINO
Hold, wife; there’s now enough of it; you din me too much. Do leave a little of your talk, that you may wrangle with me to-morrow. But what say you? Have you by this time subdued your temper, so as to do that in preference which your husband wishes to be done, rather than strive against him?
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.253:
About what matter are you speaking?
STALINO
Do you ask me? About the handmaid Casina—that she may be given in marriage to our bailiff,
2.3.255:
an honest servant, where she’ll be well off, in wood, warm water, food, and clothing, and where she may properly bring up the children which she may have, in preference to that rascally servant of an armour-bearer, a good-for-nothing and dishonest, a fellow that hasn’t this day a leaden dump of money his own.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.259: Upon my faith, I am surprised that in your old age you
2.3.260:
do not remember your duty.
STALINO
How so?
CLEOSTRATA
Because if you were to act rightly or becomingly, you’d let me manage the maid-servants, which is my own province.
STALINO
2.3.262:
Why the plague do you wish to give her to a fellow that carries a shield?
CLEOSTRATA
Because it’s our duty to gratify our only son.
STALINO
2.3.263: But although he is an only one, not a bit the more is he my only son than I am his only father.
2.3.265:
It’s more becoming for him to conform to me, than for me to him.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.266:
By my troth, sir, you’re providing for yourself a serious piece of trouble.
STALINO
(aside.)
She suspects it, I find that. (To his wife.) What, I, do you mean?
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.267:
You; but why do. you stammer so? Why do you wish for this with such anxiety?
STALINO
2.3.268:
Why, that she may rather be given to a servant that’s honest, than to a servant that’s dishonest.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.269: What if I prevail upon, and obtain of the bailiff, that for my sake
2.3.270:
he’ll give her up to the other one?
STALINO
But what if I prevail upon the armour-bearer to give her up to the other one? And I think that I can prevail upon him in this.
CLEOSTRATA
2.3.272:
That’s agreed upon. Should you like that, in your name, I should call Chalinus hither out of doors? Do you beg of him, and I’ll beg of the bailiff.
STALINO
2.3.274:
He’ll be here just now. Now we’ll make trial which of us two is the most persuasive. (She goes into the house.)
STALINO
(to himself.)
2.3.275: May Hercules and the Gods confound her!—a thing that now I’m at liberty to say. I’m wretchedly distracted with love; but she, as though on purpose, thwarts me. My wife has some suspicion now of this that I’m planning; for that reason is she purposely lending her assistance to the armour-bearer.

2.4.279:
(Enter CHALINUS, from the house.) STALINO
(aside, on seeing him.)
May all the Gods and Goddesses confound him!
CHALINUS
(addressing him.)
Your wife said that you were calling me.
STALINO
2.4.280:
Why yes, I did order you to be sent for.
CHALINUS
Tell me what you want.
STALINO
2.4.281:
In the first place, I want you to speak to me with a more cheerful countenance.
CHALINUS
2.4.282:
It would be folly for me to be morose toward you whose rule is the strongest.
STALINO
2.4.283:
Indeed! I consider you to be an honest fellow.
CHALINUS
So I find.
2.4.284:
But if you think so, why don’t you give me my freedom?
STALINO
2.4.294:
Why so I wish to do; but it’s of no use for me to wish a thing to be done, unless you aid me with your actions.
CHALINUS
2.4.287:
What you wish, I only wish myself to be acquainted with it.
STALINO
Listen then; I’ll tell you. I’ve promised to give Casina as a wife to our bailiff.
CHALINUS
2.4.290:
but whether now would you prefer yourself to be single and a free man, or, as a married man, to pass your lives, yourself and your children, in slavery? This choice is your own: whichever condition of these two you prefer, take it.
CHALINUS
2.4.293:
If I am free, I live at my own cost; at present I live at yours. As to Casina, I’m resolved to give way to no born man.
STALINO
2.4.295:
Go in-doors, and at once be quick and call my wife here, out of doors; and bring hither together with you an urn, with some water, and the lots.
CHALINUS
2.4.297:
I’ faith, in some way or other I’ll now ward off this weapon of yours; for if, as it is, I shall not be able to prevail by persuasion, at least I’ll try it by lot. There I shall take vengeance upon you and your abettors.
CHALINUS
2.4.299:
Still, for all that the lot will fall to me—
STALINO
2.4.300:
Aye, faith, for you to go to perdition with direful torments.
CHALINUS
2.4.301:
She shall marry me, contrive what you will, in any way you please.
STALINO
2.4.302:
Won’t you away hence from my sight?
CHALINUS
Unwillingly you look upon me, still I shall live on. (Goes into the house.)
STALINO
(to himself.)
2.4.303: Am I not a wretched man? Don’t all things go quite contrary with me? I’m now afraid that my wife will prevail upon Olympio not to
2.4.305: marry Casina. If that’s done, why look, it’s all over with me in my old age! If she does not prevail, there is still some tiny hope in the lots. But if the lots fail me, I’ll make a pillow of a sword, and lay me down upon it. But see, most opportunely Olympio’s coming out of doors.

2.5.309:
(Enter OLYMPIO, from the house, speaking to CLEOSTRATA, within.) OLYMPIO
By my faith, all in an instant shut me up in a hot furnace,
2.5.310:
and parch me there for a hard-baked biscuit, good mistress, before you shall gain that point of me which you desire.
STALINO
(apart.)
2.5.312:
I’m all right. My hope’s realized, according as I hear his words.
OLYMPIO
(at the door, to his MISTRESS, within.)
2.5.313: But why do you frighten me about liberty? Why, even though you should oppose it, and your son as well,
2.5.315:
against your wills and in spite of you both, for a single penny I can become free.
STALINO
(stepping forward.)
2.5.317:
What’s this? Who are you wrangling with, Olympio?
OLYMPIO
2.5.318:
With the same person that you always are.
STALINO
What, with my wife?
OLYMPIO
2.5.319: What wife are you speaking of to me? Really you are a hunter, as it were:
2.5.320:
your nights and days you pass with a female cur.
STALINO
2.5.321:
What does she say? What’s she talking to you about?
OLYMPIO
She’s begging and entreating of me that I won’t be taking Casina as my wife.
STALINO
2.5.322:
What did you say after that?
OLYMPIO
2.5.323:
Why, I declared that I wouldn’t give way to Jupiter himself, if he were to entreat me.
STALINO
2.5.324:
May the Gods preserve you for me!
OLYMPIO
2.5.325:
She’s now all in a ferment; she’s swelling so against me.
STALINO
2.5.326:
By my troth, I could like her to burst in the middle.
OLYMPIO
2.5.327: I’ faith, I fancy she will, if indeed you manage cleverly. But your amorousness, i’ faith, is a cause of trouble to me; your wife is at enmity with me, your son at enmity,
2.5.330:
my fellow-servants at enmity.
STALINO
What matters that to you? So long as (pointing to himself) this Jupiter only is propitious to you, do you take care and esteem the lesser Gods at a straw’s value.
OLYMPIO
2.5.333: That’s great nonsense; as if you didn’t know how suddenly your human Jupiters take to dying.
2.5.335:
So after all, if you, my Jupiter, are dead and gone, when your realm devolves upon the lesser Gods, who shall then come to the rescue of my back, or head, or legs?
STALINO
2.5.338:
Affairs will go with you better than you expect, if I obtain this—the enjoyment of my Casina.
OLYMPIO
2.5.340:
I’ faith, I do not think it possibly can be; so earnestly is your wife striving that she shall not be given to me.
STALINO
2.5.341:
But this way I’ll proceed: I’ll put the lots in an urn, and draw the lots for yourself and Chalinus. I find that the business has come to this pass; it’s necessary to fight with swords hand to hand.
OLYMPIO
2.5.345:
What, if the lot should turn out different from what you wish?
STALINO
2.5.346:
Speak with good omen. I rely upon the Gods; we’ll trust in the Gods.
OLYMPIO
2.5.347:
That expression I wouldn’t purchase at a rotten thread, for all people are relying upon the Gods; but still I’ve frequently seen many of those deceived who relied upon the Gods.
STALINO
2.5.350:
But hold your tongue a little while. (Pointing.)
OLYMPIO
What is it you mean?
STALINO
Why look; here’s Chalinus coming from the house, out here, with the urn and the lots. Now, with standards closing, we shall fight.

2.6.353:
(Enter CLEOSTRATA and CHALINUS, with the urn and lots.) CLEOSTRATA
Let me know, Chalinus, what my husband wants with me.
CHALINUS
2.6.354:
By my troth, he wants to see you burning outside of the Metian gate.
CLEOSTRATA
2.6.355:
I’ faith, I believe he does want that.
CHALINUS
But, by my troth, I don’t believe it, but I know it for certain.
STALINO
(aside to OLYMPIO.)
2.6.356:
I’ve got more men of business than I imagined: I’ve got this fellow, a Diviner, in my house. What, if we move our standards nearer, and go to meet them? Follow me. (Goes up to CLEOSTRATA and CHALINUS.) What are you about?
CHALINUS
2.6.358:
All the things are here which you ordered; your wife, the lots, the urn, and myself.
STALINO
2.6.359:
By yourself only, there is more here than I want.
CHALINUS
2.6.360:
I’ faith, so it seems to you indeed. I’m a stinger to you now; I’m pricking that dear little heart of yours; even now it’s palpitating from alarm.
STALINO
2.6.362:
Hold your tongue, Chalinus,
OLYMPIO
Do make that fellow be quiet.
CHALINUS
