No, that fellow rather (pointing to OLYMPIO), who has learned to misbehave.
STALINO
(to CHALINUS.)
2.6.363: Set the urn down here. (CHALINUS puts it down.) Give me the lots: lend your attention now. But I did think, my wife, that I could have prevailed upon you thus far,
2.6.365:
for Casina to be given me as my wife, and even now I think so.
OLYMPIO.
2.6.366:
She, given to you?
STALINO
Why yes, to me—dear me, I didn’t mean to say that. While I meant for myself, I said him; (aside) why really, while I’m wanting her for myself, I’ve already, i’ faith, been chattering at random.
CLEOSTRATA
(overhearing him.)
2.6.368:
Upon my word, you really have; and you are still doing so.
STALINO
2.6.369:
For him—no, no; for myself, i’ faith. Plague take it, at last, with great difficulty, I’ve got into the right road!
CLEOSTRATA
2.6.370:
Very often, i’ faith, you are making your mistakes.
STALINO
Such is the case when you desire anything very much. But each of us, both he (pointing to OLYMPIO) and I, apply to you for our rights—
CLEOSTRATA
2.6.372:
Why, I’ll tell you, my sweet. As to this Casina, you must make a present of her to this bailiff of ours.
CLEOSTRATA
2.6.373:
But, i’ faith, I neither do make it, nor do I in tend it.
STALINO
2.6.374:
In that case, then, I’ll divide the lots between them.
CLEOSTRATA
Who forbids you?
STALINO
2.6.375:
I judge with reason that that is the best and fairest way. In fine, if that happens which we desire, we shall be glad; but if otherwise, we’ll bear it with equanimity. (Giving a lot to OLYMPIO.) Take, this lot—take it; see what’s written on it.
OLYMPIO
(looking at it.)
2.6.378:
Number one.
CHALINUS
It isn’t fair, be cause that fellow has got one before me.
STALINO
(giving one to CHALINUS.)
2.6.379:
Take this, will you.
CHALINUS
(taking it.)
Give it me. Stop though; one thing has just now come into my mind.
(To CLEOSTRATA.)
2.6.380:
Do you see that there’s no other lot in there by chance at the bottom of the water.
STALINO
Whip-rascal! do you take me to be your own self?
(To CLEOSTRATA.)
2.6.381:
There is none; only set your feelings at rest.
OLYMPIO
(to CHALINUS.)
2.6.382:
May it prove lucky and fortunate to me, a great mischance to you!
CHALINUS
I’ faith, it will certainly fall to you, I fancy; I know your pious ways. But stop a bit; is that lot of yours of poplar or of fir?
OLYMPIO
2.6.385:
Why do you trouble yourself about that?
CHALINUS
Why, because I’m afraid that it may float on the surface of the water. (They go up to the urn.)
STALINO
2.6.386:
Capital!—take care! Now then, both of you, throw your lots in here. (Pointing to the urn.) Look now, wife, all’s fair. (They throw them in.)
OLYMPIO
2.6.387:
Don’t you trust your wife.
STALINO
Be of good courage.
OLYMPIO
2.6.388:
Upon my faith, I do believe that she’ll lay a spell upon the lots this very day, if she touches them.
STALINO
Hold your tongue.
OLYMPIO
2.6.389:
I’ll hold my tongue. I pray the Gods—
CHALINUS
Aye,that this day you may have to endure the chain and the bilboes.
OLYMPIO
2.6.390:
That the lot may fall to me.
CHALINUS
Aye, faith, that you may hang up by the feet.
OLYMPIO
2.6.391:
Aye, that you may blow your eyes out of your head through your nose.
CHALINUS
(to STALINO.)
2.6.392:
What are you afraid of? It must be ready by this— (Turning to OLYMPIO.) A halter for you, I mean.
OLYMPIO
(to CHALINUS.)
2.6.393:
You’re undone!
STALINO
Give attention, both of you.
OLYMPIO
I’ll be mum.
STALINO
Now you, Cleostrata, that you may not say that anything has been done cheatingly by me in this matter, or suspect it,
2.6.395:
I give you leave, do you yourself draw the lots.
OLYMPIO
(to STALINO.)
You are ruining me.
CHALINUS
He’s gaining an advantage rather.
CLEOSTRATA
(to STALINO.)
2.6.396:
You do what’s fair.
CHALINUS
(to OLYMPIO.)
I pray the Gods that your lot say run away out of the urn.
OLYMPIO
2.6.397:
Say you so? Because you are a runaway yourself, do you wish all to follow your example? I wish, indeed, that that lot of yours, as they say that of the descendants of Hercules once did, may melt away while the lots are drawing.
CHALINUS
2.6.400:
And you, that you may melt away yourself, and just now be made hot with twigs.
STALINO
2.6.401:
Attend, will you, to the business in hand, Olympio!
OLYMPIO
Yes, if this thrice-dotted fellow ’ll let me.
STALINO
2.6.402:
May this prove lucky and fortunate to me.
OLYMPIO
Yes indeed; to me as well.
CHALINUS
2.6.403:
Not so.
OLYMPIO
By my troth, yes, I say.
CHALINUS
By my troth, yes, for myself, I say.
STALINO
(to OLYMPIO.)
He’ll be the winner; you’ll live in wretchedness.
2.6.404:
Do you give him a punch in the face this instant! Well, what are you about?
CLEOSTRATA
(to OLYMPIO.)
Don’t you raise your hand.
OLYMPIO
(to STALINO.)
2.6.405:
With clenched or open hand am I to strike him?
STALINO
Do just as you please.
OLYMPIO
(striking CHALINUS.)
There’s for you, take that!
CLEOSTRATA
(to OLYMPIO.)
2.6.406:
What business have you to touch him?
OLYMPIO
Because my Jupiter (pointing to STALINO) commanded me.
CLEOSTRATA
(to CHALINUS.)
2.6.407:
Do you slap him in the face in return.
(CHALINUS strikes OLYMPIO in the face.)
OLYMPIO
(calling out to STALINO.)
I’m being murdered, I’m being punched with his fists, Jupiter!
STALINO
(to CHALINUS.)
2.6.408:
What business had you to touch him?
CHALINUS
Because this Juno of mine (pointing to CLEOSTRATA) ordered me.
STALINO
2.6.409:
I must put up with it, since, as long as I live, my wife will have the mastery.
CLEOSTRATA
(to STALINO.)
2.6.410:
He (pointing to CHALINUS) ought to be allowed to speak as much as that fellow.
OLYMPIO
Why by his talk does he occasion me an unlucky omens
STALINO
2.6.411:
I think, Chalinus, you should be on your guard against a mishap.
CHALINUS
2.6.412:
Full time, after my face has been battered!
STALINO
Come, wife, now then draw the lots. (To the SERVANTS.) Do you give your attention. (To CLEOSTRATA.) And give it, you, as well.
OLYMPIO
2.6.414: Where I am I know not. I’m undone, I’ve got my heart full of maggots, I think; it’s jumping about already;
2.6.415:
with its throbbing it beats against my breast.
CLEOSTRATA
(putting her hand into the urn.)
I’ve got hold of a lot.
STALINO
Draw it out, then.
CHALINUS
(to OLYMPIO.)
2.6.416:
Are you not dead now?
OLYMPIO
Show it. (She shows it.) It’s mine.
CHALINUS
Really this is an unlucky mishap.
CLEOSTRATA
2.6.417:
You are beaten, Chalinus.
STALINO
Then I’m glad that we are to survive after all, Olympio.
OLYMPIO
2.6.418:
Through my own piety and that of my forefathers has it happened.
STALINO
2.6.419:
Wife, go in-doors and make ready for the wedding.
CLEOSTRATA
I’ll do as you bid me.
STALINO
2.6.420:
Do you know that it’s to a distance in the country, at the farm-house,that he is to take her?
CLEOSTRATA
I know.
STALINO
2.6.421:
Go in-doors,and although this is disagreable to you, still take care and attend to it.
CLEOSTRATA
Very well. (Goes into the house.)
STALINO
(to OLYMPIO.)
2.6.422:
Let us, as well, go in-doors; let’s entreat them to make all haste.
OLYMPIO
Am I delaying at all?
2.6.423: For in his presence (pointing to CHALINUS) I don’t want there to be any further conversation. (They go into the house.)

2.7.424:
(CHALINUS, alone.) CHALINUS
(to himself.)
If now I were to hang myself, I should be losing my pains,
2.7.425: and besides my pains, putting myself to the expense of purchasing a rope, and doing a pleasure to my evil-wishers. What need is there for me, who, indeed, am dead even as it is? At the lots I’m beaten; Casina’s to be married to the bailiff. And this now is not so much to be regretted, that the bailiff has got the better,
2.7.430:
as the fact that the old man so vehemently desired that she shouldn’t be given me, and should marry him. How frightened he was, how in his misery he did bustle about, how he did caper about after the bailiff had won. By-the-bye, I’ll step aside here; I hear the door opening.
(Sees STALINO and OLYMPIO, coming out.)
2.7.435:
My well-wishers and friendsare coming out. Here in ambush I’ll lay in wait against them.
(Goes on one side.)

2.8.437:
(Enter STALINO and OLYMPIO, from the house.) OLYMPIO
Only let him come into the country; I’ll send the fellow back into the city to you with his porter’s knot, as black as a collier.
STALINO
2.8.439:
So it ought to be.
OLYMPIO
I’ll have that done and well taken care of.
STALINO
2.8.440:
I intended, if he had been at home, to send Chalinus to cater with you; that, even in his sadness, I might, in addition,inflict this misfortune upon our foe.
CHALINUS
(apart, retreating to the wall of the house.)
2.8.443: I’ll betake me back again to the wall; I’ll imitate the crab. Their conversation must be secretly picked up by me;
2.8.445:
for the one of them is tormenting me, the other wasting me with anguish. Why, this whip-rascal is marching along in his white garb, a very receptacle for stripes. My own death I defer; I’m determined to send this fellow to Acheron before me.
OLYMPIO
2.8.449: How obsequious have I been found to you! A thing that you especially
2.8.450:
desired, that same have I put in your power; this day the object that you love shall be with you, unknown to your wife.
STALINO
2.8.451:
Hush! So may the Deities kindly bless me, I can hardly withhold my lips from kissing you on account of this, my own delight!
CHALINUS
(apart.)
2.8.454:
What? Kiss him? What’s the meaning of this? What’s this delight of yours?
OLYMPIO
2.8.456:
Do you love me at all now?
STALINO
Aye, by my faith, myself even less than you. May I embrace you?
OLYMPIO
2.8.458:
How, when I touch you, I do seem to myself to be tasting honey!
CHALINUS
(apart.)
2.8.455:
I really do think he intends to choke the bailiff.
OLYMPIO
(pushing STALINO away.)
2.8.459:
Away with you, you lover; get off, with your too close acquaintanceship!
CHALINUS
(apart.)
2.8.465: I’ faith, I think that this very day they’ll be making terms. Surely,this old fellow is an universal admirer.
2.8.460:
This is the reason, this is it why he made him his bailiff; some time ago, too, when I came in his way, he wanted to make me his chamberlain upon the like terms.
OLYMPIO
2.8.463:
How subservient have I proved to you to-day, how attentive to your pleasure!
STALINO
2.8.464: How surely, so long as I live, will I prove more of a well-wisher to you than to my own self!
2.8.467:
How will I this day give full many a kiss to Casina! How will I, unknown to my wife, right pleasantly enjoy myself!
CHALINUS
(apart.)
2.8.468: Oho! Now, faith,at last I’ve got into the right track.
2.8.470:
It’s himself that’s dying for Casina. I’ve caught the fellows.
STALINO
2.8.471:
Even now, by my troth, am I longing to embrace her; even now to be kissing her.
OLYMPIO
2.8.472:
Do let her be brought out first from the house. Why the plague are you in such a hurry?
STALINO
I’m in love.
OLYMPIO
2.8.473:
But I don’t think that this can possibly be managed to-day.
STALINO
It can, if, indeed, you think that you can possibly receive your freedom to-morrow.
CHALINUS
(apart.)
2.8.475:
Why, really, I must make still better use here of my ears; now, in one thicket, I shall be cleverly catching two boars.
STALINO
(pointing to the house of ALCESIMUS.)
2.8.477:
At the house of this friend and neighbour of mine there’s a place provided; I have confided to him all my amorousness: he said that he would find me a room.
OLYMPIO
2.8.480:
What will his wife do? Where will she be?
STALINO
I’ve cleverly contrived that: my wife will invite her here, to her own house, to the wedding; to be here with her, to help her, to sleep with her. I have requested it, and my wife has said that she will do so. She’ll be sleeping here: I’ll take care her husband is away from home.
2.8.485:
You shall take your wife home into the country; that country shall be this house, for a period, until I’ve had my marriage with Casina. Hence,before daylight, you shall afterwards take her home to-morrow.Isn’t it very skilfully managed?
OLYMPIO
2.8.488:
Cleverly!
CHALINUS
(apart.)
Only do proceed; contrive away. By my troth, to your own mischance are you so clever.
STALINO
2.8.490:
Do you know what you must do now?
OLYMPIO
Tell me.
STALINO
(giving him a purse.)
Take this purse. Be off and buy some provisions: make haste. But I want it nicely done: delicate eatables, just as she herself is a delicate bit.
OLYMPIO
2.8.493:
Buy some cuttle-fish, mussels, calamaries, barley-fish.
CHALINUS
(apart.)
2.8.494:
Aye, wheaten fish, if you know what you’re about.
STALINO
2.8.495:
Some sole-fish.
CHALINUS
(apart.)
Prithee, why those rather than soles of wood, with which your head may be banged, you most vile old fellow?
OLYMPIO
2.8.497:
Should you like some tongue-fish?
STALINO
What need is there, since my wife’s at home? She is our tongue-fish, for she’s never silent.
OLYMPIO
2.8.499:
While I’m about it, I must make choice out of the supply of fish what to purchase.
STALINO
2.8.500:
You say what’s good: be off. I don’t care to spare for cost; provide abundantly. But it’s requisite also that I should see this neighbour of mine, that he may attend to what I’ve requested.
OLYMPIO
2.8.503:
Am I to go now?
STALINO
I wish you.
(Exit OLYMPIO. STALINO goes into the house of ALCESIMUS.)
CHALINUS
(coming forward.)
2.8.504: By three freedoms I could not be induced
2.8.505: this day to do other than provide a heavy retribution for them, and at once disclose all this matter to my mistress. I’ve caught and fully detected my enemies in their guilt. But if my mistress is ready now to do her duty, the cause is all our own: I’ll cleverly be beforehand with the fellows.
2.8.510:
With omens in our favour the day proceeds: just conquered, we are the conquerors. I’ll go indoors, that that which another cook has seasoned, I now, in my turn, may season after another fashion; and that for him for whom it was prepared, it may really not be prepared; and that that may be prepared for him, which before was not prepared.
(Goes into the house.)

3.1.515:
(Enter ALCESIMUS and STALINO, from the house of the former.) STALINO
Now, Alcesimus, I shall know whether you are the very picture of friend or foe to me; now is the proof upon view; now is the contest going on. But why do I do so; forbear to correct me; save yourself all that. With your hoary head, at an age unfit; save yourself that as well. One who has a wife; save yourself that like wise.
ALCESIMUS
3.1.520:
I never saw a person more distracted with love than yourself.
STALINO
3.1.521:
Do take care that the house is clear.
ALCESIMUS
Why, faith, men-servants, maid-servants, all of them I’m determined to send out of the house to yours.
STALINO
3.1.522:
Heyday! with your adroitness you are very adroit! But only take care and remember the lines which Colax repeats; take care that every one comes with his own provisions, as if they were going to Sutrium.
ALCESIMUS
3.1.525:
I’ll remember it.
STALINO
Why now there’s no public ordinance better ordered than yourself, in fact. Attend to this. I’m now going to the Forum; I shall be here just now.
ALCESIMUS
3.1.527:
Take care that your house gets a tongue.
ALCESIMUS
Why so?
STALINO
That when I come, it may invite me.
ALCESIMUS
3.1.528:
Pooh, pooh! you area person that stands in good need of a basting; you’re making too free with your fun.
STALINO
3.1.529: Of what use is it for me to be in love, unless I’m quite ready and talkative?
3.1.530:
But take you care that you haven’t to be sought for by me.
ALCESIMUS
I’ll be at home all the while.
(Exit STALINO; ALCESIMUS goes into his house.)

3.2.531:
(Enter CLEOSTRATA, from her house.) CLEOSTRATA
(to herself.)
This was the reason, then, i’ faith, why my husband entreated me, with such great earnestness, to make haste and invite my female neighbour to our house— that the house might be clear for him to be taking Casina there. Now, therefore, I shall by no means invite her,
3.2.535:
so that liberty of free range shan’t be any way given to worn-out bell-wethers. (ALCESIMUS is coming out of his house.) But look, the pillar of the Senate’s coming forward, the safeguard of the public, my neighbour, the person who is finding free range for my husband. I’ faith, the measure of wit that has been sold to him, was purchased at no cheap rate.
ALCESIMUS
(to himself.)
3.2.539: I’m wondering that my wife, who’s already waiting at home, dressed out, to be sent for, hasn’t been invited by this to my neighbour’s here.
3.2.541:
But see, here she is; she’s come to fetch her, I guess. (Going up to CLEOSTRATA.) Good day, Cleostrata!
CLEOSTRATA
And you the same, Alcesimus. Where’s your wife?
ALCESIMUS
3.2.542:
She’s waiting in-doors for you to send for her; for your husband requested me to send her to help you. Do you wish me to call her?
(Going towards the door.)
CLEOSTRATA
3.2.544:
Let it alone; I don’t care; if she’s busy.
ALCESIMUS
She’s at leisure.
CLEOSTRATA
3.2.545:
I don’t care about it; I don’t want to be troublesome to her; I’ll see her at a future time.
ALCESIMUS
3.2.546:
Are you not getting ready for a wedding there at your house?
CLEOSTRATA
I am getting ready and making preparations.
ALCESIMUS
3.2.547:
Don’t you require an assistant then?
CLEOSTRATA
We have enough at home. When the marriage has taken place, then I’ll call upon her; for the present, farewell, and bid her the same from me. (Goes into her house.)
ALCESIMUS
(to himself.)
3.2.549: What am I to do now? To my sorrow. I’ve done a most disgraceful action
3.2.550: for the sake of that vile and toothless goat, who has engaged me in this. I’ve promised the aid of my wife out of doors, as though to go lick dishes like a dog. A worthless fellow, to tell me that his wife was going to send for her, whereas she herself declares that she does not want her. And upon my faith, it’s a wonder if this female neighbour of mine hasn’t already her suspicions of this.
3.2.555:
But yet, on the other hand, when I reflect with myself on this notion, if there were anything of that, there would have been enquiries of me. I’ll go in-doors, that I may lay up the ship again in the dockyard.
(Goes into his house.) (Enter CLEOSTRATA, from her house.)
CLEOSTRATA
(to herself.)
3.2.558: Now he has been finely made a fool of. In what a bustle are these unfortunate old fellows. Now I do wish that that good-for-nothing decrepit husband of mine would come,
3.2.560: that I might make a fool of him in his turn, after I have thus fooled the other one. For I long to make a bit of a quarrel between these two. But look, he’s coming. Why, when you see him so serious, you’d think him a decent person. (She stands on one side, unseen.)

3.3.563:
(Enter STALINO.) STALINO
(aloud, to himself.)
It’s a great folly, to my notion at least, for any man that’s in love to go to the Forum
3.3.565: on that day on which the object which he loves is close at hand; as I in my folly have been doing; I’ve spent the day, standing pleading for a certain relative of mine, who, faith, I’m very delighted has lost his cause; so that he hasn’t for nothing chosen me as his advocate to-day.
3.3.570: He ought first to ask and make enquiry, whether his mind is at home or not at home, whom he’s choosing for his advocate; if he says it isn’t, without his mind he should send him off home. (Catches sight of his wife.) But look, there’s my wife before the house! Alas! wretch that I am!
3.3.575:
I’m afraid that she isn’t deaf, and has heard this.
CLEOSTRATA
(apart.)
3.3.576:
By my troth, I have heard it to your great cost.
STALINO
3.3.577:
I’ll go nearer to her. (Goes up to CLEOSTRATA.) What are you about, my delight?
CLEOSTRATA
3.3.578:
I’ faith, I was waiting for you.
STALINO
Are the things ready now? Have you by this brought over here to our house this female neighbour of yours,
3.3.580:
who was to assist you?
CLEOSTRATA
I sent for her as you requested me; but this companion of yours, your very good friend, was in a pet with his wife about something, I don’t know what; he said, when I went to fetch her, that he wouldn’t send her.
STALINO
3.3.584:
That’s your greatest fault; you are not courteous enough.
CLEOSTRATA
3.3.585:
It’s not the part of matrons, but of harlots, to be showing courtesies, my husband, to the husbands of others. Go yourself and fetch her; I wish to attend in-doors, my husband, to what is requisite to be done.
STALINO
3.3.588:
Make haste then.
CLEOSTRATA
Very well. (Aside.) Now, faith, I shall inspire some apprehensions in his heart.
3.3.590:
I’ll this day render this lovesick man completely miserable.
(She goes into the house.)

3.4.591:
(Enter ALCESIMUS, from his house.) ALCESIMUS
(to himself.)
I’ll go see here if the lover has come back home from the Forum, who, an old ghost, has been making fools of myself and my wife. But see, there he is before his house. (Addressing STALINO.) I’ faith, ’twas just in good time I was coming to your house.
STALINO
3.4.594:
And, i’ faith, I to yours. How say you, you good-for-nothing fellow? What did I enjoin you? What did I beg of you?
ALCESIMUS
3.4.596:
How nicely you’ve had your house empty for me! How well you have sent your wife over to our house here! Isn’t it through yourself that I and the opportunity are lost, both of us?
ALCESIMUS
3.4.599: Why don’t you go hang yourself? Why, ’twas you yourself said that
3.4.600:
your wife would come and fetch mine from our house?
STALINO
3.4.601:
Then she declares that she has been to fetch her, and that you said you wouldn’t let her go.
ALCESIMUS
3.4.602:
But she herself, of her own accord, said to me that she didn’t care for her assistance.
STALINO
3.4.604:
But ’tis she herself who has deputed me to come and fetch her.
ALCESIMUS
3.4.605:
But I don’t care for that.
STALINO
But you are proving my ruin.
ALCESIMUS
But that’s as it should be. But I shall still go on delaying; but I very much long for—
STALINO
3.4.607:
But—
ALCESIMUS
nothing but to do you some mischief;
but I’ll do it with pleasure. Never this day shall you have a but the more than I.
3.4.609:
But, in fine, really, upon my faith, may the Gods confound you.
STALINO
3.4.610:
What now? Are you going to send your wife to my house?
ALCESIMUS
3.4.611:
You may take her, and be off to utter and extreme perdition, both with her and with that one of yours, and with that mistress of yours as well. A way with you, and attend to something else; I’ll at once bid my wife to pass thither through the garden to your wife.
STALINO
3.4.615: Now you are proving yourself a friend to me in genuine style! (ALCESIMUS goes into his house.) Under what auspices am I to say that this passion was inflicted upon me, or what have I ever done amiss towards Venus, that when I’m thus in love crosses so many should befall me in my path? (A noise is heard.) Hey day!
3.4.620: what’s that noise, prithee, that’s going on in our house?

3.5.621:
(Enter PARDALISCA, running out of the house.) PARDALISCA
(bawling out at the door.)
I’m undone, I’m undone, I’m utterly, utterly ruined! My heart is deadened with fear. My limbs, in my misery, are all a-trembling! I know not whence to obtain or look for any assistance, safety, or refuge for myself, or any means of relief:
3.5.625:
things so surprising, in a manner so surprisingly done, have I just now witnessed in-doors, a new and unusual piece of audacity. Be on your guard, Cleostrata! prithee do get away from her,lest amid such transports she may be doing you some mischief! Tear away that sword from her, who’s not in possession of her senses!
STALINO
3.5.630:
Why, what is the matter—that she, frightened and half dead with fear, rushes hither out of doors? Pardalisca!
PARDALISCA
(looking wildly about her.)
3.5.631:
Whence do my ears catch the sound?
STALINO
3.5.632:
Just look back at me.
PARDALISCA
My master!
STALINO
What’s the matter? What?
PARDALISCA
I’m undone.
STALINO
3.5.633:
How undone?
PARDALISCA
I’m undone, and you are undone.
STALINO
Disclose it, what’s the matter with you?
PARDALISCA
3.5.634:
Woe to you!
STALINO
Aye, and the same to yourself.
PARDALISCA
That I mayn’t fall down, prithee do hold, hold me.
(Staggers, on which STALINO supports her.)
STALINO
3.5.635:
Whatever it is, tell me quickly.
PARDALISCA
Do support my throbbing breast, prithee do make a little air with your cloak.
STALINO
(fanning her with the lappet of his cloak.)
3.5.636:
I’m in alarm as to what is the matter; (aside) unless this woman has been somewhere upsetting herself with the pure cream of Bacchus.
PARDALISCA
3.5.641:
Hold my ears, pray do.
(Her head falls on her shoulder.)
STALINO
Away to utter perdition; breast, ears, head, and yourself, may the Gods confound! For, unless I quickly learn from you this matter, whatever it is, I’ll forth with be knocking your brains out, you viper,
3.5.645:
you hussey, who have thus far been making a laughing-stock of me.
PARDALISCA
3.5.646:
My master!
STALINO
What do you want, my servant?
PARDALISCA
You are too angry.
STALINO
You are saying so too soon. But whatever this is, tell it; relate in a few words what has been the disturbance in-doors.
PARDALISCA
3.5.649:
Hear this most foul crime which just now in-doors at our house your female slave began to attempt after this fashion, a thing that does not befit the regulations lations of Attica.
STALINO
3.5.653:
What is it?
PARDALISCA
Fever prevents the use of my tongue.
STALINO
3.5.654:
What is it? Can I possibly learn from you what is the matter?
PARDALISCA
I’ll tell you. Your female slave, she whom you intend to give as a wife to your bailiff, in-doors she—
STALINO
3.5.656:
In-doors what? What is it?
PARDALISCA
3.5.657:
Is imitating the wicked practices of wicked women, in threatening her husband—
STALINO
3.5.659:
What then?
PARDALISCA
Ah!
STALINO
What is it?
PARDALISCA
She says that she intends to take her husband’s life.
3.5.660:
A sword—
STALINO
(starting.)
Hah!
PARDALISCA
A sword—
STALINO
What about that sword?
PARDALISCA
3.5.661:
She has got one.
STALINO
Ah! wretch that I am! Why has she got it?
PARDALISCA
3.5.662: She is pursuing them all at home all over the house, and she won’t allow any person to approach her; and so, all, hiding in chests and under beds,
3.5.665:
are mute with fear.
STALINO
I’m murdered and ruined outright! What malady is this that has so suddenly befallen her?
PARDALISCA
3.5.667:
She is mad.
STALINO
I do think that I am the most unfortunate of men!
PARDALISCA
3.5.668:
Aye, and if you were to know the speeches she uttered to-day.
STALINO
3.5.669:
I long to know about what she said.
PARDALISCA
Listen.
3.5.670:
By all the Gods and Goddesses she swore that she would murder the person with whom she should bed.
STALINO
3.5.672:
Will she murder me?
PARDALISCA
Does that bear reference to yourself in any way?
STALINO
Pshaw!
PARDALISCA
3.5.673:
What business have you with her?
STALINO
I made a mistake; him, the bailiff, I meant to say.
PARDALISCA
3.5.675:
It’s on purpose that you are turning aside from the high road into bye-paths.
STALINO
3.5.676:
Does she threaten anything against myself?
PARDALISCA
She is hostile to you individually more than any person.
STALINO
3.5.677:
For what reason?
PARDALISCA
Because you have given her as a wife to Olympio; she says that she’ll neither suffer your life, nor her own, nor that of her husband,
3.5.679:
to be prolonged until the morrow. I have been sent hither to tell you this, that you might beware of her.
STALINO
(aside.)
3.5.681: By my troth, to my misery I’m quite undone!
3.5.682:
There neither is nor ever was any old man in love so wretched as I.
PARDALISCA
(aside, to the AUDIENCE.)
3.5.683:
Don’t I play him off cleverly? For everything that I’ve been telling him as taking place, I’ve been telling him falsely. My mistress and she who lives next door have concocted this scheme. I’ve been sent to fool him.
STALINO
3.5.689:
What is it?
STALINO
There is —
PARDALISCA
What?
STALINO
There is something that I want to enquire of you about.
PARDALISCA
3.5.690:
You are causing me delay.
STALINO
Why, you are causing me sorrow. But has Casina got that sword even still?
PARDALISCA
3.5.692:
She has; but two of them.
STALINO
Why two?
PARDALISCA
She says that this very day she’ll murder you with the one, the bailiff with the other.
STALINO
3.5.694: I am now the most utterly murdered of all people that do exist.
3.5.695:
I’ll put on me a coat of mail; I think that’s the best. What did my wife do? Didn’t she go and take them away from her?
PARDALISCA
3.5.697:
No person dares go near her.
STALINO
She should have prevailed on her.
PARDALISCA
She is entreating her. She declares that assuredly she will lay them down on no other terms, unless she understands that she shall not be given to the bailiff.
STALINO
3.5.700:
But whether she likes it or no, because she refuses, she shall marry him this day. For why shouldn’t I carry this out that I’ve begun, for her to marry me?—that, indeed, I didn’t intend to say—but, our bailiff?
PARDALISCA
3.5.703:
You’re making your mistakes pretty often.
STALINO
3.5.704: It’s alarm that impedes my words. But, prithee,
3.5.705:
do tell my wife, that I entreat her to prevail upon her to put down the sword, and allow me to return in-doors.
PARDALISCA
3.5.707:
And do you entreat her.
PARDALISCA
And I’ll entreat her.
STALINO
And in soft language, in your usual way. But do you hear me? If you manage this, I’ll give you a pair of shoes and a gold ring for your finger, and plenty of nice things.
PARDALISCA
3.5.710:
I’ll do my best.
STALINO
Take care and prevail.
PARDALISCA
3.5.711:
Now then I’ll be off; unless you detain me for anything.
STALINO
3.5.712:
Be off, and take care.
PARDALISCA
(aside.)
3.5.713: Look, his assistant is returning, at last, with the provisions; he’s bringing a train after him. (She goes into the house.)

3.6.720:
(Enter OLYMPIO, a COOK, and his ASSISTANTS, with provisions.) OLYMPIO
(to the COOK.)
See, you thief, that you lead on your briars beneath their banners.
A COOK
But how are they briars?
OLYMPIO
3.6.721:
Because that which they have touched, they instantly seize hold of; if you go to snatch it from them, they instantly rend it; so, wherever they come, wherever they are, with a twofold loss do they mulct their masters.
A COOK
3.6.723:
Heyday, indeed!
OLYMPIO
Well, well! This way I’m delaying to go meet my master with a magnificent, patrician, and patronizing air. (He struts along.)
STALINO
3.6.724:
My good man, save you.
OLYMPIO
I admit that so I am.
STALINO
How goes it?
OLYMPIO
You are in love, but I’m hungering and thirsting.
STALINO
3.6.726:
You have come capitally provided.
OLYMPIO
Pooh! pooh!
(Goes towards the door.)
STALINO
3.6.727:
But stop you, although you do hold me in contempt—
OLYMPIO
O dear, O dear! your converse has a bad smell to me. (Moving away.)
STALINO
3.6.728:
What’s the matter?
OLYMPIO
(pointing to the baskets of provisions.)
That’s the matter.
STALINO
Will you not stop there?
OLYMPIO
Why, really, you are causing me ennui.
STALINO
3.6.729:
I shall be giving you a grand coup, I fancy, if you don’t stand still forthwith. (Catches hold of him.)
OLYMPIO
3.6.730:
O mon Dieu! Can’t you get away from me, unless you would like me to be sick just now?
STALINO
3.6.732:
Do stop a bit.
OLYMPIO
How’s this? (Staring at him.) What person’s this?
STALINO
3.6.733:
I’m your master.
OLYMPIO
What master?
STALINO
He whose slave you are.
OLYMPIO
I, a slave?
STALINO
Aye, and mine.
OLYMPIO
3.6.736:
Am I not a free man? Remember! remember!
STALINO
3.6.737:
Stop and stay you there!
(Catches hold of him.)
OLYMPIO
Let me alone.
STALINO
3.6.738:
I am your slave.
OLYMPIO
That’s very good.
STALINO
My dear little Olympio, my father, my patron, I do beg of you—
OLYMPIO
3.6.739:
Well, you certainly are in your senses.
STALINO
3.6.740:
Of course I am your slave.
OLYMPIO
3.6.741:
What need have I of so worthless a slave?
STALINO
3.6.742:
Well now, how soon are you going to provide me some amusement?
OLYMPIO
3.6.743:
If the dinner were but drest.
STALINO
3.6.744:
Then let them be off this instant in-doors.
(To the COOK and his ASSISTANTS.)
Go you into the house and despatch with all haste.
3.6.746:
I’ll come in just now. Have the dinner charmingly sauced up for me; I want to have a charming meal. I really don’t care, now, to be eating in the style of your sumptuous foreigners. Be off, will you; but for the present, however, I take up my abode here.
(The COOK and his ASSISTANTS go into the house.)
OLYMPIO
3.6.748:
Is there anything that detains you here?
STALINO
3.6.749:
The servant-maid says that Casina has got a sword in-doors, to deprive you and me of life with it.
OLYMPIO
3.6.750:
I understand it. Just let her alone with it. They are imposing on you: I know these worthless baggages. However, do you now go into the house with me.
STALINO
3.6.754: But, i’ faith, I’m fearful of mischief:
3.6.755:
only do you go. Reconnoitre, first, what’s going on within.
OLYMPIO
3.6.756:
My life’s as dear to me as yours is to you.
STALINO
3.6.758:
But only do go now.
OLYMPIO
If you’ll go yourself, I’ll go in with you.
(They go into the house.)

4.1.759:
(Enter PARDALISCA, from the house, laughing aloud.) PARDALISCA
(to herself.)
Upon my faith, I do not believe that at Nemea, nor do I think that at Olympia,
4.1.760: or anywhere else, there ever where such funny games as these ridiculous games that are going on in-doors here with our old gentleman and our bailiff Olympio. In-doors, all over the house, all are in a bustle; the old man is bawling away in the kitchen, and urging on the cooks.
4.1.765: Why don’t you go to work at once? Why don’t you serve up, if you are going to serve up? Make haste; the dinner ought to have been cooked by this. And then this bailiff is strutting about with his chaplet, clothed in white and finely rigged out. And then these women are dressing up the armour-bearer in the bedroom,
4.1.770: to give him to be married to our bailiff in place of Casina; but the artful baggages very cleverly conceal what the upshot of this is really to be. Then too, in a manner quite worthy of them, the cooks are very cleverly doing their best to the end that the old gentleman mayn’t get his dinner. They are upsetting the pots, and putting out the fire with the water.
4.1.775: At the request of these ladies they are so doing; they, too, are determined to bundle the old fellow dinnerless out of doors, that they by themselves may blow out their own stomachs. I know these female gluttons; a merchant-ship full of victuals they can devour. But the door is opening.

4.2.780:
(Enter STALINO, from the house.) STALINO
(speaking to CLEOSTRATA, within.)
If you are wise, wife, you’ll dine, after all, when the dinner’s cooked. I shall dine in the country, for I’m desirous to attend the new-made husband and the newly-made bride into the country (I know the mischievous habits of persons), that no one may carry her off. Do you people indulge your appetite.
4.2.785:
But do make haste and send him and her out immediately, that at least we may get there in daylight. I shall be here tomorrow; to-morrow, wife, I’ll be having a banquet still.
PARDALISCA
(aside.)
4.2.788:
’Tis as I said it would be; the women are packing the old fellow dinnerless out of doors.
STALINO
(to PARDALISCA.)
4.2.789:
What are you doing here?
PARDALISCA
4.2.790:
I’m going whither she sent me.
STALINO
Really?
PARDALISCA
Seriously.
STALINO
4.2.791:
What are you looking for here?
PARDALISCA
Really I’m looking for nothing at all.
STALINO
Be off; you are loitering here; the others are bustling about in-doors.
PARDALISCA
4.2.793: Be off, then, will you, away from here, you jade of jades. (PARDALISCA goes into the house.) Is she gone then? I may now say here anything I please.
4.2.795: He that’s in love, i’ faith, even if he is hungry, isn’t hungry at all. But see, the bailiff, my associate, companion, and husband-in-copartnership, is coming out of doors with wreath and torch.

4.3.798:
(Enter OLYMPIO, dressed in white, with a wreath on his head, and a torch in his hand, accompanied by MUSICIANS) OLYMPIO
(to one of the MUSICIANS.)
Come, piper, while they are escorting the new-made bride out of doors, make the whole of this street resound with a sweet wedding-tune.
(He sings aloud.)
4.3.800:
Io Hymen hymenaee! Io Hymen!
STALINO
(accosting him.)
4.3.801:
How fare you, my preserver?
OLYMPIO
I’m very hungry, faith; and, in fact, I’m not thirsty a little.
STALINO
4.3.802:
But I’m in love.
OLYMPIO
Still, upon my faith, love, I shan’t be making any trial of you. For some time past my inside has been grumbling with emptiness.
STALINO
4.3.804: But why is she now delaying so long in-doors, just as though on purpose?
4.3.805:
The greater the haste I’m in, in so much the less is she.
OLYMPIO
4.3.806:
What if I were even to trill an hymeneal lay?
STALINO
4.3.807:
I agree to that; and I’ll help you at these our common nuptials.
OLYMPIO
(STALINO joining, they sing.)
4.3.809:
Upon my faith, I’m dreadfully done up; one may burst one’s self with singing this hymeneal lay; if I do burst this way, I can’t burst any other, that I may make sure of.
OLYMPIO
4.3.811:
Upon my faith, for sure, if you were a horse, you’d never be broken in.
STALINO
4.3.812:
On what grounds?
OLYMPIO
You are too hard-mouthed.
STALINO
Have you ever found me so?
OLYMPIO
4.3.813:
The Gods forbid! But the door makes a noise; they are coming out.
STALINO
4.3.814: I’ troth, the Gods do will me to be preserved at last. I already smell Casina at a distance. (They move to a distance.)

4.4.815:
(Enter, from the house, two FEMALE SERVANTS leading CHALINUS, veiled and dressed in women’s clothes, as CASINA.) TWO MAID-SERVANTS
Move on, and raise your feet a little over the threshold, newly-married bride; prosperously commence this journey, that you may always be alive for your husband, that you may be his superior in power, and the conqueror, and that your rule may gain the upper hand. Let your husband find you in clothes; you plunder your husband;
4.4.820:
by night and day to be tricking your husband, prithee, do remember.
OLYMPIO
(to STALINO.)
4.4.822:
Upon my faith, at her downright peril, the instant she offends me ever so little!
STALINO
4.4.826:
Hold your tongue.
OLYMPIO
I shall not hold my tongue.
STALINO
What’s the matter
OLYMPIO
These wicked jades are wickedly teaching her wicked lessons.
STALINO
4.4.827:
Instead of being all ready, they’ll be bringing this matter all into confusion for me. They are striving at that, wishing for it, that they may have it all undone.
TWO MAID-SERVANTS
4.4.829:
Come, Olympio, as soon as you please, receive this wife of yours from us.
(They present CHALINUS to him.)
OLYMPIO
4.4.831:
Hand her to me then, if you are going to hand her to me at all to-day.
(They hand CHALINUS to him.)
STALINO
(to the FEMALE SERVANTS.)
4.4.832:
Be off in-doors.
TWO MAID-SERVANTS
Prithee, do deal gently with her who is so young and inexperienced.
STALINO
4.4.834:
Farewell; be off now.
TWO MAID-SERVANTS
Farewell.
(They go into the house.)
STALINO
4.4.835:
Is my wife now gone?
OLYMPIO
She’s in the house; don’t be afraid.
STALINO
Hurra! Now, faith, I’m free at last. (Addressing himself to CHALINUS as CASINA.) My sweetheart, my spring-flower, my little honey!
(Embraces him.)
OLYMPIO
4.4.837:
But, hark you! you’ll beware, if you are wise, of some mishap: she’s mine.
STALINO
4.4.839:
I know that; but mine’s the first enjoyment.
OLYMPIO
(holding him the torch.)
4.4.840:
Hold this torch for me.
STALINO
Why, no, I’ll hold her in my arms in preference. All-powerful Venus, a happy existence hast thou given me in giving me the possession of her! A dear little body! a dear little honey! (Hugs CHALINUS, who pretends to struggle.)
OLYMPIO
(shouting aloud.)
4.4.842:
O my dear little wife! (Jumps about on one leg.)
STALINO
4.4.845:
What’s the matter?
OLYMPIO
She has trod upon my toes.
STALINO
(aside.)
4.4.846:
I’ll compliment her, as it were. A mist is not so soft as is— her breast.
(Pulls CHALINUS about.)
4.4.848:
A pretty little bosom, upon my faith. (CHALINUS gives him a thrust with his elbow, on which he roars out.) Woe to unfortunate me!
OLYMPIO
4.4.849:
What’s the matter?
STALINO
She struck me in the breast with her elbow.
OLYMPIO
4.4.850:
Why then, pray, do you maul her about? But she does not do so to me, who touch her gently.
(CHALINUS gives him a poke with his elbow.)
4.4.852:
O me!
STALINO
What’s the matter?
OLYMPIO
Prithee, how robust she is! she has almost laid me flat with her elbow.
STALINO
4.4.853:
She wishes, then, to go to bed.
OLYMPIO
4.4.854:
Nay but, why don’t we be off?
STALINO
(taking hold of CHALINUS.)
My pretty, pretty little dear!
(They go into the house of ALCESIMUS.)

5.1.855:
(Enter MYRRHINA and PARADALISCA, from the house of STALINO.) MYRRHINA
Having been well and handsomely entertained indoors, we’ve come out here in the street to see the wedding-sports.
5.1.859: I’d like to know how Chalinus gets on—the newly-married bride with her new-made husband.
5.1.857: Never, upon my faith, any day did I laugh so much, nor in the time that’s to come do I think I shall laugh more;
5.1.860: and no poet ever did con trive a more artful plot than this was skilfully contrived by us.
5.1.862: I’d now very much like the old fellow to come out, with his face well battered, than whom there is not a more wicked old man alive.
5.1.864:
Not even him do I deem to be more wicked who finds the room for him. Now, Pardalisca, do you be guard here (pointing to the door of her house); that whoever comes out from here, you may have some sport with him.
PARDALISCA
5.1.869:
I’ll do it with pleasure, and in my usual way.
MYRRHINA
5.1.870:
Observe from here everything that’s going on indoors.
PARDALISCA
5.1.871:
Prithee, get behind me.
MYRRHINA
You have liberty, too, to say freely and boldly to him anything you like.
PARDALISCA
(in a low voice.)
5.1.872: Be quiet; your door makes a noise. (They hide themselves.)

5.2.880: so ridiculous to be heard, to be repeated, are these mishaps which I have met with in the house. [When straightway I had led my new-made bride into the room, I fastened the bolt; but, however, the gloom there was just like the night. I placed, I propped things against the door; I struggled hard that before the old fellow with my bride.
5.2.885: Then I began to be slow in my proceedings, for I looked behind me every now and then, lest the old fellow should break in, a kiss, that provocative to lust, I asked of her first. She pushed back my hand, and allowed me not to give her a kiss in a quiet way.
5.2.889:
But then the more anxious was I, the more desirous to assert my privilege with Casina, and I longed to do the old fellow out of that task. The door I blocked up, so that the old man might not over-power me. (from the house.)
MYRRHINA
(apart to CLEOSTRATA.)
5.2.892:
Come now, you accost him. (Pointing to OLYMPIO.)
CLEOSTRATA
(accosting OLYMPIO.)
Where is your newly-made bride?
OLYMPIO
(aside.)
5.2.893:
By heavens, I’m utterly undone; the thing’s all out.
CLEOSTRATA
(overhearing him.)
It’s right, then, that you should relate the whole affair as it happened. What’s going on in-doors? How fares Casina? Is she quite obsequious to your will?
OLYMPIO
5.2.897:
I’m ashamed to tell it.
CLEOSTRATA
5.2.898:
Relate it in its order just as you proceeded.
OLYMPIO
5.2.899:
Upon my faith, I am ashamed.
CLEOSTRATA
Proceed boldly. After you went to bed, I want you to tell what took place after that.
OLYMPIO
5.2.902:
But it’s a disgraceful matter.
CLEOSTRATA
I’ll take care that those who hear it shall be on their guard as to mentioning it.
OLYMPIO
5.2.903:
That’s the principal thing.
CLEOSTRATA
You kill me with weariness. Why don’t you proceed?
OLYMPIO
—Ubi us subtus porro
5.2.906:
quid.
OLYMPIO
Babae!
CLEOSTRATA
Quid?
OLYMPIO
Papae!
5.2.907:
quid est?
OLYMPIO
Oh, erat maximum. Gladium ne haberet metui; id quaerere occœpi. Dum, gladiumne habeat, quaero, arripio capulum.
5.2.910:
Sed, quom cogito, non habuit gladium; nam id esset frigidius.
CLEOSTRATA
5.2.911:
Eloquere.
OLYMPIO
At pudet.
CLEOSTRATA
Num radix fuit?
OLYMPIO
Non fuit.
CLEOSTRATA
Num cucumis?
OLYMPIO
5.2.912:
Profecto hercle non fuit quidquam olerum; Nisi quidquid erat, calamitas profecto attigerat nunquam. Ita, quidquid erat, grande erat.
MYRRHINA
5.2.915:
Quid fit denique? Edisserta.
OLYMPIO
When I addressed Casina, Casina, said I, my dear wife, why do you slight your husband in this fashion? Really, upon my faith, you do this quite without my deserving it, inasmuch as I have given you the preference as my wife.
5.2.921:
—sepit veste id, quî estis. Ubi illum saltum video obseptum; Rogo, ut altero sinat ire. Ita, quidquid erat, grande erat. Tollo ut obvortam cubitissim Ullum mutire
She answered not a word.
5.2.925:
Surge, ut ineam in Atque illam in
MYRRHINA
5.2.928: When I attempted a kiss, a beard pricked my lips just like briars.
5.2.930:
Forthwith, as I was upon my knees, she struck my head with her feet. I tumbled headlong from the bed; she leapt down upon me and punched my face. From there in silence out of doors I came in this guise; by your leaves I say it; may the old fellow drink of the same cup that I have been drinking of.
CLEOSTRATA
5.2.933:
Most excellent. But where’s your cloak?
OLYMPIO
(pointing to the house of ALCESIMUS.)
5.2.934:
I left it here in-doors.
CLEOSTRATA
5.2.935:
Well now; hasn’t a very nice trick been played you?
OLYMPIO
Yes, and deservedly. Hush! the door makes a noise. What, is she following me, I wonder? (They go to a distance.)

5.3.937:
(Enter STALINO, in haste, from the house of ALCESIMUS.) STALINO
(aloud to himself.)
I’m branded with the greatest disgrace, nor what, under my circumstances to do, do I know. Nor yet how to look my wife in the face; so utterly undone am I! All my misdeeds are discovered.
5.3.940: In every way, to my confusion, I am ruined! So clearly am I hooked fast by the jaws! nor know I in what way to clear myself before my wife; wretch that I am, to have been stripped of my cloak! These clandestine nuptials are all discovered.
5.3.945: I judge it best for me She taught my wife the way But who is there, what person would be ready to undertake this office
5.3.950: for me? What now to do I know not, except to imitate worthless slaves, and fly from the house; for there’s no safety for my shoulder-blades if I return home. I may tell lies there; i’ faith, I shall get a basting, though much against my will, although I have earned my punishment.
5.3.955:
I’ll at once betake myself in this direction in flight.
(He begins to run.)
OLYMPIO
(coming forward with the others.)
Hallo there! Stop, this instant, you amorous one!
STALINO
(to himself.)
5.3.956:
I’m utterly undone! I’m being called back. I’ll be off, as though I didn’t hear.
(Runs on.]

5.4.963:
(Enter CHALINUS, from the house of ALCESIMUS, dressed in woman’s clothes.) CHALINUS
Where are you, you who imitate the morals of the Massilians? Now, if you wish to be taking liberties with me, is a good opportunity
5.4.965:
[ at your risk. By my troth, you are undone. Come, only step this way. Now I fancy that when a witness out of I’ll find thus out of the street I order a murmur I
STALINO
5.4.970:
Now am I in extreme danger, between the stone and the sacrifice, nor know I which way to fly The wolf-dogs it was
CHALINUS
5.4.972:
I’ faith, I do think old there now like new.]
STALINO
(turning about.)
5.4.973:
I’ll go this way. I trust that the omen of a bitch’s barking will prove the better.
CLEOSTRATA
5.4.974: What are you doing, my husband, my good man? Whence come you in this guise?
5.4.975:
What have you done with your walking-stick, or how disposed of the cloak you had?
TWO MAID-SERVANTS
5.4.976:
While he was playing his loving pranks with Casina, he lost it, I fancy.
STALINO
(aside.)
5.4.977:
Utterly undone!
CHALINUS
(coming up to STALINO.)
Shall we go to bed again? I am Casina.
STALINO
Away with you to utter perdition!
CHALINUS
5.4.978:
Don’t you love me?
CLEOSTRATA
Nay, but answer me; what has become of your cloak?
STALINO
(running about, exclaiming.)
5.4.979:
[Upon my faith, wife, the Bacchantes!
Bacchantes!
Bacchantes!
TWO MAID-SERVANTS
He’s making pretence on purpose
5.4.980:
for, upon my word, no Bacchantes are exhibiting at the present time.
STALINO
I forgot that. But still, the Bacchantes!—
CLEOSTRATA
5.4.981:
How, the Bacchantes?
Why, that cannot be.
TWO MAID-SERVANTS
5.4.982:
By my troth, you are in a fright.
STALINO
What I?
CLEOSTRATA
(to the SERVANT.)
I’ faith, do tell no lies, for it’s quite clear. ]
OLYMPIO
5.4.991:
[ who even made a notorius man of me with his flagrant acts.]
STALINO
5.4.992:
Won’t you hold your tongue?
OLYMPIO
I’ troth, I certainly shall not hold my tongue; for with the greatest earnestness you begged me to ask for Casina as my wife.
STALINO
5.4.994:
That I did
on account of my love for you.
CLEOSTRATA
I’ faith, of her rather. (Turning to CHALINUS.)
5.4.996:
He’d have been making an attack upon you, in fact.
STALINO
I been doing these things that you mention?
CLEOSTRATA
5.4.997:
And do you ask me that?
STALINO
If indeed I have done so, I’ve been doing wrong.
CLEOSTRATA
5.4.998:
Just come back in-doors here; I’ll remind you, if you have forgotten anything.
STALINO
5.4.999: Troth, I think, I’ll believe you in preference as to what you say.
5.4.1000:
But, wife, do grant pardon to your husband for this; Myrrhina, do entreat Cleostrata! If ever, from this time forward, I love Casina, or even think of it, should I love her, I say, should I ever hereafter, in fact, be guilty of such a thing, there’s no reason, wife, why you shouldn’t lash me with twigs as I hang up by the arms.
MYRRHINA
5.4.1004:
On my word, I do think that forgiveness may be granted for this.
CLEOSTRATA
(to MYRRHINA.)
I’ll do as you request me.
(To STALINO.)
5.4.1005:
On this account with the less difficulty do I now grant you this pardon, that, from being a long one, we mayn’t be making this Play still longer.
STALINO
5.4.1007:
You are not angry?
CLEOSTRATA
I am not angry.
STALINO
Am I to trust your word?
CLEOSTRATA
You may my word.
STALINO
5.4.1008:
No person ever did have a more amiable wife than I’ve got.
CHALINUS
5.4.1009:
Keep to her, then.
CLEOSTRATA
(to CHALINUS.)
Come you, give him back his walking-stick and cloak.
CHALINUS
(taking them from behind him, where he had held them.)
Take them, if you wish.
5.4.1010:
Upon my faith, a great injustice has really been most egregiously done me; I’ve been married to two husbands; neither has behaved to me as to a new-made bride.
The PLAYERS.
5.4.1012: Spectators, what’s to be done within, we’ll tell you here. This Casina will be discovered to be the daughter of this person next door, and she’ll be married to Euthynicus, our master’s son.
5.4.1015: Now it’s only fair that with your deserving hands you should give us deserved applause. He who does so, may he always keep his mistress without the knowledge of his wife. But he who doesn’t with his hands clap as loud as he can, in place of a mistress, may a he-goat, soused in bilge-water, be palmed off upon him.

1.1.1:
(Enter SILENIUM, GYMNASIUM, and PROCURESS, from the house of SILENIUM. SILENIUM
Inasmuch as hitherto I have loved you, and have deemed you to be my friend, my dear Gymnasium, and your mother as well; so have you shown it to me this day, both you and she. If you had been my own sister, how more you two could possibly have held me in esteem
1.1.5:
I know not; but, according as is my way of thinking, I conceive it could not possibly be, such ready assistance, all other things laid aside, have you given me. For this reason do I love you, and for it a vast obligation have you both conferred upon me.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.8: I’ faith, at such a price as this, indeed, it’s easy for us to give you our attendance and to do you good offices;
1.1.10:
so handsomely and so elegantly have you entertained us at breakfast at your house, as we shall ever remember.
SILENIUM
1.1.12:
It has been done with hearty good will by me, and will be done, to get those things which I shall think you are desirous of.
A PROCURESS
1.1.14: As the man said, who was borne by a prospering breeze on a calm sea:
1.1.15:
I rejoice that we came to you; in such a delightful manner have we been here this day received; nor except in the management, was there anything there at your house but what pleased me.
SILENIUM
1.1.18:
How so, prithee?
A PROCURESS
Too seldom did the servant give me something to drink, and, as it was, it clouded the colour of the wine.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.19:
Pray, is that becoming to be mentioned here?
A PROCURESS
It’s both right and proper; there’s no other person here.
SILENIUM
1.1.21:
With reason do I love you both, who esteem and honor me.
A PROCURESS
1.1.22: I’ faith, my dear Silenium, it befits this class to be kindly disposed among themselves, and carefully to keep up friendships,
1.1.25: when you see these matrons of elevated rank, born of the noblest families, how they value friendship, and how carefully they keep it united between themselves. If we do that same thing, if we imitate the same example, still as it is, with difficulty do we exist with their extreme dislike. Of their own enjoyments they would have us to be in want,
1.1.29: in resources of our own they would have us not to possess any power, and to stand in need of them in all matters, that we may be their humble servants. If you wait upon them, you’d rather be giving your room than your company. So very kind are they before the world to our class; in private, if ever there’s the opportunity,
1.1.35: underhandedly they pour cold water upon us. They declare that we are in the habit of having commerce with their husbands; they say that we are their supplanters; they attempt to crush us. Because we are the free daughters of slaves, both I and your mother, we became Courtesans; she brought up yourself, and I this girl (pointing to GYMNASIUM),
1.1.40:
by chance-fathers. Nor yet for the sake of vanity have I driven her to the calling of a Courtesan, but that I mightn’t starve.
SILENIUM
1.1.42:
But it had been better to give her in marriage to a husband in preference.
A PROCURESS
Heyday, now! Surely, faith, she’s married to a husband every day; she has both been married to one to-day, she’ll be marrying again to-night. I’ve never allowed her to go to bed a widow.
1.1.45:
For if she weren’t to be marrying, the household would perish with doleful famine.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.46:
It behoves me, mother, to be just as you wish I should be.
A PROCURESS
1.1.47: I’ troth, I don’t regret it, if you will prove such as you say you’ll be; for if, indeed, you shall be such as I intend, you’ll never be a Hecale in your old age, and you’ll ever keep that same tender age which you now have,
1.1.50:
and you’ll prove a loss to many and a profit to myself full oft, without any outlay of my own.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.51:
May the Gods grant it.
A PROCURESS
Without your own energies, the Gods cannot possibly do anything in this.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.52: I’ faith, for my own part, I’ll zealously devote my energies to it. But what mean you amid this conversation, apple of my eye, my own Silenium? (never did I see you more sad); prithee, do tell me, why does mirth so shun you?
1.1.55:
And you are not so neat as you usually are. (SILENIUM sighs.) Do look at that, please, how deep a sigh she heaved. You are pale too. Tell us both what’s the matter with you, and in what you want our aid; so that we may know. Prithee, don’t by your tears be causing me anxiety.
SILENIUM
1.1.59: My dear Gymnasium, I’m sadly affected; I feel ill, I am shockingly distrest;
1.1.60:
I am pained in spirits, I feel pain in my eyes, I am in pain from faintness. What shall I say, but that my own folly drives me to sadness?
GYMNASIUM
1.1.62:
Take you care, then, that you have your folly entombed in that very same place from which it takes its rise.
SILENIUM
1.1.63:
What shall I do?
GYMNASIUM
Hide it in darkness, in the very deepest recesses of your breast. Take you care and have it so, that you yourself are alone sensible of your own folly, without any other witnesses.
SILENIUM
1.1.65:
But I’ve got the heart-ache.
GYMNASIUM
Why so? For what reason have you the heartache, prithee, tell me, a thing that I neither have, nor any other woman whatever, according as the men say?
SILENIUM
1.1.67:
If there’s any heart to feel pain, it does feel pain; but if there isn’t, still this pains me here.
(Pointing to her left-side.)
A PROCURESS
1.1.68:
This woman’s in love.
GYMNASIUM
Come now, to begin to be in love, is it bitter, prithee?
A PROCURESS
1.1.69: Why, troth, love is most fruitful both in honey and in gall;
1.1.70:
inasmuch as it produces sweetness in a mere taste, but causes bitterness even to repletion.
SILENIUM
1.1.71:
Of that character is the malady that afflicts me, my dear Gymnasium.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.72:
Love is full of treachery.
SILENIUM
He’s taking his spoils of me, then.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.73:
Be of good courage, you’ll get the better of this malady.
SILENIUM
I trust it will be so, if the physician comes that can administer the medicine to this malady.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.75:
He will come.
SILENIUM
A hard expression is that to one in love, He will come, unless he does come. But by my own fault and foolishness, am I, wretched creature, more afflicted, because for him alone have I longed for myself, with whom to pass my life.
A PROCURESS
1.1.78: That is more suitable to a married woman, my dear Silenium, to love but one, and with him to pass her life, to whom she has once been married;
1.1.80:
but, indeed, a Courtesan is most like a flourishing city; she cannot alone increase her fortunes without a multitude of men.
SILENIUM
1.1.82: I want you to give heed to this matter; the thing on account of which you have been sent for to me, I’ll disclose. Now, my mother, because I don’t wish myself to be called a Courtesan, complied with my desire; in that matter she indulged myself who have been obedient to her;
1.1.85:
to allow me to live with him alone whom I so ardently loved.
A PROCURESS
1.1.86:
I’ faith, she acted foolishly. But look, have you ever kept company with any man?
SILENIUM
1.1.87:
With no one, indeed, except Alcesimarchus; nor has any other person whatever committed an infringement on my chastity.
A PROCURESS
1.1.88:
Prithee, by what means did this man gain your good graces?
SILENIUM
1.1.90:
my mother took me to see the procession. While I was returning home, from a secret look-out he secretly traced me even to the door; after that, he insinuated himself into the friendship of my mother and myself as well, by endearments, presents, and gifts.
A PROCURESS
1.1.93:
I should like a man of that sort to be offered me. How I’d work him.
SILENIUM
1.1.94:
What need is there of words? Through intercourse, I on the other hand began to love him, and he myself.
A PROCURESS
1.1.95:
O my dear Silenium—!
SILENIUM
What’s the matter?
A PROCURESS
1.1.96:
You ought to pretend to be in love; for if you fall in love at once, you’ll be much better consulting the interests of him whom you love than your own.
SILENIUM
1.1.98: But in solemn form he took an oath before my mother that he would take me as his wife. Now, another woman is about to be taken home by him,
1.1.100:
a Lemnian lady, his relation, who is living here hard by (pointing to DEMIPHO’S house); for his father has compelled him. Now my mother is enraged with me, because I didn’t return home to her, when I came to know of this matter, that he was about to take another as his wife.
A PROCURESS
1.1.104: Now, I entreat you that you’ll let her (pointing to GYMNASIUM) be here only for the next three days,
1.1.105:
and keep house for me; for I’ve been sent for to my mother’s house.
A PROCURESS
1.1.106:
Although this will be a troublesome three days for me, and you’ll be causing me a loss, I’ll do so.
SILENIUM
1.1.107: You act kindly and like a friend. But you, my dear Gymnasium, if in my absence Alcesimarchus shall come, don’t you chide him roughly; however he has deserved of myself, still he has my affections;
1.1.110:
but, prithee, act gently, so that you mayn’t say anything that may cause him pain. Take the keys (giving them to her); if you have need to take out anything for use, take it out. I wish to go—
GYMNASIUM
1.1.112:
(weeping.) How you have drawn tears from me.
SILENIUM
My dear Gymnasium, kindly, farewell.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.113:
Take care of yourself, there’s a dear. Prithee, will you go in this dishabille?
(Pointing to her dress.)
SILENIUM
1.1.114:
It’s right that such neglect should attend upon my prospects thus disarranged.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.115:
At least do lift up that outer garment.
SILENIUM
Let it be dragged, while I myself am being dragged down.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.116:
Since so it pleases you, fare you well and prosper.
SILENIUM
If I could, I would.
(Exit.)
GYMNASIUM
1.1.117:
Mother, do you wish anything of me, before I go indoors? Upon my faith, to me she does seem to be in love.
A PROCURESS
1.1.118:
For this reason, then, it is, that I’m repeatedly dinning it into your ears, not to be in love with any man. Go in-doors.
GYMNASIUM
1.1.119:
Do you wish anything of me?
A PROCURESS
That you may fare well.
GYMNASIUM
Fare you well.
(GYMNASIUM goes into the house of SILENTIUM.)

1.2.120:
(The PROCURESS, alone.) A PROCURESS
(to the AUDIENCE.) It’s the same fault with myself as with a great part of us women who are following this calling; who, as soon as ever we have got our load of food, are forthwith full of talk; more than is enough do we say.
1.2.126: Why, myself now, inasmuch as I’m filled to my heart’s content, and because I’ve charged myself quite full of the choicest of wine, it pleases me to use my tongue more at freedom; to my misfortune I can’t keep silent on that which it were necessary to be silent upon.
1.2.123: But once upon a time, that girl, who has gone hence in tears, from a lane I carried off a little child exposed.
1.2.125: There is here a certain youth, of the highest rank;
1.2.130: his father, of a very high family, is living at Sicyon;
1.2.131: he is dying desperately in love for this young woman, who has just. now gone hence in tears; on the other hand, she is smitten with love.
1.2.133: I made a present of her to my friend, this Courtesan: who had often made mention of it to me
1.2.135: that somewhere I must find for her a boy or a girl, just born, that she herself might pass it off as her own. As soon as ever the opportunity befell me, I immediately granted her request in that which she had asked of me.
1.2.139: After she had received this female child from me, at once
1.2.140: she was brought to bed of the same female child which she had received from me, without the aid of a midwife and without pain, just as other women bring forth, who seek a trouble to themselves; but she said that her lover was a foreigner, and that by reason of that circumstance she was palming it off.
1.2.145:
This, we two alone are aware of, I who gave the child to her, and she who received it from me; (to the AUDIENCE) except yourselves, indeed. Thus was this affair managed; if any occasion should arise, I wish you to remember this circumstance. I’m off home.
(Exit.)

1.3.149:
(Enter the GOD OF HELP, who speaks the PROLOGUE.) THE GOD OF HELP
(To the AUDIENCE.) This old woman is both a much-talker and a much-tippler.
1.3.150: Isn’t it the fact that she has hardly left room to a Divinity for him to speak, so much has she forestalled him in talking about the substitution of this girl? But if she had held her tongue, still I was about to mention it—a God, who could do it better; for my name is Help. Now (to the AUDIENCE) lend your attention,
1.3.155: that I may clearly explain this plot to you. Some time since, at Sicyon, there was the Festival of Bacchus; a merchant of Lemnos came hither to the games, and he, an ungovernable young man, ravished a maiden in the dark, in the street, at the dead of night.
1.3.160: He, as he knew that he was deserving of a heavy punishment, at once found shelter with his heels, and made off for Lemnos, where he then lived. She whom he had ravished, the ninth ensuing month completed, brought forth a daughter here. Since she did not know the person guilty of this deed, who he was,
1.3.165: she made the servant of her father partaker of her counsels, and gave to that servant the child to be exposed to death. He exposed it; this woman took up the child; that servant, who had exposed it, secretly took note whither or to what house she carried away the child.
1.3.170: As you have heard her own self confess, she gave this child to the Courtesan Melaenis; and she brought her up as being her own daughter, honestly and virtuously. But then, this Lemnian married a neighbour there, his relation, for his wife.
1.3.175: She departed this life; there she was compliant to her husband. After he had performed the due obsequies to his wife, at once he removed hither; here he married for his wife that same woman whom formerly, when a maid, he ravished. When he understood that it was she whom he had ravished,
1.3.180: she told him that, in consequence of the violation, she had brought forth a daughter, and had at once given her to a servant to be exposed. He forthwith ordered this same servant to make enquiries, if anyhow he could discover who had taken it up. Now to that task
1.3.185: is the servant always assiduously devoting his attention, if he can find out that Courtesan, whom formerly, when he himself exposed her, he from his hidingplace had seen take her up. Now, what remains unpaid, I wish to discharge, that my name may be struck out, so that I mayn’t remain a debtor.
1.3.190: A young man is here at Sicyon, his father is alive; with affection he distractedly dotes upon this exposed girl, who just now went hence in tears unto her mother; and she loves him in return, which is the most delightful love of all. As human matters go, nothing is granted for everlasting:
1.3.195: the father is wishful to give the young man a wife. When the mother came to know of this, she ordered her to be sent for home. Thus have these matters come to pass. Kindly fare you well, and conquer by inborn valour, as you have done before; defend your allies, both ancient ones and new;
1.3.200:
increase resources by your righteous laws; destroy your foes; laud and laurels gather; that, conquered by you, the Pœni may suffer the penalty.
(Exit.)

2.1.203:
(Enter ALCESIMARCHUS and MELAENIS.) ALCESIMARCHUS
I do believe that Love was the first to invent torture among mankind. This conjecture do I form from myself at home, not to go seek it out of doors;
2.1.205: I, who surpass all men, exceed them in the pangs of my feelings. I’m tossed, tormented, agitated, goaded, whirled on the wheel of love in my misery, I’m deprived of sensation, carried one way, carried another way, I’m torn and rent asunder; such clouded faculties of mind have I,
2.1.211: where I am, there I am not; where I am not, there my thoughts are; to such a degree have I now all kinds of feelings in me; what I like, then all at once I like not the same; so much does love trifle with me changing my mind,
2.1.216: drive me, pursue, desire, and seize for itself, retain, trepan, and promise; what it gives, it gives not; it deludes me; what this moment it has persuaded me, it now dissuades me from; what it has dissuaded me from, it now points out to me that same.
2.1.221: After the manner of the sea is it experienced by me; so much does it distract my enamoured feelings; and only in that, in my misery, I do not sink utterly, is there any evil removed from me thus ruined;
2.1.225:
in such a way has my father detained me these six days running in the country, at his house there; nor has it been allowed me in the meantime to visit my mistress. Isn’t this dreadful to relate?
MELAENIS
2.1.492: Are you joking for this reason, because you’ve got another wife engaged, a rich lady of Lemnos? Have her then! We are neither of a family so great as you are, nor is our wealth so substantial as yours; but still
2.1.495:
I have no fears that any one will impeach our oath; you then, if you shall feel any pain, will know for what reason you do feel pain.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.497:
May the Gods confound me—
MELAENIS
Whatever you wish for, I desire it may befall you.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.498:
If ever I’ll marry that wife which my father has engaged for me.
MELAENIS
2.1.499:
And me, if ever I give you my daughter for a wife.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.500:
Will you allow me to be forsworn?
MELAENIS
Yes, and a little more easily than myself and my affairs to go to ruin, and my daughter to be trifled with. Begone! go seek where there is confidence enough in your oaths; here now, with us, Alcesimarchus, you’ve renounced your title to our friendship.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.504:
Make trial of me but once.
MELAENIS
I have made that trial full oft; which I lament has been so made.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.505:
Give her back to me.
MELAENIS
Under new circumstances I’ll use an old proverb: What I have given, I wish I had not given; what’s left, that I shall not give.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.507:
Won’t you restore her again to me?
MELAENIS
Answer yourself for me.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.508:
You won’t restore her then?
MELAENIS
You know the whole of my resolution already.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.510:
i’ faith, I don’t at present catch these words of yours with my ears.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.511:
Not hear? Why, what are you doing?
MELAENIS
Then do you give heed at once, that you may know what you are doing.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.512:
Then, so may the Gods and Goddesses of above and below, and of middle rank, and so may Juno the queen and the daughter of supreme Jove, and so may Saturn his uncle—
MELAENIS
2.1.515:
And so may Ops the opulent, his grandam—
MELAENIS
Indeed, his mother, rather.
ALCESIMARCHUS
2.1.516:
Juno his daughter, and Saturn his uncle, supreme Jove—You are maddening me; it’s through you I make these mistakes.
MELAENIS
2.1.518:
Is it that I’m to know what conclusion you are going to come to?
MELAENIS
2.1.519:
Go on talking; I shall not send her back, that’s resolved upon.
ALCESIMARCHUS
Why then, so may Jupiter,
2.1.520: and so may Juno and Saturn, to me, so may—I don’t know what to say—Now I know—Yes, madam, listen, that you may know my mind; may all the Deities, great and small, and those honored with the platter cause me not surviving to give a kiss this day to Silenium, if I don’t this very day murder you and your daughter and myself,
2.1.525:
and after that, with the break of day, if I don’t to-morrow kill you both, and indeed, by all the powers, if at the third onset I don’t demolish you all, if you don’t send her back to me. I’ve said what I intended. Farewell.
(Goes into his FATHER’S house.)
MELAENIS
(to herself.)
2.1.528: He’s gone in-doors in a rage. What shall I do now? If she comes back to him, matters will be just in the same position. When satiety begins to take possession;
2.1.530: he’ll be turning her out of doors, when he shall be bringing home this Lemnian wife. But still I’ll go and follow him; there’s necessity for caution, lest he, in love, should be doing some mischief. In fine, since with strict justice a poor person’s not allowed to contend with a rich one, I’ll lose my labour rather than lose my daughter. But who’s this that straight along the street is directing his course this way?
2.1.535:
Both the other matter do I fear, and this do I dread; so utterly in trepidation am wretched I.
(She stands aside.)

2.2.536:
(Enter LAMPADISCUS.) LAMPADISCUS
(to himself.)
I’ve followed the old woman with my clamour through the streets; I’ve kept her most dreadfully plagued. In what a multitude of ways has she, this day, kept guard upon herself, and been able to remember nothing. How many alluring things, what advantages I’ve promised her.
2.2.540: How many inventions I’ve applied to her, how many stratagems in questioning her. With difficulty have I extorted it from her that she should tell me, because I promised to give her a cask of wine.

2.3.543:
(Enter PHANOSTRATA, from her house.) PHANOSTRATA
(to herself.)
I seemed just now to be hearing the voice of my servant Lampadiscus before the house.
LAMPADISCUS
(stepping forward.)
2.3.544:
You are not deaf, mistress, you heard aright.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.545:
What are you doing here?
LAMPADISCUS
A thing for you to rejoice at.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.546:
What’s that?
LAMPADISCUS
(pointing to the house of SILENIUM.)
A little while ago, I saw a woman coming out of that house there.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.547:
Her that took up my daughter?
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.548:
You have the matter rgiht.
PHANOSTRATA
What after that?
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.549: I told her in what way I had seen her take up the daughter of my mistress from the Hippodrome.
2.3.551:
Then she was in a fright.
MELAENIS
(apart.) Now my body’s in a shudder, my heart is throbbing; for I recollect that from the Hippodrome the little female infant was brought to me, and that I brought it up as my own.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.554: Come, prithee, do go on; my soul’s longing to hear
2.3.555:
how the matter proceeded.
MELAENIS
(apart.) I only wish you couldn’t hear.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.556: I proceed saying, This old woman calls you her daughter wrongfully. For this woman here is your foster-mother, so don’t think she is your mother. I’m to take you back and invite you to opulence, where you may be settled in a noble family,
2.3.560:
where your father may present you with twenty great talents for a portion. For this is not a place where after the Etrurian mode you are disgracefully to earn a dowry for yourself by prostitution of your person.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.564:
Is she, pray, a Courtesan, who took it up?
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.565: Yes, she was a Courtesan. But how it happened, I’ll tell you about that matter. I was now winning her over to me by my persuasion. The old woman embraced her knees, weeping and entreating that she would not forsake her; saying that she was her own daughter; and she took a solemn oath to me that she herself had borne her.
2.3.570:
Her, said she, whom you are in search of, I gave to a friend of mine to bring her up as her own daughter; and she is alive, said she. Where is she? immediately said I.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.573:
Preserve me, ye Gods, I do entreat you.
MELAENIS
(apart.)
But me you are undoing!
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.574:
You ought to have enquired to whom she gave it.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.575:
I did enquire, and she said to the Courtesan Melaenis.
MELAENIS
(apart.)
2.3.576:
He has mentioned my name? I’m utterly undone!
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.577:
When she mentioned her, I straightway asked, Where does she live? said I; take and show me. She has been carried off hence, says she, to live abroad.
MELAENIS
2.3.579:
He’s sprinkling a little cold water now.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.580:
Wherever she has been carried off, thither we will follow. Do you trifle in this fashion? You are undone, if, i’ faith, you don’t disclose this.I insisted to such a degree, that the old woman swore that she would soon inform me.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.584:
But you oughtn’t to have let her go.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.585:
She’s all safe; but she said that she wished first to meet a certain woman, a friend of hers, with whom this was a matter of interest in common, and I’m sure she’ll come.
MELAENIS
(apart.)
2.3.588:
She’ll be discovering me, and adding her own distress to mine.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.591:
Make me acquainted what you now wish me to do.
LAMPADISCUS
Go in-doors, and be of good heart. If your husband shall come, bid him wait at home, lest he should be required by me, if I want him for anything. I’m going to run back to the old woman.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.594:
Lampadio, prithee, do take care.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.595:
I’ll have this matter well managed.
PHANOSTRATA
2.3.596:
I trust in the Gods and in yourself.
LAMPADISCUS
And I in the same.—that you’ll now go home.
(PHANOSTRATA goes into her house.)
MELAENIS
(coming forward.)
2.3.597:
Young man, stay and listen.
LAMPADISCUS
What, are you calling to me, woman?
MELAENIS
2.3.598:
To you.
LAMPADISCUS
What’s the matter? For I’m fully engaged.
MELAENIS
(Pointing to the house of DEMIPHO.)
2.3.599:
Who lives there?
LAMPADISCUS
Demipho, my master.
MELAENIS
2.3.600:
It is he, I suppose, that has betrothed his daughter with such great wealth to Alcesimarchus?
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.602:
It is he himself.
MELAENIS
How now, you? What other daughter, then, are you people now in search of?
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.603:
I’ll tell you; not his daughter by his wife, but his wife’s daughter.
MELAENIS
2.3.605:
What’s the meaning of that speech?
LAMPADISCUS
By a former woman, I say, my master had a daughter born.
MELAENIS
2.3.606:
Surely, just now you said you were in search of the daughter of her who has been talking here.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.608:
Her daughter I am in search of.
MELAENIS
In what way then, pray, is she a former woman, who is now his wife?
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.609: Woman, whoever you are, you weary me with your prating.
2.3.611:
The middle woman whom he had for a wife, of her this maiden was born that’s being given to Alcesimarchus. That wife is dead. Do you understand now?
MELAENIS
2.3.613: I understand that quite well; but it’s this knotty point I’m enquiring about, how
2.3.615:
the first can be the last, the last be the first.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.616: The fact is this; this woman he ravished before he took her home as his wife; before that she was pregnant, and before that she gave birth to a daughter: after she gave birth to her, she ordered the infant to be exposed; I myself exposed her; another woman took her away;
2.3.620:
I was on the look-out; after that, my master married her. That girl, her daughter, we are now in search of. (MELAENIS turns aside her head.) Why now, with face upturned, are you looking up towards the heavens?
MELAENIS
2.3.623:
Now, then, be off at once whither you were hastening; I won’t detain you; I understand it now.
LAMPADISCUS
2.3.624: I’ troth, to the Deities I do give thanks;
2.3.625:
for if you hadn’t understood me, I do think you would never have let me go.
(Exit.)
MELAENIS
(to herself.)
2.3.626: Now it’s necessary for me to be honest, whether I will or no, although I had rather not; I find the thing is discovered. Now will I myself lay them under an obligation to me, rather than she shall peach upon me. I’ll go home,
2.3.630:
and I’ll bring Silenium to her parents.
(Exit.)

3.1.631:
(Enter MELAenis, SILENIUM, and HALISCA.) MELAENIS
I’ve disclosed the whole matter to you; follow, my Silenium, that you may rather belong to those to whom you ought to belong, than be mine. Although against my will I shall part with you, still I’ll reconcile my mind to consult that which in especial conduces to your benefit. (Giving her a casket.)
3.1.635:
For here in this are the trinkets, together with which she who gave you to me formerly brought you to me; that your parents may recognize you the more easily. Take this casket, Halisca, and then go and knock at that door (pointing to the house of DEMIPHO): say that I request that some one will come from within. Make haste, quickly.
ALCESIMARCHUS
(Enter ALCESIMARCHUS, from his FATHER’S house, with his sword drawn.) (calling aloud.)
3.1.639:
Death, receive me unto thyself, a friend and well-wisher to me!
SILENIUM
My mother, to our sorrow, we are undone!
ALCESIMARCHUS
(aloud, to himself.)
3.1.641:
Whether shall I pierce my side here (striking his right side) or on the left.
MELAENIS
(to SILENIUM.)
3.1.642:
What’s the matter with you?
SILENIUM
(pointing.)
Don’t you see Alcesimarchus? He’s grasping a sword.
ALCESIMARCHUS
(aloud, in a frantic manner.)
3.1.643:
What art about? Thou art delaying. Quit the light of day.
SILENIUM
Do run and aid him, pray, that he mayn’t kill himself.
(They run to assist him, on which HALISCA drops the casket.)
ALCESIMARCHUS
3.1.644:
O Safety more healthful than my own safety, you now, whether I wish or don’t wish, alone do cause me to live.
MELAENIS
3.1.646:
Fie on it! Were you ready to commit such violence?
ALCESIMARCHUS
I’ve nought to do with you—to you I’m dead. (Clasping SILENIUM in his arms.) Her, as I hold her, I’m determined not to lose.
