For, by heaven, I am resolved henceforth to have her entirely rivetted fast unto me. (Goes to the door of the house, and calls.) Where are you, servants? Shut the door with bolts, with bars,
3.1.650:
when I shall have carried her within the threshold!
(He carries SILENIUM into the house, followed by HALISCA.)
MELAENIS
(exclaiming, while wringing her hands.)
He’s gone off: he has carried the damsel away. I’ll go—I’ll at once follow him in-doors, that he may know of me these same things, if from being angered with me I can render him pleased.
(Goes into the house.)

4.1.653:
(Enter LAMPADISCUS.) LAMPADISCUS
I do believe I never saw a more tormenting old nag than this is. What she just now confessed to me, is she to be denying it?
4.1.655:
But look, I see my mistress. Why (seeing the casket on the ground), how’s this, that this casket is lying here with these trinkets, and that I see no other person in the street? I must act the child’s part; I’ll stoop to pick up the casket.
(Picks it up.)
PHANOSTRATA
(from her house.)
4.1.658:
What are you about, Lampadio?
LAMPADISCUS
(giving the casket to PHANOSTRATA.)
Is this casket from out of our house here, I wonder. For I picked it up, lying here near the door.
PHANOSTRATA
4.1.659:
What news do you bring about the old woman?
LAMPADISCUS
4.1.660:
That there’s not one other on earth more wicked. She denies all those things which she just now confessed to me. But, i’ faith, for me to allow that old jade to be laughing at me, it’s preferable for me to die by any kind of death.
PHANOSTRATA
4.1.663:
Ye Gods, I do adjure you by our trust in you!
(Opening the casket.)
LAMPADISCUS
4.1.664:
Why do you call upon the Gods?
PHANOSTRATA
Save us!
LAMPADISCUS
What’s the matter?
PHANOSTRATA
These are the trinkets with which you exposed my little daughter to death.
LAMPADISCUS
4.1.666:
Are you in your senses?
PHANOSTRATA
These certainly are.
LAMPADISCUS
Do you persist?
PHANOSTRATA
These are they.
LAMPADISCUS
If any other woman were to speak to me after that fashion, I should say she was drunk.
PHANOSTRATA
4.1.668:
By heaven! I’m talking no nonsense.
But prithee, whence in the world did these come, or what Deity placed this before our door? As though
4.1.670:
for a given purpose, at the very instant
sacred Hope comes to my aid?

4.2.671:
(Enter HALISCA, at a distance, from the house of the FATHER of ALCESIMARCHUS.) HALISCA
(to herself.)
Unless the Gods give me some aid, I’m utterly undone; nor do I know whence I am to seek for aid. To such a degree does carelessness possess wretched me in mind, which I sadly fear may be lighting upon my own back, if my mistress knows that I’m so negligent as I really am.
4.2.675:
The casket which I took and held in my hands here before the door, where it is I know not; except, as I fancy, it was dropt by me about this spot. (Looks about on the ground.) My good sirs (to the AUDIENCE), my kind Spectators, do give me information if any one has seen it, if any one has taken it away, or any one picked it up; and whether in this direction or that he has taken his departure?
(She pauses for a reply.)
4.2.680: I’m none the wiser for asking these persons, or for worrying them, who are always delighted at a woman’s mishaps. Now I’ll mark if there are any footsteps here; for if no one had passed this way since I went in-doors, the casket would be lying here. Why say here? It’s lost, I guess;
4.2.685: it’s done for. It’s all over with unhappy and unlucky me! It’s nowhere, and nowhere am I. This, by its loss, has proved my loss. But still, as I’ve begun, I’ll e’en go on; I’ll make search; for both within do I fear, and without I am afraid; so much, on either side, does fear agitate me now. In this are mortals intensely wretched.
4.2.690:
He is now joyous, whoever he is, that has found it, which is of no use at all to any person else; to myself it may be. But I cause delay to myself, while I’m doing this with remissness. Halisca, attend to what you are about: look down upon the ground, and look round about; search with your eyes; guess with shrewdness.
LAMPADISCUS
(apart, at a distance.)
4.2.695:
Mistress!
PHANOSTRATA
(apart.)
Well, what’s the matter?
LAMPADISCUS
(apart.)
That’s she.
(Pointing at HALISCA.)
PHANOSTRATA
(apart.)
Who?
LAMPADISCUS
(apart.)
She who let fall the casket.
4.2.696:
Why surely she’s tracing out that spot where it fell.
PHANOSTRATA
(apart.)
It seems so.
HALISCA
(to herself, looking on the ground.)
4.2.697: But that person has gone this way; this way I perceive the imprint of his shoe; this way I’ll follow him. (She moves along, still looking on the ground.) In this spot now has he stopped, along with another person. Here now a circle presents itself to my sight,
4.2.700: nor did he go straight forward this way; here he came to a pause. This way did he come out of that circle. Here was a conference with some one. It points to two persons now. Who are these? Heyday I see the footsteps of only one. But he has gone this way. I’ll consider it: hither he went from thence; from hence he has never gone.
4.2.703:
I’m troubling myself to no purpose. What’s lost is lost; my hide along with the casket. I’ll go in-doors again.
(Going towards the house of the FATHER of ALCESIMARCHUS.)
PHANOSTRATA
(calling out.)
4.2.704:
Hallo, woman-stop; there are some persons who wish to meet with you.
HALISCA
4.2.705:
Who’s calling me back?
LAMPADISCUS
A good female and a bad male want you.
HALISCA
4.2.706: Away with you, bad male; I want a good one. (To herself.) After all, he who calls knows better what he wants than I who am called; I’ll return. (Aloud.) Prithee, have you seen any person hereabouts pick up a casket with some trinkets, which I, to my misfortune, have lost here?
4.2.710:
For when, just now, we were running into the house of Alcesimarchus, that he mightn’t put an end to his life, at that moment I think that, through terror, the casket fell down from me here.
LAMPADISCUS
(aside to PHANOSTRATA.)
4.2.712:
This woman’s to our purpose; let’s then give heed to her a little, mistress.
HALISCA
4.2.713: To my sorrow, I’m utterly undone. What shall I say to my mistress, who bade me with such earnestness take care of it, through which Silenium might the more readily recognize her parents—who, when little, was adopted by my mistress as her own,
4.2.716:
and whom a certain Courtesan gave to her?
LAMPADISCUS
(aside.) She’s talking about this matter of ours. According as she gives these indications by her talk, she must surely know where your daughter is.
HALISCA
4.2.718:
Now is she desirous of her own accord to restore her to her father and mother, whose daughter she is; prithee, my good sir, you are attending to something else; I commend my matter to you.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.720:
I’m giving my attention to this, and this is as good as food to me, that you are talking of; but amid my attending to this matter, I was answering this mistress of mine what she was enquiring; now I return to you. If you have need of anything, say you, and give your orders. What were you looking, for?
HALISCA
4.2.723:
My good sir and my good madam, I greet you.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.724:
And we you. But what are you looking for?
HALISCA
I’m tracing footsteps here,
4.2.725:
the way that something has escaped me here, I don’t know how.
PHANOSTRATA
What is it?
LAMPADISCUS
What is it, pray?
HALISCA
4.2.726:
Something to bring a loss to another, and a calamity on our family.
LAMPADISCUS
(aside to PHANOSTRATA.)
4.2.727:
A worthless baggage is this, mistress, and a crafty one.
PHANOSTRATA
(aside.)
I’ faith, and so she seems.
LAMPADISCUS
(aside.)
4.2.728:
She imitates a worthless animal and a mischievous.
PHANOSTRATA
(aside.)
Which one, prithee?
LAMPADISCUS
(aside.)
4.2.729: A caterpillar, which twisting about winds itself in the leaf of the vine;
4.2.730:
just in the same way does she begin a story that twists about. (To HALISCA.) What are you looking for?
HALISCA
4.2.731:
A casket, my good young man, has flown away from me here.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.732:
You ought to have put it in a cage.
HALISCA
I’ faith, the booty was no great one.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.733:
It’s a wonder, if a whole troop of slaves isn’t there in the casket.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.734:
Do let her speak.
LAMPADISCUS
If indeed she would speak.
PHANOSTRATA
(to HALISCA.)
Come say you, what was in it?
HALISCA
4.2.735:
Trinkets only.
LAMPADISCUS
There’s a certain man, who declares that he knows where it is.
HALISCA
4.2.736:
But, by my faith, he’ll confer an obligation on a certain woman if he’ll discover it.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.737:
But this certain man wishes a reward to be given to him.
HALISCA
But, by my faith, this certain woman, that has lost this casket, declares that she has nothing to give to this certain man.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.739:
But still this certain man looks for some money.
HALISCA
But still he looks for it in vain.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.740:
But, by my faith, good woman, in no matter does this certain man give his pains for nothing.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.741:
Lend me your conversation: it will now be for your own advantage. We confess that we have got the casket.
HALISCA
4.2.742:
Then may Salvation preserve you; where is it now?
PHANOSTRATA
(producing the casket.)
4.2.743:
See, here it is, safe. But I wish to discourse with you upon a matter of importance to myself; I take you as a sharer with me in my own preservation.
HALISCA
4.2.745:
What matter is this, or who are you?
PHANOSTRATA
I am the mother of her who had these things with her, when exposed.
HALISCA
4.2.746:
Do you live here then?
(Pointing to the house.)
PHANOSTRATA
You are a diviner. But, prithee, good woman, do lay aside all mystification, and to the point; tell me at once, whence did you get these trinkets?
HALISCA
4.2.749:
This daughter of my mistress had them.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.750:
You tell a falsehood; for my own mistress’s daughter had them, not yours.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.751:
Don’t interrupt.
LAMPADISCUS
I’ll be mum.
PHANOSTRATA
Good woman, go on speaking. Where is she who had them?
HALISCA
(pointing to the house of ALCESIMARCHUS.)
4.2.753:
By the powers, surely the son-in-law of my husband is living there.
LAMPADISCUS
Surely—
PHANOSTRATA
(to LAMPADISCUS.)
Interrupting again? (To HALISCA.) Go on relating it. How many years old is she said to be?
HALISCA
4.2.756:
She is my own daughter then!
LAMPADISCUS
’Tis she, as the number of her years has proved.
HALISCA
4.2.757:
What you are seeking, you have found; I now seek what’s mine.
LAMPADISCUS
4.2.758:
Why, faith, they’ve found what’s their own, I’ll seek for number three.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.759:
My daughter, the object which I was seeking, I have discovered.
HALISCA
4.2.760: It’s proper to keep in safety what has been entrusted in confidence, lest a kindness should turn out a detriment to the well-deserving. This fosterling of ours is assuredly your daughter,
4.2.762: and my mistress is about to restore you your own, and for that purpose has she come from her house. But, prithee,
4.2.765:
enquire of her own self; I am but a servant.
PHANOSTRATA
You ask what’s just.
HALISCA
4.2.766:
To her rather do I choose this obligation to belong. But I beg that you’ll restore me that casket.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.768:
What’s to be done, Lampadio?
LAMPADISCUS
What’s your own, keep as your own.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.770:
give her the casket, and go in-doors together with her.
PHANOSTRATA
4.2.771:
I’ll follow your advice. (Giving it to HALISCA.) Take you the casket. Let’s go in-doors. But what’s the name of your mistress?
HALISCA
4.2.773:
Melaenis.
PHANOSTRATA
Go first; I’ll follow you at once.
(Exit LAMPADISCUS, and the others go into the house of the FATHER of ALCESIMARCHUS.)

5.1.774:
(Enter DEMIPHO.) DEMIPHO
What affair is this, that all persons are talking about in the street—that my daughter has been found? They say, too, that Lampadio has been seeking me in the Forum.
(Enter LAMPADISCUS.)
LAMPADISCUS
5.1.776:
Master, whence come you?
DEMIPHO
From the Senate.
LAMPADISCUS
I rejoice that through my means there is an addition to your children.
DEMIPHO
5.1.777:
But it don’t please me; I don’t want that I should be having more children by means of another person. But what is the meaning of this?
LAMPADISCUS
(pointing to the house of the FATHER of ALCESIMARCHUS.)
5.1.779:
Make haste, and go in-doors here to the house of your neighbour; you’ll at once recognize your daughter. Your wife’s in-doors there as well. Go quickly.
DEMIPHO
5.1.781:
I’m resolved that this shall, before all other matters, be attended to.
(They go into the house of the FATHER of ALCESIMARCHUS.)
The Company of COMEDIANS
5.1.782: Don’t you wait, Spectators, till they come out to you; no one will come out; they’ll all finish the business indoors; when that shall be done, they’ll lay aside their dress; then, after that,
5.1.785: he that has done amiss will get a beating; he that has not done amiss will get some drink. Now as to what’s left, Spectators, for you to do, after the manner of your ancestors, give your applause at the conclusion of the Play.

1.1.1:
(Before daybreak.) Enter at one side of the stage PHAEDROMUS, with a lighted torch, and followed by SLAVES with wine and provisions for an entertainment, and PALINURUS on the opposite side.) PALINURUS
Whither away must I say that you are going out of doors at this time o’ night, Phaedromus, with that dress and with this train?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.3: Whither Venus and Cupid summon me, and Love persuades me; whether ’tis the midnight or whether the earliest twilight,
1.1.5:
if the day is fixed for pleading your cause with your antagonist, still must you go where they command you, whether you will or no.
PALINURUS
1.1.7:
But pray, pray—
PHAEDROMUS
Pray — you are annoying to me.
PALINURUS
1.1.8:
Really that is neither pretty nor befitting you to say. You are your own servant; in your fine garb you are showing the light with your waxen torch.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.10:
And ought I not to carry that which is gathered by the labour of the little bees—which has its birth in sweets—to my own sweet one, my little honey?
PALINURUS
1.1.12:
But whither must I say that you are going?
PHAEDROMUS
If you ask me that, I’ll tell, so that you may know.
PALINURUS
1.1.13:
If I make the enquiry, what would you answer me?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.14:
This is the Temple (pointing to it) of Aesculapius.
PALINURUS
That I have known for more than a twelvemonth past.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.15:
Close to it is that door, dear as my very eyes. (Points to the door of CAPPADOX.) Hail to you! door, dear as my very eyes; have you been quite well of late?
PALINURUS
1.1.16:
Did a fever leave you but yesterday, or the day before, and did you take your dinner yesterday?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.18:
Are you laughing at me?
PALINURUS
1.1.19:
Why then, madman, are you enquiring whether the door is well or not?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.20:
I’ faith, I’ve known it as a door most comely and most discreet: never one word does it whisper; when it is opened, it is silent; and when, by night, she secretly comes out to me, it holds its peace.
PALINURUS
1.1.23: And are you not, Phaedromus, doing, or contemplating the doing of, some deed which is unworthy of yourself or of your family?
1.1.25:
Are you not laying a snare for some modest fair one, or for one that should be modest?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.26:
For no one; and may Jupiter not permit me to do so.
PALINURUS
1.1.27: I wish the same. Ever, if you are wise, so bestow your love, that if the public should know the object which you love, it may be no disgrace to you.
1.1.30:
Ever do you take care that you be not disgraced.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.32:
What means that expression?
PALINURUS
For you to proceed with caution on your path; the object that you love, love in the presence of witnesses.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.33:
Why, ’tis a Procurer that lives here.
(He points.)
PALINURUS
No one drives you away from there, nor yet forbids you, if you have the money, to buy what’s openly on sale.
1.1.35:
No one forbids any person from going along the public road, so long as he doesn’t make a path through the field that’s fenced around; so long as you keep yourself away from the wife, the widow, the maiden, youthful age, and free-born children, love what you please.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.39:
This is the house of a Procurer.
PALINURUS
A curse befall it.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.40:
Why so?
PALINURUS
Because it serves in an infamous service.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.41:
You speak out.
PALINURUS
Be it so, most especially.
PHAEDROMUS
Once more, will you hold your tongue?
PALINURUS
1.1.42:
You bade me speak out, I thought.
PHAEDROMUS
Then, now I forbid you. But, as I had begun to say, he has a young female slave—
PALINURUS
1.1.44:
This Procurer, you mean, who’s living here?
PHAEDROMUS
You have hold of it exactly.
PALINURUS
1.1.45:
The less shall I be in dread of its falling.
PHAEDROMUS
You are impertinent. He wishes to make her a courtesan, while she is desperately in love with me; whereas I don’t wish to have her upon loan.
PALINURUS
1.1.48:
Why so?
PHAEDROMUS
Because I’m for having her as my own; I love her equally as well.
PALINURUS
1.1.49:
Clandestine courtship is bad; ’tis utter ruin.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.50:
I’ troth, ’tis so as you say.
PALINURUS
Has she as yet submitted to the yoke of Venus?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.51:
For me she is as chaste as though she were my own sister, unless, indeed, she is any the more unchaste for some kissing.
PALINURUS
1.1.53: Always, do you understand, flame follows very close on smoke; with smoke, nothing can be burnt, with flame, it can.
1.1.55:
He who wishes to eat the kernel of the nut, first breaks the nut; he who wishes to seduce, opens the dance with kisses.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.57:
But she is chaste, and never yet has bestowed her favours upon man.
PALINURUS
1.1.58:
That I could believe, if any Procurer had any shame.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.59: Well, but what think you of her? When she has any opportunity,
1.1.60:
she steals away to me; when she has given me a kiss, she’s off again. This happens by reason of this, because this Procurer is lying a-bed ill in the Temple of Aesculapius; that fellow is my torturer.
PALINURUS
1.1.63:
At one time he asks me for thirty minae for her, at another for a great talent; and from him I cannot obtain any fair and just dealing.
PALINURUS
1.1.65:
You are too exacting, in requiring that of him which no Procurer possesses.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.67:
Now, I’ve sent my Parasite hence to Caria, to ask for money on loan from my friend; if he doesn’t bring me this, which way to turn myself I know not.
PALINURUS
1.1.70:
If you salute the Deities, towards the right I think; now this is this altar of Venus before their door.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.71:
I have already vowed to bring me an early breakfast for my Venus.
PALINURUS
1.1.73:
What? Will you then be giving up yourself as a breakfast to Venus?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.74:
Myself, and you, and all of these.
(Pointing to the SLAVES.)
PALINURUS
Then you would have Venus to be sick outright.
PHAEDROMUS
(to an ATTENDANT.)
1.1.75:
Here, boy, give me the bowl.
PALINURUS
What are you going to do?
PHAEDROMUS
You’ll know directly. An old hag is in the habit of sleeping here, as the keeper of the door; the name of the Procuress is Much-bibber and Neat-bibber.
PALINURUS
1.1.78:
Just as you would speak of a flagon, in which Chian wine is wont to be.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.79: What need is there of words? She is a most vinous soul;
1.1.80:
and the very moment that I’ve sprinkled this door with the wine, she knows by the smell that I’m here, and opens it forthwith.
PALINURUS
1.1.82:
Is it for her the bowl is brought with the wine?
PHAEDROMUS
Unless you object.
PALINURUS
1.1.83:
I’ faith, I do object; for I’d rather have it broken about him who has brought it. I fancied it was brought for ourselves.
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.84: Why don’t you hold your tongue?
1.1.85:
If any’s left after her, it will be enough for ourselves.
PALINURUS
1.1.86:
What river is it, pray, that the sea does not receive?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.87:
Follow me this way, Palinurus, to the door; do you be obedient to me.
PALINURUS
1.1.88:
I’ll do so.
(They advance to the door of the PROCURER’S house.)
PHAEDROMUS
(sprinkling the door with wine.)
Come, drink, you joyous door, quaff on, readily prove propitious unto me.
PALINURUS
(in an afected tone.)
1.1.90:
Door, would you like some olives or a tit-bit, or some capers?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.91:
Arouse and send out here to me your portress.
PALINURUS
1.1.92:
You’re spilling the wine; what matter is it that possesses you? (Takes hold of his arm.)
PHAEDROMUS
Let me alone. Don’t you see? This most joyous door is opening; does the hinge make a bit of creaking? ’Tis a charming one.
PALINURUS
1.1.94:
Why don’t you then give it a kiss?
PHAEDROMUS
1.1.95:
Hold your tongue; let’s keep back the light and our noise.
PALINURUS
Be it so.
(They stand apart, leaving the bowl near the door.)

1.2.96:
(Enter the PROCURESS, from the house of CAPPADOX.) PROCURESS
The savour of aged wine has reached my nostrils; the love of it has brought me in my eagerness hither in the dark; wherever it is, it’s near me. O capital, I’ve found it. (Stooping, and smelling at the bowl.) Hail to you, my soul, Joy of dear Bacchus;
1.2.100:
how enamoured am I of your old age. For in comparison with yours, the odour of all unguents were mere bilge-water; you are my myrrh, you my cinnamon, you my rose, you my saffron unguent and my cassia, you are my vine-palm scent. But, where you have been poured, there would I most earnestly hope to be buried.
PALINURUS
(apart.)
1.2.110:
This old lady’s thirsty;
how limited is her thirst?
PHAEDROMUS
(apart.)
She’s a moderate person; she swallows eight gallons only.
PALINURUS
(apart.)
1.2.111:
I’ faith, according to your account, this year’s vintage is not enough for this old woman alone.
PROCURESS
1.2.105:
But since as yet you, fragrance, alone have penetrated to my nostrils, so in its turn afford some delight to my throat. (Feels for the bowl on the ground, which PALINURUS draws away.) I find you not; where is your own dear self? I’m longing to touch you; do let me pour your liquids into me by sip-sipping. But in this direction it has gone, this way I’ll. follow it.
(Goes in the direction of PALINURUS, who has the bowl.)
PALINURUS
(apart.)
1.2.112:
It really had been more proper for her to be a dog; she has a good nose.
PROCURESS
Prithee, whose voice is it that I hear at a distance.
PHAEDROMUS
(apart.)
1.2.113:
I think that this old hag should be accosted. I’ll approach her. (Aloud.) Come back, Procuress, and look back towards me.
PROCURESS
1.2.115:
Who is it that gives his commands?
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.116:
The all-powerful in wine, jolly Bacchus; he who, when you’re hawking, parched, and half asleep, brings you a draught and comes to quench your thirst.
PROCURESS
1.2.119:
How far is he away from me?
PHAEDROMUS
(holding up the torch.)
See this light.
PROCURESS
1.2.120:
Then, prithee, do quicken your pace towards me.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.121:
Health to you.
PROCURESS
How can I have health, who am parched with thirst?
PHAEDROMUS
But you shall drink in a moment.
PROCURESS
’Tis long a-coming.
PHAEDROMUS
(extending the bowl.)
1.2.122:
Here’s for you, jolly old dame.
PROCURESS
Health to you, gentleman dear as my very eyes.
PALINURUS
1.2.123:
Come, toss this off quickly into your abyss; scour out your sink right speedily.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.124:
Hold your tongue; I won’t have her ill spoken to.
PALINURUS
(aside.)
In preference, then, I’ll do her ill.
PROCURESS
(pouring some of the residue on the altar.)
1.2.125:
Venus, of this little, this very little will I give to thee—sore against my will; for all the lovers, in their cups, to propitiate thee, expend their wine upon thee: not such windfalls often fall to me.
(Drinks again.)
PALINURUS
1.2.128:
Do look at that, please, how greedily the filthy hag swills down the pure wine into herself with distended gullet.
PROCURESS
(patting her stomach and chuckling.)
1.2.131:
Ha, ha, ha
PALINURUS
How is it? Do you like it?
PROCURESS
I do like it.
PALINURUS
And I, too, should like to goad with a spur as well.
PHAEDROMUS
(aside to PALINURUS.)
1.2.132:
Don’t you—do hold your tongue.
PALINURUS
I’ll hold my tongue; (the old woman drinks) but see, the rainbow’s drinking; I’ faith, I do believe it will rain to-day.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.129:
Troth now, I’m quite undone; what first to say to her I know not.
PALINURUS
Why, the same thing that you said to me.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.130:
What’s that?
PALINURUS
Say that you’re quite undone.
PHAEDROMUS
May the Gods confound you.
PALINURUS
Say so to her.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.133:
Am I to say then to her—?
PALINURUS
Say what?
PHAEDROMUS
That I’m quite undone.
PALINURUS
Well then, say so.
PHAEDROMUS
Old lady, do listen. I wish you to know this; to my sorrow, I’m quite undone.
PROCURESS
1.2.135:
But, i’ faith, for my part, I’m altogether brought to life. But why is it that you are pleased to say you are quite undone?
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.137:
Because I’m deprived of the object which I love. (Pretends to weep)
PROCURESS
1.2.138:
My dear Phaedromus, prithee, do not weep; do you take care that I’m not thirsty, I’ll at once bring out here for you the object which you love. (Goes into the house.)
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.140:
Assuredly, if you keep faith with me, in place of a golden statue, I’ll erect for you one of wine, which shall be a memorial of your gullet Palinurus, who on earth will be so blest as myself, if she comes to me?
PALINURUS
1.2.142:
By my faith, he who is in love, if he is in want as well, is afflicted with a dreadful malady.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.143:
Such is not the case with me; for I feel sure that this very day my Parasite will come hither to me with the money.
PALINURUS
1.2.144:
You attempt something mighty, if you expect that which nowhere exists.
PHAEDROMUS
1.2.145:
What if I approach the door, and trill a carol?
PALINURUS
If you choose; I neither bid nor request you, since, my master, I see that you are of manners and disposition thus changed.
PHAEDROMUS
(sings.)
1.2.147: Bolts, O ye bolts, with pleasure do I salute you. I love you, I court you, I seek you, and you entreat; most kindly lend your aid to me in love;
1.2.150:
become, for my sake, as though play-actors from foreign climes; leap upwards pray, and send out of doors this fair one, who drains my blood for me distractedly in love. (Addressing PALINURUS.) Look at that, how those most accursed bolts sleep on, and none the quicker for my sake do they bestir themselves.
(Addressing the door.)
1.2.155:
I see quite clearly that you don’t value my esteem at all. Hist! hush, hush!
PALINURUS
1.2.156:
I’ troth, for my part I’m silent enough.
PHAEDROMUS
I hear a noise; at last, i’ faith, these bolts have become complaisant to me.

1.3.158:
(Re-enter the PROCURESS, with PLANESIUM, from the house of CAPPADOX.) PROCURESS
(to PLANESIUM, while opening the door.)
Come softly out, and prevent the noise of the doors and the creaking of the hinges, my dear Planesium, that our master mayn’t perceive that that is going on which we are doing here.
1.3.160:
Stay, I’ll pour a little water on it.
(Pours water on the hinges.)
PALINURUS
(to PHAEDROMUS.)
Do you see how the palsied hag is giving her dose? She herself has learnt right well to drink up the wine; to the door she’s giving water for it to drink.
PLANESIUM
(looking around.)
1.3.162:
Where are you—you who have summoned me on the recognizances of Venus? To you do I present myself, and, in the same way do I call on you, on the other hand, to present yourself to me.
PHAEDROMUS
(stepping forward.)
1.3.164:
Here I am; for could I be absent, I wouldn’t repine for any misfortune to befall me, my honey.
PLANESIUM
1.3.165:
My life, it is not becoming for one thus in love to be at a distance.
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.166:
Palinurus, Palinurus!
PALINURUS
Say on; why is it that you call upon Palinurus?
PHAEDROMUS
(aside.)
1.3.167:
She is a charming one.
PALINURUS
(aside.)
Aye, too charming.
PHAEDROMUS
I am a God.
PALINURUS
Why, no—a mortal, of no great value.
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.168:
What have you seen, or what will you see, more nearly to be compared with the Gods?
PALINURUS
1.3.169:
You are not in your senses, master; a thing that’s grievous to me.
PHAEDROMUS
You are not sufficiently respectful to me: hold your tongue.
PALINURUS
1.3.170:
The person that sees the object which he loves, and enjoys not the opportunity while he may, is one who torments his own self.
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.171:
Rightly does he rebuke me; really there’s nothing which for this long time past I have more eagerly desired.
PLANESIUM
1.3.172:
Clasp me, embrace me then.
PHAEDROMUS
(embracing her.)
This, too, is a reason for which I could wish to live; because your master restrains, you, in secret do I court you.
PLANESIUM
1.3.173:
Restrain me? He neither can restrain me, nor will he restrain me, unless death should separate my soul from you.
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.178: Let monarchs keep their kingdoms to themselves, the rich their riches to themselves, to themselves their honors, to themselves their prowess, to themselves their combats, to themselves their battles;
1.3.180:
so long as they abstain from envying me, let each one of them keep what is his own.
PALINURUS
(aside.)
1.3.175:
Of a truth, I cannot refrain from giving a lecture to my master; for, really, it is good to love in a moderate degree; to distraction, it is not good; but to love to entire distraction, is the thing that my master’s doing.
(Aloud.)
1.3.181:
What say you, sir? Have you made a vow, Phaedromus, you’d watch the night through for Venus? For really, upon my faith, before very long hence the dawn will be breaking.
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.183:
Why hold my tongue? What, are you going to sleep?
PHAEDROMUS
I am asleep; don’t you make a noise.
PALINURUS
1.3.184:
Why, but you’re broad awake.
PHAEDROMUS
Aye, but after my own fashion I’m asleep; this is my slumber.
PALINURUS
(to PLANESIUM.)
1.3.185:
A word with you, madam; ’tis thoughtlessness to treat amiss one who deserves it not.
PLANESIUM
1.3.186:
You would be angry, if, when you are eating, he were to drive you away from your food.
PALINURUS
(aside.)
It’s all over with him. I see that these two are equally in love to distraction; and both of them are mad. D’ye see how intensely they hug each other? They cannot embrace enough. (Addressing them.) Are you going to part yet?
PLANESIUM
1.3.189:
No human being has blessings that last for ever. To this pleasure, then, is that plague added.
PALINURUS
1.3.190:
What say you, you shocking hussy? What, you little tipsy ninny, are even you with your owlish eyes to be calling me a plague, you whipper-snapper?
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.192:
What, you abusing my own Venus? And really, is a slave well trounced with the rod to be commencing a discussion with myself? But, by the powers, you’ve surely said that to your own misfortune.
(Strikes him.)
1.3.195:
There, take that, by way of punishment for this abusive language, that you may be able to put a check upon your speech.
PALINURUS
(to PLANESIUM.)
1.3.196:
Your aid, I pray, you night-watching Venus.
PHAEDROMUS
What, do you still persist, whip-scoundrel? (Strikes hint.)
PLANESIUM
1.3.197:
Don’t, there’s a dear, be beating a stone, lest you should hurt your hand.
PALINURUS
1.3.198: You perpetrate, Phaedromus, a flagitious and a shameful deed of great enormity; one who directs you aright, you pummel with your fists; her you are in love with, a mere nonentity.
1.3.200:
Is it right that you should behave yourself in this unreasonable manner?
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.201:
Find me a reasonable lover against his weight in gold; here, take the gold of me.
(Holds out his purse.)
PALINURUS
1.3.202:
Do you find me a person for me to serve in his sound senses against his weight in double-distilled gold.
PLANESIUM
1.3.203: Kindly fare you well, apple of my eye, for I hear the sound and creaking of doors; I think the keeper is opening the temple. But, prithee, in this same manner
1.3.205:
shall we always enjoy our love by stealth?
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.206:
Far from it; for I sent my Parasite four days since to Caria to fetch some money; he’ll be here to-day.
PLANESIUM
1.3.207:
You are very long in your contriving.
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.208:
So may Venus love me, I’ll never allow you to be three days in this house here, before I procure your liberty.
PLANESIUM
1.3.210:
Take care to remember it. Once more, before I go hence, take this kiss.
(Kisses him.)
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.211:
By heavens, really if a kingdom now were offered me, I should not obtain it with greater pleasure. When shall I see you again?
PLANESIUM
1.3.212:
Why now, for that expression get ready the Praetor’s rod; if you love me, purchase my freedom; don’t make any haggling. Take care to prevail with your offer. Kindly adieu! (Goes into the house of the PROCURER.)
PHAEDROMUS
1.3.214:
And am I then left behind? Palinurus, I’m Lilled outright.
PALINURUS
1.3.215:
And I as well, who am dying with thumps and sleepiness.
PHAEDROMUS
Do you follow me.
(They go into the house of PHAEDROMUS.)

2.1.216:
(Enter CAPPADOX, from the Temple of AESCULAPIUS.) CAPPADOX
(to himself.)
I am resolved to depart from this Temple out of doors forthwith, since thus I find the determination of Aesculapius, who sets me at nought, and chooses not that I should be healed. My health is declining, my weakness increases.
2.1.220:
For now I walk, girded with my spleen as though with a belt; in my stomach do I seem to be holding a twin offspring. I’m afraid of nothing, but that, in my misery, I should burst asunder in the middle.
(PHAEDROMUS.)
PALINURUS
(speaking to PHAEDROMUS within as he enters.)
2.1.223: If you do right, Phaedromus, you’ll listen to me, and banish this sorrow from your feelings.
2.1.225:
You are anxious because your Parasite hasn’t returned from Caria. I think he’ll bring the money; but if he doesn’t bring it, by a chain of iron he couldn’t be withheld from betaking himself to eat at his manger.
CAPPADOX
(turning round.)
2.1.229:
What person is it that speaks?
PALINURUS
(to himself.)
Whose voice is it that I hear?
CAPPADOX
2.1.230:
Isn’t this Palinurus, the servant of Phaedromus?
PALINURUS
(aside.)
Who is this fellow with extended paunch, and eyes as green as grass? From his figure I know him; from his complexion I cannot recognize him. O, now I do know him: it’s the Procurer Cappadox. I’ll accost him.
CAPPADOX
2.1.234:
Save you, Palinurus.
PALINURUS
O source of villanies, save you; how are you?
CAPPADOX
2.1.235:
I’m just alive.
PALINURUS
Just as you deserve, I suppose? But what’s the matter with you?
CAPPADOX
2.1.236:
My spleen is killing me, my reins are in torment, my lungs are being torn asunder, my liver is being tortured, my heart-strings are giving way, all my intestines are in pain.
PALINURUS
2.1.239:
The liver complaint is afflicting you, then.
CAPPADOX
2.1.244:
My spleen is expanded.
PALINURUS
Take walking exercise; that’s the best thing for the spleen.
CAPPADOX
2.1.240:
’Tis an easy matter to laugh at the afflicted.
PALINURUS
Well, then, do you hold out for some days until your intestines become putrid. Now, while the humours are pretty sound, if you do that, you yourself might sell for a worse price than those intestines of yours.
CAPPADOX
2.1.245:
Prithee, have done with this, and answer me this which I ask; can you possibly form a conjecture on it, if I relate to you what I dreamt last night in my sleep?
PALINURUS
2.1.248: Psha, this—(pointing to himself)—this is the sole person that is really skilled in divination; why, the interpreters of dreams ask advice of myself;
2.1.250: the answer that I have given them, by that opinion they all stand.

2.2.251:
(Enter a COOK, from the house of PHAEDROUMS.) COOK
Palinurus, why do you delay? Why are not the things served out for me which are needed for the breakfast to be prepared for the Parasite when he comes.
PALINURUS
2.2.253:
Wait, please, until I interpret his dream. (Pointing to CAPPADOX.)
COOK
2.2.254:
Why, you your own self, if you’ve had any dream, always apply to me.
PALINURUS
2.2.255:
I confess it.
COOK
Be off, then, and serve out the things.
PALINURUS
(to CAPPADOX.)
Come now, do you in the meantime relate your dream to him. I give you a substitute better than I am myself; for what I do know, all of it I know from him.
(Pointing to the COOK.)
CAPPADOX
2.2.257:
Let him give his attention then.
PALINURUS
He’ll give it.
CAPPADOX
2.2.258:
He does what few do, in being attentive to their masters even. (To the COOK.) Do you give me your attention then.
(PALINURUS goes into the house of PHAEDROMUS.)
COOK
2.2.259:
Although I don’t know you, I’ll give it you.
CAPPADOX
2.2.260:
Last night I seemed in my sleep to behold Aesculapius, seated at a distance far away from me; and it seemed that he didn’t come near me, or set any value upon me.
COOK
2.2.263: The other Gods will do the same, you must know; in fact, among themselves they agree with perfect unanimity.
2.2.265:
It isn’t to be wondered at, if it fares no better with you. But it had been better for you to pass the night in Jove’s Temple, who has given you his assistance in your oaths.
CAPPADOX
2.2.268:
If, indeed, those should wish to sleep there who have been guilty of perjury, it were not possible for room to be found them in the Capitol.
COOK
2.2.270:
Give your attention to this; ask peace of Aesculapius, lest perchance some great mishap befall you, which has been portended to you in your rest.
CAPPADOX
2.2.272:
You do well in advising me; I’ll go and pray to him. (Goes into the Temple.)
COOK
2.2.273:
And ill speed you with it
(Goes into the house of PHAEDROMUS.)
PALINURUS
(Enter PALINURUS, from the house.)
(looking in the distance, as he enters.)
2.2.274:
O immortal Gods, whom do I behold? Who’s that yonder?
(Pointing.)
2.2.275:
Isn’t that the Parasite, who was sent to Caria? (Goes to the door.) Hallo, come out, Phaedromus, come out, come out, come out this instant, I say.
(from the house.)
PHAEDROMUS
2.2.277:
Why are you making this noise here?
PALINURUS
I see your Parasite running; see, there he is (pointing), down at the end of the street. Let’s listen from here what he’s about.
PHAEDROMUS
2.2.279:
I think it’s as well.
(They stand aside.)

2.3.280:
(Enter CURCULIO, at a distance, walking fast.) CURCULIO
(to himself.)
Known or unknown, make way for me, while here I execute my commission; fly all of you, be off, and get out of the way, lest I should hurt any person in my speed with my head, or elbow, or breast, or with my knee. So suddenly now am I charged with a business of quickness and despatch. And be there no person ever so opulent to stop me in my way,
2.3.285: neither general, nor any tyrant, nor market-officer, nor demarch nor comarch, with their honors so great, but that down he goes, and tumbles head first from the footpath into the carriage-road. And then those Grecians with their cloaks, who walk about with covered heads, who go loaded beneath their cloaks with books, and with baskets,
2.3.290: they loiter together, and engage in gossipping among themselves, the gad-abouts; you may always see them enjoying themselves in the hot liquor-shops; when they have scraped up some trifle, with their covered pates they are drinking mulled wine, sad and maudlin they depart: if I stumble upon them here,
2.3.295:
from every single one of them I’ll squeeze out a belch from their pearled-barley diet. And then those servants of your dainty townsmen, who are playing at catch-ball in the road, both throwers and catchers, all of them I’ll pitch under foot. Would they avoid a mishap, why then, let them keep at home.
PHAEDROMUS
(apart.)
2.3.299: He points out aright, he only requires that he should speak with authority; for such manners are in vogue in the present day,
2.3.300:
such at present are the slaves; really, control cannot be held over them.
CURCULIO
(to himself.)
2.3.301:
Is there any one, I wonder, who can point out to me Phaedromus, my good Genius? The matter is of such pressing nature, I really must meet with the man this instant.
PALINURUS
(apart.)
2.3.303:
He’s looking for you.
PHAEDROMUS
(apart.)
What if we accost him? (Aloud.) Hallo! Curculio, I want you.
CURCULIO
(looking round.)
2.3.304:
Who’s calling me? Who’s mentioning my name?
PHAEDROMUS
One who wishes to meet with you.
CURCULIO
(seeing him.)
2.3.305:
You don’t wish more for me than I wish for you.
PHAEDROMUS
O my own ready occasion, Curculio, much longed-for, greetings to you.
CURCULIO
2.3.306:
Greetings to you.
PHAEDROMUS
I’m glad that you have arrived safe; give me your right hand. How stand my hopes? Troth now, prithee, do speak out.
CURCULIO
2.3.308:
To you, troth now, prithee, do speak out, how stand my own. (Makes curious gestures.)
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.309:
What’s the matter with you?
CURCULIO
A dimness is beginning to come, my knees are failing through fasting.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.310:
I’ faith, through lassitude, I think.
CURCULIO
(staggering.)
Support me, prithee, do support me.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.311:
See how pale he has turned; will you give him a seat, for him to be seated at once, and an ewer with some water? Will you make haste, this very instant?
CURCULIO
2.3.313:
Would you like some water?
CURCULIO
If it’s full of bits of meat, prithee, give it me to swallow down, i’ faith.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.314:
Woe be to that head of yours.
CURCULIO
Troth now, prithee do give me cause to rejoice at my arrival.
PHAEDROMUS
(begins to fan him.)
2.3.315:
By all means.
CURCULIO
Prithee, what’s this you’re about.
PHAEDROMUS
Some air.
CURCULIO
Really, for my part, I don’t want a breath to be raised.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.316:
What then?
CURCULIO
To eat, that I may rejoice on my arrival.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.318:
my mouth is bitter; my teeth, I find, are blunted; my jaws are clammy through fasting; with my entrails thus lank with abstinence from food am I come.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.320:
You shall eat something just now.
CURCULIO
I’ faith, I don’t want something; I’d rather have what’s fixed for certain, than your something.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.321:
Aye, but if you only knew what has been put by for you.
CURCULIO
I’d very much like to know where it is; for really it’s necessary for it and my teeth to make acquaintance.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.323:
A gammon of bacon, a sow’s stomach, some udder and kernels of the throat.
CURCULIO
What, all this do you say? Perhaps you mean that they are in the flesh-market?
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.324:
In the dishes, I mean; they’ve been got ready for you, since we knew that you were about to arrive.
CURCULIO
2.3.325:
Take care you don’t be fooling me.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.326:
So may the fair one love me whom I love, I don’t say what’s false. But as to what I sent you upon I’m none the wiser yet.
CURCULIO
2.3.330:
I saw your friend; I asked him to make me a loan of some money. In answer, you were to know that he was willing to oblige you; he didn’t wish to disappoint you, as it is only proper that a person who is a friend should be ready, and should assist his friend. In a few words he answered me, and quite in confidence, that he also was in the same extreme want of money as yourself.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.335:
By your words you ensure my undoing.
CURCULIO
Why no; I’m saving you, and wish you to be saved. After this answer was given me, I went away from him to the Forum, in sorrow that I had applied to him in vain. By accident I espied a military officer; this person I accosted, and as I approached I saluted him. Save you, said he to me, took my right hand, drew me aside, and asked me why I had come to Caria.
2.3.340: I said that I had come there for the sake of amusement. Upon this he asked me whether I knew a certain Lyco, a banker of Epidaurus. I said I knew him. Well, and the Procurer Cappadox? I answered yes, that I had seen him. But what do you want of him? said I. Because, said he, I bought of him a girl for thirty minae, her clothes and golden jewels too; and for these last ten minae more are added.
2.3.345: Have you paid the money? said I. No, said he; it is lodged with this Lyco the banker, whom I was mentioning, and I’ve instructed him that the person who should bring a letter sealed with my own ring, to him he was to give his services, that he might receive the damsel, with her jewels of gold and her clothes, from the Procurer. After he told me this, I was going away from him. At once he called me back,
2.3.350: invited me to dinner; it was a point of conscience, I was unwilling to refuse him. What if we go off home, and take our places at table? said he. The suggestion pleased me; it is neither proper to lengthen out the day, nor to curtail the night. Everything was prepared, and we, for whom it was prepared, were at our places. After we had dined and well drunk, he asked for the dice to be fetched him.
2.3.355:
He challenged me to play with him a game of hazard. I staked my cloak, he staked his ring against it; he called on the name of Planesium.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.357:
What, my mistress?
CURCULIO
Be silent a while. He threw a most losing cast. I took up the dice, and invoked Hercules as my genial patron; I threw a first-rate cast, and pledged him in a bumping cup; in return he drank it off,
2.3.360:
reclined his head, and fell fast asleep. I slily took away from him the ring, and took my legs quietly from off the couch, so that the Captain mightn’t perceive it. The servants enquired whither I was going; I said that I was going whither persons when full are wont to go. When I beheld the door, at once on the instant I betook myself away from the place.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.364:
I commend you.
CURCULIO
Commend me when I’ve brought this thing about which you desire. Now let’s go indoors, that we may seal the letter.
PHAEDROMUS
2.3.366: But let’s cram down something first, the gammon, the udder, and the kernels; these are the foundations for the stomach, with bread and roast beef, a good-sized cup and a capacious pot, that counsel enough may be forthcoming. Do you, yourself, seal the letter; he’ll do the honors (pointing to PALINURUS) while I am eating.
2.3.370:
I’ll dictate after what fashion you’re to write. Follow me this way, in-doors.
PHAEDROMUS
I follow.
(They go into the house of PHAEDROMUS.)

3.1.371:
(Enter LYCO.) LYCO
I seem to be in opulence; I’ve struck my balance, how much money I have, and how much I owe. I’m rich, if I don’t pay those to whom I’m in debt. If I do pay those to whom I’m in debt, my debts are the greatest.
3.1.375: But really, upon my faith, when I carefully consider, if they press me hard, I’ll resort to the Praetor. Most bankers have this habit, for one to borrow of the other, and to pay nobody, and to discharge the debt with their fists, if any one duns in a loudish tone.
3.1.380:
The person that has in a short time acquired wealth, unless in good time he saves it, in good time comes to starvation. I’d like to buy a servant for myself, who now, however, must be sought by me on hire: there’s occasion for my ready money.
(within.)
CURCULIO
3.1.384: Don’t you be reminding me now I’m full; I recollect and understand.
3.1.385:
I’ll render up to you all this cleverly carried out; do hold your peace. I’ faith, I’ve surely filled myself in-doors right well, and still in my stomach I’ve left room for one corner, in which to stow away the remnants of these remnants.
(Seeing LYCO.)
3.1.389: Who’s this that with covered head is saluting Aesculapius? Heyday, the very man I wanted. (To an ATTENDANT.) Follow me.
3.1.391:
I’ll make pretence as though I didn’t know him. (Aloud.) Hark you; I want you.
LYCO
(turning round.)
3.1.392:
One-eyed man, save you.
CURCULIO
Prithee, do you jeer me?
LYCO
3.1.393:
I suppose that you are of the family of the Coclites; for they are one-eyed.
CURCULIO
3.1.394: This was knocked out for me by a catapulta,
3.1.395:
at Sicyon.
LYCO
What matters it to me, pray, if it had been knocked out by a broken pot with cinders in it?
CURCULIO
(aside.)
3.1.397:
This fellow’s a wizard, surely; he tells the truth, for such catapultas are often directed at me.
(Aloud.)
3.1.399:
Young man, as I bear this mark on my face in the service of the public, prithee don’t be uncivil to me.
LYCO
3.1.401:
May I then inforize you, if I may not incomitiatize?
CURCULIO
3.1.402: You shan’t be inforizing me, indeed; and really I don’t care at all about your Forum or your Comitia. But if you can point me out this person that I’m seeking,
3.1.405:
you will be doing me a real and a great service. I’m looking for Lyco the banker.
LYCO
3.1.406:
Tell me why you are now seeking for him, or, of what country are you?
CURCULIO
3.1.407:
I’ll tell you: I’m come from Therapontigonus Platagidorus, the Captain.
LYCO
3.1.409: I’ faith, I know the name: (aside) for with that same name,
3.1.410:
when I wrote, I filled four whole sides. (To CURCULIO.) But why are you seeking for Lyco?
CURCULIO
(showing the letter.)
3.1.411:
I’ve been ordered to deliver this letter to him.
LYCO
3.1.413:
His freed-man, whom all call Summanus.
LYCO
3.1.414:
Summanus, my greetings. But why Summanus? Let me know.
CURCULIO
3.1.415:
Because, when in my drunken fit I’ve gone to sleep, I summane the garments; for that reason do all people call me Summanus.
LYCO
3.1.417:
’Twere better for you to look out for entertainment for you somewhere else; really in my own house I have no room for a Summanus. But I am the person that you are looking for.
CURCULIO
3.1.420:
Lyco the banker?
LYCO
I am.
CURCULIO
Therapontigonus requested me to give you a hearty greeting, and to deliver this letter.
LYCO
3.1.422:
What, to me?
CURCULIO
Just so. Take it, recognize the seal. Do you know it? (LYCO takes the letter.)
LYCO
3.1.423:
Why should I not know it? On which, a man, holding a shield, is cleaving an elephant asunder with a sword.
CURCULIO
3.1.425:
What’s written there he bade me request you to do immediately, if you wished for his esteem.
LYCO
3.1.427:
Step aside; I’ll look what’s written in it.
CURCULIO
(stepping aside.)
By all means, at your pleasure, so long as I receive of you that which I’m come for.
LYCO
(reads.)
3.1.429: Therapontigonus Platagidorus, the Captain, his guest, sends to his host Lyco, at Epidaurus,
3.1.431:
right hearty greeting.
CURCULIO
(aside.)
This fellow’s my own; he’s swallowing the hook.
LYCO
(going on.)
3.1.432: I beg and request of you that, the person who delivers this letter to you, to him be given up the girl whom I purchased there (which I did there in your presence, and you being the negotiator),
3.1.435:
and the golden trinkets and clothes as well. You know already how it was agreed upon. You give the money to the Procurer, and give the young woman to this person. (To CURCULIO.) Where is he himself? Why doesn’t he come?
CURCULIO
3.1.437: I’ll tell you; because it is but four days since we arrived in Caria, from India; there he now intends to order a solid golden statue
3.1.440:
to be made of Philippean gold, which is to be seven feet high—a memorial of his exploits.
LYCO
3.1.442:
For what reason this?
CURCULIO
I’ll tell you; why, because within twenty days he singly has subdued the Persians, Paphlagonians, Sinopians, Arabians, Cretans, Syrians, Rhodia and Lycia, Peredia and Bibesia,
3.1.445:
Centauromachia and Classia Unomammia, and all Libya, and all Conterebromia; one half even of all nations has he conquered unaided in twenty days.
LYCO
3.1.449:
Dear me!
CURCULIO
Why are you surprised?
LYCO
Why, because if all these people were penned up in a cage
3.1.450:
as close as chickens, even so they couldn’t be encompassed in a year. Upon my faith, I do believe that you are come from him; for you do jabber such nonsense.
CURCULIO
3.1.455:
and lo, I see (from his house.) Save you, Procurer.
CAPPADOX
May the Gods prosper you.
LYCO
3.1.456:
Do you know what this is about which I’m come to you?
CAPPADOX
Say on what you please.
LYCO
3.1.457:
You are to receive the money, and to send away the young woman with him. (Pointing to CURCULIO.)
CAPPADOX
3.1.458:
But what if I’m bound on oath to another?
LYCO
What matters that to you, so long as you get the money?
CAPPADOX
3.1.459:
He who advises is as good as an accomplice. Do you follow.
CURCULIO
3.1.461:
Procurer, take care that you don’t cause me any delay.
(They go into the house of CAPPADOX.)

4.1.462:
(Enter the CHOREGUS, as CHORUS.) THE CHOREGUS
By my faith, Phaedromus has cleverly met with this clever rogue; but whether a salt-water rogue or a dry-land one I’m the rather to say he is, I really don’t know. The costume that I’ve lent I fear I shan’t get back.
4.1.465: Although I have nothing whatever to do with him (I trusted Phaedromus himself), still I’ll keep an eye upon him. But until he comes out of doors, I’ll point out in what place you may easily meet with each person, that he mayn’t lose his labour through too much trouble, if any one wishes to meet either a rascal or one without rascality, or an honest man or a dishonest one.
4.1.470: He who desires to meet with a perjured fellow, let him go into the courts of law; he who wants a liar and a braggart, near the rites of Cloacina. The rich and erring husbands seek you at the magisterial halls of the Basilica. There, too, will be the worn-out harlots, and those who are wont to haggle for them. Contributors to pic-nic dinners you’ll find in the fishmarket.
4.1.475: In the lower part of the Forum good men and opulent do walk; in the middle, near the canal, there are the mere puffers-off. Beyond the lake of Curtius are impudent, talkative, and malevolent fellows, who boldly, without reason, utter calumnies about another, and who, themselves, have sufficient that might with truth be said against them.
4.1.480: There, at the old shops, are these who lend and those who borrow at interest. Behind the Temple of Castor there are those to whom unguardedly you may be lending to your cost. There, in the Etrurian street, are those men who hold themselves on sale. In the Velabrum you’ll find either baker, or butcher, or soothsayer; either those who sell retail themselves, or supply to others things to be sold by retail.
4.1.485:
Rich sinning husbands you’ll find at the house of Oppian Leucadia. But, meantime, the door makes a noise; I must curb my tongue.
(Exit.)

4.2.487:
(Enter, from the house of CAPPADOX, CURCULIO, leading PLANESIUM, followed by LYCO and CAPPADOX.) CURCULIO
Maiden, do you go before; what is behind me I cannot keep my eye upon. Both the trinkets of gold, and all the clothing that she had, were his own, he said.
CAPPADOX
4.2.489:
No one is going to deny it.
CURCULIO
Still, however, it’s somewhat better for me to remind you.
LYCO
4.2.490:
Remember that you’ve undertaken, that, if any one should assert in course of law that she’s properly free, all the money is to be returned to me-thirty minae.
CAPPADOX
4.2.492:
I shall remember; be easy about that; and now I say the same.
CURCULIO
4.2.493:
But I wish you to remember this well.
CAPPADOX
4.2.496: who, if anything’s entrusted them, deny it upon oath? You Procurers dispose of what belongs to others, you give liberty to what belongs to others, and what belongs to others your give your commands to; no guarantee of ownership is there in the transfer to yourselves, nor are you yourselves guarantees to another person. The race of Procurers, among mortals, in my way of thinking at least,
4.2.500:
are just like flies, gnats, bugs, lice, and fleas—a plague, a mischief, and a nuisance; you are of no serviceable use, and no respectable person dares to stand with you in the Forum; he that does associate with you, they censure him, he’s spat upon and abused; they say that he has lost his property and his honor, although he has done nothing at all.
LYCO
4.2.505:
Upon my faith, my clever one-eyed friend, in my way of thinking, you are well acquainted with the Procurers.
CURCULIO
4.2.506: You bankers, i’ faith, I put and place in the same rank; you are the very counterparts of them. They, at least, are on sale in dark corners, you in the very Forum. You tear men to pieces with usury, they by persuading them amiss and by means of their dens. Full many a proposed statute has the public confirmed on your account,
4.2.510:
which when confirmed you break; some loophole you find out; just as boiling water becomes cold, so do you deem the laws.
LYCO
(aside.)
4.2.512:
I’d rather I’d held my tongue.
CAPPADOX
Not wrongfully, and with good reason, are you abusive against them.
CURCULIO
4.2.513: If abuse is uttered against those who deserve it not, that I do hold to be abuse; but if it is uttered against those who are deserving, it is fair censure, in my way of thinking, at least.
4.2.515:
I care nothing about your warranty, nor about any other Procurer whatever. Lyco, do you want anything with me?
LYCO
4.2.516:
Heartily fare you well.
CURCULIO
Farewell. (Going.)
CAPPADOX
Hark you! I say to you—
CURCULIO
4.2.517:
Say on; what do you want?
CAPPADOX
Prithee do you take care that all’s well with her (pointing to PLANESIUM); I’ve brought her up in my house carefully and in chastity.
CURCULIO
4.2.518:
If you have such compassion for her, pray, what would you give for it to be all well with her?
CAPPADOX
4.2.519:
A plaguy mishap for yourself.
CURCULIO
You need take due care on that score about yourself.
CAPPADOX
(to PLANESIUM, who is weeping.)
4.2.520:
Why, simpleton, do you cry? Don’t be afraid; upon my faith, I’ve sold you favourably. Take care, will you, and be a good girl; now prettily accompany him, pretty one.
LYCO
4.2.522:
Summanus, do you want anything with me at present?
CURCULIO
Fare you well, and health attend you. (Aside.) For you’ve kindly given me your services and your money.
LYCO
4.2.524:
Give abundant greetings to my patron.
CURCULIO
I’ll give them.
(Exit with PLANESIUM.)
LYCO
4.2.525:
Procurer, do you wish for anything?
CAPPADOX
Give me those ten minae for me to manage for myself with, until things are better with me.
LYCO
4.2.526:
They shall be paid; order them to be fetched to-morrow.
(Exit.)
CAPPADOX
4.2.527: Since I’ve successfully finished the matter, I wish to return thanks here in the Temple. For long since, when a little girl, I bought her for ten minae; but him who sold her to me, never since then have I set eyes upon.
4.2.530:
I think he’s dead. What matters that to me? I’ve got the money. The man to whom the Gods are propitious, for him, no doubt, they throw gain in his way. Now will I give my attention to my devotions; it’s clear that he has a kind regard for me.
(Goes into the Temple.)

4.3.533:
(Enter THERAPONTIGONUS. and LYCO.) THERAPONTIGONUS
I’m come now, inflamed with wrath in no moderate degree, but with that same with which I’ve learned to deal destruction upon cities.
4.3.535:
At once now, unless this moment you make haste instantly to pay me the thirty minae which I left with you, make haste to lay down your life.
LYCO
4.3.537:
By my troth, to no little mischief do I now devote you, but to that same to which I am wont to devote that man to whom I owe nothing at all.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.539:
Don’t you be making yourself bold with me, or suppose that I shall be entreating you.
LYCO
4.3.540:
And you, indeed, shall never force me to pay you what has been paid, nor shall I give it you.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.541:
I thought this, when I entrusted you with it, that you would repay nothing at all.
LYCO
4.3.542:
Why then are you now asking it back of me?
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.543:
I wish to know to whom you have paid it.
LYCO
To your one-eyed freed-man; he said that he was called Summanus; I paid it to him, who brought me this sealed letter.
(Gives him the letter.)
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.545:
What letter of mine, what one-eyed freed-man, what people called Summanus are you dreaming about? I really have no freed-man at all.
LYCO
4.3.547:
You act more wisely than a portion of the military men who have freed-men, and then forsake them.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.549:
What have you done?
LYCO
What you requested me, I’ve done for your sake,
4.3.550:
that I mightn’t slight the messenger who had brought your seal’s impression.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.551:
More fool than fool were you to give credit to this letter.
LYCO
4.3.552:
To that by which matters both public and private are carried on ought I not to have given credit? I’ll be off; the money has been properly paid you. Warrior, farewell.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.554:
How—farewell?
LYCO
Fare you ill then, if you choose,—aye, all your life, so far as I’m concerned. (Exit.)
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.3.555: What shall I do now? Of what use is it that I have caused kings to obey me, if this obscure fellow is this day to laugh at me?

4.4.557:
(Enter CAPPADOX, from the Temple.) CAPPADOX
(to himself.)
The man to whom the Gods are propitious, they cannot, I think, be angered with him. After I ad finished my devotions, it then came into my mind, lest the banker should abscond, to go fetch the money,
4.4.560:
that I may make good cheer rather than he.
THERAPONTIGONUS
I had left my compliments for you at your house.
CAPPADOX
4.4.561:
Therapontigonus Platagidorus, save you; since you are come safe to Epidaurus this day, at my house—you won’t lick up one grain of salt.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.4.563:
You give me a kind invitation; things, however, are in a train for it to go badly with yourself. But how fares my purchase at your house?
CAPPADOX
4.4.564: Why, not at my house at all.
4.4.565:
Don’t be bringing your witnesses—assuredly, I don’t owe you anything.
THERAPONTIGONUS
How’s that?
CAPPADOX
4.4.566:
What I was bound on oath to do, I’ve done.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Will you give me up the girl or not, before I spit you with this sabre of mine, you whip-scoundrel?
CAPPADOX
4.4.568: I bid you go to perdition with all my heart; don’t you be terrifying me.
4.4.569:
She has been carried off; you shall be carried off hence away from me, beyond a doubt, if you persist in abusing me, to whom I owe nothing but a punishing.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.4.571:
What, threaten me with a punishing?
CAPPADOX
Aye, and by my troth, I’ll not be threatening, but I’ll give it, if you persist in being impertinent to me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.4.572: A Procurer, forsooth, threatening me; and are my combats in battle, so many in number, lying trodden under foot? But so may my sabre and my shield
4.4.575:
trustily aid me when fighting in the field; unless the girl is restored to me, I’ll at once cause the ants to carry you away piecemeal from this spot.
CAPPADOX
4.4.577: And so may my tweezers, my comb, my looking-glass, my crisping-iron, and my hair-scissors and scrubbing-towel love me well,
4.4.580:
I don’t value your high-sounding words, nor these big threats of yours, a bit the more than my servant-girl that washes out my sink. I’ve given her up to him who brought the money from you.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.4.582:
He said that he was Summanus, your freed-man.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Mine? You don’t say so; i’ faith, it’s that Curculio that has put a trick upon me, when I think upon it; he stole my ring from me.
CAPPADOX
(aside.)
4.4.584:
The Captain has been finely appointed to a cashiered company.
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.4.586:
Where now shall I find Curculio?
CAPPADOX
In some wheat with the greatest ease I’ll make you find even five hundred Curculios instead of one. Therefore I’m off; fare you well, and my service to you.
(Exit.)
THERAPONTIGONUS
4.4.588: Fare you ill, a plague attend you. What shall I do? Shall I stop or go away? That I should have been imposed upon in this way!
4.4.590:
I’d like to give a reward to him who would point out that fellow to me.
(Exit.)

5.1.591:
(Enter CURCULIO, with a ring, from the house of PHAEDROMUS.) CURCULIO
I’ve heard that an ancient Poet wrote in a Tragedy, that two women are worse than one; such is the fact. But a more crafty woman than is this mistress of Phaedromus, I never saw or heard of, nor, i’ faith, can one be spoken of or imagined;
5.1.595: she, as soon as ever she saw that I had got this ring, asked me whence I got it. Why do you ask that? said I. Because I’ve need to know, said she. I said I wouldn’t tell her. To get it away, she seized hold of my hand with her teeth. With much ado I betook me out of doors, and made my escape. Away with this slut.

5.2.599:
(Enter PLANESIUM, followed by PHAEDROMUS, from his house.) PLANESIUM
My Phaedromus, make haste.
PHAEDROMUS
Make haste for what?
PLANESIUM
That you mayn’t let the Parasite escape;
5.2.600:
the affair’s of consequence.
PHAEDROMUS
Nothing have I of consequence; for what I did have I quickly made away with?
(Seizes CURCULIO.)
5.2.601:
I’ve got him;
what’s the matter?
PLANESIUM
Ask him whence he got that ring: my father used to wear it.
CURCULIO
5.2.602:
Why, troth, and so did my aunt.
PLANESIUM
5.2.603:
My mother gave it him to wear.
CURCULIO
And your father, in his turn, to me.
PLANESIUM
5.2.604:
You are talking nonsense.
CURCULIO
I’m in the habit; for by reason of it I make a livelihood the more easily. What is the matter now?
PLANESIUM
5.2.605:
I entreat you, don’t be keeping me from finding my parents.
CURCULIO
5.2.606:
How can I? Have I got your father and mother hidden beneath the stone? (Holding up the ring.)
PLANESIUM
5.2.607:
I was born a free woman.
CURCULIO
And so were many others, who are now in servitude.
PLANESIUM
5.2.608:
Really now, I’m vexed.
CURCULIO
For my part, I’ve told you how this came into my possession. How often must you be told? I cheated the Captain at dice, I tell you.
(THERAPONTIGONUS.)
THERAPONTIGONUS
(eyeing CURCULIO.)
5.2.610:
I’m all right; see, here he is whom I was looking for. How do you do, good sir?
CURCULIO
I hear you; three casts of the dice, if you like, even for that scarf of yours.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.611:
Why don’t you go to very perdition, with your casts and catch-pennies? Either give me back the money or the young woman?
CURCULIO
(with an air of surprise.)
5.2.613:
What money? what rubbish are you talking about to me? What young woman are you demanding back of me?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.614:
The one that you took away this day from the Procurer, you scoundrelly fellow.
CURCULIO
5.2.615:
I took none away.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Why, surely, I see her. There she is. (Pointing to PLANESIUM.)
PHAEDROMUS
This young woman is free.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.616:
What, my female slave free, to whom I have never given her liberty?
PHAEDROMUS
5.2.617:
Who gave you possession of her, or of whom did you buy her? Let me know that?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.618:
Why, I paid the money for her through my banker—a sum which I’ll have refunded to me fourfold by you and the Procurer.
PHAEDROMUS
5.2.620:
You, who understand how to traffic in young women, kidnapped and of free birth, come you before the judge.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.621:
I shan’t come.
PHAEDROMUS
I may call my witness to the summons.
THERAPONTIGONUS
No, you mayn’t.
PHAEDROMUS
5.2.622:
May Jupiter then utterly confound you: live without witnesses then.
CURCULIO
5.2.623:
But I’m a person that he may summon.
PHAEDROMUS
(to CURCULIO.)
Do you step this way.
THERAPONTIGONUS
What? A slave summoned as a witness?
Take you care.
CURCULIO
5.2.624:
Well, that you may know it, I’m free.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Then come before the judge.
There’s for you: take that.
(Gives him a blow.)
CURCULIO
5.2.626:
O townsmen, townsmen, help.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Why do you bawl so?
PHAEDROMUS
What right have you to strike him?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.627:
Because I choose.
PHAEDROMUS
(to CURCULIO.)
Step this way you (pushes him towards the CAPTAIN); there, I’ll give him up to you. Hold your noise.
CURCULIO
5.2.628:
Phaedromus, prithee do save me.
PHAEDROMUS
As I would myself and my own good Genius. Captain, prithee, do tell me whence you got that ring,
5.2.630:
which this Parasite purloined from you.
PLANESIUM
(kneeling before the CAPTAIN.)
By your knees, I do entreat you to give us that information.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.631:
What matters that to you? You might as well ask after this sabre and this scarf, how each came into my possession.
CURCULIO
5.2.633:
What airs the swaggerer does give himself!
THERAPONTIGONUS
Send that fellow away (pointing to CURCULIO); then I’ll tell you all.
CURCULIO
5.2.634:
It’s nonsense what he says.
PHAEDROMUS
Prithee, do let me know.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.635:
I’ll tell you: (to PLANESIUM) get up. Listen to this matter, and give attention. My father Periphanes used to wear it.
PLANESIUM
5.2.637:
He, before he died, gave it to me as being his son, as it was right he should.
PLANESIUM
5.2.639:
And on that occasion he made me his heir.
PLANESIUM
O filial affection, do thou preserve me, since I have carefully preserved thee. Welcome, my brother.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.641:
How am I to believe that? Tell me, if you are speaking the truth, who was your mother?
PLANESIUM
5.2.643:
Cleobula.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Who was your nurse?
PLANESIUM
Archestrata.
5.2.644: Amid the sacred rites of Bacchus she had carried me to see the sights after we had come thither, when now she had found me a place, a whirlwind arose; the scaffolding of the stage there tumbled down; I was greatly alarmed, and then some one, I know not who, seized hold of me trembling and frightened, neither alive nor dead;
5.2.650:
and in what manner he carried me off I cannot say.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.651:
I recollect that disturbance happening; but, do you tell me, where is this person, who carried you away?
PLANESIUM
5.2.652:
I know not; but (showing a ring) this ring I have all along preserved by me, with it long since was I lost.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.654:
Give it me to look at.
CURCULIO
(to PLANESIUM.)
Are you in your senses to be trusting it to that fellow?
(Holds her arm.)
PLANESIUM
5.2.655:
Do you only leave me alone.
(She gives it to the CAPTAIN.)
THERAPONTIGONUS
(examining it.)
O Jupiter! This is the same that I presented you upon your birthday; I recognize it as easily as my own self. Welcome to you, my sister.
PLANESIUM
5.2.658:
My brother, welcome to you.
PHAEDROMUS
I trust the Gods will prosper this matter for you.
CURCULIO
5.2.659:
And I, for all of us.
(To the CAPTAIN.)
5.2.660:
Do you, as having this day arrived, give a dinner in honor of your sister he (pointing to PHAEDROMUS), to-morrow, will give one in honor of his marriage; we promise that.
PHAEDROMUS
(to CURCULIO.)
5.2.662:
Do you hold your tongue.
CURCULIO
I shan’t hold my tongue, as things are turning out so well. Captain, do you promise her to him; I’ll give the marriage-portion.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.664:
What is the marriage-portion?
CURCULIO
What, that I give? Why, that always as long as he lives he’s to feed me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.665:
I’ troth, he says what’s fair;
with my consent you shall do so.
5.2.666:
But this Procurer owes me the thirty minae.
PHAEDROMUS
5.2.667:
For what reason so?
THERAPONTIGONUS
Because he agreed with me on these terms to give it back: that if any one should assert her to be free born in due course of law, he would, without dispute, pay back all the money.
CURCULIO
5.2.670:
Then let’s go to the Procurer.
THERAPONTIGONUS
I agree.
PHAEDROMUS
This first I wish; to despatch my matter.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.671:
What’s that?
PHAEDROMUS
That you will betroth her to me.
(The CAPTAIN considers.)
CURCULIO
5.2.672:
Why do you hesitate, Captain, to give her as a wife to him?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.2.673:
If she is agreable.
PLANESIUM
My brother, it is my wish.
THERAPONTIGONUS
So be it then.
CURCULIO
You do rightly.
PHAEDROMUS
5.2.674:
Captain, do you betroth me to her for my wife?
THERAPONTIGONUS
I do betroth her.
PHAEDROMUS
(pointing to CURCULIO.)
5.2.675:
And to him do I promise support at my expense.
CURCULIO
You do kindly. But
THER,
5.2.676: But see, here’s the Procurer coming; my treasurer, I mean.

5.3.680: I say it’s neither good nor bad for them to be trusted, and that, I’ve fully experienced this day. They are not badly trusted, who never repay, but with whom it is lost outright. As for example, before this Lyco paid me the ten minae, he had to go to every banker’s counter. After there were no proceeds, I summoned the fellow with much noise; he appealed against me to the court. I was most confoundedly afraid that this day he’d be settling accounts with me before the Praetor;
5.3.685:
but my friends forced him, so he paid the money at home. Now I’m resolved to make haste to my house.
(Runs towards his door.)
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.686:
Hallo! you Procurer; I want you.
PHAEDROMUS
5.3.687:
And I want you.
CAPPADOX
But I don’t want either of you.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Stay this instant, will you.
PHAEDROMUS
5.3.688:
And make you haste to disgorge the money with all despatch.
CAPPADOX
(to PHAEDROMUS.)
What have you to do with me? (To the CAPTAIN.) Or what have you?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.689: Because this day I shall be making a javelin of you, discharged from a catapulta,
5.3.690:
and twist you with the string, just as the catapultas are in the habit of doing.
PHAEDROMUS
5.3.691:
I’ll this day make a coxcomb of you, to be sleeping with a puppy in your bed—an iron one, I mean.
CAPPADOX
5.3.692:
But I’ll make you both to be rotting in a strong-barred prison.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.693:
Seize him by the throat, and away with him to extreme torture.
PHAEDROMUS
5.3.694:
However that is, he’ll be going there of his own accord.
(The CAPTAIN seizes him.)
CAPPADOX
O Gods and men, your aid!
5.3.695:
that I, uncondemned, and without evidence against me, should thus be dragged along! Prithee, Planesium, and you, Phaedromus, do give me assistance.
PLANESIUM
5.3.697:
Brother, I do beseech you, don’t ruin him uncondemned; he treated me kindly and modestly at his house.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.698: That was through no inclination of his own; give you thanks to this Aesculapius (pointing to the Temple) that you’ve preserved your chastity;
5.3.700:
for if he had been well, he’d long ago have packed you off wherever he could.
PHAEDROMUS
5.3.701:
Now attend to me, both of you, if I can arrange between you. (To the CAPTAIN.) You let him go. Procurer, come you this way. I’ll pronounce my opinion, if indeed you are ready to abide by what I shall decide you should do.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.703:
We leave it to you.
(He lets go of the PROCURER.)
CAPPADOX
5.3.704:
So long, i’ faith, as you give a decision to the effect that no one is to take the money away from me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.705:
What, not that which you promised?
CAPPADOX
I, promised? How?
THERAPONTIGONUS
With your tongue.
CAPPADOX
With that same tongue I now gainsay it; that was given me by Nature for the purpose of speaking, not of losing my property.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.707:
He’s trifling; seize the fellow by the throat.
(Seizes him.)
CAPPADOX
I’ll at once then do as you bid me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.708:
Since you are an honest man, answer me this that I ask you.
CAPPADOX
Ask me what you please.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.709: Did you not promise, that if any one should show that she (pointing to PLANESIUM) was freeborn,
5.3.710:
you would pay back all the money?
CAPPADOX
I don’t remember saying so.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.711:
What, do you deny it?
CAPPADOX
I’ faith, I really do deny it. In whose presence? In what place was it?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.712:
In my own presence, and that of Lyco the banker.
CAPPADOX
Why don’t you hold your tongue?
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.713:
I shan’t hold my tongue.
CAPPADOX
I don’t care a rush for you; don’t be bullying me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.714:
In my own presence and that of Lyco it took place.
PHAEDROMUS
(to the CAPTAIN.)
I quite believe you.
5.3.715:
Now, therefore, Procurer, that you may know my judgment, (pointing to PLANESIUM) she is a free woman; he (pointing to the CAPTAIN) is her brother, and she is his sister; she is engaged to me; do you restore him the money; that’s my decision.
CAPPADOX
5.3.719: Upon my faith, Phaedromus, you have given this decision corruptly.
5.3.720:
It shall both be bad for you, and you, Captain,—may the Gods and Goddesses confound you.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.718:
And as for you, you shall be clapt in prison at once, unless the money’s returned me.
CAPPADOX
5.3.721:
Then follow me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
Follow you where?
CAPPADOX
To my banker—to the Praetor; for it’s there that I pay my money to all persons to whom I’m indebted.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.723:
I’ll be carrying you hence to prison, and not to the Praetor, if you don’t pay back the money.
CAPPADOX
5.3.724:
I do most earnestly wish you may come to a bad end, so don’t misunderstand me.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.725:
Do you really so?
CAPPADOX
I’ faith, I really do so.
THERAPONTIGONUS
I don’t misunderstand these fists of mine.
(Holding them up.)
CAPPADOX
5.3.726:
What then?
THERAPONTIGONUS
What then, do you ask? With these same fists, if you provoke me, I’ll be making you quiet immediately.
CAPPADOX
(taking the money from his girdle.)
5.3.727:
Well then, take this back at once.
THERAPONTIGONUS
(taking the money.)
By all means.
PHAEDROMUS
5.3.728:
Captain, you’ll dine with me; the nuptials shall take place to-day.
THERAPONTIGONUS
5.3.729:
May this matter turn out well for me and for yourselves.
An ACTOR.
Spectators, give us your applause.

1.1.1:
(Enter THESPRIO, followed by EPIDICUS. EPIDICUS
(pulling THESPRIO by the cloak.)
Harkye! young man.
THESPRIO
Who pulls me by the cloak, when thus in haste?
EPIDICUS
1.1.2:
An intimate.
THESPRIO
I confess it; for with your annoyance you are too intimate.
EPIDICUS
1.1.3:
But do look back, Thesprio!
THESPRIO
(looking round.)
What? Is it Epidicus that I see?
EPIDICUS
1.1.5:
Why surely you’ve the use of your eyes.
THESPRIO
1.1.6:
Greetings to you.
EPIDICUS
May the Gods grant what you desire. I’m glad that you’ve got here safe.
THESPRIO
1.1.7:
What besides?
EPIDICUS
According to the usage, a dinner shall be given you.
THESPRIO
1.1.8:
I agree.
EPIDICUS
What to do?
THESPRIO
That I’ll accept it, if you offer it.
EPIDICUS
1.1.9:
How are you? Fare you as you could wish?
THESPRIO
The proof’s before you.
EPIDICUS
1.1.10:
Marvellous! You seem quite plump and hearty.
THESPRIO
(pointing to his left hand.)
Thanks to this.
EPIDICUS
1.1.11:
Which, indeed, you ought to have parted with long ago.
THESPRIO
1.1.12:
I’m less of a pilferer now than formerly.
EPIDICUS
How so?
THESPRIO
I rob above-board.
EPIDICUS
1.1.13: May the immortal Gods confound you, with what huge strides you do walk! for when I caught sight of you at the harbour, I began to run at a rapid pace;
1.1.15:
I was hardly able to overtake you just now.
THESPRIO
You are a town wit.
EPIDICUS
I know that you, on the other hand, are a military gentleman.
THESPRIO
1.1.16:
Speak out as boldly as you please.
EPIDICUS
1.1.17:
How say you? Have you been well all along?
THESPRIO
In a varied way.
EPIDICUS
Those who are well in a varied way, a race of men of the goat kind or of the panther kind, don’t please me.
THESPRIO
1.1.20:
how’s our master’s son? Is he well?
THESPRIO
Stout as a boxer and an athlete.
EPIDICUS
1.1.21:
You’ve brought me joyous tidings on your arrival. But where is he?
THESPRIO
1.1.22:
I came here together with him.
EPIDICUS
Where is he then? Unless, perchance, you’ve brought him in your wallet, or, perhaps, in your knapsack.
THESPRIO
1.1.23:
May the Gods confound you!
EPIDICUS
I want to make enquiries of you. Lend me your attention; attention shall be lent you in return.
THESPRIO
1.1.25:
You say what’s law.
EPIDICUS
It becomes me to do so.
THESPRIO
But why now are you acting the Praetor over us?
EPIDICUS
1.1.26:
What other person in Athens will you say is more deserving of it than I?
THESPRIO
But still, Epidicus, one thing is wanting for your Praetorship.
EPIDICUS
1.1.27:
What, pray?
THESPRIO
You shall know; two lictors two osier bundles of twigs—
EPIDICUS
(shaking his fist at him.)
1.1.28:
Woe unto you! But how say you—?
THESPRIO
1.1.29:
What is it you ask?
EPIDICUS
Where are the arms of Stratippocles?
THESPRIO
1.1.30:
I’ faith, they’ve gone over to the enemy.
EPIDICUS
What, his arms?
THESPRIO
Aye, and quickly too.
EPIDICUS
Do you say that seriously?
THESPRIO
1.1.31:
Seriously I say it; the enemy have got them.
EPIDICUS
1.1.32:
By my troth, a disgraceful affair.
THESPRIO
Still, before now, other persons have done the same. This affair will turn out to his honor.
EPIDICUS
1.1.33:
How so?
THESPRIO
Because it has been so to others before.
EPIDICUS
1.1.34: Mulciber, I suppose, made the arms which Stratippocles had;
1.1.35:
they flew over to the enemy.
THESPRIO
