that he may carry her off hence, and have her as his own.
PERIPLECOMENUS
I wish this plan to be imparted to me.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.771:
And I, wish that ring of yours to be imparted to me.
PERIPLECOMENUS
For what purpose is it to be used?
PALAESTRIO
3.2.772:
When I have got it, I will impart the plan of my devices.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.773:
Take and use it. (Gives him the ring.)
PALAESTRIO
Take from me in return the plan of my contrivance that I have hit upon.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.774:
We are listening to you with most attentive ear.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.775:
My master is such a shocking rake among the women, that I think no one ever was his equal, nor ever will be.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.776:
I believe the same as well.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.777:
He boasts, too, that his beauty exceeds that of Alexander; and, therefore, he says that all the women in Ephesus of their own accord are courting him.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.779: Aye, faith, many there are who could wish that you were now telling an untruth about him.
3.2.780:
But I am convinced full well that it is as you say. For that reason, Palaestrio, do compress your words in as short a compass as ever you possibly can.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.782:
Can you, then, find any woman of agreable person, whose mind and body are full of merriment and subtlety?
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.784:
Free by birth, or bondwoman made free?
PALAESTRIO
I consider that a matter of indifference, so that
3.2.785:
you find one who is greedy for gain, who supports her body by her charms, who has, too, her senses all awake; as for her heart, that cannot be so, as none of them have one.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.787:
Do you want one that has taken her degrees, or one as yet a novice in the art?
PALAESTRIO
One sober but plump, a juicy bit; as taking a one as ever you can find, and one very young.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.789: Why, I have one, a dependant of mine, a courtesan, a very young woman.
3.2.790:
But what is the occasion for her?
PALAESTRIO
For you to bring her home at once to your house as your wife, and, for that reason, to bring her there dressed out, so that she may wear her locks with her hair arranged, and fillets after the fashion of matrons, and may pretend that she is your wife; so you must instruct her.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.793:
I am at a loss what road you are taking.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.794:
Well, you shall know. But what sort of a maid has she?
PERIPLECOMENUS
She is a rare clever one.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.795:
We have need of her as well; so give your instructions to the damsel and her maid, to pretend that she is your wife and is doting upon this Captain; and as though she had given this ring to her maid, then she to me, that I might deliver it to the Captain; and I must be as though it were a go-between in this matter.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.798:
I hear you; don’t stun my ears as if I were deaf.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.800:
I myself will go straightway to him; I’ll say that it has been brought and delivered to me from your wife, in order that I might introduce her to him. He’ll be distractedly longing for her at home, a scoundrel that cares for nothing else whatever but intriguing.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.2.803:
If you had commissioned the Sun himself to search them out, he couldn’t have found, better than myself, two more cleverly suited for this business. Be of good courage about it.
PALAESTRIO
3.2.805:
Take you every care then. There is need of despatch.
(Exit PERIPLECOMENUS.)

3.3.805:
PALAESTRIO
Now, do you listen, Pleusicles.
PLEUSICLES
3.3.806:
I am all attention to you.
PALAESTRIO
Take care of this. When the Captain comes home, do you remember not to call Philocomasium by her name.
PLEUSICLES
3.3.807:
What am I to call her?
PALAESTRIO
3.3.808:
Glycera.
PLEUSICLES
The same, you mean, that was agreed upon a little time since.
PALAESTRIO
Hush!—Be off.
PLEUSICLES
3.3.809:
I’ll remember; but still I don’t know what use it is to keep it in my mind.
PALAESTRIO
3.3.810:
But I will tell you, at the time, when occasion shall require. Meanwhile, be quiet; so that, bye and bye, when he too shall be acting his part, you may, on the instant, be minding your cue.
PLEUSICLES
3.3.812:
I’ll go in then.
PALAESTRIO
Go, and do take care steadily to follow my instructions.
(PLEUSICLES goes into the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)
PALAESTRIO
3.3.813: What mighty turmoils I create! What mighty engines I do set to work! This very day I shall take his mistress away from the Captain,
3.3.815: if my soldiers are only well drilled. But I’ll call him out. (Goes to the door and calls.) Hallo! Sceledrus, if you are not busy, come out to the front of the house; I, Palaestrio, call you.

3.4.818:
(Enter LUCRIO from the CAPTAIN’s house.) LUCRIO
Sceledrus is not at leisure.
PALAESTRIO
Why so?
LUCRIO
He’s fast asleep, gulping.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.819:
How, gulping?
LUCRIO
He’s snoring, ’twas that I meant to say:
3.4.820:
but, because ’tis very like gulping when you are snoring—
PALAESTRIO
3.4.821:
What! Is Sceledrus asleep in-doors?
LUCRIO
Not with his nose, in fact; for with that he is calling out loud enough.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.823: He has taken a cup by stealth; the butler has lately tapped a cask of nardine.
3.4.824:
Oho! you rascal, you are his deputy-butler. Oho!
LUCRIO
3.4.826:
What do you mean?
PALAESTRIO
How has he thought fit to go to sleep?
LUCRIO
3.4.827:
With his eyes, I suppose.
PALAESTRIO
I don’t ask you that, you vagabond. Step this way: you’re undone now, unless I know the truth. Did you draw the wine for him?
LUCRIO
3.4.829:
I did not draw it.
PALAESTRIO
Do you deny it?
LUCRIO
3.4.830:
I’ faith, I do deny it undoubtedly; for he charged me not to tell. I really didn’t just draw for him eight half pints into a pitcher, and, when drawn, he didn’t just drink it hot, at his breakfast.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.833:
And you didn’t just drink as well?
LUCRIO
The Gods confound me if I did drink—if I could drink.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.835:
for it was too hot; it burnt my throat.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.836:
Some are gloriously drunk, while others are drinking vinegar-water. The cellar’s trusted to an honest butler, as well as under-butler.
LUCRIO
3.4.838: I’ faith, you’d be doing the same, if it was entrusted to you.
3.4.839:
Since you can’t follow our example, you are envious now.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.841:
Come, now, did he ever draw any wine before this? Answer me, you rascal. And, that you may understand it, I give you this notice: if you purposely tell me an untruth, you shall be put to the torture.
LUCRIO
3.4.844: Indeed so? That you may inform, forsooth, that I told you;
3.4.845:
and then I shall be turned out of my fattening post in the cellar, that you may find another under-butler to draw for your own self.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.847:
On my honour, I will not; come, speak out boldly to me.
LUCRIO
3.4.848:
By my troth, I never saw him draw any. But thus was it; he requested me, and then I drew it.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.850:
Think of that now! very frequently, I guess, the casks were standing on their heads there.
LUCRIO
3.4.851:
No, faith, the casks would not have stood so very badly there. But there happened to be in the cellar a bit of a slippery spot; a two-pint pot was placed there, near the casks, in this fashion
(shows the way.) Frequently, that was filled ten times in a day.
3.4.856:
When the pot acted the reveller, the casks were all tottering.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.857:
Get you gone in-doors. Both of you, I find, are acting the revellers in the wine-cellar. I’ faith, I shall fetch my master home just now from the Forum.
LUCRIO
(aside.)
3.4.859: I’m ruined. My master, when he comes home, will have me tortured,
3.4.860:
when he knows of these doings. I’ faith, I’ll fly somewhither, and put off this punishment to another day. (To the AUDIENCE.) don’t you tell him, I do entreat you most earnestly.
(He is going.)
PALAESTRIO
3.4.863:
Whither are you betaking yourself?
LUCRIO
I am sent elsewhere: I’ll come back here just now.
PALAESTRIO
3.4.864:
Who has sent you?
LUCRIO
Philocomasium.
PALAESTRIO
Go; be back directly.
LUCRIO
3.4.865:
If it is divided, prithee do you only take my share of the punishment while I’m away.
(Exit LUCRIO.)

3.5.867:
(PALAESTRIO, alone.) PALAESTRIO
So—I understand what scheme the lady is upon. Because Sceledrus is asleep, she has sent her under-keeper away out of doors, whilst she may pass from our house to next door. That’s all right.
3.5.870:
(Looks down the street.) But Periplecomenus is bringing here a woman of very comely appearance, her, for whom I commissioned him. By my faith, the Gods are helping us in this matter. How becomingly drest she struts along, not like a Courtesan. This business is prospering charmingly in our hands.
(Stands aside.)

3.6.874:
(Enter PERIPLECOMENUS, with ACROTELEUTIUM and MILPHIDIPPA.) PERIPLECOMENUS
(as he advances.)
I have explained the whole affair, Acroteleutium, to you, and, Milphidippa, to you as well.
3.6.875:
If you don’t well understand this device and plan, I wish you to hear it all over again. If you comprehend it aright, there is something else that we may speak of in preference.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.878: I’ faith, it would be folly, and ignorance, and foolishness, for me to engage in the service of another, or to promise you my assistance,
3.6.880:
if, in its fabrication, I did not know how to be either mischievous or clever at deceiving.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.881:
But, ’tis better for you to be instructed.
ACROTELEUTIUM
Really I don’t understand of what great use it is for a Courtesan to be instructed. How now! have I told you all in vain, after my ears had drunk in the draughts of your discourse, in what fashion it was possible for the Captain to be cajoled?
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.885:
But no one, unaided, is sufficiently perfect; for full oft have I seen many a person lose the road to good advice before they had found it.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.887: If a woman has anything to do mischievously and maliciously, in that case her memory is immortal at remembering it for everlasting; but if anything is to be done for a good purpose, or honestly,
3.6.890:
it will fall out that those same women will become oblivious that instant, and be unable to remember.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.891:
Therefore do I fear that same, because both those things happen to be about to be done by us; for that will be a benefit to me in which you both will be acting mischievously towards the Captain.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.893:
So long as we do anything that’s good, not knowing it, don’t you fear. No woman is awkward Have no apprehensions, they are ready for the worst.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.896:
So it befits you. Do you follow me.
PALAESTRIO
(advancing.)
Why do I hesitate to go and accost them?
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.898:
Well met, and opportunely, Palaestrio. See, here they are whom you commissioned me to bring, and in the very dress.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.897: I am glad that you have come safe. I’ faith, you bring them nicely dressed.
3.6.900:
Palaestrio salutes Acroteleutium.
ACROTELEUTIUM
Prithee, who’s this, that calls me so familiarly by name?
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.902:
Health to you, master-plotter.
PALAESTRIO
And health to you. But, tell me, has he any way given you full instructions?
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.903:
I bring them both thoroughly prepared.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.904:
I’d like to hear how. I’m afraid lest you should be making some mistake.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.905:
I have added to your instructions nothing new of my own.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.906:
I suppose you wish the Captain, your master, to be gulled.
PALAESTRIO
You’ve said what’s true.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.907:
Cleverly and skilfully, adroitly and pleasantly, the whole thing is planned.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.908:
In fact, I wish you to pretend to be his wife.
(Points to PERIPLECOMENUS.)
ACROTELEUTIUM
That shall be done.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.909:
To pretend as though you had set your affection on the Captain.
ACROTELEUTIUM
And so it shall be.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.910:
And as though this affair is managed through me, as the go-between, and your servant-maid.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.911:
You might have made a good prophet; for you tell what is to be.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.912:
As though this maid of yours had conveyed from you this ring to me, which I was then to deliver to the Captain, in your name.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.914:
What need is there to mention these things now, which they remember so well?
ACROTELEUTIUM
Still, it is better.
3.6.915: For think of this, my patron; when the shipwright is skilful, if he has once laid down the keel exact to its lines, ’tis easy to build the ship, when Now this keel of ours has been skilfully laid and firmly placed; the workmen and the master-builders are not unskilled in this business.
3.6.920:
If he who furnishes the timber does not retard us in giving what is needed, I know the adroitness of our ingenuity—soon will the ship be got ready.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.922:
You know the Captain, my master, then?
ACROTELEUTIUM
’Tis strange you should ask me. How could I not know that scorn of the public, that swaggering, frizzle-headed, perfumed debauchee?
PALAESTRIO
3.6.924:
But does he know you?
ACROTELEUTIUM
He never saw me: how, then, should he know who I am?
PALAESTRIO
3.6.925:
’Tis most excellent what you say. For that reason, i’ faith, the thing will be able to be managed all the more cleverly.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.926:
Can you only find me the man, and then be easy as to the rest? If I don’t make a fool of the fellow, do you lay all the blame on me.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.928:
Well, go you in then; apply yourselves to this business with all your skill.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.930:
Come, Periplecomenus, do you conduct them at once in-doors. I’m off to the Forum; I’ll meet him, and give him this ring, and will tell him that it has been delivered to me from your wife, and that she is dying for him. As soon as we shall have come from the Forum, do you send her
(points to MILPHIDIPPA) to our house as though she were privately sent to him.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.934:
We’ll do so; trust us for that.
PALAESTRIO
3.6.935:
Do you only attend to the business; I’ll now polish him off with a pretty burden on his back.
(Exit.)
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.936: Go, with good luck to you, manage the matter cleverly. (To ACROTELEUTIUM.) But now, if I shall manage this adroitly, that my guest can this day gain the mistress of the Captain, and carry her off hence to Athens; if, I say, this day we shall succeed in this plan,
3.6.939:
what shall I give you for a present?
ACROTELEUTIUM
If now the lady seconds our efforts on her part,
3.6.941:
I think it will be right cleverly and adroitly managed.
When a comparison shall be made of our artifices, I have no fear that I shall not prove superior in the cleverness of my contrivances.
PERIPLECOMENUS
3.6.944: Let’s go in-doors, then, that we may deeply weigh these plans,
3.6.945:
that carefully and cautiously we may carry out what is to be done, so that, when the Captain comes, there may be no tripping.
ACROTELEUTIUM
3.6.946:
You are delaying us with your talk.
(They go into the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)

4.1.947:
(Enter PYRGOPOLINICES and PALAESTRIO.) PYRGOPOLINICES
’Tis a pleasure what you do, if it succeeds agreably and to your mind. For I this day have sent my Parasite to King Seleucus, to lead those soldiers, that I have levied, hence to Seleucus;
4.1.950:
in order that they may defend his kingdom till I have leisure to attend in person.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.951:
Why don’t you attend to your own concerns rather than those of Seleucus. What a charming new proposal is being offered to you through me as the negotiator.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.953:
Well then, I lay all other things aside, and I give my attention to you. Speak out: my ears, in fact, I surrender at your disposal.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.955:
Look around, then, that no one here may be an eavesdropper for our discourse; for this business was entrusted me to transact with you in private.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.957:
(looks around). There’s no one near.
PALAESTRIO
In the first place, receive from me this pledge of affection. (Gives him the ring.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.958:
What’s this? Whence comes it?
PALAESTRIO
From a charming and a handsome lady, one who loves you, and dotes upon your extreme beauty.
4.1.960:
Her maid just now gave me the ring that I might then give it to you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.961:
What? Is she free born or a freed woman, made free from a slave by the Praetor’s rod?
PALAESTRIO
4.1.962:
Pshaw! Should I presume to be the bearer of a message to you from a person once a slave, who cannot sufficiently answer the demands of the free women who are longing for you?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.964:
Is she wife, or is she widow?
PALAESTRIO
She is both wife and widow.
PYRGOPOLINICES
In what way is it possible for the same woman to be a wife and a widow?
PALAESTRIO
4.1.966:
Because she is a young woman married to an old man.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.967:
That’s good.
PALAESTRIO
She is of genteel and charming person.
PYRGOPOLINICES
Beware of misrepresenting.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.968:
It is alone worthy to be compared with your own charms.
PYRGOPOLINICES
By my faith, you make her out to be a beauty. But who is she?
PALAESTRIO
4.1.969: The wife of that old gentleman, Periplecomenus, next door.
4.1.970:
She is dying for you, and wishes to leave him; she hates the old fellow. Now she has begged me to entreat and beseech you that you will give her your support and assistance.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.972:
I’ faith, I’m ready for my part if she desires it.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.973:
Doesn’t she long for it?
PYRGOPOLINICES
What shall we do with that mistress of mine, who is at my house?
PALAESTRIO
4.1.974: Why, do you bid her to be gone about her business, wherever she chooses; as her
4.1.975:
twin-sister has come here to Ephesus, and her mother, and they are come to fetch her.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.976:
Ha! what’s that you say? Has her mother come to Ephesus?
PALAESTRIO
Those say so who know it.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.977:
I’ faith, a charming opportunity for me to turn the wench out of doors.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.978:
Aye, but do you wish to do the thing handsomely?
PYRGOPOLINICES
Speak out, and give me your advice.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.979:
Do you wish to pack her off forthwith, that she may quit you with a good grace?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.980:
I do so wish.
PALAESTRIO
Then this is the thing you must do. You have a superabundance of wealth; bid the woman to keep as a present for herself the gold and trinkets which you have supplied her with, and to take herself off from your house wherever she likes.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.983:
It pleases me what you say; but yet, only think, if I should lose her, and the other change her mind?
PALAESTRIO
4.1.984:
Pshaw! you’re over nice; a lady, that loves you as her own eyes.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.985:
Venus befriends me.
PALAESTRIO
Hist! hush! the door is opening; come this way a little out of sight. (MILPHIDIPPA comes out of the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.) This is her fly-boat—her go-between, that’s coming out there.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.987:
How so—fly-boat?
PALAESTRIO
This is her maid that is coming out of the house, she that brought that ring which I delivered to you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.1.988:
I’ faith, she too is a prettyish wench.
PALAESTRIO
4.1.989: This one is a little monkey and an owl in comparison with the other.
4.1.990:
Do you see how she hunts around with her eyes, and goes fowling about with her ears.
(They stand aside.)

4.2.991:
(Enter MILPHIDIPPA.) MILPHIDIPPA
(as she enters.)
My Circus, then, is before the house, where my sports are to take place. I’ll make pretence, as though I didn’t see them, or knew as yet that they are here.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.993:
Hush! let’s quietly listen, whether any mention is made of me.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.2.994: Is there no one near at hand here, to attend to another’s business rather than his own?—
4.2.995:
to prowl after me to see what I’m about? No one who is feeding this evening at his own expense? I dread such men as these, lest they should now come in the way, or prove an hindrance somehow, should my mistress privately pass from her house this way, who is so enamoured of his person, who so dotes upon this very charming man with his exceeding beauty—the Captain Pyrgopolinices
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.999:
And doesn’t she dote upon me, too? She is praising my beauty.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1000:
I’ faith, her language stands in need of no ashes.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1001:
For what reason?
PALAESTRIO
Why, because her language is clean spoken and far from slovenly.
4.2.1002: Whatever she says about yourself, she handles it in no slovenly way.
4.2.1003:
And, then, besides, she herself is a very pretty and a very dainty wench.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1004:
Troth, indeed, she has made an impression already, Palaestrio, at first sight.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1005:
What! before you have seen the other with your eyes?
PYRGOPOLINICES
What I see, in that I have faith for myself; for this mackerel, in the absence of the mullet, compels me to be in love with her.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1006:
I’ faith, you really mustn’t be falling in love with her, she’s engaged to me. If the other weds you to-day, forthwith I shall take this one for my wife.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1008:
Why, then, do you delay to accost her?
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1009:
Follow me this way, then.
PYRGOPOLINICES
I am your lackey at your heels.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
I wish that I had an opportunity of meeting him on account of whom I came here out of doors.
PALAESTRIO
(accosting her.)
4.2.1011:
It shall be so, and you shall have what you so greatly wish; be of good courage, don’t fear; there is a certain person who knows where that is which you are seeking.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1012:
Who’s that I hear at hand?
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1013:
The sharer of your plans and the partaker of your secrets.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1014:
I’ faith, then, what I do conceal I don’t conceal.
PALAESTRIO
Aye, but still you don’t conceal it this way.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1015:
How so?
PALAESTRIO
From the uninitiated you conceal them. I am sure and trustworthy to you.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1016:
Give me the sign, if you are one of these votaries.
PALAESTRIO
A certain lady loves a certain gentleman.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1017:
Faith, many ladies do that indeed.
PALAESTRIO
But not many ladies send a present from off their fingers.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1018:
Aye, I know now. You’ve now made the matter level for me instead of steep. But is there a certain person here?
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1019:
Either he is or he is not.
MILPHIDIPPA
Come aside with me alone, in private.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1020:
For a short or for a lengthy conversation?
MILPHIDIPPA
For three words only.
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
I’ll return to you this instant.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1021:
What? Shall I be standing here in the meanwhile, with such charms and valorous deeds, thus to no purpose?
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1022:
Submit to it and wait; for you am I doing this service.
PYRGOPOLINICES
Make haste; I am tortured with waiting.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1023:
You know that commodities of this kind are only wont to be reached step by step.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1024:
Well, well; as is most agreable to yourself.
PALAESTRIO
(aside.)
There is no stone more stupid than this fellow. I now return to you.
4.2.1025:
(To MILPHIDIPPA.) What would you with me?
(Retires with her to distance.)
MILPHIDIPPA
In the way in which I received it of you a short time since, I bring you back your clever lot;
4.2.1026:
my story is as though she were dying with love for him.
PALAESTRIO
That I understand.
4.2.1027:
Do you commend his beauty and his appearance, and make mention of his prowess.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1028: For that purpose I am armed at all points, as I have shown you before already.
4.2.1029:
On the other hand, do you give all attention, and be on the watch, and take your cue from my words.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1030:
Prithee do now, in fine, give me some share in the business; step this way this instant, I beg.
PALAESTRIO
(goes up to him.)
4.2.1031:
Here I am. If you wish for aught, give me your commands.
PYRGOPOLINICES
What is she saying to you?
PALAESTRIO
She is saying that her mistress is lamenting, and, in tears, is tormenting and afflicting herself because she wishes for you, and because she possesses you not; for that reason has she been sent here to you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1034:
Bid her approach.
PALAESTRIO
But do you know how you are to act? Pretend that you are full of disdain,
4.2.1035:
as though it pleased you not; exclaim against me, because I make you so common to the mob.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1036:
I remember, and I’ll follow your instructions.
PALAESTRIO
I’ll call her, then, who is inquiring after you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1037:
If she wants anything, let her come.
PALAESTRIO
Wench, if you want anything, step this way.
MILPHIDIPPA
(approaching.)
Save you, charmer.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1038:
She makes mention of my surname. May the Gods grant you whatever you may desire.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1039:
To pass life with you is the wish of—
PYRGOPOLINICES
You are wishing too much.
MILPHIDIPPA
I am not speaking of myself, but of my mistress, who is dying for you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1040:
Many others are wishing for the same thing, who have not the opportunity.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1041:
By my troth, ’tis not to be wondered at; you set a high value on yourself—a person so handsome, and so illustrious for his prowess, and so valorous in his deeds! O! was there ever any one more worthy to be a man?
PALAESTRIO
(aside.)
4.2.1043:
I’ faith, the filthy fellow is not a human being; indeed, I think there is something more human in a vulture.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(aside.)
4.2.1044: Now I shall make myself of importance,
4.2.1045:
since she so praises me up.
(Struts about.)
PALAESTRIO
(aside.)
Do you see the blockhead, how he struts? (To PYRGOPOLINICES.) But will you not answer her; she is the woman that’s come from the lady whom I was mentioning just now.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1047:
But from which one of them? For there are so many courting me, I cannot remember them all.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1048:
From her who strips her own fingers and adorns your fingers; for I delivered to him
(pointing to PALAESTRIO) that ring from her who is sighing for you, and then he to you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1050:
Tell me, wench, what is it you want then?
MILPHIDIPPA
That you will not despise her who is sighing for you; who lives now but in your life: whether she is to exist or not, her hope is in you alone.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1052:
What does she want then?
MILPHIDIPPA
To talk with you, to embrace you, and to be intimate with you. For unless you bring her succour, she will soon be quite desponding in her mind. Come, my Achilles, let that be done which I entreat; save her, charmer, by your charming ways.
4.2.1055:
Call forth your kind disposition, stormer of cities, slayer of kings.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1056:
O! by my troth, ’tis a vexatious thing! (To PALAESTRIO.) How often, whip-scoundrel, have I forbidden you to make promises of my attention thus common.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1057:
Do you hear that, hussy? I have told you already, and I now tell you again, unless a fee is given to this boar-pig, he cannot possibly throw away his attentions in any quarter.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1061:
A fee shall be given, as large as he shall demand.
PALAESTRIO
He requires a talent of gold, in Philippean pieces. Less he will take from no one.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1062:
O, by my troth, but that’s too little, surely.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1063:
By nature there’s no avarice in me; I have riches enough. I’ faith! I’ve more than a thousand measures full of Philippean gold coins.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1065:
Then, of silver, he has mountains, not ingots; Aetna is not so high.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aside.)
4.2.1066:
By the stars! O, what a lie!
PALAESTRIO
(to MILPHIDIPPA, aside.)
How rarely I am playing him off!
MILPHIDIPPA
(to PALAESTRIO, aside.)
And I; how do I do it? Ain’t I gulling him?
PALAESTRIO
(aside.)
4.2.1067:
Rarely.
MILPHIDIPPA
But, prithee, do let me go now.
PALAESTRIO
(to the CAPTAIN.)
But do you give her some answer, either that you will do it, or that you won’t do it.
4.2.1068:
Why cause this poor lady so much anguish of mind, who has never deserved any ill of you?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1069:
Bid her come to me herself. Tell her that I will do everything that she requires.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1070:
You now act as it is proper for you to act. since you wish the same yourself that she is wishing.
PALAESTRIO
(to himself, aside.)
4.2.1071:
No poor faculty of invention has she.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.2.1072:
Since too you have not scouted your petitioner, and have suffered me to prevail upon you. (Aside to PALAESTRIO.) How now? Haven’t I played him off?
PALAESTRIO
(aside to MILPHIDIPPA.)
4.2.1073:
Faith, I couldn’t refrain from laughing.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aside to PALAESTRIO.)
Yes; and for the same reason I turned in this direction away from you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1074: By my troth, wench, you don’t understand
4.2.1075:
how great an honor I am now paying her.
MILPHIDIPPA
I know, and I shall tell her so.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1076:
To another he could have sold his favours for his weight in gold.
MILPHIDIPPA
I’ faith, I believe you in that.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1077:
Of those that are parents by him true warriors are born, and his sons live eight hundred years.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aside to PALAESTRIO.)
4.2.1078:
Fie on you for a fibber!
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1079:
Why, straight on, from age to age, they live for a thousand years.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1080:
I spoke within limits, for the reason that she mightn’t suppose I was telling lies to her.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aside.)
4.2.1081:
I burst, I die! (Aloud.) How many years will he live himself whose sons live so long?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1082:
Wench, I was born the day after Jupiter was born of Ops.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1083:
If he had only been born the day before the other was, he would have had the realms of heaven.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aside to PALAESTRIO.)
4.2.1084:
Now, now, prithee, no more do let me get away from you, if I can, alive.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1085:
Why don’t you go then, as you have your answer?
MILPHIDIPPA
I’ll go, and I’ll bring her here, on whose behalf I am employed. Is there aught else you wish?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1086:
May I never be more handsome than I am at present; so much trouble do my good looks cause me.
PALAESTRIO
4.2.1087:
Why do you stay now? Why don’t you go?
MILPHIDIPPA
I’m going.
PALAESTRIO
(aside to MILPHIDIPPA.)
4.2.1088:
And tell her, too, do you hear, cleverly and correctly, what has passed.
MILPHIDIPPA
(to PALAESTRIO.)
So that her very heart may leap for joy.
PALAESTRIO
(aside to MILPHIDIPPA)
4.2.1089:
If Philocomasium is there, tell her to pass through into our house; that the Captain here.
MILPHIDIPPA
(to PALAESTRIO.)
4.2.1090:
She is there with my mistress for, on the sly, they have been overhearing this conversation.
PALAESTRIO
(aside to MILPHIDIPPA.)
4.2.1091:
’Twas cleverly done; here after they will take their cue the more readily from this conversation.
MILPHIDIPPA
(to PALAESTRIO.)
4.2.1092:
You are delaying me. I’m off.
PALAESTRIO
(to MILPHIDIPPA.)
I’m not delaying you, nor touching you, nor—I’m mum.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.2.1093: Bid her make haste to come out here; we’ll give our first attention to this matter especially. (MILPHIDIPPA goes into the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)

4.3.1094:
(PYRGOPOLINICES, PALAESTRIO.) PYRGOPOLINICES
What do you advise me now to do, Palaestrio,
4.3.1095:
about my mistress? For this lady can by no means be received into my house before I have sent the other away.
PALAESTRIO
4.3.1097: Why consult me what you are to do? So far as I am concerned, I have told you by what method that can be effected in the gentlest manner. The gold trinkets and female clothing with which you have furnished her, let her keep it all for herself: let her take it, be off, and carry it away:
4.3.1101:
tell her that it is high time for her to go home; say that her twin-sister and her mother are come, in company with whom she may go straight home.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1104:
How do you know that they are here?
PALAESTRIO
Because, with my own eyes, I’ve seen her sister here.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1106:
I have met her.
PYRGOPOLINICES
And did she seem a brisk wench?
PALAESTRIO
You are wishing to have everything.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1107:
Where did the sister say her mother was?
PALAESTRIO
4.3.1108: The captain that brought them told me that she was in bed, on board the ship, with sore and inflamed eyes.
4.3.1110:
This captain of the ship is lodging with them next door.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1111:
And he, too, is he a very fine fellow?
PALAESTRIO
Away with you, if you please. What have you to do with him? You have your hands quite full enough with the women. Attend to this for the present.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1114: As to that advice you were giving me,
4.3.1115:
I wish you to have a few words with her upon that subject. For, really, a conversation on that subject with her is more becoming for you.
PALAESTRIO
4.3.1117:
What is more advisable than for you to go yourself, and transact your own concerns? You must say that it is absolutely necessary for you to marry: that your relations are persuading, your friends are urging, you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1120:
And do you think so?
PALAESTRIO
Why shouldn’t I think so?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1121:
I’ll go in, then. Do you, in the mean time, keep watch here before the house, that when the other woman comes out you may call me out.
PALAESTRIO
4.3.1123:
Do you only mind the business that you are upon.
PYRGOPOLINICES
That, indeed, is resolved upon. For if she will not go out of her own accord, I’ll turn her out by force.
PALAESTRIO
4.3.1125:
Do you take care how you do that; but rather let her go from your house with a good grace, and give her those things that I mentioned. The gold trinkets and apparel, with which you furnished her, let her take away.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1128:
By my troth, I wish she would.
PALAESTRIO
I think you’ll easily prevail upon her. But go indoors; don’t linger here.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.3.1129:
I obey you.
(Goes into his house.)
PALAESTRIO
(to the AUDIENCE.)
4.3.1130: Now, does he really appear to be anything different from what, awhile ago, I told you he was, this wenching Captain? Now it is requisite that Acroteleutium should come to me, her maid too, and Pleusicles. O Jupiter! and does not opportunity favour me in every respect?
4.3.1135: For those whom I especially wished to see, I perceive at this moment coming out here from our neighbour’s.

4.4.1137:
(Enter ACROTELEUTIUM, MILPHIDIPPA, and PLEUSICLES from the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.) ACROTELEUTIUM
Follow me; at the same time look around, that there may be no overlooker.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.4.1138:
Faith, I see no one, only him whom we want to meet.
PALAESTRIO
Just as I want you.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.4.1139:
How do you do, our master-plotter?
PALAESTRIO
I, the master-plotter? Nonsense.
MILPHIDIPPA
How so?
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1140:
Because, in comparison with yourself, I am not worthy to fix a beam in a wall.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1141:
Aye, indeed so.
PALAESTRIO
She’s a very fluent and a very clever hand at mischief. How charmingly she did polish off the Captain.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.4.1143: Be of good courage all the business is now prospering under our hands. Only do you, as you have begun, still give a helping hand;
4.4.1145:
for the Captain himself has gone in-doors, to entreat his mistress to leave his house, with her mother and sister, for Athens.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1147:
Besides, all the gold trinkets and apparel which he himself has provided for the damsel, he gives her to keep as a present for herself—so have I recommended him.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1149:
Really, it’s easily done, if both she wishes it, and he desires it as well.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1150:
Don’t you know that when, from a deep well, you have ascended up to the top, there is the greatest danger lest you should thence fall back again from the top. This affair is now being carried on at the top of the well. If the Captain should have a suspicion of it, nothing whatever of his will be able to be carried off. Now, most especially, we have need of clever contrivances.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1154: I see that there is material enough at home for that purpose—
4.4.1155:
three women, yourself the fourth, I am the fifth, the old gentleman the sixth.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1156:
What an edifice of stratagems has been erected by us! I know for certain. that any town seems as though it could be taken by these plans: only do you lend your assistance.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1158:
For that purpose are we come to you, to see if you wish for anything.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1159:
You do what’s à propos. Now to you do I assign this department.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1160:
General, you shall assign me whatever you please, so far as I am capable.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1161:
I wish this Captain to be played off cleverly and adroitly.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1162:
I’ faith, you’re assigning me what’s a pleasure to me.
PALAESTRIO
But do you understand how?
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1163:
You mean that I must pretend that I am distracted with love for him.
PALAESTRIO
Right—you have it.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1164:
And as though by reason of that love I had foregone my present marriage, longing for a match with him.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1165:
Everything exactly in its due order; except only this one point; you must say that this house (pointing to the house of PERIPLECOMENUS) was your marriage-portion; that the old man had departed hence from you after you had carried out the divorce, lest he should be afraid just now to come here into the house of another man.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1169:
You advise me well.
PALAESTRIO
But when he comes out from in-doors, I wish you—standing at a distance there—
4.4.1170:
so to make pretence, as though in comparison with his beauty you despised your own, and as though you were struck with awe at his opulent circumstances; at the same time, too, praise the comeliness of his person, the beauty of his face. Are you tutored enough?
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1173:
I understand it all. Is it enough that I give you my work so nicely finished off that you cannot find a fault with it.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1175: I’m content. Now (addressing PLEUSICLES), in your turn, learn what charge I shall give to you. So soon as this shall be done, when she shall have gone in, then do you immediately take care to come here dressed in the garb of a master of a ship. Have on a broad-brimmed hat of iron-grey, a woollen shade before your eyes; have on an iron-grey cloak (for that is the seaman’s colour);
4.4.1180:
have it fastened over the left shoulder, your right arm projecting out, your clothes some way well girded up, pretend as though you are some master of a ship. And all these requisites are at the house of this old gentleman, for he keeps fishermen.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1183:
Well, when I’m dressed out, why don’t you tell me what I’m to do then?
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1184:
Come here, and, in the name of her mother, bring word to Philocomasium, that, if she would return to Athens, she must go with you to the harbour directly, and that she must order it to be carried down to the ship if she wishes anything to be put on board; that if she doesn’t go, you must weigh anchor, for the wind is favourable.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1189:
I like your plan much: do proceed.
PALAESTRIO
The Captain will at once advise her to go speedily that she may not delay her mother.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1190:
Every way you are clever.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1191:
I shall tell him that she asks for me as a helper to carry her baggage down to the harbour. I shall go, and, understand you, I shall immediately be off with you straight to Athens.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1193:
And when you have reached there, I’ll never let you be ashore three days before you’re free.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1195:
Be off speedily and equip yourself.
PLEUSICLES
Is there anything besides?
PALAESTRIO
Only to remember all this.
PLEUSICLES
4.4.1196:
I’m off.
(Exit.)
PALAESTRIO
And do you (to ACROTELEUTIUM and MILPHIDIPPA) be off hence in-doors this instant, for I’m quite sure that he’ll just now be coming out hence from in-doors.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.4.1197:
With us your command is as good as law.
PALAESTRIO
4.4.1198:
Come, then, begone. But see, the door opens opportunely.
(The women go into the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)

4.5.1200:
(Enter PYRGOPOLINICES from his house.) PYRGOPOLINICES
What I wished I have obtained just as I wished, on kind and friendly terms, that she would leave me.
PALAESTRIO
4.5.1201:
For what reason am I to say that you have been so long in-doors?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.5.1202:
I never was so sensible that I was beloved by that woman as now.
PALAESTRIO
4.5.1203:
Why so?
PYRGOPOLINICES
How many words she did utter! How the matter was protracted! But in the end I obtained what I wanted, and I granted her
4.5.1205:
what she wanted and what she asked of me. I made a present of you also to her.
PALAESTRIO
4.5.1206:
What—me, too? In what way shall I exist without you?
PYRGOPOLINICES
Come, be of good heart; I’ll make you free from exit, too. But I used all endeavours, if I could by any method persuade her to go away, and not take you with her, she forced me, however.
PALAESTRIO
4.5.1209: In the Gods and yourself I’ll place my trust. Yet, at the last,
4.5.1210:
although it is bitter to me that I must be deprived of an excellent master, yourself, at least it is a pleasure to me that, through my means, by reason of the excellence of your beauty, this has happened to you with regard to this lady neighbour, whom I am now introducing to you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.5.1213:
What need of words? I’ll give you liberty and wealth if you obtain her for me.
PALAESTRIO
4.5.1214:
I’ll win her.
PYRGOPOLINICES
But I’m impatient.
PALAESTRIO
But moderation is requisite;
4.5.1215: curb your desires; don’t be over anxious. But see, here she is herself; she is coming out of doors.

4.6.1216:
(Enter ACROTELEUTIUM and MILPHIDIPPA from the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.) MILPHIDIPPA
(in a low voice.)
Mistress, see! the Captain’s near.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(in a low voice.)
Where is he?
MILPHIDIPPA
Only look to the left.
4.6.1217:
Eye him askance, that he mayn’t perceive that we are looking at him.
ACROTELEUTIUM
4.6.1218:
I see him. Troth, now’s the time, in our mischief, for us to become supremely mischievous.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1219:
’Tis for you to begin.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
Prithee, did you see him yourself?
4.6.1220:
(Aside.) don’t spare your voice, so that he may hear.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
By my troth, I talked with his own self, at my ease, as long as I pleased, at my leisure, at my own discretion, just as I wished.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
4.6.1222:
Do you hear what she says?
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
I hear. How delighted she is because she had access to you.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1223:
O happy woman that you are!
PYRGOPOLINICES
How I do seem to be loved!
PALAESTRIO
You are deserving of it.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1224:
By my troth, ’tis passing strange what you say, that you had access to him and prevailed. They say that he is usually addressed, like a king, through letters or messengers.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.6.1226:
But, i’ faith, ’twas with difficulty I had an opportunity of approaching and beseeching him.
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
4.6.1227:
How renowned you are among the fair.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
I shall submit, since Venus wills it so.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1228: By heavens! I return to Venus grateful thanks, and her I do beseech and entreat, that I may win him whom I love and whom I seek to win,
4.6.1230:
and that to me he may prove gentle, and not make a difficulty about what I desire.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.6.1231:
I hope it may be so; although many ladies are seeking to win him for themselves, he disdains them and estranges himself from all but you alone.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1233: Therefore this fear torments me, since he is so disdainful, lest his eyes, when he beholds me, should change his sentiments,
4.6.1235:
and his own gracefulness should at once disdain my form.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.6.1236:
He will not do so; be of good heart.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
How she does slight herself!
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1237:
I fear lest your account may have surpassed my looks.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.6.1238:
I’ve taken care of this, that you shall be fairer than his expectations.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1239: Troth, if he shall refuse to take me as his wife, by heavens I’ll embrace his knees
4.6.1240:
and entreat him! If I shall be unable to prevail on him, in some way or other, I’ll put myself to death. I’m quite sure that without him I cannot live.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
4.6.1242:
I see that I must prevent this woman’s death. Shall I accost her?
PALAESTRIO
By no means; for you will be making yourself cheap if you lavish yourself away of your own accord. Let her come spontaneously, seek you, court you, strive to win you.
4.6.1245:
Unless you wish to lose that glory which you have, please have a care what you do. For I know that this was never the lot of any mortal, except two persons, yourself and Phaon of Lesbos, to be loved so desperately.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1248:
I’ll go in-doors—or, my dear Milphidippa, do you call him out of doors.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.6.1249:
Aye; let’s wait until some one comes out.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
I can’t restrain myself
4.6.1250:
from going in to him.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
The door’s fastened.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
I’ll break it in then.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
You are not in your senses.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1251:
If he has ever loved, or if he has wisdom equal to his beauty, whatever I may do through love, he will pardon me by reason of his compassionate feelings.
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
4.6.1253:
Prithee, do see, how distracted the poor thing is with love.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
’Tis mutual in us.
PALAESTRIO
4.6.1254:
Hush! don’t you let her hear.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
Why do you stand stupefied? Why don’t you knock?
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1255:
Because he is not within whom I want.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
How do you know?
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
By my troth, I do know it easily; for my nose would scent him if he were within.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
4.6.1257:
Because she is in love with me, Venus has made her prophesy.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1258:
He is somewhere or other close at hand whom I do so long to behold. I’m sure I smell him.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
4.6.1259:
Troth, now, she really sees better with her nose than with her eyes.
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
She is blind from love.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1260:
Prithee, do support me.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
Why?
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
Lest I should fall.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
Why?
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
Because I cannot stand; my senses—my senses are sinking so by reason of my eyes.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1261:
(aloud.) Heavens! you’ve seen the Captain.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1262:
I have.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
I don’t see him. Where is he?
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
Troth, you would see him if you were in tove.
MILPHIDIPPA
(aloud.)
4.6.1263:
I’ faith, you don’t love him more than I do myself, with your good leave.
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
4.6.1264:
No doubt all of the women, as soon as each has seen you, are in love with you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1265:
(to PALAESTRIO.) I don’t know whether you have heard it from me or not; I’m the grandson of Venus.
ACROTELEUTIUM
(aloud.)
4.6.1266:
My dear Milphidippa, prithee do approach and accost him.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(to PALAESTRIO.)
How she does stand in awe of me!
PALAESTRIO
(to PYRGOPOLINICES.)
4.6.1267:
She is coming towards us.
MILPHIDIPPA
(advancing.)
I wish to speak with you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
And we with you.
MILPHIDIPPA
I have brought my mistress out of the house, as you requested me.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1268:
So I see.
MILPHIDIPPA
Request her, then, to approach.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1269:
Since you have entreated it, I have prevailed upon my mind not to detest her just like other women.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1270:
I’ faith she wouldn’t be able to utter a word if she were to come near you; while she was looking at you, her eyes have in the meantime tied her tongue.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1272:
I see that this woman’s disorder must be cured.
MILPHIDIPPA
See how terrified she is since she beheld you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1273:
Even armed men are the same; don’t wonder at a woman being so. But what does she wish me to do?
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1275:
You to come to her house; she wishes to live and to pass her life with you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1276:
What!—I come home to her, when she is a married woman? Her husband is to be stood in fear of.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1277:
Why,—for your sake, she has turned her husband out of her house.
PYRGOPOLINICES
How? How could she do so?
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1278:
The house was her marriage-portion.
PYRGOPOLINICES
Was it so?
MILPHIDIPPA
It was so, on my word.
PYRGOPOLINICES
Bid her go home; I’ll be there just now.
MILPHIDIPPA
4.6.1279:
Take care, and don’t keep her in expectation; don’t torment her feelings.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1280:
Not I, indeed. Do you go then.
MILPHIDIPPA
We are going. (ACROTELEUTIUM and MILPHIDIPPA go into the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1281:
But what do I see?
PALAESTRIO
What do you see?
PYRGOPOLINICES
See there, some one is coming, I know not who, but in a sailor’s dress.
PALAESTRIO
4.6.1282:
He is surely wanting us, now; really, it is the shipmaster.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.6.1283:
He’s come, I suppose, to fetch her.
PALAESTRIO
I fancy so.

4.7.1284:
(Enter PLEUSICLES, at a distance, in a Sailor’s dress.) PLEUSICLES
(to himself.)
Did I not know that another man in other ways
4.7.1285: has done many a thing unbecomingly on account of love, I should be more ashamed by reason of love for me to be going in this garb. But since I have learned that many persons by reason of love have committed many actions, disgraceful and estranged from what is good, for I pass by how Achilles suffered his comrades to be slain—
4.7.1290: But there’s Palaestrio, he’s standing with the Captain. My talk must now be changed for another kind. Woman is surely born of tardiness itself. For every other delay, which is a delay just as much, seems a less delay than that which is on account of a woman.
4.7.1295:
I really think that this is done merely from habit. But I shall call for this Philocomasium. I’ll knock at the door then. Hallo! is there any one here?
(Knocks at the CAPTAIN’S door.)
PALAESTRIO
4.7.1297:
Young man—what is it? What do you want? Why are you knocking?
PLEUSICLES
4.7.1298: I’m come to inquire for Philocomasium; I’m come from her mother. If she’s for going, let her set off.
4.7.1300:
She is delaying us all; we wish to weigh anchor.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.7.1301:
Her things have been some time in readiness. Hearkye, Palaestrio, take some assistants with you to carry to the ship her golden trinkets, her furniture, apparel, all her precious things. All the articles are already packed up which I gave her.
PALAESTRIO
4.7.1305:
I’ll go.
(Goes into the house.)
PLEUSICLES
Troth now, prithee, do make haste.
PYRGOPOLINICES
There shall be no delay. Pray, what is it that has been done with your eye?
PLEUSICLES
4.7.1307:
Troth, hut I have my eye.
(Points to the right one.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
But the left one I mean.
PLEUSICLES
I’ll tell you. On account of the sea, I use this eye less; but if I kept away from the sea, I should use the one like the other.
4.7.1310:
But they are detaining me too long.
PYRGOPOLINICES
See, here they are coming out.

4.8.1311:
(Enter PALAESTRIO and PHILOCOMASIUM from the CAPTAIN’S house.) PALAESTRIO
(to PHILOCOMASIUM.)
Prithee, when will you this day make an end of your weeping?
PHILOCOMASIUM
What can I do but weep? I am going away hence where I have spent my days most happily.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1312:
See, there’s the man that has come from your mother and sister.
(pointing to PLEUSICLES.)
PHILOCOMASIUM
4.8.1313:
I see him.
PYRGOPOLINICES
Palaestrio, do you hear?
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1314:
What is your pleasure?
PYRGOPOLINICES
Aren’t you ordering those presents to be brought out which I gave her?
PLEUSICLES
4.8.1315:
Health to you, Philocomasium.
PHILOCOMASIUM
And health to you.
PLEUSICLES
Your mother and sister bade me give their love to you.
PHILOCOMASIUM
4.8.1317:
They beg you to set out, so that, while the wind is fair, they may set sail. But if your mother’s eyes had been well, she would have come together with me.
PHILOCOMASIUM
4.8.1319:
I’ll go; although I do it with regret—duty compels me.
PLEUSICLES
You act wisely.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1320:
If she had not been passing her life with myself, this day she would have been a blockhead.
PHILOCOMASIUM
4.8.1321:
I am distracted at this, that I am estranged from such a man. For you are able to make any woman what-ever abound in wit; and because I was living with you, for that reason I was of a very lofty spirit. I see that I must lose that loftiness of mind.
(Pretends to cry.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1324:
Don’t weep.
PHILOCOMASIUM
I can’t help it when I look upon you.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1325:
Be of good courage.
PHILOCOMASIUM
I know what pain it is to me.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1326:
I really don’t wonder now, Philocomasium, if you were here with happiness to yourself, when I, a servant—as I look at him, weep because we are parting (pretends to cry), so much have his beauty, his manners, his valour, captivated your feelings.
PHILOCOMASIUM
4.8.1329:
Prithee, do let me embrace you before I depart?
PYRGOPOLINICES
By all means
PHILOCOMASIUM
(embracing him.)
4.8.1330:
O my eyes! O my life!
PALAESTRIO
Do hold up the woman, I entreat you, lest she should fall.
(He takes hold of her, and she pretends to faint.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1331:
What means this?
PALAESTRIO
Because, after she had quitted you, she suddenly became faint, poor thing.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1332:
Run in and fetch some water.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1333:
I want no water; but I had rather you would keep at a distance. Prithee, don’t you interfere till she comes to.
PYRGOPOLINICES
(observing PLEUSICLES, who is holding PHILOCOMASIUM in his arm.)
4.8.1334: They have their heads too closely in contact between them;
4.8.1335:
I don’t like it; he is soldering his lips to hers. What the plague are you about?
PLEUSICLES
4.8.1336:
I was trying whether she was breathing or not.
PYRGOPOLINICES
You ought to have applied your ear then.
PLEUSICLES
4.8.1337:
If you had rather, I’ll let her go.
PYRGOPOLINICES
No, I don’t care; do you support her.
PALAESTRIO
To my misery, I’m quite distracted.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1338:
Go and bring here from in-doors all the things that I have given her.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1339: And even now, household God, do I salute thee before I depart;
4.8.1340:
my fellow-servants, both male and female, all farewell, and happy may you live; prithee, though absent, among yourselves bestow your blessings upon me as well.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1342:
Come, Palaestrio, be of good courage.
PALAESTRIO
Alas! alas! I cannot but weep since from you I must depart.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1343:
Bear it with patience.
PHILOCOMASIUM
(feigning to recover.)
4.8.1344:
Ha! how’s this? What means it? Hail, O light!
PLEUSICLES
4.8.1345:
Are you recovered now?
PHILOCOMASIUM
Prithee, what person am I embracing? I’m undone. Am I myself?
PLEUSICLES
(in a low voice.)
Fear not, my delight.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1347:
What means all this?
PALAESTRIO
Just now she swooned away here. I fear and dread that this at last may take place too openly.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1349:
What is that you say?
PALAESTRIO
I fear that some one may turn it to your discredit, while all these things are being carried after us through the city.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1350:
I have given away my own property, and not theirs. I care but little for other people. Be off then, go with the blessing of the Gods.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1352:
’Tis for your sake I say it.
PYRGOPOLINICES
I believe you.
PALAESTRIO
And now farewell!
PYRGOPOLINICES
And heartily farewell to you!
PALAESTRIO
(to PLEUSICLES and PHILOCOMASIUM as they leave.)
4.8.1353: Go you quickly on; I’ll overtake you directly; I wish to speak a few words with my master. (To PYRGOPOLINICES.) Although you have ever deemed others more faithful to yourself than me,
4.8.1355:
still do I owe you many thanks for all things; and if such were your feelings, I would rather be a slave to you by far than be the freedman of another.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1358:
Ah me! When it comes in my mind, how my manners must be changed, how womanish manners must be learnt, and the military ones forgotten!
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1360:
Take care and be honest.
PALAESTRIO
I can be so no longer; I have lost all inclination.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1361:
Go, follow them; don’t linger.
PALAESTRIO
Fare you right well.
PYRGOPOLINICES
And heartily fare you well.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1362:
Prithee, do remember me; if perchance I should happen to be made free, I’ll send the news to you; don’t you forsake me.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1363:
That is not my habit.
PALAESTRIO
4.8.1364: Consider every now and then how faithful I have been to you.
4.8.1365:
If you do that, then at last you’ll know who is honest towards you and who dishonest.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1366:
I know it; I have often found that true, as well before as to-day in especial.
PALAESTRIO
Do you know it? Aye, and this day I’ll make you hereafter say still more how true it is.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1370:
they may say that no one of your slaves is trustworthy except my-self. If, indeed, I thought you could do it with honor, I should advise you. But it cannot be; take care how you do so.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1373:
Then, fare you well.
PYRGOPOLINICES
’Twere better you should go with a good heart.
PALAESTRIO
Still, once more, farewell.
(Exit.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.8.1374: Before this affair, I had always thought that he was a most rascally servant;
4.8.1375: still, I find that he is faithful to me. When I consider with myself, I have done unwisely in parting with him. I’ll go hence at once now to my love here: the door, too, I perceive, makes a noise there.

4.9.1378:
(Enter a BOY from the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.) A BOY.
(to some one within.)
Don’t you be advising me; I remember my duty; this moment I’ll find him. Wherever on earth he may chance to be,
4.9.1380:
I’ll search him out; I’ll not be sparing of my pains.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.9.1381:
’Tis I he is looking for, I’ll go and meet this boy.
A BOY.
4.9.1382:
O, I’m looking for you; save you, dearest sir, one loaded by opportunity with her gifts, and whom before all others two Divinities do favour.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.9.1384:
What two?
A BOY.
Mars and Venus.
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.9.1385:
A sprightly boy.
A BOY.
She entreats that you will go in; she wishes—she longs for you, and while expecting you, she’s dying for you. Do succour one in love. Why do you stay? Why don’t you go in?
PYRGOPOLINICES
4.9.1387:
Well, I’ll go.
(Enters the house of PERIPLECOMENUS.)
A BOY.
4.9.1388: There has he entangled himself at once in the toils. The snare is prepared: the old gentleman is standing at his post
4.9.1390: to attack the letcher, who is so boastful of his good looks; who thinks that, whatever woman sees him, all are in love with him; whom all, both men and women, detest. Now I will on to the uproar; I hear a tumult within.

5.1.1394:
(Enter PERIPLECOMENUS from his house, with CARIO and other SERVANTS, dragging PYRGOPOLINICES. PERIPLECOMENUS
Bring that fellow along. If he doesn’t follow, drag him, lifted on high, out of doors.
5.1.1395:
Make him to be between heaven and earth; cut him in pieces.
(They beat him.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1396:
By my troth, I do entreat you, Periplecomenus.
PERIPLECOMENUS
By my troth, you do entreat in vain. Take care, Cario, that that knife of yours is very sharp.
CARIO
5.1.1398:
Why, it’s already longing to rip up the stomach of this letcher. I’ll make his entrails hang just as a bauble hangs from a baby’s neck.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1400:
I’m a dead man.
PERIPLECOMENUS
Not yet; you say so too soon.
CARIO
Shall I have at this fellow now?
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1401:
Aye,—but first let him be thrashed with cudgels.
CARIO
True, right lustily.
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1402:
Why have you dared, you disgraceful fellow, to seduce another man’s wife?
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1403:
So may the Gods bless me, she came to me of her own accord.
PERIPLECOMENUS
It’s a lie. Lay on.
(They are about to strike.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1404:
Stay, while I tell—
PERIPLECOMENUS
Why are you hesitating?
PYRGOPOLINICES
Will you not let me speak?
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1405:
Speak, then.
PYRGOPOLINICES
I was entreated to come here.
PERIPLECOMENUS
How did you dare? There’s for you, take that.
(Strikes him.)
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1406:
O! O! I’ve had enough. Prithee, now.
CARIO
Am I to begin cutting him up at once?
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1407:
As soon as you like. Stretch the fellow out, and spread out his pinions in opposite ways.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1408:
By heavens, prithee, do hear my words before he cuts me.
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1409:
Speak before you’re made of no sex.
PYRGOPOLINICES
I supposed that she was a widow; and so her maid, who was her go-between, informed me.
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1411:
Now take an oath that you won’t injure any person for this affair, because you have been beaten here today, or shall be beaten hereafter, if we let you go safe hence, you dear little grandson of Venus.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1414: I swear by Dione and Mars that I will hurt no one
5.1.1415:
because I have been beaten here this day; and I think that it was rightfully done; and if I don’t go hence further injured, I am rightly punished for the offence.
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1417:
But what if you don’t do so?
PYRGOPOLINICES
Then, may I always have my word not to be trusted
CARIO
5.1.1418:
Let him be beaten once more; after that I think he may be dismissed.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1419:
May the Gods ever bless you, since you so kindly come as my advocate.
CARIO
5.1.1420:
Give us a golden mina, then.
PYRGOPOLINICES
For what reason?
CARIO
That we may now let you go hence unmaimed, you little grandson of Venus; otherwise you shall not escape from here; don’t you deceive yourself.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1422:
It shall be given you.
CARIO
You’re very wise. As for your tunic, and your scarf, and sword, don’t at all hope for them; you shan’t have them.
A SERVANT.
5.1.1424:
Shall I beat him again, or do you let him go?
PYRGOPOLINICES
I’m tamed by your cudgels. I do entreat you.
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1425:
Loose him.
PYRGOPOLINICES
I return you thanks.
PERIPLECOMENUS
5.1.1426:
If I ever catch you here again, I’ll insert a disqualifying clause.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.1.1427:
Well: I make no objection.
PERIPLECOMENUS
Let’s go in, Cario.
(PERIPLECOMENUS, CARIO, and SERVANTS go into his house.)

5.2.1427:
(Enter SCLEDRUS and other SERVANTS of the CAPTAIN.) PYRGOPOLINICES
Here are some of my servants, I see. Tell me, is Philocomasium off yet.
SCELEDRUS
5.2.1429:
Aye, some time since.
PYRGOPOLINICES
Ah me!
SCELEDRUS
You would say that still more if you were to know what I know,
5.2.1430:
for that fellow who had the wool before his eye was no sailor.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.2.1431:
Who was he, then?
SCELEDRUS
A lover of Philocomasium’s.
PYRGOPOLINICES
How do you know?
SCELEDRUS
I do know: for after they had got out of the city gate, they didn’t wait a moment before falling to kissing and embracing each other at once.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.2.1433: O wretched fool that I am! I see that I have been gulled. That scoundrel of a fellow, Palaestrio,
5.2.1435:
it was he that contrived this plot against me.
SCELEDRUS
5.2.1436:
I think it was properly done. If it were so done to other letchers, there would be fewer letchers here; they would stand more in awe, and give their attention less to these pursuits.
PYRGOPOLINICES
5.2.1437:
Let’s go into my house.
AN ACTOR
(to the AUDIENCE.)
Give us your applause.

1.1.1:
(Enter, from the house of THEUROPIDES, GRUMIO, pushing out TRANIO. GRUMIO
Get out of the kitchen, will you; out of it, you whip-scoundrel, who are giving me your cavilling talk amid the platters; march out of the house, you ruin of your master. Upon my faith, if I only live, I’ll be soundly revenged upon you in the country. Get out, I say, you steam of the kitchen.
1.1.5:
Why are you skulking thus?
TRANIO
1.1.6: Why the plague are you making this noise here before the house? Do you fancy yourself to be in the country? Get out of the house; be off into the country. Go and hang yourself. Get away from the door.
1.1.9:
(Striking him.) There now, was it that you wanted?
GRUMIO
(running away.)
I’m undone! Why are you beating me?
TRANIO
1.1.11:
Because you want it.
GRUMIO
I must endure it. Only let the old gentleman return home; only let him come safe home, whom you are devouring in his absence.
TRANIO
1.1.13:
You don’t say what’s either likely or true, you blockhead, as to any one devouring a person in his absence.
GRUMIO
1.1.15: Indeed, you town wit, you minion of the mob, do you throw the country in my teeth? Really, Tranio, I do believe that you feel sure that before long you’ll be handed over to the mill. Within a short period, i’ faith, Tranio, you’ll full soon be adding to the iron-bound race in the country.
1.1.20: While you choose to, and have the opportunity, drink on, squander his property, corrupt my master’s son, a most worthy young man, drink night and day, live like Greeks, make purchase of mistresses, give them their freedom, feed parasites, feast yourselves sumptuously.
1.1.25: Was it thus that the old gentleman enjoined you when he went hence abroad? Is it after this fashion that he will find his property well husbanded? Do you suppose that this is the duty of a good servant, to be ruining both the estate and the son of his master? For I do consider him as ruined, when he devotes himself to these goings on.
1.1.30:
A person, with whom not one of all the young men of Attica was before deemed equally frugal or more steady, the same is now carrying off the palm in the opposite direction. Through your management and your tutoring has that been done.
TRANIO
1.1.34: What the plague business have you with me or with what I do?
1.1.35:
Prithee, haven’t you got your cattle in the country for you to look to? I choose to drink, to intrigue, to keep my wenches; this I do at the peril of my own back, and not of yours
GRUMIO
1.1.38:
Then with what assurance he does talk! (Turning away in disgust.) Faugh!
TRANIO
But may Jupiter and all the Deities confound you; you stink of garlick,
1.1.40:
you filth unmistakeable, you clod, you he-goat, you pig-sty, you mixture of dog and she-goat.
GRUMIO
1.1.41: What would you have to be done? It isn’t all that can smell of foreign perfumes, if you smell of them; or that can take their places at table above their master,
1.1.44: or live on such exquisite dainties as you live upon. Do you keep to yourself those turtle-doves, that fish, and poultry; let me enjoy my lot upon garlick diet. You are fortunate; I unlucky. It must be endured.
1.1.49:
Let my good fortune be awaiting me, your bad yourself.
TRANIO
1.1.51:
You seem, Grumio, as though you envied me, because I enjoy myself and you are wretched. It is quite my due. It’s proper for me to make love, and for you to feed the cattle; for me to fare handsomely, you in a miserable way.
GRUMIO
1.1.55:
O riddle for the executioner, as I guess it will turn out; they’ll be so pinking you with goads, as you carry your gibbet along the streets one day, as soon as ever the old gentleman returns here.
TRANIO
1.1.58:
How do you know whether that mayn’t happen to yourself sooner than to me?
GRUMIO
1.1.59:
Because I have never deserved it; you have deserved it, and you now deserve it.
TRANIO
1.1.60:
Do cut short the trouble of your talking, unless you wish a heavy mischance to befall you.
GRUMIO
1.1.62: Are you going to give me the tares for me to take for the cattle? If you are not, give me the money. Go on, still persist in the way in which you’ve commenced! Drink, live like Greeks,
1.1.65:
eat, stuff yourselves, slaughter your fatlings!
TRANIO
1.1.66:
Hold your tongue, and be off into the country; I intend to go to the Piraeus to get me some fish for the evening. To-morrow I’ll make some one bring you the tares to the farm. What’s the matter? Why now are you staring at me, gallows-bird?
GRUMIO
1.1.70:
I’ faith, I’ve an idea that will be your own title before long.
TRANIO
1.1.71:
So long as it is as it is, in the meantime I’ll put up with that before long.
GRUMIO
1.1.72:
That’s the way; and understand this one thing, that that which is disagreable comes much more speedily than that which you wish for.
TRANIO
1.1.74: Don’t you be annoying; now then, away with you into the country, and betake yourself off.
1.1.75:
Don’t you deceive yourself, henceforth you shan’t be causing me any impediment. (Exit.)
GRUMIO
(to himself.)
1.1.76: Is he really gone? Not to care one straw for what I’ve said! O immortal Gods, I do implore your aid, do cause this old gentleman of ours, who has now been three years absent from here, to return hither as soon as possible, before everything
1.1.80: is gone, both house and land. Unless he does return here, remnants to last for a few months only are left. Now I’ll be off to the country; but look! I see my master’s son, one who has been corrupted from having been a most excellent young man. (Exit.)

1.2.84:
(Enter PHILOLACHES, from the house of THEUROPIDES.) PHILOLACHES
(to himself.)
I’ve often thought and long reflected on it,
1.2.85: and in my breast have held many a debate, and in my heart (if any heart I have) have revolved this matter, and long discussed it, to what thing I’m to consider man as like, and what form he has when he is born?
1.2.90: I’ve now discovered this likeness. I think a man is like unto a new house when he is born. I’ll give my proofs of this fact. (To the AUDIENCE.) And does not this seem to you like the truth? But so I’ll manage that you shall think it is so.
1.2.95: Beyond a doubt I’ll convince you that it is true what I say. And this yourselves, I’m sure, when you have heard my words, will say is no otherwise than just as I now affirm that it is. Listen while I repeat my proofs of this fact;
1.2.100: I want you to be equally knowing with myself upon this matter. As soon as ever a house is built up, nicely polished off, carefully erected, and according to rule, people praise the architect and approve of the house, they take from it each one a model for himself. Each one has something similar, quite at his own expense; they do not spare their pains.
1.2.105: But when a worthless, lazy, dirty, negligent fellow betakes himself thither with an idle family, then is it imputed as a fault to the house, while a good house is being kept in bad repair. And this is often the case; a storm comes on and breaks the tiles and gutters; then
1.2.110: a careless owner takes no heed to put up others. A shower comes on and streams down the walls; the rafters admit the rain; the weather rots the labours of the builder; then the utility of the house becomes diminished; and yet this is not the fault of the builder. But a great part
1.2.115: of mankind have contracted this habit of delay; if anything can be repaired by means of money, they are always still putting it off, and don’t do it until the walls come tumbling down; then the whole house has to be built anew. These instances from buildings I’ve mentioned; and now I wish to inform you how you are to suppose that men are like houses.
1.2.120: In the first place then, the parents are the builders-up of the children, and lay the foundation for the children; they raise them up, they carefully train them to strength, and that they may be good both for service and for view before the public. They spare not either their own pains or their cost,
1.2.125: nor do they deem expense in that to be an expense. They refine them, teach them literature, the ordinances, the laws; at their own cost and labour they struggle, that others may wish for their own children to be like to them. When they repair to the army, they then find them some relation of theirs as a protector.
1.2.131: At that moment they pass out of the builder’s hands. One year’s pay has now been earned; at that period, then, a sample is on view how the building will turn out. But I was always discreet and virtuous, just as long as I was under the management of the builder.
1.2.135: After I had left him to follow the bent of my own inclinations, at once I entirely spoiled the labours of the builders. Idleness came on; that was my storm; on its arrival, upon me it brought down hail and showers, which overthrew my modesty and the bounds of virtue, and untiled them for me in an instant.
1.2.141: After that I was neglectful to cover in again; at once passion like a torrent entered my heart; it flowed down even unto my breast, and soaked through my heart. Now both property, credit, fair fame, virtue, and honor
1.2.145: have forsaken me; by usage have I become much worse, and, i’ faith (so rotten are these rafters of mine with moisture), I do not seem to myself to be able possibly to patch up my house to prevent it from falling down totally once for all, from perishing from the foundation, and from no one being able to assist me. My heart pains me, when I reflect how I now am and how I once was,
1.2.150: than whom in youthful age not one there was more active in the arts of exercise, with the quoit, the javelin, the ball, racing, arms, and horses. I then lived a joyous life; in frugality and hardihood I was an example to others;
1.2.155: all, even the most deserving, took a lesson from me for themselves. Now that I’m become worthless, to that, indeed, have I hastened through the bent of my inclinations. (He stands apart.)

1.3.157:
(Enter PHILEMATITUM and SCAPHA, with all the requisites for a toilet.) PHILEMATIUM
On my word, for this long time I’ve not bathed in cold water with more delight than just now; nor do I think that I ever was, my dear Scapha, more thoroughly cleansed than now.
SCAPHA
1.3.159:
May the upshot of everything be unto you like a plenteous year’s harvest.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.160:
What has this harvest got to do with my bathing?
SCAPHA
1.3.161:
Not a bit more than your bathing has to do with the harvest.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
O beauteous Venus, this is that storm of mine which stripped off all the modesty with which I was roofed; through which Desire and Cupid poured their shower into my breast; and never since have I been able to roof it in.
1.3.165:
Now are my walls soaking in my heart; this building is utterly undone.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.166:
Do look, my Scapha, there’s a dear, whether this dress quite becomes me. I wish to please Philolaches my protector, the apple of my eye.
SCAPHA
1.3.168:
Nay but, you set yourself off to advantage with pleasing manners, inasmuch as you yourself are pleasing. The lover isn’t in love with a woman’s dress, but with that which stuffs out the dress.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.170:
So may the Gods bless me, Scapha is waggish; the hussy’s quite knowing. How cleverly she understands all matters, the maxims of lovers too!
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.172:
Well now?
SCAPHA
What is it?
PHILEMATIUM
Why look at me and examine, how this becomes me.
SCAPHA
1.3.173:
Thanks to your good looks, it happens that whatever you put on becomes you.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.174: Now then, for that expression, Scapha, I’ll make you some present or other to-day,
1.3.175:
and I won’t allow you to have praised her for nothing who is so pleasing to me.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.176:
I don’t want you to flatter me.
SCAPHA
Really you are a very simple woman. Come now, would you rather be censured undeservedly, than be praised with truth? Upon my faith, for my own part, even though undeservedly, I’d much rather be praised than be found fault with with reason, or that other people should laugh at my appearance.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.181:
I love the truth; I wish the truth to be told me; I detest a liar.
SCAPHA
1.3.182:
So may you love me, and so may your Philolaches love you, how charming you are.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.183: How say you, you hussy? In what words did you adjure? So may I love her? Why wasn’t So may she love me added as well? I revoke the present.
1.3.185:
What I just now promised you is done for; you have lost the present.
SCAPHA
1.3.186:
Troth, for my part I am surprised that you, a person so knowing, so clever, and so well educated, are not aware that you are acting foolishly.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.187:
Then give me your advice, I beg, if I have done wrong in anything.
SCAPHA
1.3.188: I’ faith, you certainly do wrong, in setting your mind upon him alone, in fact, and humouring him in particular in this way and slighting other men.
1.3.190:
It’s the part of a married woman, and not of courtesans, to be devoted to a single lover.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.191:
O Jupiter! Why, what pest is this that has befallen my house? May all the Gods and Goddesses destroy me in the worst of fashions, if I don’t kill this old hag with thirst, and hunger, and cold.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.194:
I don’t want you, Scapha, to be giving me bad advice.
SCAPHA
You are clearly a simpleton, in thinking that he’ll for everlasting be your friend and well-wisher. I warn you of that; he’ll forsake you by reason of age and satiety.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.197:
I hope not.
SCAPHA
Things which you don’t hope happen more frequently than things which you do hope. In fine, if you cannot be persuaded by words to believe this to be the truth, judge of my words from facts; consider this instance, who I now am, and who I once was.
1.3.200:
No less than your are now, was I once beloved, and I devoted myself to one, who, faith, when with age this head changed its hue, forsook and deserted me. Depend on it, the same will happen to yourself.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.203:
I can scarcely withhold myself from flying at the eyes of this mischief-maker.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.204: I am of opinion that I ought to keep myself alone devoted to him,
1.3.205:
since to myself alone has he given freedom for himself alone.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.206:
O ye immortal Gods! what a charming woman, and of a disposition how chaste! By heaven, ’tis excellently done, and I’m rejoiced at it, that it is for her sake I’ve got nothing left.
SCAPHA
1.3.208:
On my word you really are silly.
PHILEMATIUM
For what reason?
SCAPHA
Because you care for this, whether he loves you.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.209:
Prithee, why should I not care for it?
SCAPHA
You now are free.
1.3.210:
You’ve now got what you wanted; if he didn’t still love you, as much money as he gave for your liberty, he’d lose.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.212:
Heavens, I’m a dead man if I don’t torture her to death after the most shocking fashion. That evil-persuading enticer to vice is corrupting this damsel.
PHILOLACHES
1.3.214: Scapha, I can never return him sufficient thanks for what he deserves of me;
1.3.215:
don’t you be persuading me to esteem him less.
SCAPHA
1.3.216:
But take care and reflect upon this one thing, if you devote yourself to him alone, while now you are at this youthful age, you’ll be complaining to no purpose in your aged years.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.218:
I could wish myself this instant changed into a quinsy, that I might seize the throat of that old witch, and put an end to the wicked mischief-maker.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.220:
It befits me now to have the same grateful feelings since I obtained it, as formerly before I acquired it, when I used to lavish caresses upon him.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.222:
May the Gods do towards me what they please, if for that speech I don’t make you free over again, and if I don’t torture Scapha to death.
SCAPHA
1.3.224: If you are quite assured that you will have a provision to the end,
1.3.225:
and that this lover will be your own for life, I think that you ought to devote yourself to him alone, and assume the character of a wife.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.227:
Just as a person’s character is, he’s in the habit of finding means accordingly; if I keep a good character for myself I shall be rich enough.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.229: By my troth, since selling there must be, my father shall be sold much sooner
1.3.230:
than, while I’m alive, I’ll ever permit you to be in want or go a-begging.
SCAPHA
1.3.231:
