What’s to become of the rest of those who are in love with you?
PHILEMATIUM
They’ll love me the more when they see me displaying gratitude to one who has done me services.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.233:
I do wish that news were brought me now that my father’s dead, that I might disinherit myself of my property, and that she might be my heir.
SCAPHA
1.3.235:
This property of his will certainly soon be at an end; day and night there’s eating and drinking, and no one displays thriftiness; ’tis downright cramming.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.237:
I’ faith, I’m determined to make trial on yourself for the first to be thrifty; for you shall neither eat nor drink anything at my house for the next ten days.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.239: If you choose to say anything good about him, you shall be at liberty to say it;
1.3.240:
if you speak otherwise than well, on my word you shall have a beating instantly.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.241:
Upon my faith, if I had paid sacrifice to supreme Jove with that money which I gave for her liberty, never could I have so well employed it. Do see, how, from her very heart’s core, she loves me! Oh, I’m a fortunate man; I’ve liberated in her a patron to plead my cause for me.
SCAPHA
1.3.245:
I see that, compared with Philolaches, you disregard all other men; now, that on his account I mayn’t get a beating, I’ll agree with you in preference, if you are quite satisfied that he will always prove a friend to you.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.248:
Give me the mirror, and the casket with my trinkets, directly, Scapha, that I may be quite dressed when Philolaches, my delight, comes here.
SCAPHA
1.3.250:
A woman who neglects herself and her youthful age has occasion for a mirror; what need of a mirror have you, who yourself are in especial a mirror for a mirror.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.252:
For that expression, Scapha, that you mayn’t have said anything so pretty in vain, I’ll to-day give something for your savings—to you, my Philematium.
PHILEMATIUM
(while SCAPHA is dressing her hair.)
1.3.254:
Will you see that each hair is nicely arranged in its own place?
SCAPHA
1.3.255:
When you yourself are so nice, do believe that your hair must be nice.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.256:
Out upon it! what worse thing can possibly be spoken of than this woman? Now the jade’s a flatterer, just now she was all contradictory.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.258:
Hand me the ceruse.
SCAPHA
Why, what need of ceruse have you?
PHILEMATIUM
To paint my cheeks with it.
SCAPHA
1.3.259:
On the same principle, you would want to be making ivory white with ink.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.260:
Cleverly said that, about the ink and the ivory! Bravo! I applaud you, Scapha.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.261:
Well then, do you give me the rouge.
SCAPHA
I shan’t give it. You really are a clever one. Do you wish to patch up a most clever piece with new daubing? It’s not right that any paint should touch that person, neither ceruse, nor quince-ointment, nor any other wash.
1.3.265:
Take the mirror, then. (Hands her the glass.)
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
Ah wretched me!—she gave the glass a kiss. I could much wish for a stone, with which to break the head of that glass.
SCAPHA
1.3.267:
Take the towel and wipe your hands.
PHILEMATIUM
Why so, prithee?
SCAPHA
1.3.268:
As you’ve been holding the mirror, I’m afraid that your hands may smell of silver; lest Philolaches should suspect you’ve been receiving silver somewhere.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.270:
I don’t think that I ever did see any one procuress more cunning. How cleverly and artfully did it occur to the jade’s imagination about the mirror!
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.272:
Do you think I ought to be perfumed with unguents as well?
SCAPHA
By no means do so.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.273:
For what reason?
SCAPHA
Because, i’ faith, a woman smells best when she smells of nothing at all. For those old women who are in the habit of anointing themselves with unguents, vampt up creatures,
1.3.275:
old hags, and toothless, who hide the blemishes of the person with paint, when the sweat has blended itself with the unguents, forthwith they stink just like when a cook has poured together a variety of broths; what they smell of, you don’t know, except this only, that you understand that badly they do smell.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.279: How very cleverly she does understand everything! There’s nothing more knowing than this knowing woman!
1.3.280:
(To the AUDIENCE.) This is the truth, and a very great portion, in fact, of you know it, who have old women for wives at home who purchased you with their portions.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.282:
Come now, examine my golden trinkets and my mantle; does this quite become me, Scapha?
SCAPHA
1.3.283:
It befits not me to concern myself about that.
PHILEMATIUM
Whom then, prithee?
SCAPHA
I’ll tell you;
1.3.284: Philolaches; so that he may not buy anything except that which he fancies will please you. For a lover buys the favours of a mistress for himself with gold and purple garments. What need is there for that which he doesn’t want as his own, to be shown him still? Age is to be enveloped in purple; gold ornaments are unsuitable for a woman. A beautiful woman will be more beautiful naked than drest in purple.
1.3.290:
Besides, it’s in vain she’s well-drest if she’s ill-conducted; ill-conduct soils fine ornaments worse than dirt. But if she’s beauteous, she’s sufficiently adorned.
PHILOLACHES
(apart.)
1.3.292:
Too long have I withheld my hand. (Coming forward.) What are you about here?
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.293:
I’m decking myself out to please you.
PHILOLACHES
You are dressed enough. (To SCAPHA.) Go you hence in-doors, and take away this finery. (SCAPHA goes into the house.) But, my delight,
1.3.295:
my Philematium, I have a mind to regale together with you.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.296:
And, i’ faith, so I have with you; for what you have a mind to, the same have I a mind to, my delight.
PHILOLACHES
1.3.297:
Ha! at twenty mine that expression were cheap.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.298:
Give me ten, there’s a dear; I wish to let you have that expression bought a bargain.
PHILOLACHES
1.3.299: You’ve already got ten minae with you; or reckon up the account:
1.3.300:
thirty minae I gave for your freedom—
PHILEMATIUM
Why reproach me with that?
PHILOLACHES
1.3.301:
What, I reproach you with it? Why, I had rather that I myself were reproached with it; no money whatever for this long time have I ever laid out equally well.
PHILEMATIUM
1.3.303:
Surely, in loving you, I never could have better employed my pains.
PHILOLACHES
1.3.304: The account, then, of receipts and expenditure fully tallies between ourselves;
1.3.305:
you love me, I love you. Each thinks that it is so deservedly. Those who rejoice at this, may they ever rejoice at the continuance of their own happiness. Those who envy, let not any one henceforth be ever envious of their blessings.
PHILEMATIUM
(pointing to a couch on the stage.)
1.3.308:
Come, take your place, then. (At the door, to a SERVANT, who obeys.) Boy, bring some water for the hands; put a little table here. See where are the dice. Would you like some perfumes? (They recline on the couch.)
PHILOLACHES
1.3.309: What need is there? Along with myrrh I am reclining.
1.3.310: But isn’t this my friend who’s coming hither with his mistress? ’Tis he; it’s Callidamates; look, he’s coming. Capital! my sweet one, see, our comrades are approaching; they’re coming to share the spoil.

1.4.313:
(Enter CALLIDAMATES, at a distance, drunk, and DELPHIUIM, followed by a SERVANT.) CALLIDAMATES
(to his SERVANT.)
I want you to come for me in good time to the house of Philolaches; listen you; well then! those are your orders. (Exit SERVANT.)
1.4.315:
For from the place where I was, thence did I betake myself off; so confoundedly tired was I there. with the entertainment and the discourse. Now I’ll go to Philolaches to have a bout there he’ll receive us with jovial feelings and handsomely. Do I seem to you to be fairly drenched, my bubsy?
DELPHIUM
1.4.320:
You ought always to live pursuing this course of life.
CALLIDAMATES
1.4.322:
Should you like, then, for me to hug you, and you me?
DELPHIUM
1.4.323:
If you’ve a mind to do so, of course.
CALLIDAMATES
You are a charming one. (He stumbles.) Do hold me up, there’s a dear.
DELPHIUM
(holding him by the arm.)
1.4.324:
Take care you don’t fall. Stand up.
CALLIDAMATES
1.4.325:
O! you are the apple of my eye. I’m your fosterling, my honey.
(He stumbles.)
DELPHIUM
(still holding him up.)
1.4.326:
Only do take care that you don’t recline in the street, before we get to a place where a couch is ready laid.
CALLIDAMATES
1.4.328:
Do let me fall.
DELPHIUM
Well, I’ll let you. (Lets go.)
CALLIDAMATES
(dragging her as he falls.)
1.4.330:
But that as well which I’ve got hold of in my hand.
DELPHIUM
1.4.331:
If you fall, you shan’t fall without me falling with you. Then some one shall pick us both up as we lie (Aside.) The man’s quite drenched.
CALLIDAMATES
(overhearing.)
Do you say that I am drenched, my bubsy?
DELPHIUM
1.4.332:
Give me your hand; I really do not want you hurt.
CALLIDAMATES
(giving his hand.)
1.4.333:
There now, take it.
DELPHIUM
Come, move on with me.
CALLIDAMATES
Where am I going, do you know?
DELPHIUM
I know.
CALLIDAMATES
1.4.334: It has just come into my head:
1.4.335:
why, of course I’m going home for a booze.
DELPHIUM
Why yes, really now I do remember that.
PHILOLACHES
1.4.336:
Won’t you let me go to find them, my life? Of all persons I wish well to him especially. I’ll return just now.
(Goes forward towards the door.)
PHILEMATIUM
1.4.338:
That just now is a long time to me.
CALLIDAMATES
(going to the door and knocking.)
1.4.339:
Is there any person here?
PHILOLACHES
’Tis he.
CALLIDAMATES
(turning round.)
Bravo! Philolaches,
1.4.340:
good day to you, most friendly to me of all men.
PHILOLACHES
1.4.341:
May the Gods bless you. (Pointing to a couch.) Take your place, Callidamates. (He takes his place.) Whence are you betaking yourself?
CALLIDAMATES
1.4.342:
Whence a drunken man does.
PHILOLACHES
1.4.343:
Well said. But, my Delphium, do take your place, there’s a dear.
(She takes her place on a couch.)
CALLIDAMATES
1.4.344:
Give her something to drink.
I shall go to sleep directly.
(Nods and goes to sleep.)
PHILOLACHES
1.4.345: He doesn’t do anything wonderful or strange.
1.4.346:
What shall I do with him then, my dear?
DELPHIUM
Let him alone just as he is.
PHILOLACHES
1.4.347: Come, you boy. Meanwhile, speedily pass the goblet round, beginning with Delphium.

2.1.348:
(Enter TRANIO, at a distance.) TRANIO
(to himself.)
Supreme Jove, with all his might and resources, is seeking for me and Philolaches, my master’s son, to be undone.
2.1.350: Our hopes are destroyed; nowhere is there any hold for courage; not even Salvation now could save us if she wished. Such an immense mountain of woe have I just now seen at the harbour: my master has arrived from abroad; Tranio is undone! (To the. AUDIENCE.) Is there any person who’d like to make gain of a little money,
2.1.355: who could this day endure to take my place in being tortured? Where are those fellows hardened to a flogging, the wearers-out of iron chains, or those, who, for the consideration of three didrachms, would get beneath besieging towers, where some are in the way of having their bodies pierced with fifteen spears? I’ll give a talent to that man who shall be the first to run to the cross for me;
2.1.360:
but on condition that twice his feet, twice his arms are fastened there. When that shall have been done, then ask the money down of me. But am I not a wretched fellow, not at full speed to be running home?
PHILOLACHES
2.1.363:
Here come the provisions; see, here’s Tranio; he’s come back from the harbour.
TRANIO
(running.)
2.1.364:
Philolaches!
PHILOLACHES
What’s the matter?
TRANIO
Both I and you—
PHILOLACHES
What about Both I and you?
TRANIO
Are undone!
PHILOLACHES
2.1.365:
Why so?
TRANIO
Your father’s here.
PHILOLACHES
What is it I hear of you?
TRANIO
We are finished up. Your father’s come, I say.
PHILOLACHES
(starting up.)
2.1.366:
Where is he, I do entreat you?
TRANIO
He’s coming.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.367:
Coming? Who says so? Who has seen him?
TRANIO
I saw him myself, I tell you.
PHILOLACHES
Woe unto me! what am I about?
TRANIO
2.1.368:
Why the plague now do you ask me what you are about? Taking your place at table, of course.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.369:
Did you see him?
TRANIO
I my own self, I tell you.
PHILOLACHES
For certain?
TRANIO
For certain, I tell you.
PHILOLACHES
I’m undone,
2.1.370:
if you are telling the truth.
TRANIO
What good could it be to me if I told a lie?
PHILOLACHES
2.1.371:
What shall I do now?
TRANIO
(pointing to the table and couches.)
Order all these things to be removed from here. (Pointing.) Who’s that asleep there?
PHILOLACHES
2.1.372:
Callidamates.
TRANIO
Arouse him, Delphium.
DELPHIUM
(bawling out in his ear.)
2.1.373:
Callidamates! Callidamates! awake!
CALLIDAMATES
(raising himself a little.)
I am awake; give me something to drink.
DELPHIUM
2.1.374:
Awake; the father of Philolaches has arrived from abroad.
CALLIDAMATES
I hope his father’s well.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.375:
He is well indeed; but I am utterly undone.
CALLIDAMATES
You, utterly undone? How can that be?
PHILOLACHES
2.1.376:
By heavens! do get up, I beg of you; my father has arrived.
CALLIDAMATES
Your father has come? Bid him go back again. What business had he to come back here so soon?
PHILOLACHES
2.1.378: What am I to do? My father will, just now, be coming and unfortunately finding me amid drunken carousals, and the house full of revellers and women. It’s a shocking bad job,
2.1.380:
to be digging a well at the last moment, just when thirst has gained possession of your throat; just as I, on the arrival of my father, wretch that I am, am now enquiring what I am to do.
TRANIO
(pointing at CALLIDAMATES.)
2.1.382:
Why look, he has laid down his head and gone to sleep. Do arouse him.
PHILOLACHES
(shaking him.)
2.1.383:
Will you awake now? My father, I tell you, will be here this instant.
CALLIDAMATES
How say you? Your father? Give me my shoes, that I may take up arms. On my word, I’ll kill your father this instant.
PHILOLACHES
(seizing hold of him.)
2.1.385:
You’re spoiling the whole business;
do hold your tongue.
(To DELPHIUM.) Prithee, do carry him off in your arms into the house.
CALLIDAMATES
(To DELPHIUM, who is lifting him up.)
2.1.386:
Upon my faith, I’ll be making an utensil of you just now, if you don’t find me one.
(He is led off into the house.)
PHILOLACHES
2.1.387:
I’m undone!
TRANIO
Be of good courage; I’ll cleverly find a remedy for this alarm.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.388:
I’m utterly ruined!
TRANIO
Do hold your tongue; I’ll think of something by means of which to alleviate this for you. Are you satisfied, if on his arrival I shall so manage your father,
2.1.390:
not only that he shall not enter, but even that he shall run away to a distance from the house? Do you only be off from here in-doors, and remove these things from here with all haste.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.392:
Where am I to be?
TRANIO
Where you especially desire: with her (pointing to PHILEMATIUM); with this girl, too, you’ll be. (Pointing to DELPHEIUM.)
DELPHIUM
2.1.393:
How then? Are we to go away from here?
TRANIO
Not far from here, Delphium. For carouse away in the house not a bit the less on account of this.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.395:
Ah me! I’m in a sweat with fear as to how these fine words are to end!
TRANIO
2.1.396:
Can you not be tranquil in your mind, and do as I bid you?
PHILOLACHES
I can be.
TRANIO
2.1.397:
In the first place of all, Philematium, do you go in-doors; and you, Delphium.
DELPHIUM
2.1.398:
We’ll both be obedient to you.
(They go into the house.)
TRANIO
May Jupiter grant it so! Now then, do you give attention as to what I’d have attended to.
2.1.400:
In the first place, then, before anything, cause the house to be shut up at once. Take care and don’t let any one whisper a word indoors.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.402:
Just as though no living being were dwelling within the house.
PHILOLACHES
Very well.
TRANIO
2.1.403:
And let no one answer, when the old gentleman knocks at the door.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.404:
Anything else?
TRANIO
Order the master-key of the house
2.1.405:
to be brought me at once from within; this house I’ll lock here on the outside.
PHILOLACHES
2.1.406:
To your charge I commit myself, Tranio, and my hopes. (He goes into the house, and the things are removed from the stage.)
TRANIO
(to himself.)
2.1.407: It matters not a feather whether a patron or a dependant is the nearest at hand for that man who has got no courage in his breast.
2.1.410: For to every man, whether very good or very bad, even at a moment’s notice, it is easy to act with craft; but this must be looked to, this is the duty of a prudent man, that what has been planned and done in craftiness, may all come about smoothly and without mishap;
2.1.415: so that he may not have to put up with anything by reason of which he might be loth to live; just as I shall manage, that, from the confusion which we shall here create, all shall really go on smoothly and tranquilly, and not produce us any inconvenience in the results. (Enter a BOY, from the house.) But, why have you come out?
2.1.419:
I’m undone!
(The BOY shows him the key.) O very well, you’ve obeyed my orders most opportunely.
A BOY
2.1.420:
He bade me most earnestly to entreat you some way or other to scare away his father, that he may not enter the house.
TRANIO
2.1.422: Even more, tell him this, that I’ll cause that he shan’t venture even to look at the house, and to take to flight, covering up his head with the greatest alarm.
2.1.425: Give me the key (taking it), and be off in-doors, and shut to the door, and I’ll lock it on this side. (The BOY goes into the house, and TRANIO locks the door.) Bid him now come forthwith. For the old gentleman here while still alive this day will I institute games in his presence, such as I fancy there will never be for him when he’s dead. (Moving away.) I’ll go away from the door to this spot; hence, I’ll look out afar
2.1.430: in which direction to lay the burden on the old fellow on his arrival. (Exit to a little distance.)

2.2.431:
(Enter THEUROPIDES, followed by ATTENDANTS.) THEUROPIDES
(to himself.)
Neptune, I do return extreme thanks to thee that thou hast just dismissed me from thee, though scarce alive. But if, from this time forward, thou shalt only know that I have stirred a foot upon the main, there is no reason why, that instant,
2.2.435:
thou shouldst not do with me that which thou hast now wished to do. Away with you, away with you from me henceforth for ever after to-day; what I was to entrust to thee, all of it have I now entrusted. (overhearing him.)
TRANIO
(apart.)
2.2.438:
By my troth, Neptune, you’ve been much to blame, to have lost this opportunity so fair.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.440:
After three years, I’ve arrived home from Aegypt. I shall come a welcome guest to my household, I suppose.
TRANIO
(apart.)
2.2.442:
Upon my faith, he might have come a much more welcome one, who had brought the tidings you were dead.
THEUROPIDES
(looking at the door.)
2.2.444: But what means this? Is the door shut in the daytime?
2.2.445:
I’ll knock. (Knocks at the door.) Hallo, there! is any one going to open this door for me?
TRANIO
(coming forward, and speakcing aloud.)
2.2.446:
What person is it that has come so near to our house?
THEUROPIDES
2.2.447:
Surely this is my servant Tranio.
TRANIO
O Theuropides, my master, welcome; I’m glad that you’ve arrived in safety. Haveyou been well all along?
THEUROPIDES
2.2.449:
All along, as you see.
TRANIO
That’s very good.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.450:
What about yourselves? Are you all mad?
TRANIO
Why so?
THEUROPIDES
For this reason; because you are walking about outside; not a born person is keeping watch in the house, either to open or to give an answer. With kicking with my feet I’ve almost broken in the pannels?
TRANIO
2.2.454:
How now? Have you been touching this house?
THEUROPIDES
Why shouldn’t I touch it? Why, with kicking it, I tell you, I’ve almost broken down the door.
TRANIO
2.2.457:
What, you touched it?
THEUROPIDES
I touched it, I tell you, and knocked at it.
TRANIO
Out upon you!
THEUROPIDES
Why so?
TRANIO
2.2.458:
By heavens! ’twas ill done.
THEUROPIDES
What is the matter?
TRANIO
It cannot be expressed, how shocking and dreadful a mischief you’ve been guilty of.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.460:
How so?
TRANIO
Take to flight, I beseech you, and get away from the house. Fly in this direction, fly closer to me. (He runs to wards TRANIO.) What, did you touch the door?
THEUROPIDES
2.2.462:
How could I knock, if I didn’t touch it?
TRANIO
2.2.463:
By all that’s holy, you’ve been the death—
THEUROPIDES
Of what person?
TRANIO
Of all your family.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.464:
May the Gods and Goddesses confound you with that omen.
TRANIO
2.2.465:
I’m afraid that you can’t make satisfaction for yourself and them.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.466:
For what reason, or what new affair is this that you thus suddenly bring me news of?
TRANIO
2.2.467:
And (whispering) hark you, prithee, do bid those people to move away from here.
(Pointing to the ATTENDANTS of THEUROPIDES.)
THEUROPIDES
(to the ATTENDANTS.)
2.2.468:
Move away from here.
TRANIO
Don’t you touch the house. Touch you the ground as well. (Exeunt the ATTENDANTS.)
THEUROPIDES
2.2.469:
I’ faith, prithee, do speak out now.
TRANIO
2.2.470:
Because it is now seven months that not a person has set foot within this house, and since we once for all left it.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.472:
Tell me, why so?
TRANIO
Just look around, whether there’s any person to overhear our discourse.
THEUROPIDES
(looking around.)
2.2.474:
Look around once more.
THEUROPIDES
(looking around.)
There’s nobody; now then, speak out.
TRANIO
(in a loud whisper.)
2.2.475:
The house has been guilty of a capital offence.
THEUROPIDES
I don’t understand you.
TRANIO
2.2.476:
A crime, I tell you, has been committed there, a long while ago, one of olden time and ancient date.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.477:
Of ancient date?
TRANIO
’Tis but recently, in fact, that we’ve discovered this deed.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.478:
What is this crime, or who committed it? Tell me.
TRANIO
2.2.479: A host slew his guest, seized with his hand;
2.2.480:
he, I fancy, who sold you the house.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.481:
Slew him?
TRANIO
And robbed this guest of his gold, and buried this guest there in the house, on the spot.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.483:
For what reason do you suspect that this took place?
TRANIO
2.2.484: I’ll tell you; listen. One day, when your son had dined away from home, after he returned home from dining;
2.2.486:
we all went to bed, and fell asleep. By accident, I had forgotten to put out my lamp; and he, all of a sudden, called out aloud—
THEUROPIDES
2.2.489:
What person? My son?
TRANIO
Hist! hold your peace: just listen.
2.2.490:
He said that a dead man came to him in his sleep—
THEUROPIDES
2.2.491:
In his dreams, then, you mean?
TRANIO
Just so. But only listen. He said that he had met with his death by these means—
THEUROPIDES
2.2.493:
What, in his sleep?
TRANIO
It would have been surprising if he had told him awake, who had been murdered sixty years ago.
2.2.495: On some occasions you are absurdly simple.
2.2.496: But look, what he said: I am the guest of Diapontius, from beyond the seas; here do I dwell; this has been assigned me as my abode; for Orcus would not receive me in Acheron,
2.2.500: because prematurely I lost my life. Through confiding was I deceived: my entertainer slew me here, and that villain secretly laid me in the ground without funereal rites, in this house, on the spot, for the sake of gold. Now do you depart from here; this house is accursed, this dwelling is defiled.
2.2.505: The wonders that here take place, hardly in a year could I recount them.
2.2.507:
Troth now, what has happened, prithee?
TRANIO
The door made a noise.
2.2.508:
Was it he that was knocking?
THEUROPIDES
(turning pale.)
I have not one drop of blood! Dead men are come to fetch me to Acheron, while alive!
TRANIO
(aside.)
2.2.510:
I’m undone! those people there will mar my plot. (A noise is heard from within.) How much I dread, lest he should catch me in the fact.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.512:
What are you talking about to yourself? (Goes near the door.)
TRANIO
Do get away from the door. By heavens, fly, I do beseech you.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.513:
Fly where? Fly yourself, as well.
TRANIO
2.2.514:
I am not afraid: I am at peace with the dead.
A VOICE
(from within.)
2.2.515:
Hallo! Tranio.
TRANIO
(in a low voice, near the door.)
You won’t be calling me, if you are wise. (Aloud, as if speaking to the APPARITION.) ’Tis not I that’s guilty; I did not knock at the door.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.518:
Pray, what is it that’s wrong? What matter is agitating you, Tranio? To whom are you saying these things?
TRANIO
2.2.519: Prithee, was it you that called me?
2.2.520:
So may the Gods bless me, I fancied it was this dead man expostulating because you had knocked at the door. But are you still standing there, and not doing what I advise you?
THEUROPIDES
2.2.523:
What am I to do?
TRANIO
Take care not to look back. Fly; cover up your head!
THEUROPIDES
2.2.524:
Why don’t you fly?
TRANIO
I am at peace with the dead.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.525:
I recollect. Why then were you so dreadfully alarmed just now?
TRANIO
2.2.526:
Have no care for me, I tell you; I’ll see to myself. You, as you have begun to do, fly as quick as ever you can; Hercules, too, you will invoke.
THEUROPIDES
2.2.528:
Hercules, I do invoke thee! (Runs off.)
TRANIO
(to himself.)
2.2.529: And I, as well, old fellow, that; this day he’ll send some heavy mishap upon you.
2.2.530:
O ye immortal Gods, I do implore your aid. Plague on it! what a mess I have got into to-day.
(Exit.)

3.1.535:
I cannot lend out a coin of silver to any one. (Enter TRANIO.)
TRANIO
(apart.)
3.1.536: Now, faith, I am clearly undone in an everlasting way! The Banker’s here who found the money with which his mistress was bought. The matter’s all out, unless I meet him a bit beforehand,
3.1.540: so that the old man may not at present come to know of this. I’ll go meet him. But (seeing THEUROPIDES) I wonder why he has so soon betaken himself homeward again. I’m afraid that he has heard something about this affair. I’ll meet him, and accost him. But how dreadfully frightened I am! Nothing is more wretched than the mind of a man with a guilty conscience,
3.1.545:
such as possesses myself. But however this matter turns out, I’ll proceed to perplex it still further: so does this affair require.
(Enter THEUROPIDES.)
TRANIO
(accosting him.)
3.1.547:
Whence come you?
THEUROPIDES
I met that person from whom I bought this house.
TRANIO
3.1.548:
Did you tell him anything about that which I was telling you?
THEUROPIDES
3.1.549:
I’ faith, I certainly told him everything.
TRANIO
(aside.)
Woe to unfortunate me!
3.1.550:
I’m afraid that my schemes are everlastingly undone!
THEUROPIDES
3.1.551:
What is it you are saying to yourself?
TRANIO
Why nothing. But tell me, prithee, did you really tell him?
THEUROPIDES
3.1.552:
I told him everything in its order, I tell you.
TRANIO
3.1.553:
Does he, then, confess about the guest?
THEUROPIDES
Why no; he utterly denies it.
TRANIO
3.1.554:
Does he deny it?
THEUROPIDES
Do you ask me again?
3.1.555:
I should tell you if he had confessed it. What now are you of opinion ought to be done?
TRANIO
3.1.556:
What is my opinion? By my troth, I beg of you, appoint an arbitrator together with him; but take you care that you appoint one who will believe me; you’ll overcome him as easily as a fox eats a pear.
A BANKER
(to himself.)
3.1.560:
But see, here’s Tranio, the servant of Philolaches, people who pay me neither interest nor principal on my money.
(Goes towards TRANIO, who steps forward to meet him.)
THEUROPIDES
(to TRANIO.)
3.1.565:
in such a fashion both this way and that do they find business for me. But I’ll make haste and accost him. (Moves towards the BANKER.)
A BANKER
(apart.)
3.1.566: He’s coming towards me. I’m all right I’ve some hopes of my money;
3.1.568:
The fellow’s deceived. (To the BANKER.) I heartily bid you hail, my friend Saturides.
A BANKER
3.1.569:
And hail to you. What about the money?
TRANIO
Be off with you, will you, you brute.
3.1.570:
Directly you come, you commence the attack against me.
A BANKER
(apart.)
3.1.571:
This fellow’s empty-handed.
TRANIO
(overhearing him.)
This fellow’s surely a conjurer.
A BANKER
3.1.572:
But why don’t you put an end to this trifling?
TRANIO
Tell me, then, what it is you want.
A BANKER
3.1.573:
Where is Philolaches?
TRANIO
You never could have met me more opportunely than you have met me.
A BANKER
3.1.575:
How’s that?
TRANIO
(taking him aside.)
Step this way.
A BANKER
(aloud.)
Why isn’t the money repaid me?
TRANIO
3.1.576:
I know that you have a good voice; don’t bawl out so loud.
A BANKER
(aloud.)
3.1.577:
I’ faith, I certainly shall bawl out.
TRANIO
O do humour me now.
A BANKER
3.1.578:
What do you want me to humour you in?
TRANIO
Prithee, be off hence home.
A BANKER
3.1.579:
Be off?
TRANIO
Return here about mid-day.
A BANKER
3.1.580:
Will the interest be paid then?
TRANIO
It will be paid. Be off.
A BANKER
3.1.581:
Why should I run to and fro here, or use or waste my pains? What if I remain here until mid-day in preference?
TRANIO
3.1.583:
Why no; be off home. On my word, I’m telling the truth. Only do be off.
A BANKER
(aloud.)
3.1.585:
Then do you pay me my interest. Why do you trifle with me this way?
TRANIO
3.1.586:
Bravo! faith. Really now, do be off; do attend to me.
A BANKER
(aloud.)
3.1.587:
I’ faith, I’ll call him now by name.
TRANIO
Bravo! stoutly done! Really you are quite rich now when you bawl out.
A BANKER
(aloud.)
3.1.588: I’m asking for my own. In this way you’ve been disappointing me for these many days past.
3.1.590:
If I’m troublesome, give me back the money; I’ll go away then. That expression puts an end to all replies.
TRANIO
(pretending to offer it him.)
3.1.592:
Then, take the principal.
A BANKER
(aloud.)
Why no, the interest; I want that first.
TRANIO
3.1.593: What? Have you, you fellow most foul of all fellows, come here to burst yourself? Do what lies in your power.
3.1.595:
He’s not going to pay you; he doesn’t owe it.
A BANKER
Not owe it?
TRANIO
Not a tittle, indeed, can you get from here. Would you prefer for him to go abroad, and leave the city in exile, driven hence for your sake? Why then, in preference let him pay the principal.
A BANKER
3.1.598:
But I don’t ask for it.
THEUROPIDES
(calling out to TRANIO, from a distance.)
3.1.599:
Hark you! you whip-knave, come back to me.
TRANIO
(to THEUROPIDES.)
3.1.601:
I’ll be there just now. (To the BANKER.) Don’t you be troublesome: no one’s going to pay you; do what you please. You are the only person, I suppose, that lends money upon interest.
(Moves towards THEUROPIDES.)
A BANKER
(bawling aloud.)
Don’t you be troublesome; no one’s going to pay you; do what you please. You are the only person, I suppose, that lends money upon interest.
THEUROPIDES
(to TRANIO.)
3.1.603: Give me my interest! pay me my interest! you pay my interest! Are you going to give me my interest this instant?
3.1.605:
Give me my interest!
TRANIO
Interest here, interest there! The old rogue knows how to talk about nothing but interest. I do not think that ever I saw any beast more vile than you.
A BANKER
3.1.609:
Upon my faith, you don’t alarm me now with those expressions.
This is of a hot nature; although it is at a distance off, it scorches badly.
TRANIO
3.1.610:
Pray, what interest is this that he is asking for?
TRANIO
(in a low voice, to the BANKER.)
3.1.611:
Look now; his father has arrived from abroad, not long since; he’ll pay you both interest and principal; don’t you then attempt any further to make us your enemies. See whether he puts you off.
A BANKER
3.1.614:
Nay but, I’ll take it, if anything’s offered.
THEUROPIDES
(to TRANIO, coming towards him.)
3.1.615:
What do you say, then—?
TRANIO
What is it you mean?
THEUROPIDES
Who is this? What is he asking for? Why is he thus rudely speaking of my son Philolaches in this way, and giving you abuse to your face? What’s owing him?
TRANIO
(to THEUROPIDES.)
3.1.618:
I beg of you, do order the money to be thrown in the face of this dirty brute.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.620:
I, order it?
TRANIO
Order the fellow’s face to be pelted with money.
A BANKER
(coming nearer.)
3.1.621:
I could very well put up with a pelting with money.
THEUROPIDES
(to TRANIO.)
3.1.622:
What money’s this?
TRANIO
Philolaches owes this person a little.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.623:
How much?
TRANIO
About forty minae.
A BANKER
(to THEUROPIDES.)
3.1.625:
Don’t you hear him? Troth now, prithee, doesn’t he seem just suited to be a Banker—a generation that’s most roguish?
THEUROPIDES
3.1.627: I don’t care, just now, for that, who he is or whence he is;
3.1.628: this I want to be told me, this I very much wish to know—
3.1.629:
I heard from him that there was interest owing on the money as well.
TRANIO
3.1.630: Forty-four minae are due to him.
3.1.633:
Say that you’ll pay it, that he may be off.
THEUROPIDES
I, say that I’ll pay it?
TRANIO
3.1.634:
Do say so.
THEUROPIDES
What, I?
TRANIO
You yourself. Do only say so. Do be guided by me. Do promise. Come now, I say; I beg of you.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.635:
Answer me; what has been done with this money?
TRANIO
3.1.636:
It’s safe.
THEUROPIDES
Pay it yourselves then, if it’s safe,
TRANIO
3.1.637:
Your son has bought a house.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.638:
A house?
TRANIO
A house.
THEUROPIDES
Bravo! Philolaches is taking after his father! The fellow now turns to merchandize.
3.1.640:
A house, say you?
TRANIO
A house, I tell you. But do you know of what sort?
THEUROPIDES
3.1.641:
How can I know?
TRANIO
Out with you!
THEUROPIDES
What’s the matter?
TRANIO
Don’t ask me that.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.642:
But why so?
TRANIO
Bright as a mirror, pure brilliancy itself.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.643:
Excellently done, upon my faith! Well, how much did he agree to give for it?
TRANIO
3.1.644: As many great talents as you and I put together make;
3.1.645:
but these forty minae he paid by way of earnest. (Pointing to the BANKER.) From him he received what we paid the other man. Do you quite understand? For after this house was in such a state as I mentioned to you, he at once purchased another house for himself.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.649:
Excellently done, upon my faith!
A BANKER
(touching TRANIO.)
Hark you. Mid-day is now close at hand.
TRANIO
3.1.652: Prithee, do dismiss this puking fellow, that he mayn’t worry us to death.
3.1.631:
Forty-four minae are due to him, both principal and interest.
A BANKER
’Tis just that much; I ask for nothing more.
TRANIO
3.1.632:
Upon my faith, I really could have wished that you had asked more, if only by a single coin.
THEUROPIDES
(to the BANKER.)
3.1.653:
Young man, transact the business with me.
A BANKER
I’m to ask it of you, you mean?
THEUROPIDES
3.1.654:
Come for it to-morrow.
A BANKER
I’ll be off, then; I’m quite satisfied if I get it tomorrow.
(Exit.)
TRANIO
(aside.)
3.1.655:
A plague may all the Gods and Goddesses send upon him! so utterly has he disarranged my plans. On my word, no class of men is there more disgusting, or less acquainted with fair dealing than the banking race.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.659:
In what neighbourhood did my son buy this house?
TRANIO
(aside.)
3.1.660:
Just see that, now! I’m undone!
THEUROPIDES
Are you going to tell me that which I ask you?
TRANIO
3.1.661:
I’ll tell you; but I’m thinking what was the name of the owner.
(Pretends to think.)
THEUROPIDES
3.1.662:
Well, call it to mind, then.
TRANIO
(aside.)
What am I to do now, except put the lie upon this neighbour of ours next door? I’ll say that his son has bought that house.
3.1.665:
I’ faith, I’ve heard say that a lie piping-hot is the best lie; this is piping-hot; although it is at a distance off, it scorches badly. Whatever the Gods dictate, that am I determined to say.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.667:
Well now? Have you recollected it by this?
TRANIO
(aside.)
May the Gods confound that fellow!—no this other fellow, rather.
3.1.669:
(To THEUROPIDES.) Your son has bought the house of this next-door neighbour of yours.
THEUROPIDES
In real truth?
TRANIO
3.1.671:
If, indeed, you are going to pay down the money, then in real truth; if you are not going to pay it, in real truth he has not bought it.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.673:
He hasn’t bought it in a very good situation.
TRANIO
Why yes, in a very good one.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.674:
I’ faith, I should like to look over this house; just knock at the door, and call some one to you from within, Tranio.
TRANIO
(aside.)
3.1.676:
Why just look now, again I don’t know what I’m to say. Once more, now, are the surges bearing me upon the self-same rock. What now? I’ faith, I can’t discover what I am now to do; I’m caught in the fact.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.679: Just call some one out of doors;
3.1.680:
ask him to show us round.
TRANIO
(going to the door of SIMO’s house.)
Hallo there, you! (Turning round) But there are ladies here; we must first see whether they are willing or unwilling.
THEUROPIDES
3.1.682:
You say what’s good and proper; just make enquiry, and ask. I’ll wait here outside until you come out.
TRANIO
(aside.)
3.1.684: May all the Gods and Goddesses utterly confound you, old gentleman!
3.1.685: in such a fashion are you thwarting my artful plans in every way. Bravo! very good! Look, Simo himself, the owner of the house, is coming out of doors. I’ll step aside here, until I have convened the senate of council in my mind. Then, when I’ve discovered what I am to do, I’ll join him. (THEUROPIDES and TRANIO stand at a distance from SIMO’s house, in opposite directions, THEUROPIDES being out of sight.)

3.2.690:
(Enter SIMO, from his house.) SIMO
(to himself.)
I’ve not enjoyed myself better at home this year than I have to-day, nor has at any time any meal pleased me better. My wife provided a very nice breakfast for me; now she bids me go take a nap. By no means! It instantly struck me that it didn’t so happen by chance.
3.2.695:
She provided a better breakfast than is her wont; and then, the old lady wanted to draw me away to my chamber. Sleep is not good after breakfast—out upon it! I secretly stole away from the house, out of doors. My wife, I’m sure, is now quite bursting with rage at home.
TRANIO
(apart.)
3.2.700:
A sore mischance is provided for this old fellow by the evening; for he must both dine and go to bed in-doors in sorry fashion.
SIMO
(continuing.)
3.2.702: The more I reflect upon it in my mind: if any person has a dowried wife, sleep has no charms for him.
3.2.705: I detest going to take a nap. It’s a settled matter with me to be off to the Forum from here, rather than nap it at home. And, i’ faith (to the AUDIENCE), I don’t know how your wives are in their behaviour; this wife of mine, I know right well how badly she treats me,
3.2.710:
and that she will prove more annoying to me hereafter than she has been.
TRANIO
(apart.)
3.2.711: If your escape, old gentleman, turns out amiss, there’ll be no reason for you to be accusing any one of the Gods; by very good right, you may justly lay the blame upon yourself. It’s time now for me to accost this old fellow.
3.2.715:
’Tis down upon him. I’ve hit upon a plan whereby to cajole the old fellow, by means of which to drive grief away from me. I’ll accost him. (Accosting him.) May the Gods, Simo, send on you many blessings!
(Takes him by the hand.)
SIMO
3.2.718:
Save you, Tranio!
TRANIO
How fare you?
SIMO
Not amiss. What are you about?
TRANIO
3.2.719:
Holding by the hand a very worthy man.
SIMO
You act in a friendly way,
3.2.720:
in speaking well of me.
TRANIO
It certainly is your due.
SIMO
But, i’ faith, in you I don’t hold a good servant by the hand.
THEUROPIDES
(calling from a distance, where he is not perceived by SIMO.)
3.2.721:
Hark you! you whip-knave, come back to me.
TRANIO
(turning round.)
I’ll be there just now.
SIMO
3.2.722:
Well now, how soon—?
TRANIO
What is it?
SIMO
The usual goings-on.
TRANIO
3.2.725:
reflecting, at the same time, how short life is.
TRANIO
3.2.726:
What of all this? Dear me, at last, after some difficulty, I perceive that you are talking about these goings-on of ours.
SIMO
3.2.728: I’ faith, you people are living a merry life, just as befits you:
3.2.729:
on wine, good cheer, nice dainty fish, you enjoy life.
TRANIO
3.2.731:
Why yes, so it was in time past, indeed; but now these things have come to an end all at once.
SIMO
3.2.733:
How so?
TRANIO
So utterly, Simo, are we all undone!
SIMO
3.2.734:
Won’t you hold your tongue? Everything has gone on prosperously with you hitherto.
TRANIO
3.2.735:
I don’t deny that it has been as you say; undoubtedly, we have lived heartily, just as we pleased; but, Simo, in such a way has the breeze now forsaken our ship—
SIMO
3.2.737:
What’s the matter? In what way?
TRANIO
3.2.738:
In a most shocking way.
SIMO
What, wasn’t it hauled ashorein safety?
TRANIO
3.2.739:
Ah me!
SIMO
What’s the matter?
TRANIO
Ah wretched me! I’m utterly undone!
SIMO
3.2.740:
How so?
TRANIO
Because a ship has come, to smash the hull of our ship.
SIMO
3.2.741:
I would wish as you would wish, Tranio, for your own sake. But what is the matter? Do inform me.
TRANIO
I will inform you. My master has arrived from abroad.
SIMO
3.2.742:
In that case, the cord will be stretched for you; thence to the place where iron fetters clink; after that, straight to the cross.
TRANIO
3.2.743:
Now, by your knees, I do implore you, don’t give information to my master.
SIMO
3.2.744:
Don’t you fear; he shall know nothing from me.
TRANIO
3.2.746:
Blessings on you, my patron.
SIMO
I don’t care for clients of this description for myself.
TRANIO
3.2.747:
Now as to this about which our old gentleman has sent me.
SIMO
3.2.748:
First answer me this that I ask you. As yet, has your old gentleman discovered anything of these matters?
TRANIO
3.2.750:
Nothing whatever.
SIMO
Has he censured his son at all?
TRANIO
3.2.751:
He is as calm as the calm weather is wont to be. Now he has requested me most earnestly to beg this of you, that leave may be given him to see over this house of yours.
SIMO
3.2.754:
It’s not for sale.
TRANIO
I know that indeed; but the old gentleman
3.2.755:
wishes to build a woman’s apartment here in his own house, baths, too, and a piazza, and a porch.
SIMO
3.2.757:
What has he been dreaming of?
TRANIO
I’ll tell you. He wishes to give his son a wife as soon as he can; for that purpose he wants a new apartment for the women.
3.2.760:
But he says that some builder, I don’t know who, has been praising up to him this house of yours, as being remarkably well built; now he’s desirous to take a model from it, if you don’t make any objection—
SIMO
3.2.763:
Indeed, he is really choosing a plan for himself from a piece of poor workmanship.
TRANIO
3.2.764:
It was because he heard that here the summer heat was much modified; that this house was wont to be inhabited each day all day long.
SIMO
3.2.766:
Why really, upon my faith, on the contrary, while there’s shade in every direction, in spite of it, the sun is always here from morning till night: he stands, like a dun, continually at the door; and I have no shade anywhere, unless, perhaps, there may be some in the well.
TRANIO
3.2.770:
Well now, have you one from Sarsina, if you have no woman of Umbria?
SIMO
3.2.771:
Don’t be impertinent. It is just as I tell you.
TRANIO
3.2.772:
Still, he wishes to look over it.
SIMO
He may look over it, if he likes. If there is anything that takes his fancy, let him build after my plan.
TRANIO
3.2.774:
Am I to go and call this person hither?
SIMO
Go and call him.
TRANIO
(to himself, as he goes to the other side of the stage to call THEUROPIDES.)
3.2.775: They say that Alexander the Great and Agathocles achieved two very great exploits; what shall be the lot of myself, a third, who, unaided, am achieving deeds imperishable? This old fellow is carrying his pack-saddle, the other one, as well. I’ve hit upon a novel trade for myself, not a bad one;
3.2.780:
whereas muleteers have mules to carry pack-saddles; I’ve got men to carry the pack-saddles. They are able to carry heavy burdens; whatever you put upon them, they carry. Now, I don’t know whether I am to address him. I’ll accost him, however. (Calling aloud.) Hark you, Theuropides!
THEUROPIDES
(coming forward.)
3.2.784:
Well; who’s calling me?
TRANIO
A servant most attached to his master.
3.2.786:
Where you sent me, I got it all agreed to.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.787:
Prithee, why did you stay there so long?
TRANIO
3.2.788:
The old gentleman hadn’t leisure; I was waiting until then.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.789:
You keep up that old way of yours, of being tardy.
TRANIO
3.2.790:
Hark you! if you please reflect upon this proverb: to blow and swallow at the same moment isn’t easy to be done; I couldn’t be here and there at the same time.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.793:
What now?
TRANIO
Come and look, and inspect it at your own pleasure.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.794:
Very well, you go before me.
TRANIO
Am I delaying to do so?
THEUROPIDES
I’ll follow after you.
TRANIO
(as they advance.)
3.2.795:
Look, the old gentleman himself is awaiting you before the door, but he is concerned that he has sold this house.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.797:
Why so?
TRANIO
He begs me to persuade Philolaches to let him off.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.798: I don’t think he will. Each man reaps on his own farm. If it had been bought dear,
3.2.800:
we shouldn’t have had permission to return it on his hands. Whatever profit there is, it’s proper to bring it home. It don’t, now-a-days, befit men to be showing compassion.
TRANIO
3.2.803:
I’ faith, you are losing time while you are talking. Follow me.
THEUROPIDES
Be it so.
TRANIO
(to THEUROPIDES.)
3.2.804:
I’ll give you my services.
(Pointing.) There’s the old gentleman. (To SIMO.) Well now, I’ve brought you this person.
SIMO
3.2.805:
I’m glad that you’ve arrived safely from abroad, Theuropides.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.806:
May the Gods bless you.
SIMO
Your servant was telling me that you were desirous to look over this house.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.807:
Unless it’s inconvenient to you.
SIMO
Oh no; quite convenient. Do step in-doors and look over it.
THEUROPIDES
(pausing.)
3.2.808:
But yet—the ladies—
SIMO
Take you care not to trouble yourself a straw about any lady. Walk in every direction, wherever you like, all over the house just as though it were your own.
THEUROPIDES
(apart to TRANIO.)
3.2.810:
Just as though—?
TRANIO
(whispering.)
Oh, take care that you don’t throw it in his teeth now in his concern, that you have bought it. Don’t you see him, how sad a countenance the old gentleman has?
THEUROPIDES
(apart.)
3.2.812:
I see.
TRANIO
(apart.)
Then don’t seem to exult, and to be overmuch delighted; in fact, don’t make mention that you’ve bought it.
THEUROPIDES
(apart.)
3.2.813: I understand; and I think you’ve given good advice, and that it shows a humane disposition.
3.2.815:
(Turning to SIMO.) What now?
SIMO
Won’t you go in? Look over it at your leisure, just as you like.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.816:
I consider that you are acting civilly and kindly.
SIMO
Troth, I wish to do so. Should you like some one to show you over.
THEUROPIDES
Away with any one to show me over. I don’t want him.
SIMO
Why? What’s the matter?
THEUROPIDES
I’ll go wrong, rather than any one should show me over.
TRANIO
(pointing.)
3.2.817:
Don’t you see, this vestibule before the house, and the piazza, of what a compass it is?
THEUROPIDES
3.2.818:
Troth, really handsome!
TRANIO
Well, look now, what pillars there are, with what strength they are built, and of what a thickness.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.820:
I don’t think that I ever saw handsomer pillars.
SIMO
I’ faith, they were some time since bought by me at such a price!
TRANIO
(aside, whispering.)
3.2.821:
Don’t you hear—They were once? He seems hardly able to refrain from tears.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.822:
At what price did you purchase them?
SIMO
3.2.823:
I gave three minae for the two, besides the carriage.
(He retires to some distance.)
THEUROPIDES
(after looking close at them, to TRANIO.)
3.2.824:
Why, upon my word, they are much more unsound than I thought them at first.
TRANIO
3.2.825:
Why so?
THEUROPIDES
Because, i’ faith, the woodworm has split them both from the bottom.
TRANIO
3.2.826:
I think they were cut at an improper season; that fault damages them; but even as it is, they are quite good enough, if they are covered with pitch. But it was no foreign pulse-eating artisan did this work. Don’t you see the joints in the door? (Pointing.)
THEUROPIDES
3.2.829:
I see them.
TRANIO
Look, how close together they are sleeping.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.830:
Sleeping?
TRANIO
That is, how they wink, I intended to say. Are you satisfied?
THEUROPIDES
3.2.831:
The more I look at each particular, the more it pleases me.
TRANIO
(pointing.)
3.2.832: Don’t you see the painting, where one crow is baffling two vultures?
3.2.834: The crow stands there; it’s pecking at them both in turn.
3.2.835: This way, look, prithee, towards me, that yon may be able to see the crow.
3.2.836:
(THEUROPIDES turns towards him.) Now do you see it?
THEUROPIDES
(looking about.)
For my part, I really see no crow there.
TRANIO
3.2.837:
But do you look in that direction, towards yourselves, since you cannot discover the crow, if perchance you may be able to espy the vultures. (THEUROPIDES turns towards SIMO.) Now do you see them?
THEUROPIDES
3.2.833:
Upon my faith, I don’t see them.
TRANIO
But I can see two vultures.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.839:
To make an end of it with you, I don’t see any bird at all painted here.
TRANIO
3.2.840:
Well then, I give it up. I excuse you; it is through age you cannot see.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.841:
These things which I can see, really they do all please me mightily.
SIMO
(coming forward.)
3.2.842:
Now, at length, it’s worth your while to move further on.
THEUROPIDES
Troth, you give good advice.
SIMO
(calling at the door.)
3.2.843:
Ho there, boy! take this person round this house and the apartments. But I myself would have shown you round, if I hadn’t had business at the Forum.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.845:
Away with any one to show me over. I don’t want to be shown over. Whatever it is, I’d rather go wrong than any one should show me over.
SIMO
3.2.847:
The house I’m speaking of.
THEUROPIDES
Then I’ll go in without any one to show me over.
SIMO
Go, by all means.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.848:
I’ll go in-doors, then.
TRANIO
(holding him back.)
Stop, please; let me see whether the dog—
THEUROPIDES
Very well then, look.
(TRANIO looks into the passage.)
TRANIO
3.2.849:
There is one.
THEUROPIDES
(looking in.)
Where is it?
TRANIO
(to the dog.)
Be off and be hanged! ’st, won’t you be off to utter perdition with you? What, do you still linger? ’st, away with you from here!
SIMO
(coming nearer to the door.)
3.2.851:
There’s no danger. You only move on. It’s as gentle as a woman in childbed. You may boldly step in-doors wherever you like. I’m going hence to the Forum.
THEUROPIDES
3.2.853: You’ve acted obligingly. Good speed to you. (Exit SIMO.) Tranio, come, make that dog move away from the door inside,
3.2.855:
although it isn’t to be feared.
TRANIO
Nay but (pointing), you look at it, how gently it lies. Unless you’d like yourself to appear troublesome and cowardly—
THEUROPIDES
3.2.856:
Very well, just as you like.
TRANIO
3.2.857:
Follow me this way then.
THEUROPIDES
For my part, I shall not move in any direction from your feet.
(They go into the house.)

4.1.858:
(Enter PHANISCUS.) PHANISCUS
(to himself.)
Servants who, though they are free from fault, still stand in awe of punishment, those same are wont to be serviceable to their masters.
4.1.860: But those who fear nothing, after they have merited punishment, hit upon foolish plans for themselves: they exercise themselves in running; they take to flight. But, if they are caught, they acquire from punishment a hoard, which by good means they cannot.
4.1.864: They increase from a very little, and from that they lay by a treasure. The resolution that’s in my mind is to be determined to be on my guard against punishment, before my back comes to lose its state of soundness. As hitherto it has been, so does it become my hide still to be, without a bruise, and such that I should decline its being beaten.
4.1.870: If I have any control over it, I shall keep it well covered up. When punishment is being showered down on others, don’t let it be showered down on me. But as servants wish their master to be, such is he wont to be. He is good to the good, bad to the bad. But now at our house at home there do live so many rogues,
4.1.875: lavish of their property, bearers of stripes. When they are called to go fetch their master, I shan’t go; don’t be plaguing me; I know where you are hurrying off to, is the reply. Now, faith, you mule, you’re longing to go to pasturage out of doors. With better deserts, this advantage have I reaped from them, and, in consequence, I have come from home.
4.1.881:
I alone, out of so many servants, am going to fetch my master. When, to-morrow, my master comes to know this, in the morning he will chastise them with bull’s-hide spoils. In fine, I care less for their backs than for my own. Much rather shall they be bull’s-hide-scourged than I be rope-scourged.
(Moves on.)

4.2.885:
(Enter a SERVANT.) ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
Hold you and stop this instant. Phaniscus! look round, I say!
PHANISCUS
(not turning round.)
4.2.886:
Don’t be annoying to me.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
4.2.887:
Do see how scornful the monkey is!
PHANISCUS
Are you going to stop this instant, you dirty parasite?
PHANISCUS
(turning round.)
4.2.889:
I am so for myself; I choose to be. Why do you trouble yourself about it?
(Walking on.)
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
4.2.888:
How am I a parasite?
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
Why, I’ll tell you: you can be drawn anywhere by victuals.
4.2.890:
Do you give yourself airs, because your master’s so fond of you?
PHANISCUS
(rubbing his eyes.)
O dear, my eyes do ache.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
4.2.891:
Why so?
PHANISCUS
Because the smoke’s so troublesome.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
4.2.892:
Hold your tongue, will you, you clever workman, who are in the habit of coining money out of lead.
PHANISCUS
4.2.893:
You cannot compel me to be abusive to you. My master knows me.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
4.2.894:
Why, really, his own pillow he ought to know, for resting on when drunk.
PHANISCUS
4.2.896:
If you were sober, you wouldn’t be abusive.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
Am I to give heed to you, when you won’t to me.
PHANISCUS
4.2.897:
But, you rascal, you come along with me to fetch him.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
4.2.898:
Troth now, Phaniscus, prithee, do leave off talking about these matters.
PHANISCUS
I’ll do so, and knock at the door. (Knocks at the door of the house of THEUROPIDES.) Hallo there! is there any person here to protect this door from a most serious injury? (Knocking again.) Is any one, is any one, I say, coming out here and going to open it?
4.2.900:
Why, really, no one comes out here. Just as befits such worthless fellows, so they are. But on that account, I’ve the more need to be cautious that no one may come out and use me ill.
(They stand aside.)

4.3.904:
(Enter TRANIO and THEUROPIDES, from the house of SIMO.) TRANIO
What’s your opinion of this bargain?
THEUROPIDES
I am quite delighted.
TRANIO
4.3.905:
Does it seem to you to have been bought too dear?
THEUROPIDES
I’ faith, I’m sure that I never anywhere saw a house thrown away, this one only excepted.
TRANIO
4.3.906:
Does it please you, then?
THEUROPIDES
4.3.907:
Does it please me, do you ask me? Why yes, upon my faith, it really does please me very much.
TRANIO
4.3.908:
What a fine set of rooms for the women! What a porch!
THEUROPIDES
Exceedingly fine. For my part, I don’t think that there is any Porch larger than this in the public buildings.
TRANIO
4.3.910:
Why, I myself and Philolaches have taken the measure sure of all the porches in the public buildings.
THEUROPIDES
4.3.911:
Well, what then?
TRANIO
This is far larger than all of them.
THEUROPIDES
4.3.912:
Immortal Gods—a splendid bargain! On my word, if he were now to offer six great talents of silver, ready money, for it, I would never take it.
TRANIO
4.3.914:
Upon my faith, if you were inclined to take it, I would never let you.
THEUROPIDES
4.3.915:
My money has been well invested upon this purchase.
TRANIO
4.3.916:
Boldly confess that by my advice and prompting it was done, who urged him to take up the money of the Banker upon interest, which we paid this person by way of deposit.
THEUROPIDES
4.3.918:
You’ve saved the whole ship. Eighty minae, you say, are owing for it?
TRANIO
4.3.920:
He may have it to-day.
TRANIO
By all means so, that there may be no dispute arising; or else pay them over to me, I’ll then pay them over to him.
THEUROPIDES
4.3.922:
But still, don’t let there be any taking me in, if I do give them to you.
TRANIO
4.3.923:
Could I venture to deceive you in deed or word even in jest only?
THEUROPIDES
4.3.924:
Could I venture not to be on my guard against you, so as not to trust anything to you?
TRANIO
4.3.925:
Why, have I ever imposed upon you in anything, since I was your servant?
THEUROPIDES
4.3.926:
But I’ve taken good care of that; I owe thanks to myself and my own judgment for that. If I’m only on my guard against you solely, I’m quite wise enough.
TRANIO
(aside.)
4.3.928:
Now be off into the country; tell my son that I’ve arrived.
TRANIO
I’ll do as you wish.
THEUROPIDES
4.3.929:
Run with all speed; bid him come to the city at once together with you.
TRANIO
Very well. (Aside.) Now I’ll betake myself this way by the back-door to my boon-companions; I’ll tell them that things are quiet here, and how I have kept him away from here.
(Exit.)

4.4.933:
(THEUROPIDES, PHANISCUS, and another SERVANT.) PHANISCUS
(coming forward.)
Really, I don’t hear either the sound of revellers here, as once it was, nor yet the music-girl singing, nor any one else.
(Goes towards the door.)
THEUROPIDES
4.4.935:
What’s the matter here? What are these people seeking at my house? What do they want? What are they peeping in for?
PHANISCUS
4.4.936:
I shall proceed to knock at the door. (Knocks.) Hallo there, unlock the door! Hallo, Tranio! are you going to open it, I say?
THEUROPIDES
(advancing.)
4.4.937:
What story’s this, I wonder?
PHANISCUS
(aloud.)
4.4.938:
Are you going to open it, I say? I’ve come to fetch my master Callidamates.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.939:
Harkye, you lads! what are you doing there? Why are you breaking down that door?
PHANISCUS
4.4.946:
Our master’s at a drinking-party here.
THEUROPIDES
Your master at a drinking-party here?
PHANISCUS
I say so.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.947:
You’re carrying the joke too far, my lad.
PHANISCUS
We’ve come to fetch him.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.948:
What person?
PHANISCUS
Our master. Prithee, how often must I tell you?
THEUROPIDES
4.4.949:
There’s no one living here my lad; for I do think that you are a decent lad.
PHANISCUS
4.4.950:
Doesn’t a young gentleman called Philolaches live in this house?
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
(aside.)
4.4.952:
This old fellow’s crack-brained, surely.
PHANISCUS
You are entirely mistaken, respected sir; for unless he moved from here to-day or yesterday, I know for certain that he’s living here.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.954:
Why, no one has been living here for these six months past.
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
You are dreaming.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.955:
What, I?
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
You.
THEUROPIDES
Don’t you be impertinent. Let me speak to the lad. (Pointing to PHANISCUS.)
PHANISCUS
4.4.956:
No one lives there? O dear—
THEUROPIDES
It’s the fact.
PHANISCUS
4.4.957:
Really! why, yesterday and the day before, four, five, six days ago, all along, in fact, since his father went abroad from here, eating and drinking have never ceased for a single three days here.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.959:
What is it you say?
PHANISCUS
That eating and drinking have never stopped for a single three days here,
4.4.960:
bringing in wenches, living like Greeks, hiring harpists and music-girls.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.961:
Who was it did this?
PHANISCUS
Philolaches.
THEUROPIDES
What Philolaches?
PHANISCUS
4.4.962:
He whose father I take to be Theuropides.
THEUROPIDES
(apart.)
O dear, O dear! I’m utterly undone, if he says the truth in this. I’ll continue to question him still Do you say that this Philolaches, whoever he is, has been in the habit of drinking here together
4.4.965:
with your master?
PHANISCUS
Here, I tell you.
THEUROPIDES
My lad, contrary to your appearance, you are a fool. See now, please, that you’ve not perchance been dropping in somewhere for an afternoon’s whet, and have been drinking there a little more than was enough.
PHANISCUS
4.4.968:
Just what I say: don’t be going by mistake to other persons’ houses.
PHANISCUS
4.4.969: I know where I ought to go, and the place to which I was to come.
4.4.970:
Philolaches lives here, whose father is Theuropides; and who, after his father went away to trade, made free a music-girl here.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.972:
Philolaches, say you?
PHANISCUS
Just so; Philematium, I mean.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.973:
For how much?
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
For thirty talents.
PHANISCUS
No, by Apollo; you mean minae.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.974:
Do you say that a mistress was purchased for Philolaches for thirty minae?
PHANISCUS
4.4.975:
I do say so.
THEUROPIDES
And that he gave her her freedom?
PHANISCUS
I do say so.
THEUROPIDES
And that after his father had departed hence abroad, he has been carousing here continually with your master?
PHANISCUS
4.4.977:
I do say so.
THEUROPIDES
Well, has he made purchase of the house next door here?
PHANISCUS
4.4.978:
I don’t say so.
THEUROPIDES
Has he given forty minae, too, to this person, to be as a deposit?
PHANISCUS
4.4.979:
Nor yet do I say so.
THEUROPIDES
Ah me! you’ve proved my ruin!
PHANISCUS
Aye, and he has proved the ruin of his father.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.980:
You prophesy the truth! I could wish it false!
PHANISCUS
A friend of his father, I suppose?
THEUROPIDES
4.4.981:
Ah me! Upon my faith, you do pronounce him to be a wretched father.
PHANISCUS
Why really, this is nothing at all—thirty minae, in comparison with the other expenses he has incurred in good living.
4.4.983:
He has ruined his father.
There’s one servant there a very great scoundrel, Tranio by name; he could even waste the revenue of a Hercules.
4.4.985:
On my word, I’m sadly distrest for his father; for when he comes to know that things have gone on thus, a hot coal will be scorching his breast, poor man.
THEUROPIDES
4.4.987:
If, indeed, this is the truth.
PHANISCUS
What am I to gain, that I should tell a lie?
4.4.988:
(Knocks again at the door.) Hallo, you! is any one coming to open this door?
ANOTHER SERVANT of Callidamates
Why do you knock in this way, when there’s no one in the house?
PHANISCUS
4.4.989:
I fancy that he’s gone elsewhere to carouse. Now then, let’s begone.
(They move as if going.)
THEUROPIDES
4.4.991:
What, my lad, are you off then?
Liberty’s the overcoat for your back.
PHANISCUS
4.4.992:
Nothing have I with which to cover my back, except to pay respect and service to my master.
(Exeunt PHANISCUS and SERVANT.)

4.5.993:
THEUROPIDES
(to himself.)
By my troth, I am undone! What need is there of talking? According to the words I have heard, I surely haven’t lately voyaged hence to Aegypt,
4.5.995:
but even to some desolate land and the most remote shores have I been borne about, so much am I at a loss to know where I now am. But I shall soon know; for see, here’s the person of whom my son bought the house. (Enter SIMO.)
THEUROPIDES
4.5.998:
What are you about?
SIMO
I’m coming home from the Forum.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.999:
Has anything new been going on at the Forum to-day?
SIMO
4.5.1000:
Why yes.
THEUROPIDES
What is it, pray?
SIMO
I saw a dead man being carried to burial.
THEUROPIDES
Dear me!
4.5.1001:
that is something new!
SIMO
I saw one who was dead being carried out to burial
4.5.1002:
They said that he had been alive but just before.
THEUROPIDES
Woe to that head of yours for your nonsense!
SIMO
4.5.1003:
Why are you, thus idling about, enquiring after the news?
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1004:
Because I’ve just arrived from abroad.
SIMO
I’m engaged out to dine: don’t suppose I shall invite you.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1006:
I’ faith, I don’t want.
SIMO
But, to-morrow, unless any person invites me first, I’ll even dine with you.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1008:
I’ faith, and that, too, I don’t want. Unless you are engaged with something of greater importance, lend me your attention.
SIMO
4.5.1010:
You have received, as far as I understand, forty minae of Philolaches.
SIMO
4.5.1011:
Never a coin, so far as I know.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1012:
What? Not from my servant Tranio?
SIMO
Much less is that the case.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1013:
Which he gave you by way of deposit?
SIMO
What are you dreaming about?
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1014: What, I? Why, really, ’tis yourself, who hope that, by dissembling in this manner,
4.5.1015:
you’ll be able to make void this bargain.
SIMO
4.5.1016:
Why, what do you mean?
THEUROPIDES
The business that, in my absence, my son transacted with you here.
SIMO
4.5.1018:
in your absence, transact any business with me? What pray, or on what day?
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1021:
I owe you eighty minae of silver.
SIMO
4.5.1022:
Not to me, indeed, upon my faith; but still, if you do owe them, give them me. Faith must be kept. Don’t be attempting to deny it.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1024: Assuredly, I shall not deny that I owe them; and I shall pay them.
4.5.1025:
Do you take care how you deny that you received the forty from him.
SIMO
Troth now, prithee, look this way at me, and answer me.
4.5.1027:
He said that you were wishful to give a wife to your son; for that reason, he said that you intended building on your own premises.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1029:
I, intended building here?
SIMO
So he told me.
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1030:
Ah me! I’m ruined outright! I’ve hardly any voice left. Neighbours, I’m undone, ruined quite!
SIMO
4.5.1031:
Has Tranio been causing any confusion?
THEUROPIDES
4.5.1032:
Yes; he has thrown everything into confusion. He has made a fool of me to-day in a disgraceful manner.
SIMO
4.5.1034:
What is it you say?
THEUROPIDES
This matter is just as I am telling you:
4.5.1035:
he has this day made a fool of me in an outrageous manner. Now I beseech you that you’ll kindly aid me, and lend me your assistance.
SIMO
4.5.1037:
What would you have?
THEUROPIDES
I beg of you, come this way together with me.
SIMO
4.5.1038:
Be it so.
THEUROPIDES
Lend me the assistance of your slaves and some scourges.
SIMO
4.5.1039:
Take them by all means.
THEUROPIDES
At the same time I’ll tell you about this,
4.5.1040:
in what a fashion he has this day imposed upon me.
(They go into the house of SIMO.)

5.1.1041:
(Enter TRANIO.) TRANIO
(to himself.)
The man that shall prove timid in critical matters, will not be worth a nutshell. And, really, to say what that expression, worth a nutshell, means, I don’t know. But after my master sent me into the country to fetch his son hither,
5.1.1044: I went that way (pointing) slily through the lane to our garden. At the entrance to the garden that’s in the lane, I opened the door; and by that road I led out all the troop, both men and women. After, from being in a state of siege, I had led out my troops to a place of safety, I adopted the plan of convoking a senate of my comrades,
5.1.1050: and when I had convoked it, they forthwith banished me from the senate. When I myself perceived that the matter must be decided by my own judgment, as soon as ever I could, I did the same as many others do, whose affairs are in a critical or a perplexed state; they proceed to render them more perplexed, so that nothing can be settled.
5.1.1054: But I know full well, that now by no means can this be concealed from the old man.
5.1.1062:
But how’s this, that our next neighbour’s door makes a noise? Why, surely this is my master: I’d like to have a taste of his talk.
(Goes aside, out of sight of THEUROPIDES.) (Enter THEUROPIDES, from SIMO’s house.)
THEUROPIDES
(in the doorway, speaking to SIMO’s SLAVES.)
5.1.1064: Do you stand there, in that spot within the threshold; so that, the very instant I call,
5.1.1065:
you may sally forth at once. Quickly fasten the handcuffs upon him. I’ll wait before the house for this fellow that makes a fool of me, whose hide I’ll make a fool of in fine style, if I live.
TRANIO
(apart.)
5.1.1068:
The affair’s all out. Now it’s best for you, Tranio, to consider what you are to do.
THEUROPIDES
(to himself.)
5.1.1069: I must go to work to catch him cleverly and artfully when he comes here.
5.1.1070:
I’ll not disclose to him my feelings all at once; I’ll throw out my line; I’ll conceal the fact that I know anything of these matters.
TRANIO
(apart.)
5.1.1071:
O cunning mortal! not another person in Athens can be pronounced more clever than he. One can no more this day deceive him than he can a stone. I’ll accost the man; I’ll address him.
THEUROPIDES
(to himself.)
5.1.1074:
Now I do wish that he would come here.
TRANIO
(apart.)
5.1.1075:
I’ faith, if me indeed you want, here I am ready at hand for you. (Comes forward.)
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1076:
Bravo! Tranio, what’s being done?
TRANIO
The country people are coming from the country Philolaches will be here in a moment.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1077:
I’ faith, he comes opportunely for me. This neighbour of ours I take to be a shameless and dishonest fellow.
TRANIO
5.1.1079:
Why so?
THEUROPIDES
Inasmuch as he denies that he knows you.
TRANIO
Denies it?
THEUROPIDES
And declares that you never gave him a single coin of money
TRANIO
5.1.1080:
Out with you, you are joking me, I do believe; he doesn’t deny it.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1081:
How so?
TRANIO
I am sure now that you are joking; for surely he doesn’t deny it.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1082:
Nay but, upon my faith, he really does deny it; or that he has sold this house to Philolaches.
TRANIO
5.1.1083:
Well now, pray, has he denied that the money was paid him?
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1084: Nay more, he offered to take an oath to me, if I desired it,
5.1.1085: that he had neither sold this house, nor had any money him paid been.
5.1.1087:
I told him the same that you told me.
TRANIO
What did he say?
THEUROPIDES
He offered to give up all his servants for examination.
TRANIO
5.1.1088:
Nonsense! On my faith, he never will give them up.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1089:
He really does offer them.
TRANIO
Why then, do you summon him to trial.
THEUROPIDES
Wait a bit;
5.1.1090:
I’ll make trial as I fancy. I’m determined on it.
TRANIO
Bring the fellow here to me.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1091:
or else bid the young man to demand possession of the house.
THEUROPIDES
Why no, I want to do this first—to put the servants under examination.
TRANIO
5.1.1092: I’ faith, I think it ought to be done.
5.1.1094:
Meantime, I’ll take possession of this altar.
(Runs to the altar.)
THEUROPIDES
Why so?
TRANIO
You can understand nothing.
5.1.1095:
Why, that those may not be able to take refuge here whom he shall give up for examination, I’ll keep guard here for you; so that the examination may not come to nothing.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1097:
Get up from the altar.
TRANIO
By no means.
THEUROPIDES
Prithee, don’t you take possession of the altar.
TRANIO
Why so?
THEUROPIDES
You shall hear; why, because I especially want this, for them to be taking refuge there. Do let them; so much the more easily shall I get him fined before the judge.
TRANIO
5.1.1100:
What you intend to do, do it. Why do you wish to sow further strife? You don’t know how ticklish a thing it is to go to law.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1102:
Just get up, (beckoning) this way; it’s, then, to ask your advice upon something that I want you.
TRANIO
5.1.1103:
Still, as I am, I’ll give my advice from this spot: my wits are much sharper when I’m sittings. Besides, advice is given with higher sanction from holy places.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1105:
Get up; don’t be trifling. Just look me in the face.
TRANIO
(looking at him.)
I am looking.
THEUROPIDES
Do you see me?
TRANIO
5.1.1106:
I do see—that if any third person were to step in here, he would die of hunger.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1107:
Why so?
TRANIO
Because he would get no profit; for, upon my faith, we are both artful ones.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1108:
I’m undone!
TRANIO
What’s the matter with you?
THEUROPIDES
You have deceived me.
TRANIO
How so, pray?
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1109:
Consider, please, if it wasn’t well done; is your nose running still?
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1110: Aye, all my brains besides have you been wiping out of my head as well. For all your villanies I have discovered from their very roots; and not from the roots, indeed, i’ faith, but even from beneath the very roots.
5.1.1113: Never this day, by my troth, will you have planned all this without being punished.
5.1.1114:
I shall at once, you villain, order fire and faggots to be placed around you.
TRANIO
5.1.1115:
Don’t do it; for it’s my way to be sweeter boiled than roasted.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1116:
Upon my faith, I’ll make an example of you.
TRANIO
Because I please you, you select me for an example.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1117:
Say now: what kind of a person did I leave my son, when I went away from here?
TRANIO
5.1.1118:
One with feet and hands, with fingers, ears, eyes, and lips.
THEUROPIDES
5.1.1119:
I asked you something else than that.
TRANIO
For that reason I now answer you something else.
5.1.1120: But look, I see Callidamates, the friend of your son, coming this way. Deal with me in his presence, if you want anything

5.2.1125:
he said that he was afraid to come into his presence. Now of our company I am deputed sole ambassador, to obtain peace from his father. And look, most opportunely here he is. (Accosting THEUROPIDES.) I wish you health, Theuropides, and am glad that you’ve got back safe from abroad. You must dine here with us to-day. Do so.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1130:
Callidamates, may the Gods bless you. For your dinner I offer you my thanks.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1131:
Will you come then?
TRANIO
(To THEUROPIDES.)
Do promise him; I’ll go for you, if you don’t like.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1132:
Whip-scoundrel, laughing at me still?
TRANIO
What, because I say that I’ll go to dinner for you?
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1133:
But you shan’t go. I’ll have you carried to the cross, as you deserve.
TRANIO
5.2.1134:
Come, let this pass, and say that I shall go to the dinner.
Why are you silent?
CALLIDAMATES
(to TRANIO.)
5.2.1135:
But why, you greatest of simpletons, have you taken refuge at the altar?
TRANIO
He frightened me on his arrival. (To THEUROPIDES.) Say now, what I have done amiss. Look, now there’s an umpire for us both; come, discuss the matter.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1138:
I say that you have corrupted my son.
TRANIO
Only listen. I confess that he has done amiss; that he has given freedom to his mistress; that in your absence
5.2.1140:
he has borrowed money at interest; that, I admit, is squandered away. Has he done anything different to what sons of the noblest families do?
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1142:
Upon my faith, I must be on my guard with you; you are too clever a pleader.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1143:
Just let me be umpire in this matter. (TO TRANIO.) Get up; I’ll seat myself there.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1144:
By all means: take the management of this dispute to yourself.
(Pushes him to one side of the altar.)
TRANIO
Why, this is surely a trick.
5.2.1145:
Make me, then, not to be in a fright, and yourself to be in a fright in my stead.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1146:
I consider now everything of trifling consequence, compared with the way in which he has fooled me.
TRANIO
5.2.1147:
I’ faith, ’twas cleverly done, and I rejoice that it was done. Those who have white heads ought at that age to be wiser.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1149:
What am I now to do
if my friend Demipho or Philonides—
TRANIO
5.2.1150:
Tell them in what way your servant made a fool of you. You would be affording most capital plots for Comedies.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1152:
Hold your tongue awhile; let me speak in my turn.—Listen.
THEUROPIDES
By all means.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1153: In the first place of all then, you know that I am the companion of your son;
5.2.1154: he has gone to my house, for he is ashamed to come into your presence, because he knows that you are aware what he has done. Now, I beseech you, do pardon his simplicity and youthfulness. He is your son; you know that this age is wont to play such pranks; whatever he has done, he has done in company with me. We have acted wrong:
5.2.1160:
the interest, principal, and all the sum at which the mistress was purchased, all of it we will find, and will contribute together, at our own cost, not yours.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1162: No mediator could have come to me more able to influence me than yourself. I am neither angry with him, nor do I blame him for anything: nay more, in my presence, wench on, drink, do what you please.
5.2.1165:
If he’s ashamed of this, that he has been extravagant, I have sufficient satisfaction.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1166:
I’m quite ashamed myself
TRANIO
He grants pardon thus far; now then, what is to become of me?
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1167:
Filth, tied up as you hang, you shall be beaten with stripes.
TRANIO
Even though I am ashamed?
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1168:
Upon my faith, I’ll be the death of you, if I live!
CALLIDAMATES
Make this pardon general; do, pray, forgive Tranio this offence, for my sake.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1170:
I would more readily put up with your obtaining any other request of me than that I should forbear sending to perdition this fellow for his most villanous doings.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1172:
Pray, do pardon him.
TRANIO
Do pardon me?
THEUROPIDES
Look there, don’t you see how the villain sticks there?
(Pointing to the altar.)
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1173:
Tranio, do be quiet, if you are in your senses.
THEUROPIDES
Only do you be quiet in urging this matter. I’ll subdue him with stripes, so that he shall be quiet.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1175:
Really, there is no need.
Come now, do allow yourself to be prevailed upon.
THEUROPIDES
5.2.1176:
I wish you would not request me.
CALLIDAMATES
Troth now, I do entreat you.
THEUROPIDES
I wish you would not request me, I tell you.
CALLIDAMATES
It’s in vain you wish me not; only do grant this one pardon for his offence, pray, for my sake, I do entreat you.
TRANIO
5.2.1178:
Why make this difficulty? As if to-morrow I shouldn’t be very soon committing some other fault; then, both of them, both this one and that, you’ll be able to punish soundly.
CALLIDAMATES
5.2.1180:
Do let me prevail upon you.
THEUROPIDES
Well then, have it so; begone, unpunished! (TRANIO jumps down from the altar.) There now, (pointing to CALLIDAMATES) return him thanks for it. (Coming forward.) Spectators, this Play is finished; grant us your applause.

1.1.1:
(Enter TOXILUS and SAGARISTIO, on different sides..) TOXILUS
(to himself.)
He who, falling in love, destitute of means, has first entered upon the paths of love, has in his own labours exceeded all the labours of Hercules. For with the lion, and with the Hydra, with the stag, with the Aetolian boar, with the birds of Stamphalus, with Antaeus, would I rather contend
1.1.5:
than with love. So wretched am I become with hunting after money to borrow; and yet, those whom I ask know of nothing to answer me, except I have got none.
SAGARISTIO
(apart.)
1.1.7: The servant that is desirous faithfully to serve his master, i’ troth, it surely does behove him to treasure up full many a thing in his breast which he may think will please his master, both present and abroad.
1.1.10:
I neither serve with cheerfulness, nor am I quite to my master’s satisfaction; but, as though from a running eye, my master is still unable to keep his hands off me, in giving me his commands, in making me the support of his affairs.
TOXILUS
1.1.13:
Who’s this that’s standing opposite to me?
SAGARISTIO
Who’s that that’s standing opposite to me?
TOXILUS
1.1.14:
It’s like Sagaristio.
SAGARISTIO
Surely this is my friend Toxilus.
TOXILUS
1.1.15:
Certainly it is he.
SAGARISTIO
I think it is he.
TOXILUS
