He wishes you to be informed of it, so that you mayn’t suppose that he has taken anything secretly and by stealth. He has really, I do believe, been sent here to your harvesting.
HANNO
5.2.1023:
Muphonium sucoraim.
MILPHIO
So there! do take care, please, how you do what he’s begging of you.
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1024:
What is he saying, or what is he begging? Explain it.
MILPHIO
5.2.1025:
For you to order him to be placed beneath a hurdle, and for many stones to be heaped upon it, so as to put him to death.
HANNO
5.2.1027:
Gunebel balsamen ierasan!
AGORASTOCLES
Tell me what it is that he’s saying.
MILPHIO
5.2.1028:
I’ faith, now I really don’t at all know.
HANNO
(speaking in their own language.)
5.2.1029: But that you may know, now from this moment henceforth will I speak Latin.
5.2.1030:
(To MILPHIO.) Upon my faith, you must be a worthless and bad servant, to be laughing at a person, a foreigner and a stranger.
MILPHIO
5.2.1032:
But, i’ faith, at yourself a person that’s both a swindler and a cheat, who have come here to take us in, you half-and-half Lybian, you double-tongue, just like a crawling reptile.
AGORASTOCLES
(to MILPHIO.)
5.2.1035:
Away hence with your abusiveness! do restrain your tongue. You’ll keep it from uttering abuse, if you are prudent; I don’t want you to be speaking harshly to my kinsmen. I was born at Carthage; do you remember that.
HANNO
5.2.1040:
and if you have need of anything, pray mention it, and command me for the sake of our common country.
HANNO
5.2.1041:
I return you thanks; but I’ve got a place of entertainment here; I’m in search of the son of Antidamas; do point me out Agorastocles, if you know him. Do you know any young man here named Agorastocles?
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1045:
If, indeed, you are in search of the adopted son of Antidamas, I am the very person whom you are in search of.
HANNO
(starting.)
5.2.1046:
Hah! what’s that I hear?
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1047:
That I am the son of Antidamas.
HANNO
If so it is, if you would like to compare the token of hospitality, see here, I’ve brought it.
(Shows him the ticket.)
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1049:
Come then, show it here. (He takes it in his hand, and looks at it.) It is exactly true; for I’ve got the counterpart at home.
HANNO
5.2.1050:
O my host, hail to you right earnestly; for it was your father, then, Antidamas, that was my own and my father’s guest; this was my token of hospitality with him.
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1053: Then here at my house shall hospitality be shown you; for I don’t reject either Hospitality or Carthage,
5.2.1055:
from which I sprang.
HANNO
May the Gods grant you all you may desire. How say you? How could it happen that you were born at Carthage, but had a father of Aetolia here?
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1058:
I was stolen away from there; this Antidamas, your guest, bought me, and adopted me as his son.
HANNO
5.2.1060:
He himself, likewise, was adopted by Demarchus, But about him I say no more, and return to you. Tell me, do you at all remember the names of your parents?
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1063:
I remember my father and my mother’s name.
HANNO
Repeat them, then, to me, to see if I know them, perchance, or if they are relatives of mine.
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1065:
Ampsigura was my mother, and Iachon my father.
HANNO
5.2.1066:
I could wish that your father and mother were alive.
AGORASTOCLES
5.2.1067:
Are they dead?
HANNO
So it is, a thing which I bore with much grief; for your mother Ampsigura was my cousin-german; your father—he was my uncle’s son,
5.2.1070: and when he died he made me his heir; of whom being deprived by death, I am greatly affected. But if it is the fact that you really are the son of Sachon, there ought to be a mark upon your left hand, a bite which an ape gave you when a child, playing with it.
5.2.1075:
Show it, that I may look at it;
open your hand.
AGORASTOCLES
(opening his hand.)
Look, if you like; see, there it is.
5.2.1076:
My kinsman, welcome to you!
HANNO
And welcome to you, Agorastocles! I seem to myself to be born again, in having found you.
MILPHIO
5.2.1078:
By my troth, I’m delighted that this matter has fallen out so happily for you. (To HANNO.) And would you decline to take advice?
HANNO
5.2.1079:
Really, I should wish to be advised.
MILPHIO
5.2.1080:
His father’s property ought to be restored to the son; it’s fair that he should have the property which his father possessed.
HANNO
5.2.1082:
I wish no otherwise; everything shall be restored. I’ll give his own property to him all safe, when he comes there.
MILPHIO
5.2.1084:
Take care and restore it, will you, even though he should live here still.
HANNO
5.2.1085:
Nay but, he shall have my own as well, if anything should happen to me.
MILPHIO
5.2.1086:
A pleasant project has just now come into my mind,
HANNO
5.2.1087:
What’s that?
MILPHIO
There’s need of your assistance.
HANNO
Tell me what you wish. Really, you shall have my services just as you please. What is the business?
MILPHIO
5.2.1089:
Can you act the cheat?
HANNO
5.2.1090:
Towards an enemy, I can; to a friend, it would be mere folly.
MILPHIO
5.2.1091:
I’ faith, it is an enemy of his.
(Pointing at AGORASTOCLES.)
HANNO
I could do him a mischief with pleasure.
MILPHIO
5.2.1092:
He’s in love with a person who belongs to a Procurer.
HANNO
I deem that he acts discreetly.
MILPHIO
5.2.1093:
This Procurer lives close at hand.
HANNO
I could do him a mischief with pleasure.
MILPHIO
5.2.1094: He has two slave girls, courtesans,
5.2.1095:
sisters; one of these he is desperately in love with, nor has he ever taker any liberties with her.
HANNO
5.2.1096:
It’s an unhappy kind of passion.
MILPHIO
5.2.1097:
The Procurer plays upon him.
HANNO
He’s enhancing his own profits thereby.
MILPHIO
5.2.1098:
He wishes to do him an evil turn.
HANNO
He’s right, if he does do it.
MILPHIO
5.2.1099: Now I adopt this plan, and prepare this contrivance,
5.2.1100:
that we should cite you; you are to affirm that they are your daughters, and that they were stolen when little from Carthage, and to maintain the cause of both in an action on their freedom, as though they were both your own daughters. Do you understand?
HANNO
5.2.1104: On my faith, I do understand; for I likewise did have two daughters
5.2.1105:
who were stolen away when little children, together with their nurse.
MILPHIO
5.2.1106:
Upon my word, you do feign it cleverly. At the very commencement this amuses me.
HANNO
(aside, weeping.)
5.2.1107:
Much more, i’ troth, than I could wish.
MILPHIO
(aside to AGORASTOCLES.)
Dear me! a subtle person, upon my word, artful and knowing, both tricky and crafty! How he does whimper, in order that with his gestures he may effect this all the more easily.
5.2.1110:
Even myself, now, the master-workman, does he excel in skill.
HANNO
5.2.1111:
But their nurse, of what appearance was she? Tell me.
MILPHIO
5.2.1112:
Of stature not tall, of a dusky complexion.
HANNO
’Tis the very person.
MILPHIO
5.2.1113:
Of agreable form, with a small mouth, and very dark eyes.
HANNO
5.2.1114:
I’ faith, you really have depicted her form exactly in your words.
MILPHIO
5.2.1115:
Should you like to see her?
HANNO
I’d rather see my daughters. Still, go and call her out of doors. If they are my daughters, if she is their nurse, she’ll recognize me at once.
MILPHIO
(knocking at the door of the PROCURER’S house.)
5.2.1118: Hallo there! is there any one here? Tell Giddeneme to come out of doors; there’s a person wants to see her.

5.3.1120:
(Enter GIDDENEME and a BOY, from the house.) GIDDENEME
Who is it that knocks?
MILPHIO
One that’s a near acquaintance of yours.
GIDDENEME
What do you want?
MILPHIO
Come now (pointing to HANNO.) do you know that person in the tunic, who it is?
GIDDENEME
5.3.1122:
Why, whom do I behold? O supreme Jupiter! this sure is my master, the father of my foster-children, Hanno, the Carthaginian!
MILPHIO
5.3.1124:
Now, do see the cunning hussey this Carthaginian is really a clever juggler; he has brought all over to his own opinion.
GIDDENEME
(running up to HANNO.)
5.3.1127: O my master! welcome to you, Hanno! most unhoped for by myself and your daughters, welcome to you! But look you, don’t be wondering, or gazing so intently upon me.
5.3.1130:
Don’t you know Giddeneme, your female slave?
HANNO
5.3.1131:
I know her. But where are my daughters? That I’m longing to know.
GIDDENEME
5.3.1132:
At the Temple of Venus.
HANNO
What are they doing there? Tell me.
GIDDENEME
5.3.1133:
To-day is the Aphrodisia, the festive day of Venus! they have gone there to entreat the Goddess to be propitious to them.
MILPHIO
5.3.1135:
I’ faith, they’ve fully prevailed, I’m sure, inasmuch as he has arrived here.
AGORASTOCLES
(aside to GIDDENEME.)
5.3.1136:
How now, are these his daughters?
GIDDENEME
Just as you say. (To HANNO.) Your kindness has clearly come to our rescue, in your having arrived here to-day at the very time; for this day their names were to have been changed,
5.3.1140:
and they were to have made a livelihood, disgraceful to their station, by their persons.
A BOY
5.3.1141:
Haudones illi.
GIDDENEME
Havon bene si illi, in mustine.
5.3.1142:
Me ipsi et eneste dum et alamna cestinum.
AGORASTOCLES
5.3.1143:
What is it they are saying among themselves? Tell me.
MILPHIO
5.3.1144:
He’s saluting his mother, and she this her son.
HANNO
5.3.1145:
Hold your peace, and let alone the woman’s gear.
MILPHIO
5.3.1146:
What gear is that?
HANNO
Loud talking
without limit.
5.3.1147:
(To MILPHIO.) Do you lead these people in-doors (pointing to his SERVANTS.) and bid this nurse to come away together with you to your house.
AGORASTOCLES
(to MILPHIO.)
5.3.1148:
Do as he requests.
GIDDENEME
(to HANNO.)
5.3.1149:
But who’s to point them out to you?
AGORASTOCLES
I will, right skilfully.
GIDDENEME
5.3.1150:
I’ll go away then.
AGORASTOCLES
I’d only rather that you would do so, than say so.
(She goes into the house of AGORASTOCLES.)
MILPHIO
5.3.1169: Upon my faith, I do think that this day the very thing that I said by way of joke
5.3.1170: will be coming to pass both soberly and seriously,
5.3.1171:
that these will be discovered to-day to be his daughters.
AGORASTOCLES
5.3.1172: Troth, that very thing is quite certain now. Do you, Milphio, take them (pointing to the SERVANTS) in-doors; we’ll wait here for these damsels.
5.3.1151:
I wish a dinner to be got ready for my kinsman on his arrival.
MILPHIO
5.3.1152:
Lachananim you! (aside to the SERVANTS.) whom I’ll just now be packing off to the mill-stones, and from there after that to the dungeon and the oaken log. I’ll give you reason to praise your treatment here but slightly.
AGORASTOCLES
(to HANNO.)
5.3.1155:
Do you hear, kinsman? I say, don’t you revoke what has been said; promise me your elder daughter in marriage.
HANNO
5.3.1157:
Consider the thing as agreed on.
AGORASTOCLES
Do you promise her, then?
HANNO
I do promise her.
AGORASTOCLES
5.3.1158: My kinsman, blessings on you! for now you are mine beyond a doubt; now at length shall I converse with her without restraint.
5.3.1160:
Now, kinsman, if you wish to see your daughters, follow me.
HANNO
5.3.1161:
Why, really, this long time I’ve been longing for it, and I’ll follow you.
AGORASTOCLES
5.3.1162:
What if we go and meet them?
HANNO
But I’m afraid lest we should pass them on the road. Great Jupiter, do now reinstate my fortunes for me as being certain instead of uncertain!
AGORASTOCLES
5.3.1165:
I trust that my charmer will be my own. But look, I catch sight of them.
HANNO
5.3.1166:
What, are these my daughters? How tall from being such little creatures have they now become!
AGORASTOCLES
5.3.1167:
Do you know how it is? These are Grecian columns; they are wont to be erect.
(They stand aside.)

5.4.1174:
(Enter ADELPHASIUM and ANTERBASTYLIS, from the Temple of Venus.) ADELPHASIUM
’Twas worth the while, to-day, of him who has a taste for loveliness
5.4.1175: to afford a feast to his eyes, in coming hither to the Temple this day to see the sights. Upon my faith, I was charmed there to-day with the most elegant offerings of the courtesans, worthy of Venus, the most handsome Goddess; nor did I despise her worship this day; so great an abundance of beauteous objects was there there, each nicely arranged in its own place.
5.4.1179:
The odours of Arabia and of myrrh filled everything. The festive day seemed to be affected with no gloom, Venus, nor did thy Temple; so great a throng of her dependants was there, who had come to Venus of Calydon.
ANTERASTYLIS
5.4.1181:
But certainly, as far indeed as regarded us two, sister, we were all-powerful in our prayers, beauteous and gainers of her favour; neither were we there held in ridicule by the young men, which, i’ faith, sister, happened to all the rest.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1184:
I’d rather that it should so appear to other persons, than that you, sister, should praise yourself.
ANTERASTYLIS
5.4.1185:
Indeed, I trust so.
ADELPHASIUM
Troth, and so do I, when I reflect of what breeding we and the others are. We were born in that station, that it befits us to be unblemished by faultiness.
HANNO
(apart.)
5.4.1187: Jupiter, who dost preserve and feed the race of men, through whom we pass this mortal life, in whose hands are the hopes of life in all men, prithee, do grant this day as a prosperous one
5.4.1189: for my fortunes! Those whom I’ve missed for many years,
5.4.1190:
and whom when little I lost from their native land, to them restore their liberty, that I may be sure that for an indomitable sense of duty there is a reward.
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
5.4.1191:
I’ll engage that Jove shall do it all; for to me he is indebted, and stands in awe of me.
HANNO
(apart.)
Prithee, do hold your peace.
(He weeps.)
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
Kinsman, do not weep.
ANTERASTYLIS
(apart.)
5.4.1192:
As it is a pleasure for a man, my sister, if he succeeds in anything, to have the credit of victory, just so did we this day among the rest excel them all in beauty.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1194: Sister, you are more silly than I could wish. Prithee, do you really think yourself a beauty,
5.4.1195:
if your face has not been besmeared with soot?
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
O kinsman! O kinsman, dearest of all kinsmen to me!
HANNO
(apart.)
What is it, son of my cousin? My son, tell me, what is it you wish?
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
5.4.1196:
Why, really, I do wish you to attend to this.
HANNO
(apart.)
Why, really, I am attending to it.
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
5.4.1197:
Kinsman, kinsman, dearest of all kinsmen to me!
HANNO
(apart.)
What’s the matter?
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
She’s a clever and a nice girl. How shrewd she is!
HANNO
(apart.)
5.4.1198:
She has her father’s disposition in being shrewd.
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
5.4.1199: How’s that? This long time, i’ faith, she has surely used up your shrewdness.
5.4.1200:
’Tis from here (pointing to himself) she now derives her shrewdness; ’tis from here her sense; whatever she does shrewdly, through my love does she act so shrewdly.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1201:
We are not born of that rank, although we are slaves, sister, that it should befit us to do anything which any man may laugh at. Many are the faults of women; but of the many, this one is the greatest, to please themselves too much, and to give their attention too little to pleasing the men.
ANTERASTYLIS
5.4.1205:
It was a very great delight that was portended in our sacrifice of the entrails, sister, and what the soothsayer said about us both—
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
5.4.1206:
I wish he had said something about me!
ANTERASTYLIS
5.4.1207:
That we should be free in a few days, in spite of our owner. I don’t know why I should hope for that, unless the Gods or our parents do something.
AGORASTOCLES
(apart.)
5.4.1209: ’Twas through confidence in me, kinsman, upon my faith, that the soothsayer promised them
5.4.1210:
liberty, I’m sure of it, because he knows I’m in love with her.
ADELPHASIUM
Sister, follow me this way.
(Moves as if going.)
ANTERASTYLIS
I follow.
(Moves also.)
HANNO
(stepping forward.)
5.4.1211:
Before you go away, I want you both. Unless it’s inconvenient, stop.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1212:
Who’s calling us back?
AGORASTOCLES
One who wishes to do you a kindness.
ADELPHASIUM
There’s opportunity for doing it. But who is the person?
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1213:
A friend of yours.
ADELPHASIUM
One who is not an enemy, in fact.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1214:
This is a good man, my love.
ADELPHASIUM
I’ faith, I should prefer him rather than a bad one.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1215:
If, indeed, friendship must be engaged in, with such a person ought it to be engaged in.
ADELPHASIUM
I don’t beg for it.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1216:
He wishes to do you many services.
ADELPHASIUM
Being good yourself you will be doing good to the good.
HANNO
5.4.1217:
I will cause you joy—
ADELPHASIUM
And, i’ faith, we pleasure to you.
HANNO
5.4.1218:
And liberty.
ADELPHASIUM
At that price you’ll easily make us your own.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1219: My kinsman, so may the Gods bless me, if I were Jupiter,
5.4.1220:
upon my faith I’d at once marry her for my wife, and pack Juno out of doors. How quietly did she utter her words, how considerately and becomingly! how modestly did she frame her speech! certainly she is my own!
HANNO
(apart to AGORASTOCLES.)
5.4.1222:
But how skilfully I accosted her!
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1223:
Cleverly and becomingly, upon my faith.
HANNO
5.4.1224:
Am I still to go on testing them?
AGORASTOCLES
Compress it in a few words; the people who are sitting here are getting thirsty.
HANNO
5.4.1225:
Well, why don’t we proceed to do that which was to be done? (To the WOMEN.) I summon you to justice.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1226:
Seize hold of this one, kinsman, if you are wise. Should you like me to catch hold of her?
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1227:
Is this person your kinsman, Agorastocles?
AGORASTOCLES
I’ll soon let you know. Now, by my word, I’ll be nicely revenged on you; for I’ll make—you my bride.
HANNO
5.4.1229:
Come before a court of justice; don’t delay!
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1230:
Summon me as your witness, and take me; I’ll be a witness for you; and after that, her (pointing to ADELPHASIUM) will I love and embrace. But ’twas this, indeed, I intended to say—why yes, I did say that which I intended to say.
HANNO
(to the DAMSELS.)
5.4.1232:
You are lingering. I summon you to justice, unless it is more becoming for you to be dragged thither.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1233:
Why do you summon us to justice? What are we in your debt?
AGORASTOCLES
He’ll tell it there.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1235:
give me a kiss in place of a piece of meat; present your lips in place of a bone: that way I’ll render this dog more smooth for you than oil.
HANNO
5.4.1237:
Come on, if you are coming.
ADELPHASIUM
What have we done to you?
HANNO
You are thieves, both of you.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1238:
What, we, as regards you?
HANNO
You, I say.
AGORASTOCLES
And I know it.
ADELPHASIUM
What theft is this?
AGORASTOCLES
Enquire of him.
HANNO
5.4.1239: Because for many years you have been concealing my daughters from me,
5.4.1240:
and, in fact, persons free-born, and free, and born of the highest rank.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1241:
I’ faith, you’ll never find that villany to have been committed by us.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1242:
Make a bet of a kiss now, if you are not forsworn, which is to give it to the other.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1243:
I’ve nothing to do with you; prithee, get you gone.
AGORASTOCLES
But, i’ faith, I’ve got something to do with you; for he is my kinsman; it’s necessary for me to be his advocate.
5.4.1245:
And I’ll inform him how you are guilty of many a theft, and in what way you have got his daughters as slaves at your house, whom you know to be free women stolen from their native land.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1248:
Where are these, or who are they, prithee?
AGORASTOCLES
(aside to HANNO.)
They have been teased sufficiently.
HANNO
(aside.)
5.4.1249:
Why not speak out, then?
AGORASTOCLES
(aside.)
I’ faith, I’m of that opinion, kinsman.
ADELPHASIUM
I’m dreadfully afraid
5.4.1250:
what this business can mean, my sister; so astounded am I, I stand here without my senses.
HANNO
5.4.1251: Damsels, give me your attention. In the first place, if it could possibly come to pass, for the Gods not to send upon the innocent what is undeserved, that could I have wished to happen; now for the good the Gods bestow upon me, upon yourselves and upon your nurse, ’tis due that we should give to the Deities our endless thanks,
5.4.1255:
since the immortal Gods approve and reward our piety. You are my daughters, both of you, and this is your relation, Agorastocles, the son of my cousin.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1257:
Prithee, are they deluding us with imaginary joys?
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1258:
Really, so may the Deities preserve me, this is your father. Give him your hands.
ADELPHASIUM
(embracing him.)
5.4.1259:
Welcome, father! unhoped-for by us, allow us to embrace you!
ANTERASTYLIS
(embracing him.)
5.4.1260: Welcome, father! much wished and longed for!
5.4.1262:
Who’ll be for embracing me in the next place?
HANNO
Now am I happy! Now with this delight do I allay the miseries of many a year.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1264:
We hardly seem to believe this.
HANNO
I’ll tell you something to make you believe it the more:
5.4.1265:
why, it was your nurse who recognized me first.
ADELPHASIUM
Prithee, where is she?
HANNO
(pointing to AGORASTOCLES.)
5.4.1266:
She’s at his house.
AGORASTOCLES
(to ADELPHASIUM, who is embracing her father.)
Pray, why does it please you to clasp his neck so long,
5.4.1268:
before he has betrothed you to me?
Dear one, much longed-for, blessings on you!
(He embraces her.)
ADELPHASIUM
(struggling.)
I will leave off.
5.4.1267:
Do leave off your salutations!
AGORASTOCLES
And you the other one.
(To ANTERASTYLIS, whom he embraces.
ANTERASTYLIS
(struggling.)
I don’t want that; you torment me to death!
HANNO
5.4.1269: Let us each clasp the other in our arms,
5.4.1270:
than whom is there anything on earth more happy?
AGORASTOCLES
Blessings befall the deserving.
5.4.1271:
(Pointing to HANNO.) At last his wishes are realized!
O Apelles! O Zeuxis the painter! why did you die too soon? Would that you could paint a subject after this! For I don’t care for other common painters to be treating subjects of this description.
HANNO
5.4.1274: Gods and Goddesses all! I return you deservedly extreme thanks,
5.4.1275:
for having blest me with this gladness so supreme and with these joys so great; as my daughters have returned to me and into my possession.
ADELPHASIUM
5.4.1277:
My father, your own piety has clearly come to our aid.
AGORASTOCLES
5.4.1278:
Kinsman, take care and keep it in memory that you’ve betrothed your elder daughter to me—
HANNO
5.4.1279:
I remember it.
AGORASTOCLES
The portion, too, that you promised.

5.5.1280:
(Enter ANTHEMONIDES, from the house of LYCUS.) ANTHEMONIDES
(to himself.)
If I don’t take full revenge for that mina which I gave to the Procurer, then really may the townspeople make a butt of me! This most rascally fellow even brought me to his house to breakfast. He himself went away out of doors, and left me as his chamberlain in the house. When neither the Procurer nor these women came back, nor anything was given me to eat,
5.5.1285: for the best part of the breakfast I took a pledge, and came out of doors. This way I’ll pay him. I’ll touch up the rascally Procurer in the military way of payment. He did get hold of a person for him to bamboozle out of a mina of silver! But I wish that my mistress would now come in my way while thus enraged. Then, by my troth, with my fists I’d make her quite black all over;
5.5.1290:
I’d cover her so with swarthiness, that she should be much more swarthy than the Egyptians, or than those who carry the buckets at the games in the Circus.
ADELPHASIUM
(running to AGORASTOCLES.)
5.5.1292:
Do hold me fast, please, my love; I sadly fear the kites; this is an evil animal—lest perchance he may carry me off, your chick.
ANTERASTYLIS
(embracing her FATHER.)
5.5.1294:
I cannot clasp you fast enough, my father!
ANTHEMONIDES
(to himself.)
I’m delaying.
5.5.1295: (Looking in his hand.) I can now pretty nearly cater a breakfast for myself with this. (Raising his eyes.) But what’s this? How’s this? What’s this? What’s this I see? How now? What means this strange conjunction? What’s this coupling together? Who’s this fellow with the long skirts, just like a tavern-boy? Do I quite see with my eyes? Isn’t this my mistress, Anterastylis?
5.5.1300: Why, surely it is she. For some time past I’ve perceived that I’m set at nought. Isn’t the girl ashamed to be hugging a tawny fellow in the middle of the street? I faith, I shall give him up forthwith to the executioner to be tortured all over. Surely this is a womanish race, with their tunics hanging down to their heels. But I’m determined to accost this African female lover.
5.5.1305:
(To HANNO.) Hallo! you woman, I say, are you not ashamed? What business have you with her, pray? Tell me.
HANNO
5.5.1307:
Young man, greetings to you.
ANTHEMONIDES
I don’t want them; that’s nothing to you. What business have you to touch her with a finger?
HANNO
5.5.1309:
You choose?
HANNO
I say so.
ANTHEMONIDES
Away to utter perdition, you shoe-latchet!
5.5.1310:
What, do you dare to be acting the lover here, you great toe of a man, or to be meddling with an object which masculine men are fond of, you skinnea pilchard, you deformed image of Serapis, you half-apron, you sheepskin-jacket, you pot of stinking sea-salt; more crammed, too, to boot, with leeks and garlick than the Roman rowers?
AGORASTOCLES
5.5.1315:
Young man, do your jaws or your teeth itch, that you are annoying this person, or are you in search of a heavy mishap?
ANTHEMONIDES
5.5.1317:
Why didn’t you use a drum while you were saying that? For I take you to be more of an effeminate wretch than a real man.
AGORASTOCLES
5.5.1319: Do you understand what sort of effeminate wretch I am? (Calling aloud.) Servants, come out of doors,
5.5.1320:
bring out some cudgels!
ANTHEMONIDES
Hark you, if I have said anything in a joke, don’t you be for taking it seriously.
ANTERASTYLIS
5.5.1322: Prithee, what pleasure have you, Anthemonides, in speaking rudely to our kinsman and father? For this is our father; he has just now recognized us,
5.5.1325:
and him as the son of his cousin.
ANTHEMONIDES
So may Jupiter kindly bless me, I heartily rejoice that it is so, and I am delighted, if, in fact, any great misfortune befalls this Procurer, and since a fortune awaits you equal to your merits.
ANTERASTYLIS
5.5.1329:
I’ faith, he says what’s worthy of belief; do believe him, my father.
HANNO
5.5.1330:
I do believe him.
AGORASTOCLES
And I believe him. But look (pointing.) I espy the Procurer Lycus,
5.5.1332:
the worthy fellow; look, there he is—he’s betaking himself homeward.
HANNO
5.5.1333:
Who is this?
AGORASTOCLES
He’s which you please, both the Procurer and Lycus. He has been keeping your daughters in servitude,
5.5.1335:
and from myself he has stolen some gold.
HANNO
A pretty fellow for you to be acquainted with!
AGORASTOCLES
5.5.1336:
Let’s bring him to justice.
HANNO
By no means.
AGORASTOCLES
For what reason?
HANNO
Because ’twere better for an action of damages to be brought against him.

5.6.1338:
(Enter LYCUS.) LYCUS
(to himself.)
No one, in my opinion at least, is deceived, who rightly states his case to his friends.
5.6.1340:
But by all my friends the one same thing is agreed upon, that I ought to hang myself, so as not to be adjudged to Agorastocles.
AGORASTOCLES
(stepping forward.)
5.6.1342:
Procurer, let’s away to the court of justice.
LYCUS
I do entreat you, Agorastocles, that I may be at liberty to hang myself.
HANNO
5.6.1343:
I summon you to justice.
LYCUS
5.6.1344:
But what have you to do with me?
HANNO
(pointing at his DAUGHTERS.)
Because I affirm that both of these are my daughters, free women, and free by birth,
5.6.1346:
who, when little, were kidnapped together with their nurse.
LYCUS
5.6.1347:
Indeed, I knew that already, and I wondered that no one came to assert their freedom; they really are none of mine, indeed.
ANTHEMONIDES
5.6.1349:
Procurer, you must come to justice.
LYCUS
5.6.1350:
You are talking about the breakfast; it is owing to you; I’ll give it.
AGORASTOCLES
5.6.1351:
Twofold compensation I must have for the theft.
LYCUS
(pointing to his neck.)
Take it out of this, then.
HANNO
5.6.1352:
And I require a full satisfaction.
LYCUS
(pointing to his neck.)
Take out of this whatever you please.
ANTHEMONIDES
5.6.1353:
And I, indeed, a mina of silver.
LYCUS
(pointing to his neck.)
Take out of this whatever you please. I’ll at once settle the matter for all with my neck, just like a porter.
AGORASTOCLES
5.6.1355:
Do you refuse me in any way?
LYCUS
Not a word, in fact.
AGORASTOCLES
5.6.1356:
Go in-doors, then, damsels. But (to HANNO.) my kinsman, betroth me your daughter, as you promised.
HANNO
5.6.1358:
I should not venture to do otherwise.
ANTHEMONIDES
Kindly farewell!
AGORASTOCLES
And kindly farewell to you!
ANTHEMONIDES
(holding up what he has got in his hand.)
5.6.1359:
Procurer, I take this as a pledge with me for my mina.
LYCUS
5.6.1360:
By heavens, I am ruined!
AGORASTOCLES
Why yes, before very long, when you’ve come to justice.
LYCUS
5.6.1361:
Nay but, I own myself your slave. What need of the Praetor have we? But I beseech you that I may be allowed to pay the simple sum, three hundred Philippeans. I think it can be scraped together; to-morrow I’ll have an auction.
AGORASTOCLES
5.6.1365:
that you shall be in wooden custody at my house.
LYCUS
5.6.1366:
So be it.
AGORASTOCLES
Follow me in-doors, my kinsman, that we may keep this festive day in joyousness, upon his misfortune and our good fortune. (To the AUDIENCE.) Heartily fare you well. To great length have we gone; at last all these misfortunes fall upon the Procurer.
5.6.1370: Now—that which is the last seasoning for our Play—if it has pleased you, our Comedy asks applause.

5.7.1372:
(AGORASTOCLES, LYCUS, HANNO, ANTHEMONIDES, ADELPHASIUM, and ANTERASTYLIS. AGORASTOCLES
What is it you are about, Captain? Why does it please you to speak rudely to my relative? Don’t be surprised that the damsels do follow after him; he has just now discovered that both of them are his own daughters.
LYCUS
(starting.)
5.7.1375: Hah! what speech was it that reached my ears? Now I am undone!
5.7.1376:
(To AGORASTOCLES.) From what house were these females lost?
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1377:
They are Carthaginians.
LYCUS
Then I am ruined. I was always in dread of that, lest some one should recognize them, a thing which has now come to pass. Woe unto wretched me!
5.7.1380:
My eighteen minae are lost, I guess, which I paid for them.
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1381:
And you yourself are lost, Lycus.
HANNO
5.7.1382:
Who is this?
AGORASTOCLES
Which you please, he’s either the Procurer or Lycus. He has been keeping your daughters in servitude, and from myself he has stolen some gold.
HANNO
5.7.1384:
A pretty fellow for you to be acquainted with!
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1385:
Procurer, I always deemed you to be avaricious, but they know you to be a thief as well, who know more of you.
LYCUS
5.7.1387: I’ll approach him. (He falls on the ground before AGORASTOCLES.) By your knees I do beseech you, and by him (pointing to HANNO.) whom I understand to be your relative; since you are deserving persons, as it befits deserving persons to do,
5.7.1390: do then come to the aid of your suppliant! Indeed, already did I know them to be free women, and was waiting for some one to claim their freedom, for really they are none of mine. Then besides, I’ll restore your gold that I’ve got in my house, and I’ll make oath
5.7.1395:
that I have done nothing, Agorastocles, with ill intent.
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1396:
As it’s right for me to do, I shall still consult my own notions. Let go of my knees.
LYCUS
5.7.1397:
I’ll let them go, if such is your determination.
(He rises from the ground, and retires to a distance.)
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1398:
Hark you! Procurer.
LYCUS
What do you want with a Procurer amid business?
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1399:
You to restore me my money before I take you hence to be laid in fetters.
LYCUS
5.7.1400:
May the Gods grant better things!
AGORASTOCLES
Even so; you’ll be dining away from home. I see Gold, silver, and your neck, Procurer, the three things are you now owing to me all at once.
HANNO
5.7.1402:
What it befits me to do in this matter, I’m considering with myself. If I should attempt to take vengeance on this fellow, I shall be engaging in litigation in a strange city. So far as I hear, his disposition and manners, of the nature that they are—
ADELPHASIUM
5.7.1405:
My father, do have no dealings with this man, I conjure you.
ANTERASTYLIS
5.7.1406:
Do listen to my sister. Come, put an end to your strife with the rascal.
HANNO
5.7.1407:
Attend to this, will you, Procurer. Although I know that you deserve to come to ruin, I’ll not try the matter with you.
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1408:
Nor I, if you restore me my gold; Procurer, when let go from the fetters—you may get thrust into prison.
LYCUS
5.7.1410:
What, your old habit still?
ANTHEMONIDES
Carthaginian, I wish to excuse myself to you. If I have said anything in my passion against the inclination of your feelings, I beg that you will pardon it; and as you have found these daughters of yours, so may the Deities bless me, it is a pleasure to me.
HANNO
5.7.1413:
I both forgive and believe you.
ANTERLASTYIS
5.7.1414:
Procurer, do you take care either to find me a mistress, or return me the mina of gold.
LYCUS
5.7.1415:
Should you like to have my music-girl?
ANTHEMONIDES
I don’t care for a music-girl; you don’t know which is the greater, their cheeks or their bosoms.
LYCUS
5.7.1417:
I’ll find one to please you.
ANTHEMONIDES
Mind that.
LYCUS
(to AGORASTOCLES.)
To-morrow I’ll bring back your gold to your house.
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1418:
Take care that you keep that in memory.
Captain, follow me.
ANTHEMONIDES
Yes, I’ll follow you.
(LYCUS goes into his house.)
AGORASTOCLES
(to HANNO.)
5.7.1419: How say you, kinsman? When are you thinking of leaving here for Carthage?—
5.7.1420:
for I’m determined to go together with you.
HANNO
As soon as ever I can, that instant I shall go.
AGORASTOCLES
5.7.1421:
It’s necessary for you to stop here some days, until I’ve had an auction.
HANNO
5.7.1422:
I’ll do just as you wish.
AGORASTOCLES
Come, please, let’s be off; let’s enjoy ourselves. (To the AUDIENCE.) Grant us your applause.]

0.0.0:
PROLOGUE
ATTEND to me this day; good things I bring upon the stage; for I think ’tis very just that to the good good things should be brought; as likewise bad things to the bad; that those who are bad may have what’s bad, those who are good what’s good; bad men are bad because they hate the good; because the good contemn the bad, needs must be that they are good; and therefore, you are good since you have ever abhorred the bad; and both by your laws, Quirites, and by your legions, have you routed them with good success. In like manner now do you give your goodly attention to this goodly company, which is a good one, and. to good people brings this day good things. Ears, eyes, and understanding, shall be amply filled. He that comes hungry or thirsty to the theatre, the same shall carefully give his attention both through laughter and a sharpened stomach; while those who are full will laugh, the hungry will be carping. Now, if you are wise, you hungry ones, give place, and go away; you who are full, stand—aye, sit you down, and give attention. I shall not now divulge the plot, nor yet the name of this play—Pseudolus will fully do that. I imagine then and I think that this is enough which I have said to you. Where mirth, jokes, laughter, wine, and jollity, are the order of the day, the Graces, too, and propriety, joyousness, and delight; he who seeks for other things, that person appears to seek for evil. Away, then, with evil cares, as being men at your ease this day.
0.0.1: ’Tis better for your loins to be stretched, and for you to arise. A long play of Plautus is coming upon the stage.

1.1.3:
(Enter CALIDORUS and PSEUDOLUS from SIMO’S house.) PSEUDOLUS
If, master, by your being silent, I could be informed what miseries are afflicting you so sadly,
1.1.5: I would willingly have spared the trouble of two persons—of myself in asking you, and of yourself in answering me. Since, however, that cannot be, necessity compels me to enquire of you. Answer me: What’s the reason that, out of spirits for these many days past,
1.1.10:
you’ve been carrying a letter about with you, washing it with your tears, and making no person the sharer of your purpose? Speak out, that what I am ignorant of, I may know together with yourself.
CALIDORUS
1.1.13:
I am wretchedly miserable, Pseudolus.
PSEUDOLUS
May Jupiter forbid it!
CALIDORUS
1.1.14: This belongs not at all to the arbitration of Jupiter;
1.1.15:
under the sway of Venus am I harassed, not under that of Jove.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.16:
Is it allowable for me to know what it is? For hitherto you have had me as chief confidant in your plans.
CALIDORUS
1.1.18:
The same is now my intention.
PSEUDOLUS
Let me know then what’s the matter with you. I’ll aid you either with resources, or with my efforts, or with good counsel.
CALIDORUS
1.1.20:
Do you take this letter: do you thence inform yourself what misery and what care are wasting me away.
PSEUDOLUS
(taking the letter.)
1.1.22:
Compliance shall be given you. But, prithee, how’s this?
CALIDORUS
What’s the matter?
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.23:
As I think, these letters are very loving; they are climbing on each other’s backs.
CALIDORUS
1.1.24:
Are you making sport of me with your foolery?
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.25:
I’ faith, I really do believe that unless the Sibyl can read them, nobody else can possibly interpret them.
CALIDORUS
1.1.27:
Why speak you unkindly of those sweet letters— sweet tablets too, written upon by a hand as sweet.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.29: Troth now, have hens, prithee, such hands?
1.1.30:
For certainly a hen has written these letters.
CALIDORUS
You are annoying me. Either read it or return the letter.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.31:
Very well then, I’ll read it through. Give me your attention.
CALIDORUS
1.1.32:
That’s not here.
PSEUDOLUS
Do you summon it then.
CALIDORUS
1.1.33:
Well, I’ll be silent; do you summon it from that wax there; for there my attention is at present, not in my breast.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.35:
I see your mistress, Calidorus.
CALIDORUS
Where is she, prithee?
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.36:
See, here she is at full length in the letter; she’s lying upon the wax.
CALIDORUS
1.1.37:
Now, may the Gods and Goddesses, inasmuch—
PSEUDOLUS
Preserve me from harm, to wit.
CALIDORUS
1.1.38:
For a short season have I been like a summer plant; suddenly have I sprung up, suddenly have I withered.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.40:
Be silent, while I read the letter through.
CALIDORUS
Why don’t you read it then?
PSEUDOLUS
(reading.)
1.1.41:
Phœnicium to her lover, Calidorus, by means of wax and string and letters, her exponents, sends health, and safety does she beg of you, weeping, and with palpitating feelings, heart, and breast.
CALIDORUS
1.1.45:
I’m undone; I nowhere find, Pseudolus, this safety for me to send her back.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.46:
What safety?
CALIDORUS
A silver one.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.47:
And do you wish to send her back a silver safety for one on wood? Consider what you’re about.
CALIDORUS
1.1.49: Read on now; I’ll soon cause you to know from the letter
1.1.50:
how suddenly there’s need for me for one of silver to be found.
PSEUDOLUS
(reading on.)
1.1.51: The procurer has sold me, my love, for twenty minae, to a Macedonian officer from abroad. Before he departed hence, the Captain paid him fifteen minae; only five minae now are remaining unpaid.
1.1.55:
On that account the Captain left here a token—his own likeness impressed on wax by his ring—that he who should bring hither a token like to that, together with him the procurer might send me. The next day hence, on the Festival of Bacchus, is the one fixed for this matter.
CALIDORUS
1.1.61:
Let me read it through.
CALIDORUS
1.1.62:
I permit you; for I seem to myself to be talking to her. Read on; the sweet and the hitter are you now mingling together for me.
PSEUDOLUS
(reading on.)
1.1.64: Now our loves, our tenderness, our intimacy,
1.1.65: our mirth, our dalliance, our talking, our sweet kisses, the close embrace of us lovers equally fond, the soft, dear kisses impressed on our tender lips, the delicious pressing of the swelling bosom; of all these delights, I say, for me and for you as well,
1.1.70:
the severance, the destruction, and the downfal is at hand, unless there is some rescue for me in you or for you in me. I have taken care that you should know all these things that I have written; now shall I make trial how far you love me, and how far you pretend to do so.
CALIDORUS
1.1.74:
’Tis written, Pseudolus, in wretchedness.
PSEUDOLUS
Alas! very wretchedly.
CALIDORUS
1.1.75:
Why don’t you weep, then?
PSEUDOLUS
I’ve eyes of pumice stone; I can’t prevail upon them to squeeze out one tear even.
CALIDORUS
1.1.77:
Why so?
PSEUDOLUS
My family was always a dryeyed one.
CALIDORUS
1.1.78:
Won’t you attempt to assist me at all?
PSEUDOLUS
What shall I do for you?
CALIDORUS
1.1.79:
Alas!
PSEUDOLUS
Alas! do you say? Well, don’t be sparing of them, i’ faith; I’ll give you plenty.
CALIDORUS
1.1.80:
I’m distracted. I nowhere can find any money to borrow.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.81:
Alas!
CALIDORUS
Nor is there a single coin in the house.
PSEUDOLUS
Alas!
CALIDORUS
1.1.82:
He’s going to carry the damsel away to-morrow.
PSEUDOLUS
Alas!
CALIDORUS
1.1.83:
Is it in that fashion that you help me?
PSEUDOLUS
I give you that which I have; for I’ve a perpetual supply of those treasures in my house.
CALIDORUS
1.1.85:
It’s all over with me this very day. But can you now lend me one drachma, which I’ll pay you back to-morrow
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.87:
I’ faith, I hardly think I could, even though I should pawn myself for it. But what do you want to do with this drachma?
CALIDORUS
1.1.88:
I want to purchase a halter for myself.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.89:
For what reason?
CALIDORUS
With which to hang myself.
1.1.90:
I’m determined, ere ’tis dark, to take a leap in the dark.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.91:
Who then shall pay me back my drachma ? Do you wish purposely to hang yourself for the very reason, that you may cheat mo out of my drachma if I lend it you?
CALIDORUS
1.1.94: At all events, I can in nowise survive
1.1.95:
if she’s removed and carried off from me.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.96:
Why do you weep, you cuckoo? You shall survive.
CALIDORUS
Why should I not weep, who have neither a coin of silver in ready money, nor have the hope of a groat anywhere in the world?
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.99: As I understand the tenor of this letter,
1.1.100: unless you weep for her with tears of silver, the affection which you wish yourself by those tears to prove is of no more value than if you were to pour water into a sieve. But have no fear, I’ll not forsake you in your love. In troth, I do trust that this day, from some quarter or other, by my good aid
1.1.105:
I shall find you help in the money line. But whence that is to come,—that whence I know not how to pronounce; except only that so it shall be; my eyebrow twitches to that effect.
CALIDORUS
1.1.108:
As to what you say, I trust that your deeds may be as good as your words.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.109: I’ faith, you surely know, if I set my plans a-going,
1.1.110:
after what fashion and how great is the bustle that I am in the habit of causing.
CALIDORUS
1.1.111:
In you are now centred all the hopes of my existence.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.112:
Is it enough, if I this day make this damsel to be yours, or if I find you twenty minae?
CALIDORUS
1.1.114:
’Tis enough, if so it is to be.
PSEUDOLUS
Ask of me twenty minae,
1.1.115:
that you may be assured that I’ll procure for you that which I have promised. Ask them of me, by my troth, prithee do; I long to make the promise.
CALIDORUS
1.1.117:
Will you this day find me twenty minae of silver?
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.118: I will find them; be no more troublesome to me then. And this I tell you first, that you mayn’t deny that it was told you;
1.1.120:
if I can no one else, I’ll diddle your father out of the money.
CALIDORUS
1.1.121:
So far as filial affection is concerned, even my mother as well. May the Gods always preserve you for me. But what if you are not able?
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.123:
Upon that matter do you go to sleep with either eye.
CALIDORUS
1.1.124:
With the eye or with the ear?
PSEUDOLUS
The latter is too common an expression.
1.1.125:
Now, that no one may affirm that it wasn’t told him, I tell you all (to the AUDIENCE), in the presence of the youths in this audience, and of all the people, to all my friends and all my acquaintances I give notice, that for this day they must guard against me, and not trust me.
CALIDORUS
1.1.129:
Hist! be silent, prithee, by all the powers!
PSEUDOLUS
What’s the matter?
CALIDORUS
There was a noise at the procurer’s door.
PSEUDOLUS
1.1.131:
I could only wish it were his legs in preference.
CALIDORUS
1.1.132:
Yes, and he himself is coming out from in-doors, the perjured scoundrel.
(They stand at a distance.)

1.2.133:
(Enter BALLIO, with several MALE and FEMALE SLAVES, from his house.) BALLIO
Get out, come, out with you, you rascals, kept at a loss and bought at a loss, in the minds of not one of whom aught ever comes to do aright,
1.2.135: of whom I can’t make a bit of use, unless I try it after this fashion. (He flogs the men all round.) At no time did I ever see human beings more like asses; so hardened are your ribs with stripes; when you flog them, you hurt yourself the most. Of such a disposition are these whipping-posts who follow this line of conduct; when the opportunity is given, pilfer, purloin, prig, plunder, drink, eat, and run away’s the word. This
1.2.140: is their method, so that you would choose rather to leave wolves among sheep, than these fellows on guard in your house. Yet, when you look at their appearance, they don’t seem amiss; by their doings they deceive you. Now, therefore, unless you all of you give your attention to this charge, unless you remove drowsiness and sloth from your breasts and eyes,
1.2.145: I’ll make your sides to be right thoroughly marked with thongs, so much so that not even Campanian coverlets are coloured as well, nor yet Alexandrian tapestry of purple embroidered with beasts all over. Even yesterday I already gave you all notice, and assigned to each his own respective employment; but so utterly worthless are you, so neglectful, of such stubborn dispositions,
1.2.150: that you compel me to put you in mind of your duty with a basting. You are so minded I suppose, to get the better of this scourge and myself through the hardness of your hides. Never, i’ faith, will your hides prove harder, than is this cow-hide of mine. (He dangles it before them.) Do look at that, please; they are minding other matters. Attend to this, and give heed to this.
1.2.155:
(He flogs one of them.) How now? Does it pain? Ah, that’s the way it’s laid on when any slave slights his master. Stand all of you before me, you race of mortals born to be thrashed; turn your ears this way; give attention all of you to what I say. You fellow who are holding the pitcher, do you fetch the water; do you take care that the cauldron’s full this instant. You, with the axe, I appoint over the wood-cutting department.
SLAVES of Ballio.
1.2.160: yet am I for that reason any the less to enjoy your services? My orders I give to you, that the house be made clean. You have what you are to do; make haste, and go in-doors. (Exit FIRST SLAVE.) Be you the one that makes the couches smooth. Do you wash the plate clean, and arrange it in order as well, Take care that when I return from the Forum, I find things done; that all be swept, sprinkled, scoured, made smooth, cleaned, and arranged in order.
1.2.165: For this day is my birthday; it befits you all to celebrate it. Take care to lay the gammon of bacon, the brawn, the collared neck, and the udder, in water; do you hear me? I wish to entertain tip-top men in first-rate style, that they may fancy that I have property. Go you in-doors, and get these things ready quickly, that there may be no delay when the cook comes. I’m going to market, that I may make purchase of whatever fish is there.
1.2.170: Boy, go you before me; I must have a care that no one cuts away my purse. Or wait there; there’s something that I had almost forgotten to say at home. Do you hear me, you women? I have this charge for you—you, misses of distinction, who spend your time with illustrious men in refinements, luxury, and delights; now shall I know and make trial this day,
1.2.175: which one has regard for her liberty, which for her appetite which thinks on her business, which on sleeping only: this day I’ll make trial which I must think of as a freed-woman, and which as one to be sold. Take you care that many a present from your lovers comes in for me this day; for if your year’s board isn’t picked up for me, to-morrow I’ll turn you adrift on the public. You know that this is my birthday; where are those youths, the apples of whose eyes you are,
1.2.180: whose very existence, whose delight you are? Where are your kisses, where your bosoms sweet as honey? Make the bearers of presents to come here then, for my sake, before this house, in whole regiments. Why am I to find clothes for you, gold trinkets, and those things which you need? What have I, you jades, through your means, except vexation, you women, eager for nothing but the wine? You are a-soaking away yourselves and your paunches too, at the very time that I’m here a-dry.
1.2.185: Now, therefore, this is the best thing to do; for me to call you each by her name, that no one of you may be declaring to me by-and-by that her business hasn’t been told her. Give attention, all of you. In the first place, Hedylium, my business is with you—you, who are the favorite of the corn-merchants, men who have, all of them, immense mountains of wheat piled up at home;
1.2.190:
take you care that wheat is brought here for me, to suffice this year to come for myself and all my household, and that I may so abound in corn that the city may change my name for me, and instead of the procurer Ballio proclaim me King lasions.
CALIDORUS
(apart.)
1.2.194:
Do you hear what the gallows-bird is saying? Doesn’t he seem a regular boaster to you?
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
1.2.195:
I’ troth the fellow does, and a wicked one as well. But hush now, and give attention to this.
BALLIO
1.2.196: Aeschrodora, you who have for your patrons the butchers, those rivals of the procurers, who, just like ourselves, by false oaths seek their gains, do you listen; unless the three larders shall be crammed for me this day with carcases of ample weight, to-morrow, just as they say that formerly the two sons of Jupiter fastened Dirce
1.2.200:
to the bull, aye, this day as well, will I tie you up to the larder; that, in fact, shall be your bull.
CALIDORUS
(apart.)
1.2.201: I’m quite enraged by the talk of this fellow;
1.2.202: that we should suffer the youth of Attica to encourage here this fellow! Where are they—where are they skulking, they of mature age, who have their amorous dealings with this procurer? Why don’t they meet? Why don’t they one and all deliver the public from this pestilence?
1.2.205:
But I am very simple, and very ignorant; they would venture, of course, to do that to those, to whom their passions compel them, to their misfortune, to be subservient, and, at the same time, prevent them from doing that against them which they would rather wish to do.
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
1.2.206:
Hush!
CALIDORUS
(apart.)
What’s the matter?
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
1.2.208:
Pshaw! you are not very obliging. Why are you drowning his talk by your noise?
CALIDORUS
(apart.)
1.2.209:
I’ll be silent.
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
But I’d much rather you would be silent, than that you should say you will be silent.
BALLIO
And you,
1.2.210: Xystilis, take you care and give me your attention—you whose fanciers have large quantities of oil at home. If oil shall not be brought me here forthwith in leathern bags, I’ll to-morrow cause yourself to be carried off in a leathern bag to the prostitutes’ shambles.
1.2.215: There a bed shall be given you, I warrant, where you can have no rest, but where, even to downright fainting— You understand what’s the tendency of that which I’m saying? Will you tell me, you viper you, you who have so many of your fanciers so right well laden with their oil,
1.2.219: is now the head of any one of your fellow-slaves a bit the better anointed by your means, or do I, myself, get my dainty morsels a bit the better seasoned with oil for it? But I understand— you don’t care much about oil; with wine you anoint yourself. Only wait a bit; by my troth I’ll punish you for all at one spell, unless indeed this day you contrive to manage all these things that I’ve been speaking of.
1.2.225:
But as for you, Phœnicium, I tell you this, you pet of the mighty men—you who have been for so long a time always paying down to me your money for your liberty—you who only know how to promise, but don’t know how to pay what you have promised; unless this day all your keep is brought me here out of the stores of your customers, to-morrow, Phœnicium, with a true Phœnician hide, you’ll pay a visit to the strumpets’ shambles.
(The SLAVES go into the house of BALLIO.)

1.3.230:
(CALIDORUS and PSEUDOLUS come forward. BALLIO stands near his door.) CALIDORUS
Pseudolus, don’t you hear what he says?
PSEUDOLUS
I hear it, master, and I give good heed.
CALIDORUS
1.3.231:
What do you advise me to send him, that he mayn’t devote my mistress to dishonor?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.232:
Don’t you trouble yourself about that; be of cheerful mind. I’ll manage for myself and for you. For some time past I’ve been on terms of goodwill with him, and he with me; and our friendship is of old standing. I’ll send him this day, on his birthday, a mischief heavy and well-matured.
CALIDORUS
1.3.235:
What’s the plan?
PSEUDOLUS
Can’t you attend to something else?
CALIDORUS
But—
PSEUDOLUS
Tut.
CALIDORUS
I’m distracted.
PSEUDOLUS
Harden your heart.
CALIDORUS
1.3.236:
I cannot.
PSEUDOLUS
Make yourself to can.
CALIDORUS
By what means, pray, can I prevail upon my feelings?
PSEUDOLUS
Carry you out that which is to your advantage, rather than give heed with your feelings to the thing that’s disadvantageous.
CALIDORUS
1.3.238:
That’s nonsense; there is no pleasure, unless a lover acts like a fool.
PSEUDOLUS
Do you persist?
CALIDORUS
1.3.239:
O my dear Pseudolus, let me be undone—do let me, please.
PSEUDOLUS
I’ll let you; only let me go.
(Going.)
CALIDORUS
1.3.240:
Stay, stay. As you shall, then, wish me to be, so will I be.
PSEUDOLUS
Now, at last, you are in your senses.
BALLIO
(coming forward from the door of his house to the other side of the stage.)
1.3.241:
The day is passing; I’m causing delay to myself. Boy, do you go before me.
(Moves as if going.)
CALIDORUS
Hallo there! he’s going; why don’t you call him back?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.242:
Why in such a hurry? Gently.
CALIDORUS
But before he’s gone.
BALLIO
Why the plague do you go so slowly, boy?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.243: You born on this day, hallo! you born on this day; I’m calling to you; hallo! you born on this day, come you back and look at us. Although you are busy,
1.3.245:
we want you; stop—it’s because some persons want to speak to you.
BALLIO
1.3.246:
What’s this? Who is it, when I’m busy, causes me unseasonable delay?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.247:
He that has been your supporter.
BALLIO
1.3.248:
He’s dead that has been; only he that is, is now alive.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.249:
You are too saucy.
BALLIO
You are too troublesome.
(Turns away to go on.)
CALIDORUS
Seize the fellow: follow him up.
BALLIO
Go on, boy.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.250:
Let’s go and meet him this way.
(They run and stand before him.)
BALLIO
May Jupiter confound you, whoever you are.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.251:
That for yourself I wish.
BALLIO
And for both of you do I. Turn you this way, boy.
(Takes another direction.)
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.252:
May we not speak with you?
BALLIO
1.3.253:
Why, it doesn’t please me.
PSEUDOLUS
But if it’s something to your advantage?
BALLIO
1.3.254:
Am I allowed to go away, pray, or am I not?
PSEUDOLUS
Pshaw!
1.3.255:
Stop.
(Catches hold of him.)
BALLIO
Let me go.
CALIDORUS
Ballio, listen.
BALLIO
I’m deaf.
CALIDORUS
Really, you are uncivil.
BALLIO
You are a chatterer of nonsense.
CALIDORUS
1.3.256:
I gave you money so long as I had it.
BALLIO
I’m not asking what you gave.
CALIDORUS
1.3.257:
I’ll give you some when I have it.
BALLIO
When you have it, bring it to me.
CALIDORUS
1.3.258:
Alas, alas! In what a foolish fashion have I lavished what I brought to you, and what I gave you.
BALLIO
1.3.260:
you now are talking about it; you are a simpleton, a cause that has been tried you are trying over again.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.261:
At least consider him, who he is.
BALLIO
I’ve known for a long time now who he was; who he now is, let him know himself. Do you walk on (to the BOY).
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.263:
And can’t you, Ballio, only once give a look this way for your own profit?
BALLIO
1.3.265:
At that price I’ll give a look; for if I were sacrificing to supreme Jupiter, and were presenting the entrails in my hands to lay them on the altar, if in the meanwhile anything in the way of profit were offered, I should in preference forsake the sacrifice. There’s no being able to resist that sort of piety, however other things go.
PSEUDOLUS
(aside.)
1.3.269:
The very Gods, whom it is especially our duty to reverence—them he esteems of little value.
BALLIO
1.3.270:
I’ll speak to him. Hail to you, right heartily, the very vilest slave in Athens.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.271:
May the Gods and Goddesses favour you, Ballio, both at his wish and at my own; or, if you are deserving of other terms, let them neither favour nor bless you.
BALLIO
1.3.273:
What’s the matter, Calidorus?
CALIDORUS
Love and pinching want are the matter.
BALLIO
1.3.274:
I would pity you, if, upon pity I could support my establishment.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.275:
Aye, aye, we know you quite well, what sort of character you are; don’t be proclaiming it. But do you know what we want?
BALLIO
1.3.276:
I’ faith, I know it pretty nearly; that there may be something unfortunate for me.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.277:
Both to that and this for which we called you back, prithee do give your attention.
BALLIO
I am attending; but compress into a few words what you want, as I’m busy now.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.279: He (pointing to CALIDORUS) is quite ashamed about what he promised you, and the day for which he promised it,
1.3.280:
that he hasn’t even yet paid you those twenty minae for his mistress.
BALLIO
1.3.281:
That which we are ashamed at is much more easily endured than that which we are vexed at. At not having paid the money, he is ashamed; I, because I have not received it, am vexed.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.283:
Still, he’ll pay it, he’ll procure it; do you only wait some days to come. But he has been afraid of this, that you’ll sell her on account of his embarrassment.
BALLIO
1.3.285:
He had an opportunity, had he wished, of paying the money long ago.
CALIDORUS
1.3.286:
What if I had it not?
BALLIO
If you had been in love, you would have found it on loan. You would have gone to the usurer; you would have paid the interest; or else you would have pilfered it from your father.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.288:
Ought he to have pilfered it from his father, you most shameless villain? There is no fear that you’ll point out to him anything that’s right.
BALLIO
1.3.289:
That’s not like a procurer.
CALIDORUS
1.3.290:
And could I possibly pilfer anything from my father, an old man so much on his guard? And besides, if I could do so, filial affection forbids.
BALLIO
1.3.291: I understand you; do you then at night embrace filial affection in place of Phœnicium. But since I see you prefer your filial affection to your love—are all men your fathers? Is there no one for you to ask
1.3.295:
to lend you some money?
CALIDORUS
Why, the very name of lending’s dead and gone by this.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.296:
Look you now; since, i’ faith, those fellows arose from the banker’s table, with a filled skin, who, when they called in their own, paid what they had borrowed to no born creature, since then, I say, all people have been more cautious not to trust another.
CALIDORUS
1.3.299: Most wretched am I; nowhere am I able to find a coin of silver;
1.3.300:
so distractedly am I perishing both through love and want of money.
BALLIO
1.3.301:
Buy oil on credit, and sell it for ready money; then, i’ faith, even two hundred minae ready money might be raised.
CALIDORUS
1.3.303:
There I’m done; the twenty-five year old law founders me. All are afraid to trust me.
BALLIO
1.3.304:
The same law have I. I’m afraid to trust you.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.305:
To trust him, indeed! How now, do you repent of the great profit he has been to you?
BALLIO
1.3.306:
No lover is a profitable one, except him who keeps continually making presents. Either let him be always giving, or when he has nothing, let him at the same time cease to be in love.
CALIDORUS
1.3.308:
And don’t you pity me at all?
BALLIO
You come empty-handed; words don’t chink. But I wish you life and health.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.309:
Heyday! Is he dead already?
BALLIO
1.3.310:
However he is, to me indeed, at all events, with these speeches, he is dead. Then, does a lover really live, when he comes begging to a procurer? Do you always come to me with a complaint that brings its money. As for that, which you are now lamenting about, that you have got no money, complain of it to your stepmother.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.314:
Why, have you ever been married to his father, pray?
BALLIO
1.3.315:
May the Gods grant better things.
PSEUDOLUS
Do what we ask you, Ballio, on my credit, if you are afraid to trust him. Within the next three days, from some quarter, in some way, either by land or sea, I’ll rout up this money for you.
BALLIO
1.3.318:
I, trust you?
PSEUDOLUS
Why not?
BALLIO
Because, i’ faith, on the same principle that I trust you, on that principle I should tie a run-away dog to a lamb’s fry.
CALIDORUS
1.3.320:
Is the obligation thus ungratefully returned by you to me, who have deserved so well of you?
BALLIO
1.3.321:
What do you want now?
CALIDORUS
That you will only wait these six days of the Feast, and will not sell her or prove the death of the person who loves her.
BALLIO
1.3.322:
Be of good courage; I’ll wait six months even.
CALIDORUS
1.3.324:
Aye; and do you wish, too, that from joyful I should make you even more joyous?
CALIDORUS
1.3.325:
How so?
BALLIO
Why, because I’ve got no Phœnicium to sell.
CALIDORUS
1.3.326:
Not got her?
BALLIO
I’ faith, not I, indeed.
CALIDORUS
Pseudolus, go fetch the sacrifice, the victims, the sacrificers, that I may make offering to this supreme Jove. For this Jupiter is now much more mighty to me than is Jupiter himself.
BALLIO
1.3.329:
I want no victims; with the entrails of minae I wish to be appeased.
CALIDORUS
(to PSEUDOLUS.)
1.3.330:
Make haste. Why do you hesitate? Go fetch the lambs; do you hear what Jupiter says?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.331:
I’ll be here this moment; but first I must run as far as beyond the gate.
CALIDORUS
1.3.332:
Why thither?
PSEUDOLUS
I’ll fetch two sacrificers thence, with their bells; at the same time I’ll fetch thence two bundles of elm twigs, that this day a sufficiency may be provided for the sacrifice to this Jove.
BALLIO
1.3.335:
Away to utter perdition.
PSEUDOLUS
Thither shall the pimping Jupiter go.
BALLIO
1.3.338:
It isn’t for your interest that I should die.
PSEUDOLUS
How so?
BALLIO
This way; because, if I’m dead, there will be no one worse than yourself in Athens. For your interest (to CALIDORUS) it is that I should die.
CALIDORUS
1.3.336:
How so?
BALLIO
I’ll tell you; because, i’ faith, so long as I shall be alive, you’ll never be a man well to do.
CALIDORUS
1.3.340:
Troth now, prithee, in serious truth, tell me this that I ask you—have you not got my mistress, Phœnicium, on sale?
BALLIO
1.3.342:
By my faith, I really have not; for I’ve now sold her already.
CALIDORUS
1.3.343:
In what way?
BALLIO
Without her trappings, with all her inwards.
CALIDORUS
1.3.344:
What? Have you sold my mistress?
BALLIO
1.3.345:
For twenty minae?
BALLIO
Or, in other words, for four times five minae, whichever you please, to a Macedonian Captain; and I’ve already got fifteen of the minae at home.
CALIDORUS
1.3.347:
What is it that I hear of you?
BALLIO
That your mistress has been turned into money.
CALIDORUS
1.3.348:
Why did you dare to do so?
BALLIO
’Twas my pleasure; she was my own.
CALIDORUS
Hallo! Pseudolus. Run, fetch me a sword.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.349:
What need is there of a sword?
CALIDORUS
With which to kill this fellow this instant, and then myself.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.350:
But why not kill yourself only rather? For famine will soon be killing him.
CALIDORUS
1.3.351:
What do you say, most perjured of men as many as are living upon the earth? Did you not take an oath that you would sell her to no person besides myself?
BALLIO
1.3.353:
I confess it.
CALIDORUS
In solemn form, to wit.
BALLIO
Aye, and well considered too.
CALIDORUS
1.3.354:
You have proved perjured, you villain.
BALLIO
I sacked the money at home, however.
1.3.355:
Villain as I am, I am now able to draw upon a stock of silver in my house; whereas you who are so dutiful, and born of that grand family, haven’t a single coin.
CALIDORUS
1.3.357:
Pseudolus, stand by him on the other side and load this fellow with imprecations.
PSEUDOLUS
Very well. Never would I run to the Praetor with equal speed that I might be made free.
(Stands on the other side of BALLIO.)
CALIDORUS
1.3.359:
Heap on him a multitude of curses.
PSEUDOLUS
Now will I publish you with my rebukes.
1.3.360:
Thou lackshame!
BALLIO
’Tis the fact.
PSEUDOLUS
Villain!
BALLIO
You say the truth.
PSEUDOLUS
Whipping-post!
BALLIO
1.3.361:
Why not?
PSEUDOLUS
Robber of tombs!
BALLIO
No doubt.
PSEUDOLUS
Gallows-bird!
BALLIO
Very well done.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.362:
Cheater of your friends!
BALLIO
That’s in my way.
PSEUDOLUS
Parricide!
BALLIO
Proceed, you.
CALIDORUS
1.3.363:
Committer of sacrilege!
BALLIO
I own it.
CALIDORUS
Perjurer!
BALLIO
You’re telling nothing new.
CALIDORUS
1.3.364:
Lawbreaker!
BALLIO
Very much so.
PSEUDOLUS
Pest of youth!
BALLIO
Most severely said.
CALIDORUS
1.3.365:
Thief!
BALLIO
Oh! wonderful!
PSEUDOLUS
Vagabond!
BALLIO
Pooh! pooh!
CALIDORUS
Defrauder of the public!
BALLIO
Most decidedly so.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.366:
Cheating scoundrel!
CALIDORUS
Filthy
pander!
PSEUDOLUS
Lump of filth!
BALLIO
A capital chorus.
CALIDORUS
1.3.367:
You beat your father and mother.
BALLIO
Aye, and killed them, too, rather than find them food; did I do wrong at all?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.369:
We are pouring our words into a pierced cask: we are losing our pains.
BALLIO
1.3.370:
Would you like to call me anything else besides?
CALIDORUS
Is there anything that shames you?
BALLIO
1.3.371: Yes; that you have been found to be a lover as empty as a rotten nut. But although you have used towards me expressions many and harsh, unless the Captain shall bring me this day the five minae that he owes me, as this was the last day appointed for the payment of that money,
1.3.375:
if he doesn’t bring it, I think that I am able to do my duty.
CALIDORUS
1.3.376:
What is that duty?
BALLIO
If you bring the money, I’ll break faith with him; that’s my duty. If it were more worth my while, I would talk further with you. But, without a coin of money, ’tis in vain that you request me to have pity upon you. Such is my determination; but do you, from this, consider what you have henceforth to do?
(Moves.)
CALIDORUS
1.3.380:
Are you going then?
BALLIO
At present I am full of business.
(Exit.)
PSEUDOLUS
Before long you’ll be more so. That man is my own, unless all Gods and men forsake me. I’ll bone him just in the same fashion that a cook does a lamprey. Now, Calidorus, I wish you to give me your attention.
CALIDORUS
1.3.383:
What do you bid me do?
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.384: I wish to lay siege to this town, that this day it may be taken.
1.3.385:
For that purpose, I have need of an artful, clever, knowing, and crafty fellow, who may despatch out of hand what he is ordered, not one to go to sleep upon his watch.
CALIDORUS
1.3.387:
Tell me, then, what you are going to do?
PSEUDOLUS
In good time I’ll let you know. I don’t care for it to be repeated twice; stories are made too long that way.
CALIDORUS
1.3.389:
You plead what’s very fair and very just.
PSEUDOLUS
Make haste; bring the fellow hither quickly.
CALIDORUS
1.3.390:
Out of many, there are but few friends that are to be depended upon by a person.
PSEUDOLUS
1.3.391:
I know that; therefore, get for yourself now a choice of both, and seek out of these many one that can be depended upon.
CALIDORUS
1.3.393:
I’ll have him here this instant.
PSEUDOLUS
Can’t you be off then? You create delay for yourself by your talking.
(Exit CALIDORUS.)

1.4.394:
(PSEUDOLUS, alone.) PSEUDOLUS
Since he has gone hence, you are now standing alone, Pseudolus.
1.4.395: What are you to do now, after you have so largely promised costly delights to your master’s son by your speeches? You, for whom not even one drop of sure counsel is ready, nor yet of silver nor have you where first you must begin your undertaking,
1.4.400: nor yet fixed limits for finishing off your web. But just as the poet, when he has taken up his tablets, seeks what nowhere in the world exists, and still finds it, and makes that like truth which really is a fiction; now I’ll become a poet; twenty minae,
1.4.405: which no-where in the world are now existing, still will I find. And some time since had I said that I would find them for him, and I had attempted to throw a net over our old gentleman; however, by what means I know not, he perceived it beforehand. But my voice and my talking must be stopped;
1.4.410:
for, see! I perceive my master, Simo, coming this way, together with his neighbour, Callipho. Out of this old sepulchre will I dig twenty minae this day, to give them to my master’s son. Now I’ll step aside here, that I may pick up their conversation.
(He stands apart.)

1.5.415:
(Enter SIMO and CALLIPHO.) SIMO
If now a Dictator were to be appointed at Athens of Attica out of the spendthrifts or out of the gallants, I do think that no one would surpass my son. For now the only talk of all throughout the city is to the effect that he is trying to set his mistress free,
1.5.420:
and is seeking after money for that purpose. Some people bring me word of this; and, in fact, I had long ago perceived it, and had suspected it, but I dissembled on it.
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
1.5.422: Already is his son suspected by him; this affair is nipt in the bud, this business is at a stand-still.
1.5.424: The way is now entirely blocked up against me, by which I had intended to go a-foraging for the money.
1.5.426:
He has perceived it beforehand. There’s no booty for the marauders.
CALLIPHO
1.5.427: Those men who carry about and who listen to accusations, should all be hanged, if so it could be at my decision, the carriers by their tongues, the listeners by their ears.
1.5.430: For these things that are told you, that your son in his amour is desirous to chouse you out of money, the chance is that these things so told you are all lies. But sappose they are true, as habits are, now-a-days especially, what has he done so surprising? What new thing, if a young man
1.5.435:
does love, and if he does liberate his mistress?
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
A delightful old gentleman.
SIMO
1.5.436:
I don’t wish him to follow the old-fashioned habits.
CALLIPHO
But still, in vain do you object; or you yourself shouldn’t have done the like in your youthful days. It befits the father to be immaculate, who wishes his son to be more immaculate than he has been himself.
1.5.440:
But the mischief and the profligacy you were guilty of might have been distributed throughout the whole population, a share for each man. Are you surprised at it, if the son does take after the father?
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
1.5.443:
O Zeus, Zeus! how few in number are you considerate men. See, that’s being a father to a son, just as is proper.
SIMO
1.5.445:
Who is it that’s speaking here? (Looking round.) Why, surely ’tis my servant Pseudolus. ’Tis he corrupts my son, the wicked scoundrel; he is his leader, he his tutor. I long for him to be put to extreme torture.
CALLIPHO
1.5.448: This is folly now, thus to keep your anger in readiness. How much better were it
1.5.450:
to accost him with kind words and to make all enquiries, whether these things are true or not that they tell you of?
SIMO
1.5.453:
I’ll take your advice.
PSEUDOLUS
(apart.)
They are making towards you, Pseudolus; prepare your speech to meet the old fellow.
1.5.455:
Good courage in a bad case is half the evil got over. (Aloud, as he advances to meet them.) First, I salute my master, as is proper; and alter that, if anything is left, that I bestow upon his neighbour.
SIMO
1.5.457:
Good day to you. What are you about?
PSEUDOLUS
About standing here in this fashion (assuming an attitude).
SIMO
1.5.458:
See the attitude of the fellow, Callipho; how like that of a man of rank.
CALLIPHO
1.5.459:
I consider that he is standing properly and with boldness.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.460:
It befits a servant innocent and guileless, as he is, to be bold, most especially before his master.
CALLIPHO
1.5.462:
There are some things about which we wish to inquire of you, which we ourselves know and have heard of as though through a cloud of mist.
SIMO
1.5.464: He’ll manage you now with his speeches, so that you shall think
1.5.465:
it isn’t Pseudolus but Socrates that’s talking to you. What do you say?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.466:
For a long time you have held me in contempt, I know. I see that you have but little confidence in me. You wish me to be a villain; still, I will be of strict honesty.
SIMO
1.5.469: Take care, please, and make the recesses of your ears free, Pseudolus,
1.5.470:
that my words may be enabled to enter where I desire.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.471:
Come, say anything you please, although I am angry at you.
SIMO
1.5.472:
What, you, a slave, angry at me your master?
PSEUDOLUS
And does that seem wonderful to you?
SIMO
1.5.473: Why, by my troth, according to what you say, I must be on my guard against you in your anger, and you are thinking of beating me in no other way than I am wont to beat yourself.
1.5.476:
What do you think?
(To CALLIPHO.)
CALLIPHO
I’ faith, I think that he’s angry with good reason, since you have so little confidence in him.
SIMO
1.5.477:
I’ll leave him alone then. Let him be angry: I’ll take care that he shall do me no harm. But what do you say? What as to that which I was asking you?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.479: If you want anything, ask me.
1.5.480:
What I know, do you consider given you as a response at Delphi.
SIMO
1.5.481:
Give your attention then, and take care and please mind your promise. What do you say? Do you know that my son is in love with a certain music-girl?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.483:
Yea, verily.
SIMO
Whom he is trying to make free?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.484:
Yea, verily and indeed.
SIMO
And you are scheming by cajolery and by cunning tricks to get twenty minae in ready money out of me?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.486:
I, get them out of you?
SIMO
1.5.487:
Just so; to give them to my son, with which to liberate his mistress. Do you confess it? Speak out.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.489:
He confesses it.
Didn’t I tell you so just now, Callipho?
CALLIPHO
1.5.490:
So I remember.
SIMO
Why, directly you knew of these things, were they kept concealed from me? Why wasn’t I made acquainted with them?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.491:
I’ll tell you: because I was unwilling that a bad custom should originate in me, for a servant to accuse his master before his master.
SIMO
1.5.494:
Wouldn’t you order this fellow to be dragged head first to the treadmills?
CALLIPHO
1.5.495:
Has he done anything amiss, Simo?
SIMO
Yes, very much so.
PSEUDOLUS
(to CALLIPHO.)
1.5.496:
Be quiet, I quite well understand my own affairs, Callipho. Is this a fault? Now then, give your attention to the reason why I you kept ignorant of this amour. I knew that the treadmill was close at hand, if I told you.
SIMO
1.5.500:
And didn’t you know, as well, that the treadmill would be close at hand when you kept silent on it?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.501:
I did know it.
SIMO
Why wasn’t it told me?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.502:
The one evil was close at hand, the other at a greater distance; the one was at the moment, the other was a few days off.
SIMO
1.5.504: What will you be doing now? For assuredly the money cannot be got in this quarter out of me, who have especially detected it.
1.5.506:
I shall forthwith give notice to all that no one is to trust him the money.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.507:
I’ faith, I’ll never go begging to any person, so long, at all events, as you shall be alive; troth, you shall find me the money; and as for me, I shall take it from you.
SIMO
1.5.509:
You, take it from me?
PSEUDOLUS
Undoubtedly.
SIMO
1.5.510:
Troth, now, knock out my eye, if I do find it.
PSEUDOLUS
You shall provide it. I warn you then to be on your guard against me.
SIMO
1.5.511:
By my troth, I know this for sure; if you do take it away, you will have done a wonderful and a great exploit.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.513:
I will do it, however.
SIMO
But if you don’t carry it off?
PSEUDOLUS
Then flog me with rods. But what if I do carry it off?
SIMO
1.5.514: I give you Jupiter as your witness,
1.5.515:
that you shall pass your life free from punishment.
PSEUDOLUS
Take care and remember that.
SIMO
1.5.516:
Could I possibly be unable to be on my guard, who am forewarned?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.517:
I forewarn you to be on your guard. I say you must be on your guard, I tell you. Keep watch. Look, now, with those same hands will you this day give me the money
SIMO
1.5.519:
By my troth, ’tis a clever mortal if he keeps his word.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.520:
Carry me away to be your slave if I don’t do it.
SIMO
1.5.521:
You speak kindly and obligingly; for at present you are not mine, I suppose.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.522:
Would you like me to tell you, too, what you will still more wonder at?
SIMO
1.5.523:
Come, then; i’ faith, I long to hear it; I listen to you with pleasure.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.524: Before I fight that battle, I shall first
1.5.525:
fight another battle, famous and memorable.
SIMO
1.5.530:
and I surely will have both of these things effected this very day, before the evening.
SIMO
1.5.531:
Well, if you accomplish these tasks as you say, you will surpass in might King Agathocles. But if you don’t do it, is there any reason why I shouldn’t forthwith put you in the treadmill?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.535:
i’ faith, for all, whatever the time. But if I effect it, will you not at once give me the money of your own free will for me to pay to the procurer?
CALLIPHO
1.5.537:
Pseudolus is making a fair claim; say I’ll give it.
SIMO
1.5.538: But still, do you know what comes into my mind? Suppose they have made an arrangement, Callipho,
1.5.540:
among themselves, or are acting in concert, and on a preconcerted plan, to bamboozle me out of the money?
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.541:
Who would be more audacious than myself, if I dared to do such an action? Well, Simo, if we are thus in collusion, or have ever arranged any plan, do you mark me quite all over with elm-tree stripes, just as when letters are written in a book with a reed.
SIMO
1.5.546:
Now then, proclaim the games as soon as you please.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.547:
Give me your attention, Callipho, I beg you, for this day, so that you may not any way employ yourself upon other business.
CALLIPHO
1.5.549:
Why, now, I had made up my mind yesterday to go into the country.
PSEUDOLUS
1.5.550:
Still, do you now change the plan which you had resolved upon.
CALLIPHO
1.5.551:
I am now resolved not to go away on account of this; I have an inclination to be a spectator of your games, Pseudolus; and if I shall find that he doesn’t give you the money which he has promised, rather than it shouldn’t be done, I’ll give it.
SIMO
1.5.555:
I shall not change my purpose.
PSEUDOLUS
