since I’m empowered to touch you. How hardly can I persuade myself of this, that I am holding you. Prithee, do embrace me (they embrace), my only hope; how you are now easing me of all my woes.
PALAESTRA
1.4.248:
You are beforehand with me in using expressions which belong to me. Now it befits us to be going hence.
AMPELISCA
1.4.249:
Prithee, whither shall we go?
PALAESTRA
1.4.250:
Let’s keep along this sea-shore.
(Pointing to the shore.)
AMPELISCA
Wherever you please, I’ll follow.
PALAESTRA
1.4.251:
Shall we go along thus with our wet clothing?
AMPELISCA
1.4.252:
That which exists, the same must of necessity be borne. (Looking up at the Temple.) But, pray, what’s this?
PALAESTRA
1.4.253:
What is it?
AMPELISCA
Prithee, don’t you see this Temple?
(Pointing towards it.)
PALAESTRA
1.4.254:
Where is it?
AMPELISCA
On the right hand.
PALAESTRA
1.4.255:
I seem to be looking at a place becoming the Divinities.
AMPELISCA
1.4.256:
There must be people not far hence; it is so delightful a spot. Whoever the God is, I pray him to relieve us from these troubles, and to succour us females, wretched, helpless, and in distress.
(They advance towards the Temple, and kneel down before it.)

1.5.259:
(Enter PTOLEMOCRATIA, the Priestess, from the Temple of Venus.) PTOLEMOCRATIA
Who are these, that in their prayers are soliciting aid from my Patroness?
1.5.260:
For the voice of suppliants has brought me hither out of doors. They pay suit to a kind and compliant Goddess and a Patroness that makes no difficulties, and one who is very benevolent.
PALAESTRA
1.5.263:
Mother, we bid you hail.
PTOLEMOCRATIA
Maidens, hail to you. But, prithee, whence
1.5.265:
am I to say that you are hither come with your wet garments, thus wofully arrayed?
PALAESTRA
1.5.266:
Just now, we came from a place there (pointing towards the shore), not a great way from this spot; but it is a great way off from here, whence we have been brought hither.
PTOLEMOCRATIA
1.5.268:
Have you been borne, do you mean, by a ship, the wooden steed, over the azure paths?
PALAESTRA
1.5.269:
Even so.
PTOLEMOCRATIA
Then it were more fitting that you should have come
1.5.270:
arrayed in white and provided with victims; it isn’t the practice for people to come to this Temple in that fashion.
(Pointing at their dresses.)
PALAESTRA
1.5.272: Prithee, whence would you have us, who have been both cast away at sea, to be bringing victims hither? Now, in want of assistance, do we embrace your knees,
1.5.275:
we who are of hopes undefined in places unknown, that you may receive us under your roof and shelter us, and that you will pity the miseries of us both, who have neither any place of refuge nor hope at hand, nor have anything whatever of our own beyond that which you see.
PTOLEMOCRATIA
1.5.280:
Give me your hands, arise, both of you, from off your knees; no one among women is more compassionate than I. (They arise from the ground.) But, maidens, my circumstances are poor and limited; with difficulty I support my own existence; Venus I serve for my maintenance.
AMPELISCA
1.5.284:
Prithee, is this a Temple of Venus?
PTOLEMOCRATIA
1.5.285:
I will admit it; I am styled the Priestess of this Temple. But whatever it is, it shall be done by me with a hearty welcome, so far as my means shall suffice. Come with me this way.
PALAESTRA
1.5.288:
Kindly and attentively, mother, do you show your attentions to us.
PTOLEMOCRATIA
1.5.289:
So I ought to do.
(They go into the Temple.)

2.1.290:
(Ente some FISHERMEN, with lines and nets.) A FISHERMAN
Persons who are poor live wretchedly in every way, especially those who have no calling and have learned no art. Of necessity must that be deemed enough, whatever they have at home. From our garb, then, you pretty well understand how wealthy we are. These hooks and these rods here are as good to us as a calling and as our clothing.
2.1.295: Each day from the city do we come out hither to the sea to seek for forage. Instead of exertion in the wrestling-school and the place for exercise, we have this: sea-urchins, rock-mussels, oysters, limpets, cockles, sea-nettles, sea-mussels and spotted crabs, we catch. After that, we commence our fishing with the hook and among the rocks,
2.1.300: and thus we take our food from out of the sea. If success does not befall us, and not any fish is taken, soaked in salt water and thoroughly drenched, we quietly betake ourselves home, and without dinner go to sleep. And since the sea is now in waves so boisterous, no hopes have we; unless we take some cockles, without a doubt we’ve had our dinners.
2.1.305:
Now let’s adore good Venus here, that she may kindly befriend us to-day.
(They advance towards the door of the Temple.)

2.2.306:
(Enter TRACHALIO, at a distance, in haste.) TRACHALIO
(to himself.)
I’ve carefully given all attention that I mightn’t pass my master anywhere; for when some time since he went out of the house, he said that he was going to the harbour, and he ordered me to come here to meet him at the Temple of Venus. But see, opportunely do I espy some people standing here of whom I may enquire; I’ll accost them.
2.2.310:
(Goes up to the FISHERMEN.) Save you, thieves of the sea, shellfish-gatherers and hook-fishers, hungry race of men, how fare ye? How perish apace?
FISHERMEN of Cyrene
2.2.312:
Just as befits a fisherman with hunger, thirst, and expectation.
TRACHALIO
2.2.313: Have you seen to-day, while you’ve been standing here, any young man, of courageous aspect, ruddy, stout, of genteel appearance, come by this way,
2.2.315:
who was taking with him three men in scarfs, with swords?
FISHERMEN of Cyrene
2.2.316:
We know of no one coming this way of that appearance which you mention.
TRACHALIO
Have you seen any old fellow, bald on the forehead and snub-nosed, of big stature, pot-bellied, with eyebrows awry, a narrow forehead, a knave, the scorn of Gods and men, a scoundrel, one full of vile dishonesty and of iniquity,
2.2.320:
who had along with him two very pretty-looking young women?
FISHERMEN of Cyrene
2.2.321:
One who has been born with qualities and endowments of that sort, ’twere really fitter for him to resort to the executioner than to the Temple of Venus.
TRACHALIO
2.2.323:
But tell me if you have seen him.
FISHERMEN of Cyrene
Really, no one has passed this way. Fare you well.
TRACHALIO
2.2.324: Fare ye well. (Exeunt FISHERMEN.) (to himself.) I thought so; it has come to pass as I suspected;
2.2.325: my master has been deceived; the cursed Procurer has taken himself off to distant lands. He has embarked on board ship, and carried the women away; I’m a wizard. He invited my master here to breakfast, as well, this very spawn of wickedness. Now what is better for me than to wait here in this spot until my master comes? At the same time, if this Priestess of Venus knows anything more,
2.2.330: if I see her, I’ll make enquiries; she’ll give me the information.

2.3.331:
(Enter AMPELISCA, from the Temple.) AMPELISCA
(to the PRIESTESS, within.)
I understand; here at this cottage (pointing to it), which is close by the Temple of Venus, you’ve requested me to knock and ask for water.
TRACHALIO
2.3.332:
Whose voice is it that has flown to my ears?
AMPELISCA
2.3.333:
Prithee, who’s speaking here? Who is it that I see?
TRACHALIO
2.3.334:
Isn’t this Ampelisca that’s coming out from the Temple?
AMPELISCA
Isn’t this
2.3.335:
Trachalio that I see, the servant of Plesidippus?
TRACHALIO
2.3.336:
It is she.
AMPELISCA
It is he; Trachalio, health to you.
TRACHALIO
Health, Ampelisca, to you; how fare you?
AMPELISCA
2.3.337:
In misery I pass a life not far advanced.
TRACHALIO
Do give some better omen.
AMPELISCA
2.3.338:
Still it behoves all prudent persons to confer and talk together. But, prithee, where’s your master, Plesidippus?
TRACHALIO
2.3.339:
Marry, well said, indeed; as if he wasn’t within there.
(Pointing to the Temple.)
AMPELISCA
2.3.340:
By my troth, he isn’t, nor, in fact, has he come here at all.
TRACHALIO
2.3.341:
He hasn’t come?
AMPELISCA
You say the truth.
TRACHALIO
That’s not my way, Ampelisca. But how nearly is the breakfast got ready?
AMPELISCA
2.3.342:
What breakfast, I beg of you?
TRACHALIO
2.3.343:
The sacrifice, I mean, that you are performing here.
AMPELISCA
Prithee, what is it you are dreaming about?
TRACHALIO
2.3.344:
For certain, Labrax invited Plesidippus hither to a breakfast, your master, my master.
AMPELISCA
2.3.345:
By my troth, you’re telling of no wondrous facts: if he has deceived Gods and men, he has only acted after the fashion of Procurers.
TRACHALIO
2.3.347:
Then neither yourselves nor my master are here performing a sacrifice.
AMPELISCA
You are a wizard.
TRACHALIO
2.3.348:
What are you doing then?
AMPELISCA
The Priestess of Venus has received here into her abode both myself and Palaestra, after many mishaps and dreadful alarm, and from being in danger of our lives, destitute of aid and of resources.
TRACHALIO
2.3.351:
Prithee, is Palaestra here, the beloved of my master?
AMPELISCA
Assuredly.
TRACHALIO
2.3.352:
Great joyousness is there in your news, my dear Ampelisca. But I greatly long to know what was this danger of yours.
AMPELISCA
2.3.354:
Last night our ship was wrecked, my dear Trachalio.
TRACHALIO
2.3.355:
How, ship? What story’s this?
AMPELISCA
Prithee, have you not heard in what way the Procurer intended secretly to carry us away hence to Sicily, and how, whatever there was at home, he placed on board ship? That has all gone to the bottom now.
TRACHALIO
2.3.358: O clever Neptune, hail to thee! Surely, no dicer is more skilful than thyself. Decidedly
2.3.360:
a right pleasant throw hast thou made; thou didst break a-villain. But where now is the Procurer Labrax?
AMPELISCA
2.3.361:
Perished through drinking, I suppose; Neptune last night invited him to deep potations.
TRACHALIO
2.3.363: By my troth, I fancy it was given him to drink by way of cup of necessity. How much I do love you, my dear Ampelisca; how pleasing you are; what honied words you do utter.
2.3.365:
But you and Palaestra, in what way were you saved?
AMPELISCA
I’ll let you know. Both in affright, we leapt from the ship into a boat, because we saw that the ship was being borne upon a rock; in haste, I unloosed the rope, while they were in dismay. The storm separated us from them with the boat in a direction to the right. And so, tossed about by winds and waves,
2.3.370:
in a multitude of ways, we, wretched creatures, during the livelong night half dead, the wind this day has scarce borne us to the shore.
TRACHALIO
2.3.372:
I understand; thus is Neptune wont to do; he is a very dainty Aedile; if any wares are bad, over he throws them all.
AMPELISCA
2.3.374:
Woe to your head and life!
TRACHALIO
To your own, my dear Ampelisca. I was sure that the Procurer would do that which he has done; I often said so. It were better I should let my hair grow, and set up for a soothsayer.
AMPELISCA
2.3.378:
Did you not take care then, you and your master, that he shouldn’t go away, when you knew this?
TRACHALIO
2.3.379:
What could he do?
AMPELISCA
If he was in love, do you ask what he could do?
2.3.380:
Both night and day he should have kept watch; he should have been always on his guard. But, by my troth, he has done like many others; thus finely has Plesidippus taken care of her.
TRACHALIO
2.3.382:
For what reason do you say that?
AMPELISCA
The thing is evident.
TRACHALIO
Don’t you know this? Even he who goes to the bath to bathe, while there he carefully keeps an eye upon his garments, still they are stolen; inasmuch as some one of those that he is watching is a rogue;
2.3.385:
the thief easily marks him for whom he’s upon the watch; the keeper knows not which one is the thief. But bring me to her; where is she?
AMPELISCA
2.3.386:
Well then, go here into the Temple of Venus; you’ll find her sitting there, and in tears.
TRACHALIO
2.3.387:
How disagreable is that to me already. But why is she weeping?
AMPELISCA
2.3.388: I’ll tell you; she’s afflicting herself in mind for this; because the Procurer took away a casket from her which she had,
2.3.390:
and in which she kept that by which she might be enabled to recognize her parents; she fears that this has been lost.
TRACHALIO
2.3.391:
Where was that little casket, pray?
AMPELISCA
There, on board the ship; he himself locked it up in his wallet, that there mightn’t be the means by which she might recognize her parents.
TRACHALIO
2.3.393:
O scandalous deed! to require her to be a slave, who ought to be a free woman.
AMPELISCA
2.3.395:
Therefore she now laments that it has gone to the bottom along with the ship. There, too, was all the gold and silver of the Procurer.
TRACHALIO
2.3.397:
Some one, I trust, has dived and brought it up.
AMPELISCA
For this reason is she sad and disconsolate, that she has met with the loss of them.
TRACHALIO
2.3.398: Then have I the greater occasion to do this, to go in and console her, that she mayn’t thus distress herself in mind.
2.3.400:
For I know that many a lucky thing has happened to many a one beyond their hopes.
AMPELISCA
2.3.401:
But I know too that hope has deceived many who have hoped.
TRACHALIO
2.3.402:
Therefore a patient mind is the best remedy for affliction. I’ll go in, unless you wish for anything.
(Goes into the Temple.)
AMPELISCA
2.3.403: Go. (To herself.) I’ll do that which the Priestess requested me, and I’ll ask for some water here at the neighbour’s;
2.3.405: for she said that if I asked for it in her name, they would give it directly. And I do think that I never saw a more worthy old lady, one to whom I should think that it is more befitting for Gods and men to show kindness. How courteously, how heartily, how kindly, how, without the least difficulty, she received us into her home, trembling, in want, drenched, shipwrecked, half dead;
2.3.410: not otherwise, in fact, than if we had been her own offspring. How kindly did she herself, just now, tucking up her garments, make the water warm for us to bathe. Now, that I mayn’t keep her waiting, I’ll fetch some water from the place where she requested me. (Knocking at the door of DAEMONES.) Hallo, there, is there any one in the cottage? is any one going to open this door? Will any one come out?

2.4.414:
(Enter SCEPARNIO, from the cottage of DAEMONES.) SCEPARNIO
Who is it so furiously making an attack upon our door?
AMPELISCA
2.4.415:
It’s I.
SCEPARNIO
Well now, what good news is there? (Aside.) Dear me, a lass of comely appearance, i’ troth.
AMPELISCA
2.4.416:
Greeting to you, young man.
SCEPARNIO
And many greetings to you, young woman.
AMPELISCA
2.4.417:
I’m come to you—
SCEPARNIO
I’ll receive you with a welcome, if you come in the evening, by-and-by, just such as I could like; for just now I’ve no means to receive you, a damsel, thus early in the morning But what have you to say, my smiling, pretty one.
(Chucks her under the chin.)
AMPELISCA
2.4.419:
Oh, you’re handling me too familiarly.
(Moves away.)
SCEPARNIO
2.4.420:
O ye immortal Gods! she’s the very image of Venus. What joyousness there is in her eyes, and, only do see, what a skin ’tis of the vulture’s tint,—rather, the eagle’s, indeed, I meant to say. Her breasts, too, how beautiful; and then what expression on her lips!
(Takes hold of her.)
AMPELISCA
(struggling.)
2.4.424:
I’m no common commodity for the whole township; can’t you keep your hands off me?
SCEPARNIO
(patting her.)
2.4.425:
Won’t you let me touch you, gentle one, in this manner, gently and lovingly?
AMPELISCA
2.4.426:
When I have leisure, then I’ll be giving my attention to toying and dalliance to please you; for the present, prithee, do either say me Yes or No to the matter for which I was sent hither.
SCEPARNIO
2.4.428:
What now is it that you wish?
AMPELISCA
(pointing to her pitcher.)
To a shrewd person, my equipment would give indications of what it is I want.
SCEPARNIO
2.4.429:
To a shrewd woman, this equipment, too, of mine, would give indication of what it is I want.
AMPELISCA
(pointing to the Temple.)
2.4.430:
The Priestess there of Venus, requested me to fetch some water from your house here.
SCEPARNIO
2.4.431:
But I’m a lordly sort of person; unless you entreat me, you shan’t have a drop. We dug this well with danger to ourselves, and with tools of iron. Not a drop can be got out of me except by means of plenty of blandishments.
AMPELISCA
2.4.434:
Prithee, why do you make so much fuss about the water—a thing that even enemy affords to enemy?
SCEPARNIO
2.4.435:
Why do you make so much fuss about granting a favour to me, that citizen grants to citizen?
AMPELISCA
2.4.436:
On the contrary, my sweet one, I’ll even do everything for you that you wish.
SCEPARNIO
2.4.437:
O charming! I am favoured; she’s now calling me her sweet one. The water shall be given you, so that you mayn’t be coaxing me in vain. Give me the pitcher.
AMPELISCA
2.4.438:
Take it (gives it to him): make haste and bring it out, there’s a dear.
SCEPARNIO
2.4.439:
Stay a moment; I’ll be here this instant, my sweet one. (Goes into the cottage.)
AMPELISCA
2.4.440: What shall I say to the Priestess for having delayed here so long a time? How, even still, in my wretchedness do I tremble, when with my eyes I look upon the sea. (She looks towards the shore.)
2.4.442: But what, to my sorrow, do I see afar upon the shore? My master, the Procurer, and his Sicilian guest. both of whom wretched I supposed to have perished in the deep. Still does thus much more of evil survive for us than we had imagined. But why do I delay to run off into the Temple, and to tell
2.4.455:
Palaestra this, that we may take refuge at the altar before this scoundrel of a Procurer can come hither and seize us here? I’ll betake myself away from this spot; for the necessity suddenly arises for me to do so.
(Runs into the Temple.)

2.5.458:
(Enter SCEPARNIO, from the cottage.) SCEPARNIO
(to himself.)
O ye immortal Gods, I never did imagine that there was so great delight in water; how heartily I did draw this.
2.5.460: The well seemed much less deep than formerly. How entirely without exertion did I draw this up. With all deference to myself, am I not a very silly fellow,in having only to-day made a commencement of being in love? (Turning slowly round, he holds out the pitcher.) Here’s the water for you, my pretty one; here now, I would have you carry it with as much pleasure as I carry it, that you may please me.
2.5.465: (Stares around him.) But where are you, my tit-bit? Do take this water, please; where are you? (Again looks about.) I’ troth, she’s in love with me, as I fancy; the roguish one’s playing bo-peep. Where are you? Are you going now to take this pitcher? Where are you, I say? You’ve carried the joke far enough. Really, do be serious at last. Once more, are you going to take this pitcher? Where in the world are you?
2.5.470: (Looks about.) I’ troth, I don’t see her anywhere, for my part; she’s making fun of me. I’ faith, I shall now set down this pitcher in the middle of the road. But yet, suppose any person should carry away from here this sacred pitcher of Venus, he would be causing me some trouble. I’ faith, I’m afraid that this woman’s laying a trap for me,
2.5.475: that I may be caught with the sacred pitcher of Venus. In such case, with very good reason, the magistrate will be letting me die in prison, if any one shall see me holding this. For it’s marked with the name; itself tells its own tale, whose property it is. Troth now, I’ll call that Priestess here out of doors,
2.5.480:
that she may take this pitcher. I’ll go there to the door. (He knocks.) Hallo there! Ptolemocratia. (Calling aloud.) Take this pitcher of yours, please; some young woman, I don’t know who, brought it here to me. (A pause.) It must then be carried in-doors by me. I’ve found myself a job, if, in fact, of my own accord, water is to be carried by me for these people as well.
(Goes into the Temple with the pitcher.)

2.6.485:
(Enter LABRAX, dripping wet, followed by CHARMIDES, at a distance, in the same plight.) LABRAX
(grumbling to himself.)
The person that chooses himself to be wretched and a beggar, let him trust himself and his life to Neptune. For if any one has any dealings at all with him, he sends him back home equipped in this guise.
2.6.489: (Surveying himself.) By my troth, Liberty, you were a clever one, who were never willing to put even a foot, I’ faith, on board ship with me.
2.6.491:
But (looking round) where’s this guest of mine that has proved my ruin? Oh, see, here he comes.
CHARMIDES
2.6.492:
Where the plague are you hurrying to, Labrax? For really I cannot follow you so fast.
LABRAX
2.6.494: I only wish that you had perished by direful tornments in Sicily before I had looked upon you with my eyes,
2.6.496:
you on whose account this misfortune has befallen me.
CHARMIDES
2.6.497: I only wish that on the day on which you admitted me into your house, I had laid me down in a prison sooner. I pray the immortal Gods, that so long as you live,
2.6.500:
you may have all your guests just like your own self.
LABRAX
2.6.501:
In your person I admitted misfortune into my house. What business had I to listen to a rogue like you, or what to depart hence? Or why to go on board ship, where I have lost even more wealth than I was possessor of?
CHARMIDES
2.6.505:
Troth, I’m far from being surprised if your ship has been wrecked, which was carrying yourself, a villain, and your property villanously acquired.
LABRAX
2.6.507:
You’ve utterly ruined me with your wheedling speeches.
CHARMIDES
2.6.508:
A more accursed dinner of yours have I been dining upon than the ones that were set before Thyestes and Tereus.
LABRAX
2.6.510:
I’m dying; I’m sick at heart. Prithee, do hold up my head.
CHARMIDES
2.6.511:
By my troth, I could very much wish that you would vomit up your lungs.
LABRAX
2.6.512:
Alas! Palaestra and Ampelisca, where are you now?
CHARMIDES
2.6.513:
Supplying food for the fishes at the bottom, I suppose.
LABRAX
2.6.514: You have brought beggary upon me by your means,
2.6.515:
while I was listening to your bragging lies.
CHARMIDES
2.6.516:
You have reason deservedly to give me many hearty thanks, who from an insipid morsel by my agency have made you salt.
LABRAX
2.6.518:
Nay, but do you get out from me to extreme and utter perdition.
CHARMIDES
2.6.519:
You be off; I was just going to do that very thing.
LABRAX
2.6.520:
Alas! what mortal being is there living more wretched than I?
CHARMIDES
2.6.521:
I am by very far much more wretched, Labrax, than yourself.
LABRAX
2.6.522:
How so?
CHARMIDES
Because I am not deserving of it, whereas you are deserving.
LABRAX
2.6.523:
O bulrush, bulrush, I do praise your lot, who always maintain your credit for dryness.
CHARMIDES
(his teeth chattering.)
2.6.525:
For my part, I’m exercising myself for a skirmishing fight, for, from my shivering, I utter all my words in piecemeal flashes.
LABRAX
2.6.527: By my troth, Neptune, you are a purveyor of chilly baths; since I got away from you with my clothes, I’ve been freezing.
2.6.529: No hot liquor-shop at all for sure does he provide;
2.6.530:
so salt and cold the potions that he prepares.
CHARMIDES
2.6.531:
How lucky are the blacksmiths who are always sitting among hot coals; they are always warm.
LABRAX
2.6.533:
I only wish that I were now enjoying the lot of the duck, so as, although I had just come from out of the water, still to be dry.
CHARMIDES
2.6.535:
What if I some way or other let myself out at the games for a hobgoblin?
LABRAX
2.6.536:
For what reason?
CHARMIDES
Because, I’ faith, I’m chattering aloud with my teeth.
2.6.537:
But I’m of opinion that, with very good reason, I’ve had this ducking.
LABRAX
2.6.538:
How so?
CHARMIDES
Why, haven’t I ventured to go on board ship with yourself, who have been stirring up the ocean for me from the very bottom?
LABRAX
2.6.540:
I listened to you when advising me; you assured me that there in Sicily was very great profit from courtesans; there, you used to say, I should be able to amass wealth.
CHARMIDES
2.6.543:
Did you expect, then, you unclean beast, that you were going to gobble up the whole island of Sicily?
LABRAX
2.6.545:
What whale, I wonder, has gobbled up my wallet where all my gold and silver was packed up?
CHARMIDES
2.6.547:
That same one, I suppose, that has swallowed my purse, which was full of silver in my travelling-bag.
LABRAX
2.6.549: Alas! I’m reduced even to this one poor tunic (stretching it out)
2.6.550:
and to this poor shabby cloak; I’m done for to all intents.
CHARMIDES
2.6.551:
Then you may even go into partnership with me; we have got equal shares.
LABRAX
2.6.552: If at least my damsels had been saved, there would have been some hope. Now, if the young man Plesidippus should be seeing me,
2.6.555:
from whom I received the earnest for Palaestra, he’ll then be causing me some trouble in consequence.
(He begins to cry.)
CHARMIDES
2.6.557: Why cry, you fool? Really, by my troth, so long as your tongue shall exist, you have abundance with which to make payment to everybody.

2.7.559:
(Enter SCEPARNIO, from the Temple.) SCEPARNIO
(to himself, aloud.)
What to-do is this, I’d like to know, that two young women
2.7.560:
here in the Temple, in tears, are holding in their embrace the statue of Venus, dreading I know not what in their wretchedness? But they say that this last night they have been tossed about, and to-day cast on shore from the waves.
LABRAX
(overhearing.)
2.7.563:
Troth now, young man, prithee, where are these young women that you are talking of?
SCEPARNIO
2.7.564:
Here (pointing) in the Temple of Venus.
LABRAX
How many are there?
SCEPARNIO
Just as many as you and I make.
LABRAX
2.7.565:
Surely, they are mine.
SCEPARNIO
Surely, I know nothing about that.
LABRAX
Of what appearance are they?
SCEPARNIO
Good-looking; I could even fall in love with either of them, if I were well liquored.
LABRAX
2.7.567:
Surely, they are the damsels.
SCEPARNIO
Surely, you are a nuisance; be off, go in and see, if you like.
LABRAX
2.7.568:
These must be my wenches in here, my dear Charmides.
CHARMIDES
2.7.569:
Jupiter confound you, both if they are and still if they are not.
LABRAX
2.7.570:
I’ll straightway burst into this Temple of Venus here.
CHARMIDES
Into the bottomless pit, I would rather. (LABRAX rushes into the Temple, and shuts the door.) Prithee, stranger, show me some spot where I may go to sleep.
SCEPARNIO
2.7.572:
Go to sleep there, wherever you please (points to the ground); no one hinders, it’s free to the public.
CHARMIDES
(pointing to his clothes.)
2.7.573: But do you see me, in what wet clothes I’m dressed? Do take me under shelter; lend me some dry clothes,
2.7.575:
while my own are drying; on some occasion I’ll return you the favour.
SCEPARNIO
2.7.576:
See, here’s my outer coat, which alone is dry; that, if you like, I’ll lend you. (Takes it off and holds it out to him.) In that same I’m wont to be clothed, by that same protected, when it rains. Do you give me those clothes of yours; I’ll soon have them dried.
CHARMIDES
2.7.578:
How now, are you afraid that, as I’ve been washed bare last night at sea, I mayn’t be made bare again here upon shore?
SCEPARNIO
2.7.580:
Wash you bare, or anoint you well, I don’t care one fig. I shall never entrust anything to you unless upon a pledge being taken. Do you either sweat away or perish with cold, be you either sick or well. I’ll put up with no stranger-guest in my house; I’ve had disagreements enough.
(Puts on his coat again, and goes into the house of DAEMONES.)
CHARMIDES
2.7.584: What, are you off? (A pause.) He’s a trafficker in slaves for money; whoever he is,
2.7.585: he has no bowels of compassion. But why in my wretchedness am I standing here, soaking? Why don’t I rather go away from here into the Temple of Venus, that I may sleep off this debauch which I got with drinking last night against the bent of my inclination? Neptune has been drenching us with salt water as though we were Greek wines, and so he hoped that our stomachs might be vomited up with his salt draughts.
2.7.590:
What need of words? If he had persisted in inviting us a little longer, we should have gone fast asleep there; as it is, hardly alive has he sent us off home. Now I’ll go see the Procurer, my boon companion, what he’s doing within.
(Goes into the Temple.)

3.1.593:
(Enter DAEMONES, from his house.) DAEMONES
(to himnself.)
In wondrous ways do the Gods make sport of men, in wondrous fashions do they send dreams in sleep.
3.1.595: Not the sleeping, even, do they allow to rest. As, for example, I, this last night which has gone by, dreamed a wonderful and a curious dream. A she-ape seemed to be endeavouring to climb up to a swallow’s nest;
3.1.600: and she was not able thence to take them out. After that, the ape seemed to come to me to beg me to lend a ladder to her. I in these terms gave answer to the ape, that swallows are the descendants of Philomela and of Progne.
3.1.605: I expostulated with her, that she might not hurt those of my country. But then she began to be much more violent, and seemed gratuitously to be threatening me with vengeance. She summoned me to a court of justice. Then, in my anger, I seemed to seize hold of the ape by the middle, in what fashion I know not;
3.1.610: and I fastened up with chains this most worthless beast. Now to what purpose I shall say that this dream tends, never have I this day been able to come to any conclusion. (A loud noise is heard in the Temple.) But what’s this noise that arises in this Temple of Venus, my neighbour? My mind’s in wonder about it.

3.2.615:
(Enter TRACHALIO, in haste, from the Temple.) TRACHALIO
(aloud.)
O citizens of Cyrene, I implore your aid, countrymen, you who are near neighbours to these spots, bring aid to helplessness, and utterly crush a most vile attempt. Inflict vengeance, that the power of the wicked, who wish themselves to be distinguished by crimes, may not be stronger than of the guiltless.
3.2.620: Make an example for the shameless man, give its reward to modest virtue; cause that one may be allowed to live here rather under the control of the laws than of brute force. Hasten hither into the Temple of Venus; again do I implore your aid, you who are here at hand and who hear my cries.
3.2.624: Bring assistance to those who, after the recognized usage, have entrusted their lives to Venus and to the Priestess of Venus, under their protection.
3.2.626:
Wring ye the neck of iniquity before it reaches yourselves.
DAEMONES
3.2.627:
What’s all this to-do?
TRACHALIO
(embracing his knees.)
By these knees of yours, I do entreat you, old gentleman, whoever you are—
DAEMONES
3.2.628:
Nay, but do you let go my knees, then, and tell me why it is that you are making a noise?
TRACHALIO
3.2.629: I do beg and entreat you, that if you hope
3.2.630:
this year that you will have abundance of laserwort and silphium, and that that export will arrive at Capua safe and sound, and that you may ever enjoy freedom from diseased eyes—
DAEMONES
3.2.633:
Are you in your senses?
TRACHALIO
—Or whether you trust that you will have plenty of juice of silphium, that you will not hesitate to give me the aid which I shall entreat of you, aged sir.
DAEMONES
3.2.635:
And I, by your legs, and ancles, and back, do entreat you that, if you hope that you will have a crop of elm-twigs, and that a fruitful harvest of beatings will this year be your lot, you will tell me what’s the matter here, by reason of which you are making this uproar.
TRACHALIO
3.2.639:
Why do you choose to speak me ill? For my part, I wished you everything that’s good.
DAEMONES
3.2.640:
And for my part, I’m speaking you well, in praying that things which you deserve may befall you.
TRACHALIO
3.2.641:
Prithee, do prevent this.
DAEMONES
What’s the matter, then?
TRACHALIO
(pointing to the Temple.)
Two innocent women are inside here, in need of your aid, on whom, against law and justice, an injury has been, is being, glaringly committed here in the Temple of Venus. Besides, the Priestess of Venus
3.2.645:
is being disgracefully insulted.
DAEMONES
What person is there of effrontery so great as to dare to injure the Priestess? But these women, who are they? Or what injury is being done to them?
TRACHALIO
3.2.647:
If you give me your attention, I’ll tell you. They have clung to the statue of Venus; a most audacious fellow is now trying to tear them away. They ought, by rights, both of them to be free.
DAEMONES
3.2.650:
What fellow is it that so lightly holds the Gods? In a few words tell me.
TRACHALIO
3.2.651:
One most full of fraud, villany, parricide, and perjury; a lawbreaker, an immodest, unclean, most shameless fellow; to sum up all in one word, he is a Procurer; why need I say more about him?
DAEMONES
3.2.654:
Troth now, you tell of a man that ought to be handed over to retribution.
TRACHALIO
3.2.655:
A villain, to seize the Priestess by the throat.
DAEMONES
3.2.656:
By my troth, but he has done it at his own great peril. (Calls aloud at his door.) Come you out of doors here, Turbalio and Sparax; where are you?
TRACHALIO
3.2.657:
Prithee, do go in, and hasten to their rescue.
DAEMONES
(impatiently.)
3.2.658:
And am I to call for them once more?
(from the cottage.)
DAEMONES
Follow me this way.
TRACHALIO
Come on now this instant, bid them tear his eyes out, just in the way that cooks do cuttle-fish.
DAEMONES
3.2.660:
Drag the fellow out here by his legs, just like a slaughtered pig.
(DAEMONES and his SERVANTS go into the Temple.)
TRACHALIO
(listening at the door.)
3.2.661: I hear a scuffling; the Procurer, I guess, is being belaboured with their fists; I’d very much like them to knock the teeth out of the jaws of the most villanous fellow. But see, here are the women themselves coming out of the Temple in consternation.

3.3.664:
(Enter PALAESTRA and AMPELISCA, in haste, from the Temple, with dishevelled locks.) PALAESTRA
Now is that time arrived when destitution of all resources and aid,
3.3.665: succour and defence, overtakes us. Neither hope nor means is there to bring us aid, nor know we in what direction we should commence to proceed. In exceeding terror now are we both, in this our wretchedness. Such cruelty and such outrage
3.3.670: have been committed towards us just now in-doors here by our master, who, in his villany, pushed down the old lady, the Priestess, headlong, and struck her in a very disgraceful manner, and with his violence tore us away from the inner side of the statue. But as our lot and fortunes are now showing themselves,
3.3.675:
’twere best to die, nor in our miseries is there anything better than death.
TRACHALIO
(behind.)
3.3.676: What’s this? Whose words are those? Why do I delay to console them? (Aloud.) Harkye, Palaestra,
3.3.678:
Ampelisca, harkye!
PALAESTRA
Prithee, who is it that calls us?
AMPELISCA
3.3.679:
Who is it that calls me by name?
TRACHALIO
If you turn round and look, you’ll know.
PALAESTRA
(turning round.)
3.3.680:
O hope of my safety!
TRACHALIO
Be silent and of good courage; trust me.
PALAESTRA
If only it can be so, let not violence overwhelm us.
TRACHALIO
3.3.681:
What violence?
PALAESTRA
That same which is driving me to commit violence on myself.
TRACHALIO
Oh, do leave off; you are very silly.
PALAESTRA
3.3.682:
Then do you leave off at once your consoling me in my misery with words.
AMPELISCA
3.3.683:
Unless you afford us protection in reality, Trachalio, it’s all over with us.
PALAESTRA
3.3.684:
I’m resolved to die sooner than suffer this Procurer to get me in his power. But still I am of woman’s heart; when, in my misery, death comes into my mind, fear takes possession of my limbs.
TRACHALIO
3.3.686: By my troth, although this is a bitter affliction,
3.3.687:
do have a good heart.
PALAESTRA
Why where, pray, is a good heart to be found for me?
TRACHALIO
3.3.688:
Don’t you fear, I tell you; sit you down here by the altar.
(Points to it.)
AMPELISCA
What can this altar possibly avail us more than the statue here within the Temple
3.3.690:
of Venus, from which just now, embracing it, in our wretchedness, we were torn by force?
TRACHALIO
3.3.691:
Only you be seated here; then I’ll protect you in this spot. This altar you possess as though your bulwarks; these your fortifications; from this spot will I defend you. With the aid of Venus, I’ll march against the wickedness of the Procurer.
PALAESTRA
3.3.694: We follow your instructions (they advance to the altar and kneel); and genial Venus, we both of us, in tears, implore thee,
3.3.695: embracing this thy altar, bending upon our knees, that thou wilt receive us into thy guardianship, and be our protector; that thou wilt punish those wretches who have set at nought thy Temple, and that thou wilt suffer us to occupy this thy altar with thy permission, we who last night were by the might of Neptune cast away;
3.3.700:
hold us not in scorn, and do not for that reason impute it to us as a fault, if there is anything that thou shouldst think is not so well attended to by us as it ought to have been.
TRACHALIO
3.3.702: I think they ask what’s just; it ought, Venus, by thee to be granted. Thou oughtst to pardon them; ’tis terror forces them to do this. They say that thou wast born from a shell; take thou care that thou dost not despise the shells of these.
3.3.705:
But see, most opportunely the old gentleman is coming out, both my protector and your own.
(He goes to the altar.)

3.4.706:
(Enter DAEMONES, from the Temple, with his two SERVANTS dragging out LABRAX.) DAEMONES
Come out of the Temple, you most sacrilegious of men, as many as have ever been born. Do you go (calling to the WOMEN) and sit by the altar. (Not seeing them near the door.) But where are they?
TRACHALIO
3.4.708: Very good; I wanted that. Now bid him come this way. (To LABRAX.) Are you attempting here among us to commit a violation of the laws against the Deities?
3.4.710:
(To the SERVANTS, who obey with alacrity.) Punch his face with your fists.
LABRAX
I’m suffering these indignities at your own cost.
DAEMONES
3.4.711:
Why, the insolent fellow’s threatening even.
LABRAX
I’ve been robbed of my rights; you are robbing me of my female slaves against my will.
TRACHALIO
3.4.712: Do you then find some wealthy man of the Senate of Cyrene as judge, whether these women ought to be yours, or whether they oughtn’t to be free,
3.4.715:
or whether it isn’t right that you should be clapped into prison, and there spend your life, until you have worn the whole gaol out with your feet.
LABRAX
3.4.717:
I wasn’t prepared to prophesy for this day that I should be talking with a hang-gallows like yourself. (Turning to DAEMONES.) You do I summon to judgment.
DAEMONES
(pointing to TRACHALIO.)
3.4.718:
In the first place, try it with him who knows you.
LABRAX
(to DAEMONES.)
3.4.719:
My suit is with yourself.
TRACHALIO
But it must be with myself. (Pointing to the WOMEN.) Are these your female slaves?
LABRAX
3.4.720:
They are.
TRACHALIO
Just come then, touch either of them with your little finger only.
LABRAX
3.4.721:
What if I do touch them?
TRACHALIO
That very instant, upon my faith, I’ll make a hand-ball of you, and while you’re in the air I’ll belabour you with my fists, you most perjured villain.
LABRAX
3.4.723:
Am I not to be allowed to take away my female slaves from the altar of Venus?
DAEMONES
3.4.724:
You may not; such is the law with us.
LABRAX
I’ve no concern with your laws; for my part, I shall at once carry them both away from here.
3.4.726:
If you are in love with them, old gentleman (holding out his hand), you must down here with the ready cash.
DAEMONES
3.4.727:
But these women have proved pleasing to Venus.
LABRAX
She may have them, if she pays the money.
DAEMONES
3.4.728: A Goddess, pay you money? Now then, that you may understand my determination, only do you commence in mere joke to offer them the very slightest violence;
3.4.730:
I’ll send you away from here with such a dressing, that you won’t know your own self. You, therefore (turning to his SERVANTS), when I give you the signal, if you don’t beat his eyes out of his head, I’ll trim you round about with rods just like beds of myrtle with bulrushes.
LABRAX
3.4.733:
You are treating me with violence.
TRACHALIO
What, do you even upbraid us with violence, you flagrant specimen of flagitiousness?
LABRAX
3.4.734:
You, you thrice-dotted villain, do you dare to speak abusively to me?
TRACHALIO
3.4.735:
I am a thrice-dotted villain; I confess it; you are a strictly honorable man; ought these women a bit the less to be free?
LABRAX
3.4.737:
Aye, and your mistresses, too, I’ faith, and from genuine Greece; for one of them was born at Athens of free-born parents.
DAEMONES
3.4.739:
What is it I hear from you?
TRACHALIO
That she (pointing to PALAESTRA) was born at Athens, a free-born woman.
DAEMONES
(to TRACHALIO.)
3.4.740:
Prithee is she a countrywoman of mine?
TRACHALIO
Are you not a Cyrenian?
DAEMONES
3.4.741:
No; born at Athens in Attica, bred and educated there.
TRACHALIO
3.4.742:
Prithee, aged sir, do protect your countrywomen.
DAEMONES
(aside.)
O daughter, when I look on her, separated from me you remind me of my miseries: (aloud) she who was lost by me when three years old; now, if she is living, she’s just about as tall, I’m sure, as she.
(Pointing to PALAESTRA.)
LABRAX
3.4.745:
I paid the money down for these two, to their owners, of whatever country they were. What matters it to me whether they were born at Athens or at Thebes, so long as they are rightfully in servitude as my slaves?
TRACHALIO
3.4.747: Is it so, you impudent fellow? What, are you, a cat prowling after maidens, to be keeping children here kidnapped from their parents and destroying them in your disgraceful calling?
3.4.750:
But as for this other one, I really don’t know what her country is; I only know that she’s more deserving than yourself, you most abominable rascal.
LABRAX
3.4.752:
Are these women your property?
TRACHALIO
Come to the trial, then, which of the two according to his back is the more truthful; if you don’t bear more compliments upon your back than any ship of war has nails, then I’m the greatest of liars.
3.4.755:
Afterwards, do you examine mine, when I’ve examined yours; if it shall not prove to be so untouched, that any leather flask maker will say that it is a hide most capital and most sound for the purposes of his business, what reason is there why I shouldn’t mangle you with stripes, even till you have your belly full? Why do you stare at them? If you touch them I’ll tear your eyes out.
LABRAX
3.4.760:
Yet notwithstanding, although you forbid me to do so, I’ll at once carry them off both together with me.
DAEMONES
3.4.761:
What will you do?
LABRAX
I’ll bring Vulcan; he is an enemy to Venus.
(Goes towards DAEMONES’ cottage.)
TRACHALIO
3.4.762:
Whither is he going?
LABRAX
(calling at the door.)
Hallo! Is there anybody here? Hallo! I say.
DAEMONES
If you touch the door, that very instant, upon my faith, you shall get a harvest upon your face with fists for your pitchforks.
SERVANT
3.4.764:
We keep no fire, we live upon dried figs.
DAEMONES
3.4.765:
I’ll find the fire, if only I have the opportunity of kindling it upon your head.
LABRAX
3.4.766:
Faith, I’ll go somewhere to look for some fire.
DAEMONES
What, when you’ve found it?
LABRAX
3.4.767:
I’ll be making a great fire here.
DAEMONES
What, to be burning a mortuary sacrifice for yourself?
LABRAX
3.4.768:
No, but I’ll burn both of these alive here upon the altar.
DAEMONES
3.4.769: I’d like that. For, by my troth, I’ll forthwith seize you by the head and throw you into the fire,
3.4.770:
and, half-roasted, I’ll throw you out as food for the great birds. (Aside.) When I come to a consideration of it with myself, this is that ape, that wanted to take away those swallows from the nest against my will, as I was dreaming in my sleep.
TRACHALIO
3.4.773:
Aged sir, do you know what I request of you? That you will protect these females and defend them from violence, until I fetch my master.
DAEMONES
3.4.775:
Go look for your master, and fetch him here.
TRACHALIO
But don’t let him—
DAEMONES
At his own extreme peril, if he touches them, or if he attempts to do so.
TRACHALIO
3.4.776:
Take care.
DAEMONES
Due care is taken; do you be off.
TRACHALIO
3.4.777:
And watch him too, that he doesn’t go away anywhere. For we have promised either to give the executioner a great talent, or else to produce this fellow this very day.
DAEMONES
3.4.779:
Do you only be off. I’ll not let him get away, while you are absent.
TRACHALIO
I’ll be back here soon.
(Exit TRACHALIO.)

3.5.780:
(DAEMONES, LABRAX, PALAESTRA, AMPELISCA, and SERVANTS.) DAEMONES
(to LABRAX, who is struggling with the SERVANTS.)
Which, you Procurer, had you rather do, be quiet with a thrashing, or e’en as it is, without the thrashing, if you had the choice?
LABRAX
3.5.782:
Old fellow, I don’t care a straw for what you say. My own women, in fact, I shall drag away this instant from the altar by the hair, in spite of yourself, and Venus, and supreme Jove.
DAEMONES
3.5.784:
Just touch them.
LABRAX
(going towards them)
3.5.785:
I’ troth, I surely will touch them.
DAEMONES
Just come then; only approach this way.
LABRAX
3.5.786:
Only bid both those fellows, then, to move away from there.
DAEMONES
3.5.787:
On the contrary, they shall move towards you.
LABRAX
I’ faith, for my own part, I don’t think so.
DAEMONES
3.5.788:
If they do move nearer to you, what will you do?
LABRAX
I’ll retire. But, old fellow, if ever I catch you in the city,
3.5.790:
never again, upon my faith, shall any one call me a Procurer, if I don’t give you some most disagreable sport.
DAEMONES
3.5.792:
Do what you threaten. But now, in the meantime, if you do touch them, a heavy punishment shall be inflicted on you.
LABRAX
3.5.794:
How heavy, in fact?
DAEMONES
Just as much as is sufficient for a Procurer.
LABRAX
3.5.795:
These threats of yours I don’t value one straw; I certainly shall seize them both this instant without your leave.
DAEMONES
3.5.797:
By my troth, I surely will touch them.
DAEMONES
You will touch them, but do you know with what result? Go then, Turbalio, with all haste, and bring hither from out of the house two cudgels.
LABRAX
3.5.799:
Cudgels?
DAEMONES
Aye, good ones; make haste speedily. (TURBALIO goes in.)
3.5.800:
I’ll let you have a reception this day in proper style, as you are deserving of.
LABRAX
(aside.)
3.5.801:
Alas! cursedly unfortunate. I lost my headpiece in the ship; it would now have been handy for me, if it had been saved. (To DAEMONES.) May I at least address these women?
DAEMONES
3.5.804:
(TURBALIO enters bringing two cudgels.) Well now, by my faith, look, the cudgel-man is coming very opportunely here.
LABRAX
(aside.)
3.5.806:
By my troth, this surely is a tingling for my ears.
DAEMONES
3.5.807: Come, Sparax, do you take this other cudgel. (Giving him one.) Come, take your stand, one on one side, the other on one other. Take your stations both of you. (They stand with lifted cudgels on each side of he altar.) Just so. Now then attend to me:
3.5.810: if, I’ faith, that fellow there should this day touch these women with his finger against their inclination, if you don’t give him a reception with these cudgels even to that degree that he shan’t know which way he is to get home, you are undone, both of you. If he shall call for any one, do you make answer to this fellow in their stead.
3.5.815:
But if he himself shall attempt to get away from here, that instant, as hard a you can, lay on to his legs with your sticks.
LABRAX
3.5.817:
Are they not even to allow me to go away from here?
DAEMONES
I’ve said sufficient. And when that servant comes here with his master, he that has gone to fetch his master, do you at once go home.
3.5.820:
Attend to this with great diligence, will you.
(DAEMONES goes into his house.)
LABRAX
3.5.821: O rare, by my troth, the Temple here is surely changed all of a sudden; this is now the Temple of Hercules which was that of Venus before; in such fashion has the old fellow planted two statues here with clubs. I’ faith, I don’t know now whither in the world I shall fly from here;
3.5.825:
so greatly are they both raging now against me, both land and sea. Palaestra!
SERVANT
3.5.826:
What do you want?
LABRAX
Away with you, there is a misunderstanding between us; that, indeed, is not my Palaestra that answers. Harkye, Ampelisca.
SERVANT
3.5.828:
Beware of a mishap, will you.
LABRAX
(aside.)
3.5.829: So far as they can, the worthless fellows advise me rightly enough.
3.5.830:
(Aloud.) But, harkye, I ask you, whether it is any harm to you for me to come nearer to these women?
SERVANT
3.5.831:
Why none at all to ourselves.
LABRAX
3.5.832:
Will there be any harm to myself?
SERVANT
None at all, if you only take care.
LABRAX
3.5.833:
What is it that I’m to take care against?
SERVANT
Why, look you, against a heavy mishap.
LABRAX
3.5.834:
Troth now, prithee, do let me approach them.
SERVANT
Approach them, if you like.
LABRAX
3.5.835:
I’ faith, obligingly done; I return you thanks, I’ll go nearer to them.
(Approaches them.)
SERVANT
3.5.836:
Do you stand there on the spot, where you are.
(Drags him to his place, with the cudgel over his head.)
LABRAX
(aside.)
3.5.837: By my faith, I’ve come scurvily off in many ways. Still, I’m resolved to get the better of them this day by constantly besieging them.

3.6.839:
(Enter PLESIDIPPUS and TRACHALIO, at a distance, on the other side of the stage.) PLESIDIPPUS
And did the Procurer attempt by force and violence
3.6.840:
to drag my mistress away from the altar of Venus?
TRACHALIO
Even so.
PLESIDIPPUS
3.6.841:
Why didn’t you kill him on the instant?
TRACHALIO
I hadn’t a sword.
PLESIDIPPUS
3.6.842:
You should have taken either a stick or a stone.
TRACHALIO
What! ought I to have pelted this most villanous fellow with stones like a dog?
LABRAX
(aside, on seeing them.)
3.6.844: By my troth, but I’m undone now; see, here’s Plesidippus;
3.6.845:
he’ll be sweeping me away altogether this moment with the dust.
PLESIDIPPUS
3.6.846:
Were the damsels sitting on the altar even then when you set out to come to me?
TRACHALIO
3.6.847:
Yes, and now they are sitting in the same place.
PLESIDIPPUS
3.6.850:
he is now protecting them with his servants—I committed them to his charge.
PLESIDIPPUS
3.6.851:
Lead me straight to the Procurer. Where is this fellow?
(They go towards LABRAX.)
LABRAX
3.6.852:
Health to you.
PLESIDIPPUS
I want none of your healths. Make your choice quickly, whether you lad rather be seized by your throat wrenched, or be dragged along; choose whichever you please, while you may.
LABRAX
3.6.855: Be off then, Trachalio, with all speed to the sea-shore; bid those persons that I brought with me to hand over this rascal to the executioner, to come from the harbour to the city to meet me; afterwards return hither and keep guard here. I’ll now drag this scoundrelly outcast to justice. (Exit TRACHALIO. Pleusicles addresses LABRAX.)
3.6.860:
Come, proceed to a court of justice.
LABRAX
In what have I offended?
PLESIDIPPUS
Do you ask? Didn’t you receive an earnest of me for this woman (pointing to PALAESTRA), and carry her off from here?
LABRAX
3.6.862:
I didn’t carry her off.
PLESIDIPPUS
Why do you deny it?
LABRAX
3.6.863: Troth now, because I put her on board ship; carry her off unfortunately, I couldn’t. For my part, I told you that this day I would make my appearance
3.6.865:
at the Temple of Venus; have I swerved at all from that? Am I not there?
PLESIDIPPUS
3.6.866:
Plead your cause in the court of justice; here a word is enough. Follow me.
(They lay hold of him.)
LABRAX
(calling aloud.)
3.6.867:
I entreat you, my dear Charmides, do come to my rescue; I am being seized with my throat wrenched.
(Enter CHARMIDES, from the Temple.)
CHARMIDES
(looking about.)
3.6.869:
Do you see me how I’m being seized?
CHARMIDES
I see, and view it with pleasure.
LABRAX
3.6.870:
Don’t you venture to assist me?
CHARMIDES
What person is seizing you?
LABRAX
3.6.871:
Young Plesidippus.
CHARMIDES
What you’ve got, put up with; ’twere better for you, with a cheerful spirit, to slink to gaol; that has befallen you which many greatly wish for for themselves.
LABRAX
3.6.874:
What’s that?
CHARMIDES
To find for themselves that which they are seeking.
LABRAX
3.6.875:
I entreat you, do follow me.
CHARMIDES
You try to persuade me, just like what you are: you are being taken off to gaol, for that reason is it you entreat me to follow you?
PLESIDIPPUS
(to LABRAX.)
3.6.877:
Do you still resist?
LABRAX
I’m undone.
PLESIDIPPUS
I trust that may prove the truth. You, my dear Palaestra and Ampelisca, do you remain here in the meanwhile, until I return hither.
SERVANT
3.6.880:
rather to go to our house, until you return.
PLESIDIPPUS
I’m quite agreable; you act obligingly.
(The SERVANTS open the door of the cottage, and PALAESTRA and AMPELISCA go in.)
LABRAX
3.6.881:
You are thieves to me.
SERVANT
How, thieves?
PLESIDIPPUS
Lead him along.
(The SERVANTS seize him.)
LABRAX
(calling out.)
3.6.882:
I pray and entreat you, Palaestra.
PLESIDIPPUS
Follow, you hang-dog.
LABRAX
3.6.883:
Guest, Charmides!
CHARMIDES
I am no guest of yours; I repudiate your hospitality.
LABRAX
3.6.884:
What, do you slight me in this fashion?
CHARMIDES
I do so; I’ve been drinking with you once already.
LABRAX
3.6.885:
May the Deities confound you.
CHARMIDES
To that person of yours, say that. (PLESIDIPPUS leads LABRAX off, followed by the SERVANTS.) I do believe that men are transformed, each into a different beast. That Procurer, I guess, is transformed into a stock-dove; for, before long, his neck will be in the stocks. He’ll to-day be building his nest in the gaol.
3.6.890: Still, however, I’ll go, that I may be his advocate,—if by my aid he may possibly be sentenced any the sooner.

4.1.892:
(Enter DAEMONES, from his cottage. DAEMONES
(to himself.)
’Twas rightly done, and it is a pleasure this day for me to have given aid to these young women; I have now found some dependants, and both of them of comely looks and youthful age.
4.1.895: But my plaguy wife is watching me in all ways, lest I should be giving any hint to the young women. But I wonder what in the world my servant Gripus is about, who went last night to the sea to fish. Troth, he had done wiser if he had slept at home;
4.1.900: for now he throws away both his pains and his nets, seeing what a storm there now is and was last night. I’ll thoroughly cook upon my fingers what he has caught to-day; so violently do I see the ocean heaving. (A bell rings.) But my wife’s calling me to breakfast; I’ll return home.
4.1.905:
She’ll now be filling my ears with her silly prating.
(Goes into the cottage.)

4.2.906:
(Enter GRIPUS, dragging a net enclosing a wallet, by a rope.) GRIPUS
(to himself.)
These thanks do I return to Neptune, my patron, who dwells in the salt retreats, the abode of fishes, inasmuch as he has despatched me finely laden on my return from his retreats, and from his Temples, laden with most abundant booty,
4.2.910: with safety to my boat, which in the stormy sea made me master of a singular and rich haul. In a wondrous and incredible manner has this haul turned out prosperously for me, nor yet have I this day taken a single ounce weight of fish, but only that which I am here bringing with me in my net.
4.2.914: For when I arose in the middle of the night, and without sloth, I preferred profit to sleep and rest; in the raging tempest, I determined to try how I might lighten the poverty of my master and my own servitude, not sparing of my own exertions.
4.2.920: Most worthless is the man that is slothful, and most detestably do I hate that kind of men. It behoves him to be vigilant who wishes to do his duty in good time; for it befits him not to be waiting until his master arouses him to his duties. For those who sleep on for the love of it, rest without profit to themselves and to their own cost.
4.2.924: But now I, who have not been slothful, have found that for myself through which to be slothful if I should choose.
4.2.925: (Points to the wallet.) This have I found in the sea to-day; whatever’s in it, it’s something heavy that’s in it; I think it’s gold that’s in it. And not a single person is there my confidant in the matter. Now, Gripus, this opportunity has befallen you, that the Praetor might make you a free man from among the multitude. Now, thus shall I do, this is my determination; I’ll come to my master cleverly and cunningly, little by little I’ll promise money for my freedom, that I may be free.
4.2.930: Now, when I shall be free, then, in fine, I’ll provide me land and houses and slaves: I’ll carry on merchandize with large ships: among the grandees I shall be considered a grandee. Afterwards, for the sake of pleasing myself, I’ll build me a ship and I’ll imitate Stratonicus, and I’ll be carried about from town to town. When my greatness is far-spread, I shall fortify some great city: to that city I shall give the name of Gripus,
4.2.935:
a memorial of my fame and exploits, and there I’ll establish a mighty kingdom. I am resolving here in my mind to prepare for mighty matters. At present I’ll hide this booty. But this grandee (pointing to himself) is about to breakfast upon vinegar and salt, without any good substantial meat.
(Gathers up the net, and drags it after him.)

4.3.938:
(Enter TRACHALIO, in haste.) TRACHALIO
Hallo there! stop.
GRIPUS
Why should I stop?
TRACHALIO
While I coil up this rope for you that you are dragging.
GRIPUS
4.3.939:
Now let it alone.
TRACHALIO
Troth, but I’ll assist you. What’s kindly done to worthy men, isn’t thrown away.
GRIPUS
4.3.940:
There was a boisterous tempest yesterday; no fish have I, young man; don’t you be supposing I have. Don’t you see that I’m carrying my dripping net without the scaly race?
TRACHALIO
4.3.943:
I’ faith, I’m not wishing for fish so much as I am in need of your conversation.
GRIPUS
4.3.944:
Then, whoever you are, you are worrying me to death with your annoyance.
TRACHALIO
(takes hold of him.)
I’ll not allow you to go away from here; stop.
GRIPUS
4.3.945:
Take you care of a mishap, if you please; but why the plague are you dragging me back?
TRACHALIO
Listen.
GRIPUS
4.3.946:
I won’t listen.
TRACHALIO
But, upon my faith, you shall listen.
GRIPUS
Nay but, another time, tell me what you want.
TRACHALIO
4.3.947:
Come now, it’s worth your while at once to hear what I want to tell you.
GRIPUS
4.3.948:
Say on, whatever it is.
TRACHALIO
See whether any person is following near us.
(Looks back.)
GRIPUS
4.3.950:
but can you give me some good advice?
GRIPUS
4.3.951:
What’s the business? Only tell me.
TRACHALIO
I’ll tell you; keep silence; if only you’ll give me your word that you won’t prove treacherous to me.
GRIPUS
4.3.955: I knew the owner to whom that same property belonged. Afterwards I came myself to the thief, and I made him a proposal in these terms: I know the person on whom that theft was committed; now if you are ready to give me half, I’ll not make a discovery to the owner.
4.3.960:
He didn’t even give me an answer. What is it fair should be given me out of it? Half, I trust you will say.
GRIPUS
4.3.961:
Aye, even more; but unless he gives it you, I think it ought to be told to the owner.
TRACHALIO
4.3.962:
I’ll act on your advice. Now give me your attention; for it is to yourself all this relates.
GRIPUS
What has been done by me?
TRACHALIO
(pointing at the wallet.)
4.3.963:
I’ve known the person for a long time to whom that wallet belongs.
GRIPUS
What do you mean?
TRACHALIO
4.3.965:
and I know the person who found it, and who is now the owner. That, I’ faith, is not a bit the more your matter than it is my own. I know the person to whom it now belongs; you, the person to whom it formerly belonged. This shall no individual get away from me; don’t you be expecting to get it in a hurry.
TRACHALIO
4.3.969:
If the owner comes, shan’t he get it away?
GRIPUS
That you mayn’t be mistaken, no born person is there that’s owner of this but my own self—who took this in my own fishing.
TRACHALIO
4.3.971:
Was it really so?
GRIPUS
Which fish in the sea will you say is my own? When I catch them, if indeed I do catch them, they are my own; as my own I keep them. They are not claimed as having a right to freedom nor does any person demand a share in them. In the market I sell them all openly as my own wares.
4.3.975:
Indeed, the sea is, surely, common to all persons.
TRACHALIO
I agree to that; prithee, then, why any the less is it proper that this wallet should be common to me? It was found in the sea.
GRIPUS
4.3.977: Assuredly you are an outrageously impudent fellow; for if this is justice which you are saying, then fishermen would be ruined. Inasmuch as, the moment that the fish were exposed upon the stalls,
4.3.980:
no one would buy them; every person would be demanding his own share of the fish for himself; he would be saying that they were caught in the sea that was common to all.
TRACHALIO
4.3.981:
What do you say, you impudent fellow? Do you dare to compare a wallet with fish? Pray, does it appear to be the same thing?
GRIPUS
4.3.983: The matter doesn’t lie in my power; when I’ve cast my hook and net into the sea, whatever has adhered I draw out.
4.3.985:
Whatever my net and hooks have got, that in especial is my own.
TRACHALIO
4.3.986:
Nay but, I’ faith, it is not; if, indeed, you’ve fished up any article that’s made
GRIPUS
Philosopher, you.
TRACHALIO
4.3.987: But look now, you conjurer, did you ever see a fisherman who caught a wallet-fish, or exposed one for sale in the market? But, indeed, you shan’t here be taking possession of all the profits that you choose;
4.3.990:
you expect, you dirty fellow, to be both a maker of wallets and a fisherman. Either you must show me a fish that is a wallet, or else you shall carry nothing off that wasn’t produced in the sea and has no scales.
GRIPUS
4.3.993:
What, did you never hear before to-day that a wallet was a fish?
TRACHALIO
Villain, there is no such fish.
GRIPUS
4.3.994: Yes, there certainly is; I, who am a fisherman, know it.
4.3.995:
But it is seldom caught; no fish more rarely comes near the land.
TRACHALIO
4.3.996:
It’s to no purpose; you hope that you can be cheating me, you rogue. Of what colour is it?
GRIPUS
(looking at the wallet.)
4.3.997:
Of this colour very few are caught: some are of a purple skin, there are great and black ones also.
TRACHALIO
4.3.998: I understand; by my troth, you’ll be turning into a wallet-fish I fancy, if you don’t take care;
4.3.1000:
your skin will be purple, and then afterwards black.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
4.3.1001:
What a villain this that I have met with to-day!
TRACHALIO
We are wasting words; the day wears apace. Consider, please, by whose arbitration do you wish us to proceed?
GRIPUS
4.3.1002:
By the arbitration of the wallet.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1003:
Really so, indeed? You are a fool.
GRIPUS
My respects to you, Mister Thales
(Going.)
TRACHALIO
(holding him.)
4.3.1004: You shan’t carry that off this day, unless you find a place of safe keeping for it, or an umpire,
4.3.1005:
by whose arbitration this matter may be settled.
GRIPUS
Prithee, are you in your senses?
TRACHALIO
4.3.1006:
I’m mad, in need of hellebore.
GRIPUS
But I’m troubled with sprites; still I shan’t let this go.
(Hugs the wallet.)
TRACHALIO
4.3.1007:
Only add a single word more, that instant I’ll drive my fists smash into your brains. This instant on this spot, just as a new napkin is wont to be wrung, I’ll wring out of you whatever moisture there is, if you don’t let this go.
(Seizes the wallet.)
GRIPUS
4.3.1010:
Touch me; I’ll dash you down on the ground just in such fashion as I’m in the habit of doing with a polypus fish. Would you like to fight?
(Assumes a boxing attitude.)
TRACHALIO
4.3.1011:
What need is there? Nay, in preference, divide the booty.
GRIPUS
4.3.1012:
You can’t get anything from here but harm to yourself, so don’t expect it. I’m taking myself off.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1013:
But I’ll turn aside your ship from that direction, that you mayn’t be off anywhere—stop.
(Stands in front of him, and holds the rope.)
GRIPUS
4.3.1014: If you are the helmsman of this ship, I’ll be the pilot.
4.3.1015:
Let go of the rope now, you villain.
TRACHALIO
I will let go; do you let go of the wallet.
GRIPUS
4.3.1016:
I’ faith, you shall never this day become a scrap the more wealthy from this.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1017:
You cannot convince me by repeatedly denying, unless either a part is given me, or it is referred to arbitration, or it is placed in safe keeping.
GRIPUS
4.3.1019:
What, that which I got out of the sea—?
TRACHALIO
But I spied it out from the shore.
GRIPUS
4.3.1020:
—With my own pains and labour, and net and boat.
TRACHALIO
If now the owner, whose property it is, were to come, how am I, who espied from afar that you had taken this, a bit the less the thief than yourself?
GRIPUS
4.3.1022:
None whatever.
(Going.)
TRACHALIO
(seizing the net.)
Stop, you whip-knave; just let me learn of you by what reasoning I am not the sharer, and yet the thief.
GRIPUS
4.3.1024: I don’t know; neither do I know these city laws of yours,
4.3.1025:
only that I affirm that this is mine.
(Looks at the wallet.)
TRACHALIO
And I, too, say that it is mine.
GRIPUS
4.3.1026:
Stay now; I’ve discovered by what method you may be neither thief nor sharer.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1027:
By what method?
GRIPUS
Let me go away from here; you quietly go your own way, and don’t you inform against me to any one, and I won’t give anything to you. You hold your tongue; I’ll be mum. This is the best and the fairest plan.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1030:
Well, what proposition do you venture to make?
GRIPUS
I’ve made it already; for you to go away, to let go of the rope, and not to be a nuisance to me.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1032:
Stop while I propose terms.
GRIPUS
I’ faith, do, prithee, dispose of yourself forthwith.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1033:
Do you know any one in these parts?
GRIPUS
My own neighbours I must know.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1034:
Where do you live here?
GRIPUS
(pointing.)
At a distance out away yonder, as far off as the farthest fields.
TRACHALIO
(pointing to the cottage of DAEMONES.)
4.3.1035:
The person that lives in that cottage, should you like it to be decided by his arbitration?
GRIPUS
4.3.1036:
Let go of the rope for a moment while I step aside and consider.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1037:
Be it so.
(Lets go of the rope.)
GRIPUS
(aside.)
Capital, the thing’s all right; the whole of this booty is my own. He’s inviting me here inside of my own abode to my own master as umpire. By my troth, he never this day will award three obols away from his own servant.
4.3.1040:
Assuredly, this fellow doesn’t know what proposal he has been making. (To TRACHALIO.) I’ll go to the arbitrator with you.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1041:
What then?
GRIPUS
Although I know for sure that this is my own lawful right, let that be done rather than I should now be fighting with you.
TRACHALIO
4.3.1043: Although you are driving me before an arbitrator whom I don’t know, if he shall administer justice, although he is unknown, he is as good as known to me; if he doesn’t, though known, he is the same as though entirely unknown.

4.4.1045:
(Enter DAEMONES, from his cottage, with PALAESTRA and AMPELISCA, and SERVANTS.) DAEMONES
(to the WOMEN.)
Seriously, upon my faith, young women, although I wish what you desire, I’m afraid that on your account my wife will be turning me out of doors, who’ll be saying that I’ve brought harlots here before her very eyes. Do you take refuge at the altar rather than I.
THE WOMEN
4.4.1048:
We, wretched creatures, are undone.
(They weep.)
DAEMONES
4.4.1049: I’ll place you in safety; don’t you fear. But why (turning to the SERVANTS) are you following me out of doors?
4.4.1050: Since I’m here, no one shall do them harm.
4.4.1051:
Now then, be off, I say, in-doors, both of you, you guards from off guard.
(They go in.)
GRIPUS
4.4.1052:
O master, save you.
DAEMONES
Save you. How goes it?
TRACHALIO
(pointing to GRIPUS.)
Is he your servant?
GRIPUS
4.4.1053:
I’m not ashamed to say yes.
TRACHALIO
I’ve nothing to do with you.
GRIPUS
Then get you gone hence, will you.
TRACHALIO
Prithee, do answer me, aged sir; is he your servant?
DAEMONES
4.4.1054:
He is mine.
TRACHALIO
Oh then, that is very good, since he is yours.
4.4.1055:
Again I salute you.
DAEMONES
And I you. Are you he who, not long since, went away from here to fetch his master?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1056:
I am he.
DAEMONES
What now is it that you want?
TRACHALIO
(pointing to GRIPUS.)
4.4.1057:
This is your servant, you say?
DAEMONES
He is mine.
TRACHALIO
That is very good, since he is yours.
DAEMONES
4.4.1058:
What’s the matter?
TRACHALIO
(pointing to GRIPUS.)
That’s a rascally fellow there.
DAEMONES
What has the rascally fellow done to you?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1059:
I wish the ancles of that fellow were smashed.
DAEMONES
4.4.1060:
What’s the thing about which you are now disputing between yourselves?
TRACHALIO
I’ll tell you.
GRIPUS
4.4.1061:
No, I’ll tell you.
TRACHALIO
I fancy I’m to move the matter first.
GRIPUS
If indeed you were a decent person, you would be moving yourself off from here.
DAEMONES
4.4.1062:
Gripus, give attention, and hold your tongue
GRIPUS
4.4.1063:
In order that that fellow may speak first?
DAEMONES
Attend, Itell you. (To TRACHALIO.) Do you say on.
GRIPUS
Will you give the right of speaking to a stranger sooner than to your own servant?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1064: O dear! how impossible it is for him to be kept quiet.
4.4.1065:
As I was beginning to say, that Procurer, whom some little time since you turned out of the Temple of Venus—see (pointing at the wallet), he has got his wallet.
GRIPUS
4.4.1067:
I haven’t got it.
TRACHALIO
Do you deny that which I see with my own eyes?
GRIPUS
But I only wish you couldn’t see. I have got it, and I haven’t got it; why do you trouble yourself about me, what things I do?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1069:
In what way you got it does matter, whether rightfully or wrongfully.
GRIPUS
4.4.1070:
If I didn’t take it in the sea, there’s not a reason why you shouldn’t deliver me up to the cross. If I took it in the sea with my net, how is it yours rather than my own?
TRACHALIO
(to DAEMONES.)
4.4.1072:
He is deceiving you; the matter happened in this way, as I am telling you.
GRIPUS
What do you say?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1073:
So long as the person that has the first right to speak is speaking, do (to DAEMONES) put a check on him, please, if he belongs to you.
GRIPUS
4.4.1074: What, do you wish the same thing to be done to myself, that your master has been accustomed to do to yourself?
4.4.1075:
If he is in the habit of putting a check upon you, this master of ours isn’t in the habit of doing so with us.
DAEMONES
(to TRACUALIO.)
4.4.1076:
In that remark only has he got the better of you. What do you want now? Tell me.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1077:
For my part, I neither ask for a share of that wallet there, nor have I ever said this day that it is my own; but in it there is a little casket that belongs to this female (pointing to PALAESTRA), whom a short time since I averred to be free born.
DAEMONES
4.4.1080:
You are speaking of her, I suppose, whom a short time since you said was my countrywoman?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1081:
Just so; and those trinkets which formerly, when little, she used to wear, are there in that casket, which is in that wallet. This thing is of no service to him, and will be of utility to her, poor creature, if he gives it up, by means of which to seek for her parents.
DAEMONES
4.4.1084:
I’ll make him give it up; hold your tongue.
GRIPUS
4.4.1085:
I’ faith, I’m going to give nothing to that fellow.
TRACHALIO
I ask for nothing but the casket and the trinkets.
GRIPUS
4.4.1086:
What if they are made of gold?
TRACHALIO
What’s that to you? Gold shall be paid for gold, silver shall have its weight in silver in return.
GRIPUS
4.4.1088:
Please let me see the gold; after that I’ll let you see the casket.
DAEMONES
(to GRIPUS.)
4.4.1089:
Do you beware of punishment, and hold your tongue. (To TRACHALIO.) As you commenced to speak do you go on.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1090:
This one thing I entreat of you, that you will have compassion on this female, if, indeed, this wallet is that Procurer’s, which I suspect it is. In this matter, I’m saying nothing of certainty to you, but only on conjecture.
GRIPUS
4.4.1093:
Do you see how the rascal’s wheedling him?
TRACHALIO
Allow me to say on as I commenced. If this is the wallet that belongs to that villain whose I say it is,
4.4.1095:
these women here will be able to recognize it; order him to show it to them.
GRIPUS
Say you so? To show it to them?
DAEMONES
4.4.1096:
He doesn’t say unreasonably, Gripus, that the wallet should be shown.
GRIPUS
4.4.1097:
Yes, I’ faith, confoundedly unreasonably.
DAEMONES
How so?
GRIPUS
Because, if I do show it, at once they’ll say, of course, that they recognize it.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1098:
Source of villany, do you suppose that all other people are just like yourself, you author of perjury?
GRIPUS
4.4.1100:
All this I easily put up with, so long as he (pointing to DAEMONES) is of my way of thinking.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1101:
But now he is against you; from this (pointing to the wallet) will he obtain true testimony.
DAEMONES
4.4.1102:
Gripus, do you pay attention. (To TRACHALIO.) You explain in a few words what it is you want?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1103: For my part, I have stated it; but if you haven’t understood me, I’ll state it over again. Both of these women (pointing to them), as I said a short time since, ought to be free;
4.4.1105:
(pointing to PALAESTRA) she was stolen at Athens when a little girl.
GRIPUS
Tell me what that has got to do with the wallet, whether they are slaves or whether free women?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1107:
You wish it all to be told over again, you rascal, so that the day may fail us.
DAEMONES
4.4.1108:
Leave off your abuse, and explain to me what I’ve been asking.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1109: There ought to be a casket of wicker-work in that wallet,
4.4.1110:
in which are tokens by means of which she may be enabled to recognize her parents, by whom, when little, she was lost at Athens, as I said before.
GRIPUS
4.4.1112:
May Jupiter and the Gods confound you. What do you say, you sorcerer of a fellow? What, are these women dumb, that they are not able to speak for themselves?
TRACHALIO
4.4.1114:
They are silent for this reason, because a silent woman is always better than a talking one.
GRIPUS
4.4.1115:
Then, I’ faith, by your way of speaking, you are neither a man nor a woman to my notion.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1116:
How so?
GRIPUS
Why, because neither talking nor silent are you ever good for anything. Prithee (to DAEMONES), shall I ever be allowed to-day to speak?
DAEMONES
4.4.1117:
If you utter a single word more this day, I’ll break your head for you.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1119: As I had commenced to say it, old gentleman, I beg you
4.4.1120:
to order him to give up that casket to these young women; if for it he asks any reward for himself, it shall be paid; whatever else is there besides, let him keep for himself.
GRIPUS
4.4.1122:
Now at last you say that, because you are aware it is my right; just now you were asking to go halves.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1123:
Aye, and even still I ask it.
GRIPUS
4.4.1124:
I’ve seen a kite making a swoop, even when he got nothing at all however.
DAEMONES
(to GRIPUS.)
4.4.1125:
Can’t I shut your mouth without a drubbing?
GRIPUS
(pointing to TRACHALIO.)
If that fellow is silent, I’ll be silent; if he talks, allow me to talk in my own behalf.
DAEMONES
4.4.1127:
Please now give me this wallet, Gripus.
GRIPUS
I’ll trust it to you; but for you to return it me, if there are none of those things in it.
DAEMONES
4.4.1128:
It shall be returned.
GRIPUS
Take it.
(Gives him the wallet.)
DAEMONES
4.4.1129: Now then listen, Palaestra and Ampelisca, to this which I say:
4.4.1130:
is this the wallet, in which this Procurer said that your casket was?
PALAESTRA
It is the same.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
4.4.1131:
Troth, to my sorrow, I’m undone; how on the instant, before she well saw it, she said that it was it.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1132: I’ll make this matter plain to you, instead of difficult. There ought to be a casket of wicker-work there in that wallet; whatever is in there I’ll state by name; don’t you
4.4.1135:
show me anything. If I say wrong, I shall then have said this to no purpose; then you shall keep these things, whatever is in there for yourselves. But if the truth, then I entreat you that what is my own may be restored to me.
DAEMONES
4.4.1137:
I agree; you ask for bare justice only, in my way of thinking, at least.
GRIPUS
4.4.1138: But, I’ faith, in mine, for extreme injustice; what if she is a witch or a sorceress,
4.4.1140:
and shall mention exactly everything that’s in it. Is a sorceress to have it?
DAEMONES
4.4.1141:
She shan’t get it, unless she tells the truth; in vain will she be conjuring. Unloose the wallet, then (giving it to GRIPUS), that as soon as possible I may know what is the truth.
GRIPUS
(first unfastens the straps of the wallet, and then hands it to his MASTER.)
4.4.1143:
Take it, it’s unfastened. (DAEMONES takes out the casket.) Alas, I’m undone; I see the casket.
DAEMONES
(holding it up, and addressing PALAESTRA.)
Is this it?
PALAESTRA
4.4.1144: That is it. O my parents, here do I keep you locked up;
4.4.1145:
here have I enclosed both my wealth and my hopes of recognizing you.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
4.4.1146:
Then, by my faith, the Gods must be enraged with you, whoever you are, who fasten up your parents in so narrow a compass.
DAEMONES
4.4.1148: Gripus, come hither, your cause is being tried. (To PALAESTRA.) Do you, young woman, away at a distance there say what’s in it, and of what appearance; mention them all.
4.4.1150:
By my troth, if you make ever so slight a mistake, even if afterwards you wish, madam, to correct yourself, you’ll be making a great mistake.
GRIPUS
4.4.1152:
You demand what’s real justice.
TRACHALIO
By my troth, then, he doesn’t demand yourself; for you are the opposite of justice.
DAEMONES
4.4.1153:
Now then, say on, young woman. Gripus, give attention and hold your tongue.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1154:
There are some trinkets.
DAEMONES
(looking in the casket.)
See, here they are, I espy them.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
In the first onset I am worsted;
4.4.1155:
(takes hold of the arm of DAEMONES) hold, don’t be showing.
DAEMONES
Of what description are they? Answer in their order.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1156:
In the first place, there’s a little sword of gold, with an inscription.
DAEMONES
Just tell me, what the characters are upon that little sword.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1157:
The name of my father. Next, on the other side, there’s a little two-edged axe, of gold likewise, with an inscription: there on the axe is the name of my mother.
DAEMONES
4.4.1160:
tell me, what’s the name of your father upon the little sword?
PALAESTRA
Daemones.
DAEMONES
4.4.1161:
Immortal Gods! where in the world are my hopes?
GRIPUS
Aye, by my troth, and where are mine?
DAEMONES
4.4.1162:
Do proceed forthwith, I entreat you.
GRIPUS
Cautiously, or else (aside) away to utter perdition.
DAEMONES
4.4.1163:
Say, what’s the name of your mother, here upon the little axe?
PALAESTRA
4.4.1164:
Daedalis.
DAEMONES
The Gods will that I should be preserved.
GRIPUS
But that I should be ruined.
DAEMONES
4.4.1165:
This must be my own daughter, Gripus.
GRIPUS
She may be for me, indeed. (To TRACHALIO.) May all the Gods confound you who this day saw me with your eyes, and myself as well for a blockhead, who didn’t look about a hundred times first to see that no one was watching me, before I drew the net out of the water.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1169: Next, there’s a little knife of silver, and two little hands linked together, and
4.4.1170:
then a little sow.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
Nay, then, go and be hanged, you with your little sow and with your little pigs.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1171:
There’s also a golden drop, which my father presented to me upon my birthday.
DAEMONES
4.4.1172:
