Undoubtedly there is; but I cannot restrain myself any longer from embracing you. My daughter, blessings on you; I am that father who begot you; I am Daemones, and see, your mother Daedalis is in the house here (pointing to his cottage).
AMPELISCA
(embracing him.)
4.4.1175:
Blessings on you, my unlooked-for father.
DAEMONES
Blessings on you; how joyously do I embrace you.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1176:
’Tis a pleasure to me, inasmuch as this falls to your lot from your feelings of affection.
DAEMONES
4.4.1177:
Come then, Trachalio, if you can, bring that wallet into the house.
TRACHALIO
(taking the wallet.)
4.4.1178:
See the villany of Gripus; inasmuch, Gripus, as this matter has turned out unfortunately for you, I congratulate you.
DAEMONES
4.4.1179: Come, then, let’s go, my daughter, to your mother,
4.4.1180:
who will be better able to enquire of you into this matter from proofs; who had you more in her hands, and is more thoroughly acquainted with your tokens.
TRACHALIO
4.4.1182:
Let’s all go hence in-doors, since we are giving our common aid.
PALAESTRA
4.4.1183:
Follow me, Ampelisca.
AMPELISCA
That the Gods favour you, it is a pleasure to me.
(They all go into the cottage of DAEMONES, exceptGRIPUS.)
GRIPUS
(to himself.)
4.4.1184: Am I not a blockhead of a fellow, to have this day fished up that wallet?
4.4.1185: Or, when I had fished it up, not to have hidden it somewhere in a secret spot? By my troth, I guessed that it would be a troublesome booty for me, because it fell to me in such troublous weather. I’ faith, I guess that there’s plenty of gold and silver there. What is there better for me than to be off hence in-doors and secretly hang myself—
4.4.1190:
at least for a little time, until this vexation passes away from me?
(Goes into the cottage.)

4.5.1191:
(Enter DAEMONES, from his cottage.) DAEMONES
(to himself.)
O ye immortal Gods, what person is there more fortunate than I, who unexpectedly have discovered my daughter? Isn’t it the fact, that if the Gods will a blessing to befall any person, that longed-for pleasure by some means or other, falls to the lot of the virtuous?
4.5.1195: I this day, a thing that I never hoped for nor yet believed, have unexpectedly discovered my daughter, and I shall bestow her upon a respectable young man of noble family, an Athenian, and my kinsman. For that reason I wish him to be fetched hither to me as soon as possible,
4.5.1200: and I’ve requested my servant to come out here, that he may go to the Forum. Still, I’m surprised at it that he isn’t yet come out. I think I’ll go to the door. (Opens the door, and looks in.) What do I behold? Embracing her, my wife is clasping my daughter around her neck. Her caressing is really almost too foolish and sickening.

4.6.1205:
DAEMONES
(Goes to the door again, and calls out.)
’Twere better, wife, for an end to be made at last of your kissing; and make all ready that I may perform a sacrifice, when I come in-doors, in honor of the household Gods, inasmuch as they have increased our family. At home I have lambs and swine for sacred use. But why, ladies, are you detaining that Trachalio? Oh, I see he’s coming out of doors, very seasonably.
(Enter TRACHALIO, from the cottage.)
TRACHALIO
(speaking to those within.)
4.6.1210:
Wheresoever he shall be, I’ll seek Plesidippus out at once, and bring him together with me to you.
DAEMONES
4.6.1211:
Tell him how this matter has fallen out about my daughter. Request him to leave other occupations and to come here.
TRACHALIO
4.6.1213:
Tell him that I’ll give him my daughter for a wife.
TRACHALIO
Very well.
DAEMONES
4.6.1214:
And that I knew his father, and that he is a relation of my own.
TRACHALIO
Very well.
DAEMONES
4.6.1215:
But do make haste.
TRACHALIO
Very well.
DAEMONES
Take care and let a dinner be prepared here at once.
TRACHALIO
Very well.
DAEMONES
4.6.1216:
What, all very well?
TRACHALIO
Very well. But do you know what it is I want of you? That you’ll remember what you promised, that this day I’m to be free.
DAEMONES
4.6.1218:
Take care and entreat Plesidippus to give me my freedom.
DAEMONES
Very well.
TRACHALIO
4.6.1219:
And let your daughter request it; she’ll easily prevail.
DAEMONES
Very well.
TRACHALIO
4.6.1220:
And that Ampelisca may marry me, when I’m a free man.
DAEMONES
Very well.
TRACHALIO
4.6.1221:
And that I may experience a pleasing return to myself in kindness for my actions.
DAEMONES
Very well.
TRACHALIO
4.6.1222:
What, all very well?
DAEMONES
Very well. Again I return you thanks. But do you make haste to proceed to the city forthwith, and betake yourself hither again.
TRACHALIO
4.6.1223:
Very well. I’ll be here directly. In the meanwhile, do you make the other preparations that are necessary.
(Exit TRACHALIO.)
DAEMONES
4.6.1225: may Hercules ill befriend him with his very-welling; he has so stuffed my ears with it. Whatever it was I said, very well was the answer.

4.7.1227:
(Enter GRIPUS, from the cottage.) GRIPUS
How soon may I have a word with you, Daemones?
DAEMONES
4.7.1228:
What’s your business, Gripus?
GRIPUS
Touching that wallet, if you are wise, be wise; keep what goods the Gods provide you.
DAEMONES
4.7.1230:
Does it seem right to you, that, what belongs to another I should assert to be my own?
GRIPUS
4.7.1231:
What, not a thing that I found in the sea?
DAEMONES
4.7.1232:
So much the better does it happen for him who lost it; none the more is it necessary that it should be your wallet.
GRIPUS
4.7.1234:
For this reason are you poor because you are too scrupulously righteous.
DAEMONES
4.7.1235: O Gripus, Gripus, in the life of man very many traps there are, in what they are deceived by guile. And, by my troth, full often is a bait placed in them, which bait if any greedy person greedily snaps at, through his own greediness he is caught in the trap.
4.7.1240: He who prudently, skilfully, and warily, takes precaution, full long he may enjoy that which is honestly acquired. This booty seems to me to be about to be made a booty of by me, that it may go hence with a greater blessing than it first came. What, ought I to conceal what I know was brought to me as belonging to another?
4.7.1245:
By no means will my friend Daemones do that. ’Tis ever most becoming for prudent men to be on their guard against this, that they be not themselves confederates with their servants in evil-doing. Except only when I’m gaming, I don’t care for any gain.
GRIPUS
4.7.1249: At times, I’ve seen the Comedians, when acting, in this fashion
4.7.1250:
repeat sayings in a wise manner, and be applauded for them, when they pointed out this prudent conduct to the public. But when each person went thence his own way home, there wasn’t one after the fashion which they had recommended.
DAEMONES
4.7.1254:
Go in-doors, don’t be troublesome, moderate your tongue. I’m going to give you nothing, don’t you deceive yourself.
GRIPUS
(apart.)
4.7.1256:
Then I pray the Gods that whatever’s in that wallet, whether it’s gold, or whether silver, it may all become ashes.
(Goes into the cottage.)
DAEMONES
4.7.1258: This is the reason why we have bad servants. For this master, if he had combined with any servant,
4.7.1260:
would have made both himself and the other guilty of a theft. While he was thinking that he himself had made a capture, in the meantime he himself would have been made a capture: capture would have led to capture. Now will I go in-doors from here and sacrifice; after that, I’ll at once order the dinner to be cooked for us.
(Goes into the cottage.)

4.8.1265:
(Enter PLESIDIPPUS and TRACHALIO, at the further end of the stage.) PLESIDIPPUS
Tell me all these things over again my life, my Trachalio, my freed-man, my patron, aye rather, my father; has Palaestra found her father and mother?
TRACHALIO
4.8.1268:
And is she my countrywoman?
TRACHALIO
So I think.
PLESIDIPPUS
And is she to marry me?
TRACHALIO
So I suspect.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1269:
Prithee, do you reckon that he will betroth her to me?
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1270:
Well, shall I congratulate her father too upon his finding her?
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1271:
Well, her mother too?
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
What then do you reckon?
TRACHALIO
What you ask me, I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1272:
Tell me then how much do you reckon it at?
TRACHALIO
What I, I reckon—
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1273:
Then really, do carry over. Don’t be always making a reckoning.
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1274:
What if I run?
(Pretends to run.)
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
Or rather gently, this way?
(He walks slowly.)
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1275:
Ought I to salute her as well when I arrive?
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
Her father too?
TRACHALIO
4.8.1276:
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
After that, her mother?
TRACHALIO
So I reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
And what after that? When I arrive, should I also embrace her father?
TRACHALIO
4.8.1278:
Well, her mother?
TRACHALIO
So I don’t reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
Well, her own self?
TRACHALIO
So I don’t reckon.
PLESIDIPPUS
4.8.1279:
Confusion, he has closed his reckoning; now when I wish him, he doesn’t reckon.
TRACHALIO
4.8.1280:
You are not in your senses; follow me.
PLESIDIPPUS
Conduct me, my patron, where you please.
(They go into the cottage of DAEMONES.)

5.1.1285:
so much do all persons make sport if any misfortune befalls a Procurer. Now I’ll go look here, in the Temple of Venus, for that other female, that her at least I may take away, the only portion of my property that remains.
(He retires a little distance.)

5.2.1288:
(Enter GRIPUS, from the cottage of DAEMONES, with a spit in his hand.) GRIPUS
(calling to the PEOPLE within.)
By the powers, you shall never this day at nightfall behold Gripus alive, unless the wallet is restored to me.
LABRAX
(behind.)
5.2.1289:
I’m ready to die; when I hear mentior made anywhere of a wallet, I’m thumped, as it were with a stake, upon the breast.
GRIPUS
(at the door, continuing.)
5.2.1291:
That scoundrel is free; I, the person that held the net in the sea, and drew up the wallet, to him you refuse to give anything.
LABRAX
(behind.)
5.2.1293:
O ye immortal Gods! by his talk this person has made me prick up my ears.
GRIPUS
(continuing.)
5.2.1294: By my troth, in letters a cubit long, I’ll immediately post it up in every quarter,
5.2.1295:
If any person has lost a wallet with plenty of gold and silver, let him come to Gripus. You shan’t keep it as you are wishing.
LABRAX
(behind.)
5.2.1297:
I’ faith, this person knows, as I think, who has got the wallet. This person must be accosted by me; ye Gods, aid me, I do entreat you.
(Some one calls GRIPUS, from within.)
GRIPUS
5.2.1299: Why are you calling me back in-doors? (He rubs away at the spit.) I want to clean this here before the door.
5.2.1300:
But surely this, I’ faith, has been made of rust, and not of iron; so that the more I rub it, it becomes quite red and more slender. Why surely this spit has been drugged; it does waste away so in my hands.
LABRAX
(accosting him.)
5.2.1303:
Save you, young man.
GRIPUS
May the Gods prosper you with your shorn pate.
LABRAX
What’s going on?
GRIPUS
5.2.1304:
A spit being cleaned.
LABRAX
How do you do?
GRIPUS
What are you? Prithee, are you a medicant?
LABRAX
5.2.1305:
No, I’ faith, I am more than a medicant by one letter.
GRIPUS
Then you are a mendicant.
LABRAX
5.2.1306:
You’ve hit it to a nicety.
GRIPUS
Your appearance seems suitable to it. But what’s the matter with you?
LABRAX
5.2.1307:
Troth, this last night I was shipwrecked at sea the vessel was cast away, and to my misfortune I lost there everything that I had.
GRIPUS
5.2.1309:
What did you lose?
LABRAX
A wallet with plenty of gold and silver.
GRIPUS
5.2.1310:
Do you at all remember what there was in the wallet which was lost?
LABRAX
5.2.1311:
What matters for us now to be talking of it, if, in spite of it, it’s lost?
GRIPUS
5.2.1312:
What if I know who has found it? I wish to learn from you the tokens.
LABRAX
5.2.1313:
Eight hundred golden pieces were there in a purse, besides a hundred Philippean minae in a wash-leather bag apart.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
5.2.1315:
Troth, it is a noble prize; I shall be getting a handsome reward. The Gods show respect to mortals; therefore I shall come off bounteously rewarded. No doubt, it is this man’s wallet. (To LABRAX.) Do you proceed to relate the rest.
LABRAX
5.2.1318:
A large talent of silver of full weight was in a purse, besides a bowl, a goblet, a beaker, a boat, and a cup.
GRIPUS
5.2.1320:
Astonishing! you really did have some splendid riches.
LABRAX
5.2.1321:
A shocking expression is that, and a most abominable one. You did have, and now have not.
GRIPUS
5.2.1322:
What would you be ready to give to one who should find these out for you, and give you information? Say, speedily and at once.
LABRAX
5.2.1323:
Three hundred didrachms.
GRIPUS
Rubbish.
LABRAX
5.2.1324:
Four hundred.
GRIPUS
Old thrums.
LABRAX
Five hundred.
GRIPUS
A rotten nut.
LABRAX
5.2.1325:
Six hundred.
GRIPUS
You are prating about mere tiny weevils.
LABRAX
5.2.1326:
I’ll give seven hundred.
GRIPUS
Your mouth is hot, you are cooling it just now.
LABRAX
5.2.1327:
I’ll give a thousand didrachms.
GRIPUS
You are dreaming.
LABRAX
I add no more;
be off with you.
GRIPUS
Hear me then; if, I’ faith, I should be off from here, I shan’t be here.
LABRAX
5.2.1328:
Would you like a hundred as well as the thousand?
GRIPUS
You are asleep.
LABRAX
5.2.1329:
Say how much you ask.
GRIPUS
That you mayn’t be adding anything against your inclination,
5.2.1330:
a great talent; it’s not possible for three obols to be bated thence; then do you say either yes or no at once.
LABRAX
(aside.)
5.2.1331:
What’s to be done here? It’s a matter of necessity, I see: (to GRIPUS) the talent shall be paid.
GRIPUS
(going towards the altar.)
5.2.1332:
Just step this way; I wish Venus here to put the question to you.
LABRAX
5.2.1333:
Whatever you please, that command me.
GRIPUS
Touch this altar of Venus.
LABRAX
(touching it.)
I am touching it.
GRIPUS
5.2.1334:
By Venus here must you swear to me.
LABRAX
What must I swear?
GRIPUS
What I shall bid you.
LABRAX
5.2.1335:
Dictate in words just as you like. (Aside.) What I’ve got at home, I shall never beg of any one else.
GRIPUS
5.2.1336:
Take hold of this altar.
LABRAX
(taking hold of it.)
I am taking hold of it.
GRIPUS
Swear that you will pay me the money on that same day on which you shall gain possession of the wallet.
LABRAX
5.2.1337:
Be it so.
GRIPUS
(speaking, while LABRAX repeats after him.)
5.2.1338: Venus of Cyrene, I invoke thee as my witness, if I shall find that wallet which I lost in the ship,
5.2.1340:
safe with the gold and silver, and it shall come into my possession—Then to this Gripus do I promise; say so and place your hand upon me.
LABRAX
5.2.1343:
Then to this Gripus do I promise, Venus, do thou hear me—
GRIPUS
(followed by LABRAX.)
5.2.1344:
That I will forthwith give him a great talent of silver."
GRIPUS
5.2.1345:
If you defraud me, say, may Venus utterly destroy your body, and your existence in your calling. (Aside.) As it is, do you have this for yourself, when you’ve once taken the oath.
LABRAX
5.2.1348:
If, Venus, I shall do anything amiss against this oath, I supplicate thee that all Procurers may henceforth be wretched.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
5.2.1350:
As it is, it shall be so, even if you do keep your oath. Do you wait here; (going towards the cottage)—I’ll at once make the old gentleman come out; do you forthwith demand of him that wallet.
(Goes in.)
LABRAX
(to himself.)
5.2.1353: If ever so much he shall restore to me this wallet, I’m not this day indebted to him three obols even.
5.2.1355: It’s according to my own intention what my tongue swears. (The door opens.) But I’ll hold my peace; see, here he’s coming out, and bringing the old man.

5.3.1357:
(Enter GRIPUS, followed by DAEMONES, with the wallet.) GRIPUS
Follow this way.
Where is this Procurer?
Hark you (to LABRAX), see now; this person (pointing at DAEMONES) has got your wallet.
DAEMONES
5.3.1358: I have got it, and I confess that it is in my possession; and if it’s yours, you may have it. Everything, just as each particular was in it, shall in like manner be given safe to you.
5.3.1360:
(Holding it out.) Take it, if it’s yours.
LABRAX
Immortal Gods, it is mine. (Takes it.) Welcome, dear wallet.
DAEMONES
5.3.1361:
Is it yours?
LABRAX
Do you ask the question? If indeed, I’ faith, it were in Jove’s possession, still it is my own.
DAEMONES
5.3.1362:
Everything in it is safe; there has only been one casket taken out of it, with some trinkets, by means of which this day I have found my daughter.
LABRAX
5.3.1364:
What person?
DAEMONES
Palaestra, who was your property, she has been discovered to be my own daughter.
LABRAX
5.3.1365:
By my troth, it has happily turned out so; since this matter has happened so fortunately for you according to your wishes, I’m rejoiced.
DAEMONES
5.3.1366:
In that I don’t readily believe you.
LABRAX
5.3.1367:
Aye, by my faith, that you may be sure that I’m rejoiced, you shan’t give me three obols for her; I excuse you.
DAEMONES
5.3.1368:
I’ faith, you are acting kindly.
LABRAX
5.3.1369:
No, troth; it’s really yourself, indeed, that’s doing so.
(Going off with the wallet.)
GRIPUS
Hark you, you’ve got the wallet now.
LABRAX
5.3.1370:
I have got it.
GRIPUS
Make haste.
LABRAX
Make haste about what?
GRIPUS
To pay me the money.
LABRAX
5.3.1371:
By my troth, I’ll neither give you anything nor do I owe you anything.
GRIPUS
What mode of proceeding is this? Don’t you owe it me?
LABRAX
5.3.1372:
Troth, not I indeed.
GRIPUS
Didn’t you promise it me upon your oath?
LABRAX
5.3.1373:
I did take an oath, and now I’ll take an oath, if it is in any way my own pleasure; oaths were invented for preserving property, not for losing it.
GRIPUS
5.3.1375:
Give me, will you, a great talent of silver, you most perjured fellow.
DAEMONES
5.3.1376:
Gripus, what talent is it you are asking him for?
GRIPUS
He promised it me on oath.
LABRAX
5.3.1377:
I chose to swear; (turning to DAEMONES) are you the priest as to my perjury?
DAEMONES
(to GRIPUS.)
5.3.1378:
For what reason did he promise you the money?
GRIPUS
If I restored this wallet into his hands, he swore that he would give
5.3.1380:
me a great talent of silver.
LABRAX
Find me a person with whom I may go to the judge, to decide whether you did not make the bargain with wicked fraudulence, and whether I am yet five-and-twenty years old.
GRIPUS
(pointing to DAEMONES.)
5.3.1382:
Go to the judge with him.
LABRAX
No; I must have some other person.
DAEMONES
(to LABRAX.)
5.3.1383:
Then I shan’t allow you to take it away from him, unless I shall have found him guilty. Did you promise him the money?
LABRAX
5.3.1384:
I confess it.
DAEMONES
What you promised my slave
5.3.1385:
must needs be my own. Don’t you be supposing, Procurer, that you are to be using your pimping honesty here. That can’t be.
GRIPUS
(to LABRAX.)
5.3.1386:
Did you fancy now that you had got hold of a person whom you might cheat? It must be paid down here (holding his hand), good silver coin; I shall, at once, pay it to him (pointing to DAEMONES), so that he may give me my liberty.
DAEMONES
5.3.1389:
Inasmuch, therefore, as I have acted courteously towards you, and by my means these things (pointing to the wallet) have been saved for you—
GRIPUS
5.3.1390:
I’ faith, by my means, rather; don’t say by yours.
DAEMONES
(to GRIPUS.)
5.3.1391:
If you are prudent you’ll hold your tongue. (To LABRAX.) Then it befits you in a like courteous manner kindly to return the obligation to myself, who so well merit the same.
LABRAX
5.3.1392:
You are pleading, of course, for my right?
DAEMONES
(ironically.)
5.3.1393:
It would be a wonder if I didn’t, at a loss to myself, ask you to forego your right.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
5.3.1394:
I’m all right; the Procurer’s giving way; my freedom is at hand.
DAEMONES
(pointing to GRIPUS.)
5.3.1395:
He found this wallet; he is my slave. I therefore have preserved this for you, together with a large sum of money.
LABRAX
5.3.1397:
I return you thanks, and with regard to the talent that I promised on oath to him, there’s no reason that you shouldn’t receive it.
GRIPUS
5.3.1398:
Hark you, give it me then, if you are wise.
DAEMONES
(to GRIPUS.)
5.3.1399:
Will you hold your tongue, or not?
GRIPUS
You pretend to be acting on my side: I tell you
5.3.1400:
by my troth, you shan’t do me out of that, if I did lose the other booty.
DAEMONES
5.3.1401:
You shall have a beating if you add a single word.
GRIPUS
Troth now, do you kill me even; I’ll never be silent on any terms, unless my mouth is shut with the talent.
LABRAX
5.3.1403:
For yourself, in fact, is he using his exertions; do hold your tongue.
DAEMONES
Step this way, Procurer.
LABRAX
Very well.
(They walk on one side.)
GRIPUS
5.3.1404:
Proceed openly; I don’t want any whisperings or mumblings to be going on.
DAEMONES
5.3.1405:
Tell me, at what price did you buy that other young woman, Ampelisca?
LABRAX
5.3.1406:
I paid down a thousand didrachms.
DAEMONES
Should you like me to make you a handsome offer?
LABRAX
5.3.1407:
I should like it much.
DAEMONES
5.3.1408:
I’ll divide the talent.
LABRAX
You act fairly.
DAEMONES
For that other woman Ampelisca, that she may be free, take you one half, and give the other half to him.
LABRAX
5.3.1410:
By all means.
DAEMONES
For that half I’ll give his freedom to Gripus, by means of whom you found your wallet, and I my daughter.
LABRAX
5.3.1411:
You act fairly; I return you many thanks.
(They return to GRIPUS.)
GRIPUS
5.3.1412:
How soon then is the money to be returned to me?
DAEMONES
5.3.1413:
The money’s paid, Gripus; I’ve got it.
GRIPUS
You, faith; but I had rather it were myself.
DAEMONES
5.3.1414:
I’ faith, there’s nothing for you here, so don’t you be expecting it. I wish you to release him from his oath.
GRIPUS
(aside.)
5.3.1415:
Troth, I’m undone; if I don’t hang myself, I’m utterly done for. (Aloud.) I’ faith, after this day you certainly shall never be cheating me again.
DAEMONES
5.3.1417:
Dine here to-day, Procurer.
LABRAX
Be it so; the proposal is to my taste.
DAEMONES
5.3.1418: Do you both follow me in-doors. (He comes forward and addresses the AUDIENCE.) Spectators, I would invite you to dinner as well, were it not that I’m going to give nothing, and that there is no good cheer at all at home;
5.3.1420:
and if, too, I didn’t believe that you are invited to dinner elsewhere. But if you shall be willing to give hearty applause to this Play, do you all come to make merry at my house some sixteen years hence. Do you (to LABRAX and GRIPUS) both dine here with me to-day.
GRIPUS
5.3.1423:
Be it so.
An ACTOR
(To the AUDIENCE)
Now give us your applause.

1.1.1:
(Enter PHILUMENA and PAMPHILA. PHILUMENA
Sister, I think that Penelope was wretched from her very soul, who was so long deprived of her husband; for from our own fortunes, whose husbands are absent from us, we judge of her feelings;
1.1.5:
for whose affairs, still, in their absence, both night and day, sister, as is becoming, we are ever anxious.
PAMPHILA
1.1.7:
’Tis right that we should do our duty; and we do not that any further than affection bids us.
PHILUMENA
1.1.9: But, sister, step this way a moment; I want
1.1.10:
to speak about the affairs of my husband.
PAMPHILA
Ain’t they prospering, pray?
PHILUMENA
1.1.11: I hope and wish so, indeed. But, sister, at this am I vexed, that your and my father, one who is esteemed as especially honorable among all his fellow-citizens, should be now acting the part of a dishonorable man;
1.1.15:
who is undeservedly doing so great an injustice to our absent husbands, and is wishing to separate us from them. These things, sister, render me tired of existence; these things are a care and a vexation to me.
(She sheds tears.)
PAMPHILA
1.1.20: Weep not, sister, nor do that to your feelings which your father is threatening to do. ’Tis to be hoped that he will act more righteously. I know him well; he says these things in jest; and he would not earn for himself the mountains of the Persians,
1.1.25: which are said to be of gold, to do that of which you are in dread. Still, if he does do it, it befits you by no means to be angry; nor will it happen without some reason.
1.1.29:
For this is the third year since our husbands have been away from home.
PHILUMENA
1.1.31:
’Tis as you say; while, in the meantime, they may be living, and may be well, they do not make us acquainted where they are, what they are doing, whether they are doing well, neither do they return.
PAMPHILA
1.1.34:
And do you, sister, regret this, that they do not observe their duty, whereas you do yours?
PHILUMENA
1.1.37:
Hold your peace, if you please; take care, please, that I hear not that same thing from you in future.
PHILUMENA
1.1.39: Because, i’ faith, in my opinion, ’tis proper for all prudent people
1.1.40: to observe and to do their duty. For that reason, sister, although you are the older, I advise you to remember your duty; and if they are unjust and act otherwise to us than is right, then, i’ faith, in exactly the same degree,
1.1.45:
that there may be no further mischief, it befits us studiously to remember our duty by all means in our power.
PHILUMENA
1.1.47:
’Tis good; I’m silenced.
PAMPHILA
But do take care and remember it.
PHILUMENA
1.1.48: I do not wish, sister, to be thought to be unmindful of my husband; nor has he thrown away the distinction that he conferred upon me.
1.1.50:
For, by my troth, his kindness is pleasing and delightful to me; and, really, this choice of mine is not now irksome to me, nor is there any reason why I should wish to abandon this match. But, in fine, ’tis placed in our father’s power; that must be done by us which our relatives enjoin.
PAMPHILA
1.1.55:
I know it, and in thinking of it I am overwhelmed with grief; for already has he almost disclosed his sentiments.
PHILUMENA
1.1.57: Let us consider, then, what is necessary for us to do.

1.2.58:
(Enter ANTIPHO from his house, speaking at the door to his SERVANTS.) ANTIPHO
The man in condition of a servant who always waits to be told his duty, and doesn’t remember to do it of his own accord, that servant, I say, is not of a deserving character.
1.2.60: You remember well on each returning Calends to ask for your allotment of provisions; why, then, do you less remember to do what is necessary to do about the house? Now, therefore, if, when I return, the furniture shall not be set for me, each piece in its proper place, I’ll be putting you in mind with a bull’s hide remembrancer. Not human beings seem to be living with me, but pigs.
1.2.65:
Take care, if you please, that my house is clean, when I return home. I shall soon be back home; I’m going to her house, to see my eldest daughter. If any one should enquire for me, call me thence, some of you; or—I shall be here soon myself.
PHILUMENA
(aside.)
1.2.68:
What are we to do, sister, if our father shall resolve against us?
PAMPHILA
It befits us to submit to what he does whose power is the stronger.
1.2.70:
By entreating, not by opposing, I think we must use our endeavours. If with mildness we ask for favour, I trust to obtain it of him. Oppose him we cannot, without disgrace and extreme criminality; I will neither do that myself, nor will I give you the advice to do it, but rather that we should entreat him. I know our family; he will yield to entreaty.
ANTIPHO
(speaking to himself.)
1.2.75: In the first place, in what manner I should make a beginning with them, about that I am in doubt; whether I should accost them in language couched in ambiguous terms, after this fashion, as though I had never pretended anything at all against them, or whether as though I had heard that they were deserving of some censure against them; whether I should rather try them gently or with threats. I know that there will be opposition; I know my daughters right well.
1.2.80: If they should prefer to remain here rather than to marry afresh, why, let them do so. What need is there for me, the term of my life run out, to be waging war with my children, when I think that they don’t at all deserve that I should do so? By no means; I’ll have no disturbances. But I think that this is the best thing to be done by me; I’ll do thus; I’ll pretend as though they had themselves been guilty of some fault;
1.2.85:
I’ll terribly terrify their minds this day by some ambiguous expressions; ana then, after that, as I shall feel disposed, I’ll disclose myself. I know that many words will be spoken; I’ll go in. (Goes to the door of PHILUMENA’S house.) But the door’s open.
PHILUMENA
1.2.88:
Why, surely the sound of my father’s voice reached my ears.
PAMPHILA
1.2.89:
I’ troth, ’tis he; let’s hasten to meet him with a kiss.
(They both run to kiss him.)
PHILUMENA
1.2.90:
My father, my respects.
ANTIPHO
And to you the same. Away this instant, and be off from me,
(Removes her.)
PHILUMENA
1.2.91:
One kiss.
ANTIPHO
I’ve had enough of your kissing.
PHILUMENA
Prithee, father, why so?
ANTIPHO
1.2.92:
Because, as it is, the seasoning of your affection has reached my soul.
PAMPHILA
Sit down here, father.
(Points to a chair.)
ANTIPHO
1.2.93:
I’ll not sit there; do you sit down; I’ll sit on the bench.
(Sits on a bench.)
PAMPHILA
1.2.94:
Wait till I fetch a cushion.
ANTIPHO
You take kind care of me; I’m nicely seated now as I am.
PAMPHILA
1.2.95:
Do let me, father.
(Goes into the house.)
ANTIPHO
What need is there?
PAMPHILA
There is need.
(Coming out, and bringing a cushion.)
ANTIPHO
I’ll submit to you. (Arranging the cushion.) Yes, this does very well.
PAMPHILA
1.2.96:
Why, daughters can never take too much care of their parent. Whom is it proper that we should esteem more dear than yourself? And then, in the next place, father, our husbands, for whom you have chosen that we should be the mothers of families.
ANTIPHO
1.2.99: You do as it is proper for good wives to do, in esteeming your husbands,
1.2.100:
though absent, just as though they were present.
PAMPHILA
’Tis propriety, father, for us to highly honor those who have chosen us as companions for themselves.
ANTIPHO
1.2.102:
Is there any other person here to listen with his ears to our conversation?
PHILUMENA
1.2.103:
There’s no one except us and yourself.
ANTIPHO
I wish your attention to be given; for, unacquainted with female matters and ways,
1.2.105:
I come now as a pupil to you, my instructresses; in order that each of you may tell me what endowments matrons ought to have, who are the best esteemed.
PAMPHILA
1.2.107:
What’s the reason that you come hither to enquire about the ways of females?
ANTIPHO
1.2.108:
Troth, I’m looking for a wife, as your mother’s dead and gone.
PAMPHILA
1.2.109: You’ll easily find, father, one both worse and of worse morals
1.2.110:
than she was; one better you’ll neither find nor does the sun behold.
ANTIPHO
1.2.111:
But I’m making the enquiry of you, and of this sister of yours.
PAMPHILA
I’ faith, father, I know how they should be, if they are to be such as I think right.
ANTIPHO
1.2.113:
I wish, then, to know what you do think right.
PAMPHILA
That when they walk through the city, they should shut the mouths of all, so that none can speak ill of them with good reason.
ANTIPHO
(to PHILUMENA.)
1.2.115:
And now speak you in your turn.
PHILUMENA
What do you wish that I should speak to you about, father?
ANTIPHO
1.2.116:
How is the woman most easily distinguished, who is of a good disposition?
PHILUMENA
1.2.117:
When she, who has the power of doing ill, refrains from doing so.
ANTIPHO
1.2.118:
Not bad that. (To PAMPHILA.) Come, say you, which choice is the preferable, to marry a maiden or a widow?
PAMPHILA
1.2.119: So far as my skill extends,
1.2.120: of many evils, that which is the least evil, the same is the least an evil.
1.2.121:
He that can avoid the women, let him avoid them,
so that each day he takes care, the day before, not to do that which, the day after, he may regret.
ANTIPHO
1.2.123:
What sort of woman, pray, seems to you by far the wisest?
PHILUMENA
1.2.124: She who, when affairs are prosperous, shall still be able to know herself,
1.2.125:
and who with equanimity can endure it to be worse with her than it has been.
ANTIPHO
1.2.126:
By my troth, in merry mood have I been trying the bent of your dispositions. But ’tis this for which I am come to you, and for which I wished to meet you both. My friends are advising me to the effect that I should remove you hence to my own house.
PAMPHILA
1.2.129: But still, we, whose interests are concerned, are advising you quite otherwise.
1.2.130:
For either, father, we ought not formerly to have been bestowed in marriage, unless our husbands pleased you, or, it is not right for us now to be taken away when they are absent.
ANTIPHO
1.2.132:
And shall I suffer you while I am alive to remain married to men who are beggars?
PAMPHILA
1.2.133:
This beggar of mine is agreable to me; her own king is agreable to the queen. In poverty have I the same feelings that once I had in riches.
ANTIPHO
1.2.135:
And do you set such high value on thieves and beggars?
PHILUMENA
1.2.136:
You did not, as I think, give me in marriage to the money, but to the man.
ANTIPHO
1.2.137:
Why are you still in expectation of those who have been absent for now three years? Why don’t you accept an eligible match in place of a very bad one?
PAMPHILA
1.2.139: ’Tis folly, father, to lead unwilling dogs to hunt.
1.2.140:
That wife is an enemy, who is given to a man in marriage against her will.
ANTIPHO
1.2.141:
Are you then determined that neither of you will obey the command of your father?
PHILUMENA
1.2.142:
We do obey; for where you gave us in marriage, thence are we unwilling to depart.
ANTIPHO
1.2.143:
Kindly good b’ye; I’ll go and tell my friends your resolutions.
PAMPHILA
1.2.144:
They will, I doubt not, think us the more honorable, if you tell them to honorable men.
ANTIPHO
1.2.145:
Take you care, then, of their domestic concerns, the best way that you can.
(Exit.)
PHILUMENA
Now you gratify us, when you direct us aright: now we will hearken to you. Now, sister, let’s go indoors.
PAMPHILA
1.2.147:
Well, first I’ll take a look at home. If, perchance, any news should come to you from your husband, take you care that I know it.
PHILUMENA
1.2.149: Neither will I conceal it from you, nor do you conceal from me what you may know.
1.2.150:
(Calls at the door of her house.) Ho there, Crocotium, go, fetch hither Gelasimus, the Parasite; bring him here with you. For, i’ faith, I wish to send him to the harbour, to see if, perchance, any ship from Asia has arrived there yesterday or to-day. But, one servant has been sitting at the harbour whole days in waiting; still, however, I wish it to be visited every now and then. Make haste, and return immediately.
(Each goes into her own house.)

1.3.155:
(Enter GELASIMUS.) GELASIMUS
I do suspect that Famine was my mother; for since I was born I have never been filled with victuals. And no man could better return the favour to his mother, than do I right unwillingly return it to my mother, Famine. For in her womb, for ten months she bore me,
1.3.160: whereas I have been carrying her for more than ten years in my stomach. She, too, carried me but a little child, wherefore I judge that she endured the less labour; in my stomach no little Famine do I bear, but of full growth, i’ faith, and extremely heavy.
1.3.165: The labour-pains arise with me each day, but I’m unable to bring forth my mother, nor know I what to do. I’ve often heard it so said that the elephant is wont to be pregnant ten whole years; for sure this hunger of mine is of its breed.
1.3.170: For now for many a year has it been clinging to, my inside. Now, if any person wants a droll fellow, I am on sale, with all my equipage: of a filling-up for these chasms am I in search. When little, my father gave me the name of Gelasimus,
1.3.175: because, even from a tiny child, I was a droll chap. By reason of poverty, in fact, did I acquire this name, because, it was poverty that made me to be a droll; for whenever she reaches a person, she instructs him thoroughly in every art. My father used to say that I was born when provisions were dear;
1.3.180: for that reason, I do believe, I am now the more sharply set. But on our family such complacence has been bestowed—I am in the habit of refusing no person, if any one asks me out to eat. One form of expression has most unfortunately died away with people, and one, i’ faith, most beseeming and most elegant to my thinking,
1.3.185: which formerly they employed: Come here to dinner—do so—really, do promise—don’t make any difficulties—is it convenient?—I wish it to be so, I say; I’ll not part with you unless you come. But now, in the present day, they have found a substitute for these expressions—a saying, by my faith, truly right worthless and most vile:
1.3.190: I’d invite you to dinner, were I not dining; out myself. I’ faith, I wish the very loins of that phrase broken, that it mayn’t repeat its perjury if he does dine at his own house. These phrases reduce me to learn foreign habits, and to spare the necessity for an auctioneer,
1.3.195:
and so proclaim the auction, and put myself up for sale.
(Enter CROCOTIUM from the house of PHILUMENA, unseen by GELASIMUS.)
CROCOTIUM
(aside.)
1.3.196:
This is the Parasite, whom I’ve been sent to fetch. I’ll listen to what he’s saying, before I accost him.
GELASIMUS
1.3.198: Now there are a good many curious mischief-makers here, who, with extreme zeal, busy themselves with the affairs of other people,
1.3.200: and who have themselves no affairs of their own to busy themselves with. They, when they know that any one is about to have an auction, go forthwith and sift out what’s the reason; whether a debt compels it, or whether he has purchased a farm; or whether, on a divorce, her marriage-portion is to be repaid to his wife.
1.3.205: All these, although, i’ faith, I don’t judge them undeserving, in their most wretched state, to go toiling on, I don’t care about. I’ll proclaim the reason of my auction, that they may rejoice in my mishaps, for there’s no person a busybody but what he’s ill-natured too. Very great mishaps, alas! have befallen wretched me.
1.3.210: So dreadfully afflicted has my property rendered me: my many drinking-bouts are dead and gone; how many dinners, too, that I’ve bewailed, are dead! how many a draught of honeyed wine; how many breakfasts, too, that I have lost within these last three years!
1.3.215:
In my wretchedness, for very grief and vexation have I quite grown old. I’m almost dead with hunger.
CROCOTIUM
(aside.)
1.3.217:
There’s no one such a droll, as he is when he is hungry.
GELASIMUS
1.3.218: Now am I resolved that I’ll make a sale: out of doors am I obliged to sell whatever I possess.
1.3.220: Attend, if you please; the bargains will be for those who are present. I’ve funny bon mots to sell. Come, bid your price. Who bids a dinner? Does any one bid a breakfast? They’ll cost vou an Herculean breakfast or dinner. Ho, there! (to one of the SPECTATORS) did you nod to me? No one will offer you better—
1.3.225: I won’t allow that any Parasite has better
1.3.228: quibbles, cajoleries, and parasitical white lies.
1.3.230: I’m selling a rusty flesh-scraper, too; a rusty-coloured brown bottle
1.3.226: for the Greek unguents at the sweating-baths; delicate after-dinner powders;
1.3.231:
an empty Parasite as well (pointing to himself), in whom to lay by your scraps. ’Tis needful that these should be sold at once for as much as they can; that, if I offer the tenth part. to Hercules, on that account it may be greater
CROCOTIUM
(aside.)
1.3.234:
An auction of no great value, by my troth. Hunger has taken hold of the very deepest recess of the fellow’s stomach. I’ll accost the man.
(Moves towards him.)
GELASIMUS
1.3.237:
Who’s this that’s coming towards me? Why, surely this is Crocotium, the maid-servant of Epignomus.
CROCOTIUM
1.3.239:
My respects, Gelasimus.
GELASIMUS
That’s not my name.
CROCOTIUM
1.3.240:
I’ faith, for sure that used to be your name.
GELASIMUS
1.3.241:
Distinctly it was so, but I’ve lost it by use. Now I’m called Miccotrogus from what is fact.
CROCOTIUM
1.3.243:
O dear! I’ve laughed a good deal at you to-day.
GELASIMUS
When? or in what place?
CROCOTIUM
1.3.244:
Here, when you were carrying on a most worthless auction.
GELASIMUS
How now; did you really hear it?
CROCOTIUM
1.3.246:
Aye, and one really right worthy of yourself.
GELASIMUS
1.3.247:
Where are you bound for now?
CROCOTIUM
For yourself.
GELASIMUS
Why have you come?
CROCOTIUM
Philumena bade me ask you by all means to come to visit her at her house this instant, together with me.
GELASIMUS
1.3.250:
I’ faith, but I’ll surely come there as fast as I can. Are the entrails cooked by this? With how many lambs has she been sacrificing?
CROCOTIUM
1.3.252:
Indeed, she hasn’t been sacrificing at all.
GELASIMUS
How? What does she want with me, then?
CROCOTIUM
1.3.253:
I think that she’s going to ask you for ten measures of wheat.
GELASIMUS
1.3.254:
Or me rather ask it of her?
CROCOTIUM
1.3.255:
No; that you yourself should lend them to us.
GELASIMUS
1.3.256:
Tell her that I’ve nothing to give myself, or that she could wish to borrow, nor anything whatever, except this cloak that I have on. Even my very tongue that so freely used to offer itself I’ve sold as well.
CROCOTIUM
1.3.258:
How? Have you got no tongue?
GELASIMUS
1.3.259:
Why, the former one, that used to say here, take me, I’ve lost: see, here’s one now that says give me.
(Puts out his tongue.)
CROCOTIUM
1.3.262:
A curse may the Gods give you
GELASIMUS
Aye, if a curse you want, this same tongue will give you that.
CROCOTIUM
1.3.264: tell her I’ll be there this moment; make haste and be off. (CROCOTIUM goes into the house.)
1.3.266: I wonder why she has requested me to be fetched to her, who has never, before this day, requested that I should be fetched to her, ever since her husband left. I wonder what it can be; except it is for some experiment to be made upon me; I’ll go see what she wants.
1.3.270:
But see, here’s her boy, Pinacium. Look at that now; how very facetiously and just like a picture does he stand? Full many a time, for sure, in good troth, has he poured out for me the wine, almost unmixed, right cleverly into a very tiny cup indeed.
(Stands aside.)

2.1.274:
(Enter PINACIUM at a distance, with a fishing-rod, hooks, and a basket in his hand.) PINACIUM
(to himself.)
Mercury, who is said to be the messenger of Jove, never bore such pleasing tidings to his father, as I shall e’en now be telling to my mistress.
2.1.276: So loaded do I bear my breast with joy and with delight; and really I don’t care to speak a syllable but in a highflown style. The charms of all the loves and graces do I bring; my heart, too, is overleaping its banks, and overflowing with joyousness.
2.1.280: Now have you the means of acquiring glory, fame, and honor; make haste, Pinacium, exhort your feet to swiftness, grace your message by your deeds, and come to the rescue of your mistress in her need who is so wretched in awaiting the arrival of her husband, Epignomus; just as becomes her does she dote upon her husband, and anxiously long for him. Now, Pinacium,
2.1.285:
do as pleases you, run on, just as you like; take care and regard no person at the value of a straw; thrust them from the path with your elbows; make right smooth your way. If a, king shall come in your way, upset the king himself forthwith.
GELASIMUS
(apart.)
2.1.288:
Why, I wonder, is Pinacium running so overladen with baggage? He’s carrying a rod, and a basket, and a fish-hook.
PINACIUM
(to himself.)
2.1.290: But yet, I think ’tis proper that my mistress should come with entreaty to me, and that she should send envoys to me, and gifts of gold, and chariots in which for me to be borne, for I can’t go on foot. Therefore I shall now go back. (Turns back.) I think it is only proper that I should be approached and addressed with entreaties. And do you really think that it’s mere nonsense or nothing at all that I am now acquainted with?
2.1.295: Blessings so great am I carrying from the harbour, joys so extensive am I bringing, that hardly could my mistress herself presume to wish this of the Gods, if she were to know it. And am I to carry it, then, of my own accord? It pleases me not, nor do I think that the duty of a man. This way does it seem to be better suited to this news of mine; let her come to meet me, let her entreat me to communicate to her this news.
2.1.300: Haughtiness and pride befit prosperous fortunes. But, at last, when I reconsider it, how could she know that I know this? (Turning round.) Well, I can’t do otherwise than return, than speak, than relate it at length, and relieve my mistress of her grief, and both mightily increase the good deeds of my ancestors, and present her with a comfort unhoped for and opportune.
2.1.305: I’ll outdo the deeds of Talthybius, and I’ll set all messengers at nought, and at the same time I’ll think about the running at the Olympic games. But this distance is far too short for the course; how sorry for it I am. How’s this? I see the door’s closed. I’ll go and knock at the door. (Knocks at the door of PHILUMENA’S house.) Open, and make haste, cause the door to be thrown open; away with all delay.
2.1.310:
This matter is attended to too carelessly; see how long I’ve been standing here and knocking. Are you indulging yourselves with a nap? I’ll try whether the door or my arms and feet are the stronger. (Knocks and kicks.) I wish much that this door would run away from its master, that for that reason it might meet with a heavy punishment. I’m tired of knocking. Well, be this the last for you.
(Knocks again.)
GELASIMUS
(apart.)
2.1.315:
I’ll go and accost him. (Accosts PINACIUM.) Good day to you.
PINACIUM
2.1.316:
And good day to you.
GELASIMUS
2.1.317:
Are you turned fisherman, then?
PINACIUM
2.1.318:
How long is it since you ate?
GELASIMUS
2.1.319:
Whence come you? What are you carrying? Why are you in a hurry?
PINACIUM
About that which is no business of yours, don’t you trouble yourself.
GELASIMUS
2.1.321:
What’s there in that?
(Taking up the lid of the basket.)
PINACIUM
Snakes, for you to eat.
GELASIMUS
Why are you so pettish?
PINACIUM
If you had any shame, you wouldn’t address me.
GELASIMUS
2.1.323:
May I learn the truth from you?
PINACIUM
2.1.324: You may; this day you’ll get no dinner.

2.2.326:
(Enter PHILUMENA from her house.) PHILUMENA
Who now, pray, is breaking this door down? (To GELASIMUS.) Are you doing this? Do you come to me like an enemy?
GELASIMUS
2.2.327:
My respects to you; I come at your bidding.
PHILUMENA
And is it for that reason you are breaking down my door?
GELASIMUS
2.2.328:
Scold your own people; the offenders are your own. I came to see what you wanted me for. Why, for my own part, I pitied this door.
PINACIUM
2.2.329:
For that reason your assistance was given so very readily.
PHILUMENA
2.2.330:
Pray, who’s that, talking here so near to us?
GELASIMUS
Pinacium.
PHILUMENA
Where is he?
(Looks on each side.)
PINACIUM
(coming forward.)
2.2.331:
Attend to me, and leave alone that needy Parasite, Philumena.
PHILUMENA
2.2.332:
Pinacium.
PINACIUM
That name my elders gave me.
PHILUMENA
2.2.333:
What’s your business
PINACIUM
What’s my business, do you ask?
PHILUMENA
Why shouldn’t I ask it?
PINACIUM
What’s yours with me?
PHILUMENA
2.2.334:
Do you insult me, impudent fellow? Answer me, this very instant, Pinacium.
PINACIUM
2.2.335:
Bid those, then, to let me alone, who are detaining me.
PHILUMENA
Who are detaining you?
PINACIUM
Do you ask me that? A lassitude is in possession of all my limbs.
PHILUMENA
2.2.336:
Well, I know right well that it’s not in possession of your tongue.
PINACIUM
2.2.337:
With such rapid speed have I been hastening from the harbour, for the sake of your own well-doing.
PHILUMENA
2.2.338:
Why, do you bring any good news?
PINACIUM
2.2.339:
I bring more, by very much, than you expect.
PHILUMENA
I’m saved, then.
PINACIUM
2.2.340:
And I’m done for; lassitude is drinking up my marrow apace.
GELASIMUS
2.2.341:
What, then, am I, the marrow of whose stomach, to my sorrow, famine has seized upon?
PHILUMENA
2.2.342:
Did you meet any one?
PINACIUM
Many.
PHILUMENA
But any man?
PINACIUM
Very many; but, of the many, not one a greater rascal than he is.
(Points at GELASIMUS.)
PHILUMENA
2.2.344:
I have been affronted already at his saying uncivil things to me. If you irritate me any further—
(Holds up his fist to PINACIUM.)
PINACIUM
2.2.345:
I’ faith, you’ll be plaguy hungry to eat me.
GELASIMUS
2.2.346:
I’ll cause you to know that assuredly you’ve said that with reason.
PINACIUM
2.2.347:
I wish everything to be made clean. (Calls to the SERVANTS from the door.) Bring out here your brooms, and a reed as well, that I may destroy all the labours of the spiders and their plaguy webs, and rout out all their looms.
(The SERVANTS bring some brooms.)
GELASIMUS
2.2.349:
The poor things will be cold in future.
PINACIUM
2.2.350:
What? Do you think that they are just like yourself, with only one coat? Take this broom.
(Gives him a broom.)
GELASIMUS
2.2.351:
I’ll take it.
PINACIUM
This I’ll take myself. Do you sweep away there.
GELASIMUS
I’ll do so.
(Sweeps away.)
PINACIUM
(calling aloud.)
2.2.352:
Will some one bring here a pail and water?
GELASIMUS
Really, this fellow’s playing the Aedile without the vote of the public even.
(The water is brought.)
PINACIUM
2.2.353:
Come, do you quickly sweep the ground, and sprinkle before the house.
GELASIMUS
2.2.354:
I’ll do so.
PINACIUM
It needs be done.
2.2.355:
I’ll knock down the spider-webs there from the door and from the wall.
GELASIMUS
2.2.356:
I’ faith, a troublesome business, this.
PHILUMENA
Still, I don’t at all understand what it means; unless, perchance, some guests are about to come?
PINACIUM
(ordering the SERVANTS.)
2.2.357:
Do you spread the couches.
GELASIMUS
(aside.)
2.2.360:
take you down the gammon of bacon and the collar of brawn.
GELASIMUS
(aside.)
I’ faith, this is a very sensible fellow.
PHILUMENA
2.2.361:
By my troth, as I imagine, you haven’t quite minded the directions of your mistress.
PINACIUM
2.2.362:
Why, I’ve left all matters unattended to by reason of what you wished.
PHILUMENA
2.2.363:
Then do you inform me upon that, on account of which you were sent to the harbour?
PINACIUM
2.2.364: I’ll tell you. After, with the daybreak, you had sent me to the harbour,
2.2.365: the sun with its beams opportunely arose from out of the sea. While I was enquiring of the revenue officers whether any ship had arrived from Asia, and they were saying none had come, I beheld, in the meantime, a bark, than which I think I never saw a greater one. With a favouring breeze, and in full sail, it came into harbour.
2.2.370:
We were enquiring one of another whose ship it was, and what it carried? In the meantime I espied your husband and his servant Stichus.
PHILUMENA
2.2.372:
Ha! what? Did you mention Epignomus?
GELASIMUS
Your husband
and my own life.
PINACIUM
2.2.373:
He has arrived, I say.
PHILUMENA
Did you see him yourself?
PINACIUM
Yes, and with pleasure too.
GELASIMUS
2.2.375:
I’ faith, I’ll surely take the broom, and sweep this place with pleasure.
PINACIUM
2.2.374:
He has brought a great amount of silver and gold.
GELASIMUS
’Tis right cleverly done.
PINACIUM
2.2.376:
Wool and purple in plenty.
GELASIMUS
Aye, for me to clothe my carcase with.
PINACIUM
2.2.377:
Couches, adorned with ivory and gold.
GELASIMUS
I’ll recline at table right regally.
PINACIUM
2.2.378:
Besides—Babylonian coverings for couches, and carpets dyed in purple, has he brought.
GELASIMUS
2.2.379:
Abundance of fine things.
I’ faith, his business has been successful.
PINACIUM
2.2.380:
Then, as I began to say, female players on the harp, on the pipe, sackbuts too, has he brought with him, of surprising beauty.
GELASIMUS
2.2.381:
Capital! When I’m at my wine, I’ll be quite sportive; then am I in merriest pin.
PINACIUM
2.2.383:
Besides many unguents of numerous kinds.
GELASIMUS
I’ll not sell my bon mots; I’ll not have an auction now; I’ve got an estate in fee.
2.2.385:
Let the mischievous hunters of auctions go to perdition. Hercules, I congratulate thee that the tenths which I vowed to thee are increased. ’Tis my hope that at length, by some means or other, I may expel this plaguy famine from my stomach.
PINACIUM
2.2.388:
And then, besides, he has brought some Parasites with him.
GELASIMUS
Alas! to my confusion, I’m undone.
PINACIUM
2.2.389:
Right funny fellows.
GELASIMUS
I’ faith, I’ll sweep this dust back, which I just now swept together. (Sweeps it back.)
2.2.393: Those bon mots are now on sale, which I was saying I wouldn’t sell. I’m done for: now there is occasion for spiteful persons to rejoice at my misfortune.
2.2.395:
Hercules, thou who art a God, thou really hast departed not opportunely.
PHILUMENA
2.2.390:
Did you see Pamphilus, the husband of my sister?
PINACIUM
No.
PHILUMENA
Isn’t he there?
PINACIUM
2.2.391:
Yes, they said that he had come as well. I ran hither before them, with all speed, that I might bring the welcome tidings.
PHILUMENA
2.2.396:
Go in-doors, Pinacium; bid the servants prepare the sacred things for me. (To GELASIMUS.) Fare you well!
GELASIMUS
2.2.397:
Do you want me to assist?
PHILUMENA
I have servants enough in the house.
(PHILUMENA and PINACIUM go into the house.)
GELASIMUS
(to himself.)
2.2.398: In good sooth, Gelasimus, I doubt you have come to but little purpose, if neither he that is here gives you any aid, nor yet he that’s coming.
2.2.400:
I’ll off indoors to my books, and take my instructions from the cleverest sayings; for if I don’t drive away those fellows, the Parasites that are coming, most surely I’m undone.
(Exit.)

3.1.402:
(Enter EPIGNOMUS and STICHUS, followed by some SLAVES.) EPIGNOMUS
Inasmuch as, my business prosperously carried on, I am returned safe home, thanks do I return to Neptune and to his tempests; to Mercury as well, who in my traffic
3.1.405: has aided me, and by my profits has rendered my property fourfold. Those whom formerly I affected with sorrow at my departure, the same shall I now make joyous at my arrival. But already have I met my connexion Antipho, and from bad terms have I returned to friendship with him.
3.1.410: See, prithee, what money can effect. Since, my affairs prospering, he sees that I’ve returned, and brought home great wealth, without any mediators, there on board the ship, upon the deck, we have returned to friendship and good feeling.
3.1.415:
Both he and my brother dine with me this day; for yesterday we were both in the same harbour together; but to-day my ship weighed anchor a little the soonest. Take these people in-doors, Stichus, whom I’ve brought with me.
STICHUS
3.1.419: Master, whether I’m silent or speak, I’m sure you know
3.1.420:
how many hardships I’ve endured in your service; now, on my arrival home, I wish to spend in freedom this one day after these many hardships.
EPIGNOMUS
3.1.423: You ask what’s just and right. Stlchus, you may take this day for yourself; I don’t object to it. Go where you like.
3.1.425:
A cask, too, of old wine, I give you to drink.
STICHUS
O, grand! I’ll have my mistress this day.
EPIGNOMUS
3.1.426:
Even ten, so long as it is at your own expense.
STICHUS
3.1.430:
Where do you dine to-day?
STICHUS
This plan have I thus resolved upon. I have a mistress here in the neighbourhood, Stephanium, the servantmaid of your brother. I’m going to invite her; I’ll take her to a pic-nic entertainment at her fellow-servant’s, Sagarinus We both have the same mistress; we are rivals.
EPIGNOMUS
3.1.435:
Come then, conduct them in. I grant you this day.
STICHUS
3.1.436: Hold me to blame if I don’t make the most of it. Troth now, I’ll pass through the garden to my mistress, to engage her beforehand for me this evening; at the same time I’ll give my contribution, and bid the dinner to be cooked at Sagarinus’s,
3.1.440: or else I’ll go myself and make my marketing as caterer. Sagarinus, a servant for my with stripes to take him home well thrashed,
3.1.445: I’ll make all things to be in readiness here; but I’m delaying myself. And don’t you be surprised (to the AUDIENCE) that men, who are slaves, drink, court, and give invitations to dinner? This is allowed us at Athens. But when I think of it, rather than meet with censure, there’s here, too,
3.1.450:
another door to the back buildings of our house. I’ll go that way to market; by that way I’ll bring back the provisions—through the garden there’s a passage that communicates with both houses. (To the SLAVES.) Do you follow me this way. I surely will pull this day to bits.
(Goes into the house of EPIGNOMUS.)

3.2.454:
(Enter GELASIMUS.) GELASIMUS
(to himself.)
I’ve consulted my books; I’m as sure as possible,
3.2.455:
that by my funny bon mots I shall recover my patron. Now I’m going to see whether he has arrived by this from the harbour, that when he comes I may smooth him down with my speeches.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.458:
Surely, this is Gelasimus, the Parasite, that’s coming.
GELASIMUS
(to himself.)
3.2.459: With lucky auspices, by my troth, this day did I come out of doors;
3.2.460: since an omen auspiciously befel me. This was beheld by me; how a weasel carried off a mouse close at my feet. For as she found sustenance for herself this day, so do I hope that I shall do, as the augury predicts.
3.2.465:
(Sees EPIGNOMUS.) Surely this is Epignomus that’s standing here; I’ll go and address him. My dear Epignomus, how pleased I am to see you now; how my tears are starting forth for very joy. Have you all along enjoyed your health?
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.467:
With care it has been preserved.
GELASIMUS
3.2.468:
Right heartily I wish you health.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.469:
You speak kindly, and like a friend. May the Gods grant what you wish.
GELASIMUS
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.470:
I, sup there with you?
GELASIMUS
Since you are returned safe.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.472:
Really, an engagement has been made already; but I give you thanks.
GELASIMUS
3.2.473:
Do promise me.
EPIGNOMUS
It’s settled.
GELASIMUS
But do, I say.
EPIGNOMUS
The thing’s agreed on.
GELASIMUS
3.2.474:
By my troth, you’d do it with much pleasure to me.
EPIGNOMUS
I know that well.
3.2.475:
When an opportunity shall come, it shall be so.
GELASIMUS
Now, then, is the opportunity.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.476:
I’ faith, I cannot.
GELASIMUS
Why make difficulties? Do consider; I have I know not what luxuries at hand.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.477:
Do be off, now; seek for yourself another guest for to-day.
GELASIMUS
3.2.479:
You promise, then?
EPIGNOMUS
I would make no difficulty if I could.
GELASIMUS
3.2.480:
Really, on my word, one thing, for sure, I promise you, I’d entertain you with pleasure, beyond a doubt, if you would promise.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.482:
Adieu!
(Moving.)
GELASIMUS
Have you resolved?
EPIGNOMUS
I have resolved. I shall dine at home.
GELASIMUS
(aside.)
3.2.484: Since nothing has been effected this way, I’ll therefore approach him by a more open path, and I’ll speak plainly out.
3.2.483: (To EPIGNOMUS.) Since you, yourself, are not willing to promise to come to me,
3.2.486:
should you like that I should come to dine with you?
EPIGNOMUS
If it were possible, I should like it; but here are nine other people coming to dine at my house.
GELASIMUS
3.2.488:
For my part, I don’t ask that I should recline on the couch; you know that I’m a man for the lower seats.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.490:
But these are deputies of a people, tip-top men they come here as public ambassadors from Ambracia.
GELASIMUS
3.2.492:
Let then the deputies of a people, your tip-top men, recline at the tip-top place; I, the lowest, in the lowest quarter.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.494:
It isn’t proper for you to be entertained among deputies.
GELASIMUS
3.2.495:
I ’faith, and I—I’m a deputy, too, but little it does avail me.
EPIGNOMUS
3.2.496:
I intend that to-morrow we shall dine upon the scraps. Sincerely, farewell.
(Goes into his house.)
GELASIMUS
3.2.497: By my troth, ’tis clear that I’m undone, and by no fault of my own. The number is less than it was before by one Gelasimus. I’m resolved, hereafter, never to believe in a weasel,
3.2.500:
for I know of no beast more uncertain than her. She who herself is ten times a day shifting her place, from her have I taken my omens in matters of life and death to me! I’m determined to call my friends together, to take counsel how by rule I must starve henceforth.
(Exit.)

4.1.505:
(Enter ANTIPHO and PAMPHILUS.) ANTIPHO
So may the Gods favour me, and preserve for me my daughters, it is a pleasure to me, Pamphilus, that I see you both return home to your native land, your business prosperously managed, yourself and your brother.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.508:
I should have heard enough from you, Antipho, did I not see that you are friendly to me; now, since I’ve found that you are my friend, I’ll give you credence.
ANTIPHO
4.1.510: I would invite you to my house to dinner, had not your brother told me that you were going to dine at his house to-day, when he invited myself to his house to dinner. And it would have been more proper for me to give you an entertainment on your arrival, than to engage myself to him, were it not that I didn’t wish to disoblige him. Now I don’t wish with words alone to insinuate myself into your favour;
4.1.515:
to-morrow you shall be at my house, both you and he, with your wives.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.516:
Then, the day after, at my house; for it was yesterday he invited me for to-day. But am I quite reconciled to you, Antipho?
ANTIPHO
4.1.518: Since you have thus thrived in your affairs, as it behoves yourselves and persons friendly disposed to wish, let there be good-will and intercourse between us. Take you care to think of this;
4.1.520:
according as wealth is obtained by each man, so does he experience his friends. If his fortunes are flourishing, so are his friends true; if his prospects decline, so, too, do his friends decline. Fortune finds friends.
(from his house.)
EPIGNOMUS
(to himself.)
4.1.523: I’m now returned. ’Tis a great delight, if you have been long from home, when you return home again, if no anxieties come in contact with your feelings.
4.1.525:
But, in my absence, so well has my wife taken care of my private affairs, that she has made me free and unembarrassed by anxieties. But, see, here’s my brother Pamphilus, walking with his father-in-law.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.528:
How fares it, Epignomus?
EPIGNOMUS
How with you? How long since you came into harbour?
PAMPHILUS
4.1.529:
Not very long ago.
EPIGNOMUS
(aside.)
And is it since then that he has become on smooth terms with you?
ANTIPHO
(overhearing.)
4.1.530:
More smooth than the sea, on which you have both been borne.
EPIGNOMUS
You do as you are wont to do other things. Do we unlade the ship to-day, brother?
PAMPHILUS
4.1.531:
I would rather go quietly to work. Let’s rather lade ourselves with delights in their turn. How soon will the dinner be cooked? I haven’t breakfasted to-day.
EPIGNOMUS
4.1.533:
Go in-doors to my house and bathe.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.534: I’ll only step home to my own house, to salute the Gods and my wife.
4.1.535:
If I do that as I wish, I’ll forthwith return to your house.
EPIGNOMUS
4.1.536:
But your wife is hastening to come here with her sister.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.537:
’Tis very good; there will then be the less delay on that account. I shall be at your house this instant.
ANTIPHO
(to PAMPHILUS.)
4.1.538:
Before you go away, in your presence I wish to relate a single story to him.
EPIGNOMUS
4.1.539:
By all means.
ANTIPHO
There was once an old gentleman, just as I now am; he had two daughters, such as mine now are; they were married to two brothers,
4.1.541:
just as mine now are to yourselves.
PAMPHILUS
I wonder how the story is to turn out?
ANTIPHO
4.1.542:
One of these young men had, as you (to PAMPHILUS) now have, a damsel, a music-girl; he had brought her from abroad, as you have now done. Now, this old gentleman was a widower, just as I now am.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.544:
Do proceed; this story is really à propos.
ANTIPHO
4.1.545:
Then said this old gentleman to him to whom the music-girl belonged, just as I now say to you—
PAMPHILUS
4.1.546:
I’m listening, and carefully giving heed.
ANTIPHO
4.1.547:
I gave you my daughter, to be a comfortable bedfellow for you; now, I think it fair that one should be given me in return by you, to be my bed-fellow.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.549:
Who says that? Does he say it just as though you were to say it?
ANTIPHO
Just as I now say it to you.
4.1.550:
Aye, I’ll give you two of them, says this young man, if one’s too little; and if you are not satisfied with two, says he, two more shall be added.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.552:
Prithee, who says that? Does he say it just as though I were to say it?
ANTIPHO
He says it just as though you were to say it. Then says this old gentleman, just as though I were to say it, Well, give me four, if you like, so long only as, i’ faith, you find them something to eat as well, that they mayn’t consume my victuals.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.555:
Why surely it must have been a stingy old chap to say that, in asking food as well of him who promised them to him.
ANTIPHO
4.1.557: Why surely, this young man must have been a good-for-nothing fellow, who forthwith, when the other asked him, refused to give him a grain of wheat. But, i’ troth, the old gentleman asked what was fair, inasmuch as
4.1.560:
the dowry which he had given to his daughter, he wished him to have as an equivalent for the music-girl.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.561:
I’ faith, for sure I really do think that the young man was well advised, who wouldn’t give a mistress to that old fellow in return for the dower.
ANTIPHO
4.1.563: The old gentleman wished, indeed, if he could, to bargain for their maintenance; because he couldn’t, he said he wished it to be done on what terms it might.
4.1.565:
Done, said this young man. You do me a kindness, said the old gentleman. Have I the thing agreed upon? said he. I’ll do even as you wish it to be done, said the other. But I’ll be off in-doors, and congratulate my daughters on your arrival. Then I’ll go wash me at the bath; there will I take all care of my old age; after that, when I’ve bathed, lying down, I’ll await you at my leisure.
(Exit.)
PAMPHILUS
4.1.570: A funny mortal, Antipho; how cleverly he did make up his story.
4.1.571: Even yet the rogue considers himself a young man. A mistress shall be given to the fellow, to sing to the old chap at night in bed; for, i’ faith, indeed, I know not of what other use a mistress can be to him.
4.1.574:
But how fares our Parasite, Gelasimus? Is he well, too?
EPIGNOMUS
4.1.575:
I’ faith, I saw the fellow not so very long ago.
PAMPHILUS
How fares he?
EPIGNOMUS
Like one half-starved.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.576:
Why didn’t you invite the fellow to your house to dinner?
EPIGNOMUS
That on my arrival I mightn’t be wasting anything. But see, here’s the wolf in the Fable; here he is in person with his ravenous fit.
PAMPHILUS
4.1.578:
We’ll have some sport with the fellow.
EPIGNOMUS
You put me in mind of a plan I had already resolved on.

4.2.579:
(Enter GELASIMUS.) GELASIMUS
(to the AUDIENCE.)
But as I had begun to tell you; while I have been absent hence,
4.2.580: I’ve now been consulting with my friends and with my relatives. They have been my advisers to the effect that I should this very day kill myself with starvation. But don’t I see Pamphilus with his brother Epignomus? Yes, ’tis he. I’ll accost the man. (Goes up to PAMPHILUS.) O longed-for Pamphilus! O my salvation! O my life! O my delight! right welcome. I rejoice that
4.2.585:
you’ve returned safe from abroad to your native land. Welcome.
PAMPHILUS
Welcome, Gelasimus.
GELASIMUS
4.2.586:
Have you been quite well?
PAMPHILUS
I have taken good care of my health.
GELASIMUS
I’ troth, I’m glad of it. I’ faith, I confoundedly wish I had now a thousand measures of silver.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.588:
What need have you of it?
GELASIMUS
I’ faith, that I might invite him to dinner, and not invite you.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.589:
You are talking against your own interest.
GELASIMUS
This, then, that I might invite you both
4.2.590:
for my part I should not avoid there is nothing so as this
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.592:
Troth, now, I’d ask you with pleasure, if there were room left.
GELASIMUS
4.2.593:
Well, standing, then, I’ll gobble down a bit in the scramble.
EPIGNOMUS
No, only this one thing can be done.
GELASIMUS
4.2.594:
What?
EPIGNOMUS
When the guests have gone, that then you may come—
GELASIMUS
Hurra! capital!
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.595:
To wash the pots, I mean; not to dinner.
GELASIMUS
The Gods confound you! What say you, Pamphilus?
PAMPHILUS
4.2.596:
I’ troth, this day I’m engaged to dine elsewhere abroad.
GELASIMUS
4.2.597:
How, abroad?
PAMPHILUS
Really abroad, on my word.
GELASIMUS
How the plague do you like, thus wearied, to be supping abroad?
PAMPHILUS
4.2.598:
Which do you advise me?
GELASIMUS
Order a dinner to be cooked at home, and word to be sent to him who invited you.
PAMPHILUS
4.2.599:
Shall I dine at home, alone?
GELASIMUS
4.2.600:
Why, not alone; invite me.
PAMPHILUS
But I’m afraid lest he should scold me, who has been to this expense for my sake.
GELASIMUS
4.2.601:
It may easily be excused—only listen to me; do order a dinner to be cooked at home.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.602:
Not by my advice, indeed, will he act so as to disappoint that person this day.
GELASIMUS
4.2.603: Will you not be off from here? Perhaps you suppose that I don’t see what you’re about. Do you look to yourself, please.
4.2.605:
(To PAMPHILUS.) How that fellow is gaping after your property just like a hungry wolf. Don’t you know how men are set upon here in the street at night?
PAMPHILUS
4.2.607:
So many the more servants will I bid to come and fetch me, that they may protect me.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.608:
He won’t stir—he won’t stir; because you persuade him so earnestly not to go out.
GELASIMUS
Do order a dinner to be cooked at home with all speed for me and for yourself and your wife.
4.2.610:
Troth, if you do so, I don’t think you’ll say that you are deceived.
PAMPHILUS
4.2.611:
So far as that dinner is concerned, Gelasimus, you may be dinnerless to-day.
GELASIMUS
4.2.612:
Are you going abroad to dine?
PAMPHILUS
I’m going to dine at my brother’s, hard by.
GELASIMUS
4.2.613:
Is that fixed?
PAMPHILUS
Fixed.
GELASIMUS
By my troth, I hope you may be struck with a stone this day.
PAMPHILUS
4.2.614:
I’m not afraid; I shall go through the garden; I’ll not go abroad.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.615:
What say you to that, Gelasimus?
GELASIMUS
You’re entertaining your deputies; keep them to yourself.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.616:
Why, faith, ’tis your own business.
GELASIMUS
If, indeed, ’tis my own business, avail yourself of my assistance; invite me.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.617:
By my faith, I see, as I fancy, one place still for yourself only, where you may recline.
PAMPHILUS
4.2.618:
Really, I do think it may be managed.
GELASIMUS
O light of the city!
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.619:
If you can manage to recline in a small compass.
GELASIMUS
Aye, even between two wedges of iron.
4.2.620:
As little space as a puppy can lie in, the same will be enough for me.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.621:
I’ll beg for it some way or other; come along.
(Pulls him along.)
GELASIMUS
What? This way?
EPIGNOMUS
Yes, to prison. For here, indeed, you’ll not find any further entertainment. Let’s be off, you Pamphilus.
PAMPHILUS
4.2.623:
I’ll but salute the Gods: then I’ll pass through to your house forthwith.
GELASIMUS
4.2.624:
What then?
EPIGNOMUS
Why, I said that you might go to prison.
GELASIMUS
Well, if you order it,
4.2.625:
I’ll go there even.
EPIGNOMUS
Immortal Gods! really, by my troth, this fellow might be induced by a dinner or a breakfast to bear extreme torture.
GELASIMUS
4.2.626:
Such is my nature; with anything can I struggle much more easily than with hunger.
EPIGNOMUS
4.2.629:
I know it: at my house
full long enough has this facility of yours been experienced by me
4.2.628: while you were the Parasite of myself and my brother, we ruined our fortunes.
4.2.630:
Now I don’t wish you to be made by me from a Gelasimus into a Catagelasimus.
(EPIGNOMUS and PAMPHILUS go into their houses.)
GELASIMUS
4.2.631: And are you gone now? Surely he is gone. Now have I need of a wise resolution. Both are gone; consider, Gelasimus, what plan you must adopt. What, I? Yes, you. What, for myself? Yes, for yourself. Don’t you see how dear provisions are? Don’t you see how the kindness and the heartiness of men have vanished? Don’t you see how drolls are set at nought, and how they themselves are sponged upon?
4.2.635:
By my troth, not a person shall ever behold me alive on the morrow; for, this instant, in-doors will I load my throat with a bulrush dose. And by this I shall not give cause for men to say that I died of hunger.
(Exit.)

5.1.641:
(Enter STICHUS, and provisions, a table, and couches on the stage.) STICHUS
Foolishly and unwisely is it done in my opinion, if people are in the habit, if they are expecting a person; of looking out for him; faith, ne doesn’t on that account come a bit the faster. I’m now doing that same thing, in looking out for Sagarinus;
5.1.645:
who, still, for that reason won’t come a jot the faster. Troth, I shall just now be taking my place alone, if he doesn’t come here. I’ll now fetch that cask of wine hither from home, and then I’ll take my place. The day, like snow, is melting away apace.
(Goes into the house of EPIGNOMUS.)

5.2.649:
(Enter SAGARINUS.) SAGARINUS
Hail! Athens, thou nurse of Greece;
5.2.650: country of my master, hail! How joyously do I behold thee. But I have a wish to see how my mistress and fellow-servant, Stephanium, is faring. For I bade Stichus to give her my regards, and to tell her that I should come to-day, so that she might cook a dinner in good time.
5.2.655:
But, surely, here’s Stichus.
(with a cask of wine)
STICHUS
(to himself.)
A clever thing you did, master, when you presented your servant, Stichus, with this gift. O ye immortal Gods! how many delights do I carry, how many smiles, how many jokes, how many a kiss, dancing, dalliance, and good-fellowship.
SAGARINUS
5.2.660:
Stichus,
how fare you?
STICHUS
Right well, Sagarinus, most delightfully; I’m bringing Dionysus, as my guest and yours. For, i’ faith, the dinner’s cooked; free range has been given me and you at your house. For at our house there’s an entertainment; your master’s dining there with his wife, and Antipho as well;
5.2.665:
there, too, is my master. This was given me as a present.
(Points to the cask.)
SAGARINUS
5.2.666:
How? Are you dreaming?
STICHUS
I’ faith, I’m telling you the truth.
SAGARINUS
Who then gave you this?
STICHUS
What matters that to you?
5.2.669: I wish us this day to wash away everything of foreign climes.
5.2.670: Leave them alone; let’s now attend to Athens; follow me.
5.2.667:
Do you at once make haste, and bathe.
SAGARINUS
I have bathed.
STICHUS
Very good follow me, then, this. way in-doors, Sagarinus.
SAGARINUS
5.2.671:
Of course, I follow. By my troth, this beginning pleases me as I return home; a happy omen and augury has met me in my path.
(They go into the house of PAMPHILUS.)

5.3.673:
(Enter STEPHANIUM from the house of EPIGNOMUS.) STEPHANIUM
(to the AUDIENCE.)
I wish that it may appear wondrous to no one of you, Spectators,
5.3.674: why I who live there (pointing to the house of PAMPHILUS) am come out hither from this other house: I’ll inform you thereon. Just now was I sent for to this house by the back way. For as soon as news was brought that the husbands of these ladies were about to come, we all hurried thither. We attended to laying the couches, and setting all in order. Still, amid these duties, I had a care for my friends,
5.3.680:
Stichus and my fellow-servant Sagarinus, that their dinner should be cooked. Stichus has been caterer; but for cooking it, I’ve appointed one my deputy. Now, I’ll be off hence, and attend to my friends, who, I see, are coming here.
(Goes into the house of PAMPHILUS.)

5.4.683:
(Enter STICHUS and SAGARINUS from the house of PAMPHILUS with provisions, a PIPER following.) SAGARINUS
Come, out of doors with you; lead on the procession. Stichus, I appoint you commander of the cask. I’m resolved to prove our banquet in every fashion this day.
5.4.685:
So may the Gods love me, we are well entertained in being feasted in this place. I will that each person that passes by shall be invited to join the banquet.
STICHUS
5.4.686:
Agreed, so long only as, i’ faith, each man comes with his own wine; for of this, a mouthful shall be given to no person but ourselves, this day. Eating alone, let’s wait upon ourselves.
SAGARINUS
5.4.690:
for our means, is quite sufficient, with its nuts, beans, figs, a dish of olives, pounded lupines, and a cake.
STICHUS
5.4.692: It better becomes a man who is a slave to bring his expenses within moderation than beyond. Each one to his own station; they, who have wealth at home, drink from cups, goblets, and bowls; we, if we are now
5.4.695:
drinking from our Samian jug, still build our walls according to our means.
SAGARINUS
5.4.701:
But while she who is your mistress and mine is arranging her hair, and bedecking herself, I wish us to have some diversion among ourselves. I appoint you the commander of this feast.
STICHUS
5.4.703:
Very aptly does it suggest itself to your mind.
SAGARINUS
5.4.704:
Wouldn’t we be more suitably entertained like Cynics on benches here, than upon couches?
STICHUS
Aye, but this is far the most pleasant.
SAGARINUS
5.4.696:
On which side is each of us to recline by our mistress?
STICHUS
Of course you go to the upper place. And, so that you may understand it, I make a division with you on these terms: consider, and take which province you would even like now to take.
(They take their places.)
SAGARINUS
5.4.699:
But what’s your meaning about this province?
STICHUS
Whether you would choose to hold the command over the water or over Bacchus.
SAGARINUS
5.4.705:
But, in the meantime, general of ours, why stands this goblet here? See how many cups we have drunk.
STICHUS
5.4.706:
As many as there are fingers on your hand. The Greek song is, Drink either your five cups or your three, but not your four.
SAGARINUS
(about to drink.)
5.4.708:
I pledge you. Do you take for yourself the tenth part from the fountain, if you are wise. Here’s luck to you, luck to us; here’s luck to thee, luck to me; luck to our Stephanium as well.
STICHUS
5.4.712:
’Tis bravely done. I pledge you in a goblet.
(Drinks.)
SAGARINUS
5.4.713:
Keep your wine; I’d very much like something by way of a relish.
STICHUS
If you are not satisfied with what’s here, there’s nothing else. Take some water.
SAGARINUS
5.4.714: You say right; I care for no dainties.
5.4.715:
Drink away, Piper; drink, if you do drink. I’ faith, this must be drunk—don’t shirk it. (Holds the goblet to the PIPER.) Why flinch at what you see must be done by you? Why don’t you drink? Do it, if you are to do it. Take it, I tell you, for the public pays for this. That’s not your way to shirk your drink. Take your pipes out of your mouth.
(The PIPER drinks.)
STICHUS
5.4.719: When he has drunk, either do you mind my rules, or else I’ll give up.
5.4.720:
I don’t wish us to drink this straight out; we shall soon be about nothing; for, by my faith, almost all in a moment, the cask might be turned head downwards.
SAGARINUS
(to the PIPER.)
5.4.722: How now? Although you did make a fuss about it, still it didn’t hurt you. Come, Piper, when you’ve done drinking, put back your pipes to your lips; quickly puff out your cheeks, just like a reptile serpent.
5.4.725:
Come now, Stichus, whichever of the two breaks order, shall be fined a cup.
STICHUS
5.4.726:
You propose a good regulation. You ought to have your way, who only ask what’s fair.
SAGARINUS
5.4.727:
Mind it then; if you offend, I’ll forthwith take the forfeit on the spot.
STICHUS
5.4.728:
You ask what’s quite right and just.
SAGARINUS
(pledging STICHUS.)
Here’s to you first of all.
STICHUS
